stem: A 4-week-old white male is brought to your office with a 2-week history of increasing dyspnea, cough, and poor feeding. The child appears nontoxic and is afebrile. On examination you note conjunctivitis, and a chest examination reveals tachypnea and crackles. A chest film shows hyperinflation and diffuse interstitial infiltrates and a WBC count reveals eosinophilia. What is the most likely etiologic agent?

bullets.text: Chlamydial pneumonia presents subacutely in infants 3–16 weeks old with tachypnea, prominent cough, diffuse crackles, possible conjunctivitis, and characteristic chest film findings, distinguishable from RSV by its subacute onset, absence of fever, and mild wheezing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Chlamydial pneumonia is usually seen in infants 3–16 weeks of age, and these patients frequently have been sick for several weeks. The infant appears nontoxic and is afebrile, but is tachypneic with a prominent cough. The physical examination will reveal diffuse crackles with few wheezes, and conjunctivitis is present in about 50% of cases. A chest film will show hyperinflation and diffuse interstitial or patchy infiltrates. Chlamydial infections can be differentiated from respiratory syncytial virus infections by a history of conjunctivitis, the subacute onset and absence of fever, and the mild wheezing. There may also be eosinophilia.

bullets.text: Staphylococcal pneumonia has a sudden, severe onset with fever, wheeze, abdominal distress, tachypnea, dyspnea, bronchopneumonia or lobar disease, and prominent leukocytosis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Staphylococcal pneumonia has a sudden onset. The infant appears very ill and has a fever, and initially may have an expiratory wheeze simulating bronchiolitis. Signs of abdominal distress, tachypnea, dyspnea, and localized or diffuse bronchopneumonia or lobar disease may be present. The WBC count will show a prominent leukocytosis.

bullets.text: RSV begins with rhinorrhea and pharyngitis, progresses to cough, wheezing, and possible air hunger, with variable fever, normal or elevated WBC, and occasional rash or conjunctivitis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Respiratory syncytial virus infections start with rhinorrhea and pharyngitis, followed in 1–3 days by a cough and wheezing. Auscultation of the lungs will reveal diffuse rhonchi, fine crackles, and wheezes, but the chest film is often normal. If the illness progresses, coughing and wheezing increase, air hunger and intercostal retractions develop, and evidence of hyperexpansion of the chest is seen. In some infants the course of the illness may be similar to that of pneumonia. Rash or conjunctivitis may occur occasionally, and fever is an inconsistent sign. The WBC count will be normal or elevated, and the differential may be normal or shifted either to the right or left.

bullets.text: Parainfluenza virus causes typical cold symptoms and predominantly affects the upper respiratory tract, accounting for ~50% of laryngotracheitis and ~15% each of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia in hospitalized children.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Parainfluenza virus infection presents with typical cold symptoms. Eight percent of infections affect the upper respiratory tract. In children hospitalized for severe respiratory illness, parainfluenza viruses account for about 50% of the cases of laryngotracheitis and about 15% each of the cases of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia.

explanation_raw:
**Chlamydial Pneumonia**
• Chlamydial pneumonia presents subacutely in infants 3–16 weeks old with tachypnea, prominent cough, diffuse crackles, possible conjunctivitis, and characteristic chest film findings, distinguishable from RSV by its subacute onset, absence of fever, and mild wheezing.
  - Chlamydial pneumonia is usually seen in infants 3–16 weeks of age, and these patients frequently have been sick for several weeks.
  - The infant appears nontoxic and is afebrile, but is tachypneic with a prominent cough.
  - The physical examination will reveal diffuse crackles with few wheezes, and conjunctivitis is present in about 50% of cases.
  - A chest film will show hyperinflation and diffuse interstitial or patchy infiltrates.
  - Chlamydial infections can be differentiated from respiratory syncytial virus infections by a history of conjunctivitis, the subacute onset and absence of fever, and the mild wheezing.
  - There may also be eosinophilia.

**Staphylococcal Pneumonia**
• Staphylococcal pneumonia has a sudden, severe onset with fever, wheeze, abdominal distress, tachypnea, dyspnea, bronchopneumonia or lobar disease, and prominent leukocytosis.
  - Staphylococcal pneumonia has a sudden onset.
  - The infant appears very ill and has a fever, and initially may have an expiratory wheeze simulating bronchiolitis.
  - Signs of abdominal distress, tachypnea, dyspnea, and localized or diffuse bronchopneumonia or lobar disease may be present.
  - The WBC count will show a prominent leukocytosis.

**Respiratory Syncytial Virus**
• RSV begins with rhinorrhea and pharyngitis, progresses to cough, wheezing, and possible air hunger, with variable fever, normal or elevated WBC, and occasional rash or conjunctivitis.
  - Respiratory syncytial virus infections start with rhinorrhea and pharyngitis, followed in 1–3 days by a cough and wheezing.
  - Auscultation of the lungs will reveal diffuse rhonchi, fine crackles, and wheezes, but the chest film is often normal.
  - If the illness progresses, coughing and wheezing increase, air hunger and intercostal retractions develop, and evidence of hyperexpansion of the chest is seen.
  - In some infants the course of the illness may be similar to that of pneumonia.
  - Rash or conjunctivitis may occur occasionally, and fever is an inconsistent sign.
  - The WBC count will be normal or elevated, and the differential may be normal or shifted either to the right or left.

**Parainfluenza Virus**
• Parainfluenza virus causes typical cold symptoms and predominantly affects the upper respiratory tract, accounting for ~50% of laryngotracheitis and ~15% each of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia in hospitalized children.
  - Parainfluenza virus infection presents with typical cold symptoms.
  - Eight percent of infections affect the upper respiratory tract.
  - In children hospitalized for severe respiratory illness, parainfluenza viruses account for about 50% of the cases of laryngotracheitis and about 15% each of the cases of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia.

stem: A 36-year-old obese female presents to your office with a chief complaint of amenorrhea. On examination you note hirsutism and body acne. She is on no medications and a pregnancy test is negative. Serum testosterone is at the upper limits of normal and TSH is within normal limits. In addition to weight loss and exercise, which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial management?

bullets.text: PCOS requires hyperandrogenism plus either polycystic ovaries or ovulatory dysfunction, confirmed by clinical, lab, and ultrasound findings.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has polycystic ovary syndrome, which is characterized by hyperandrogenism on clinical and laboratory evaluations, polycystic ovaries on pelvic ultrasonography, and ovulatory dysfunction. Hyperandrogenism and either polycystic ovaries or ovulatory dysfunction are necessary to make the diagnosis.

bullets.text: In obese PCOS patients, lifestyle modification is first-line, metformin improves menstruation (SOR A), and OCPs reduce endometrial cancer risk from unopposed estrogen; levothyroxine is not indicated without thyroid dysfunction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The first-line recommendation in obese patients is lifestyle modification, but metformin may improve abnormal menstruation (SOR A). Low-dose combined oral contraceptives are more frequently used to reduce the risk of endometrial cancer in patients with chronic anovulation and the resulting unopposed estrogen secretion. This patient does not have thyroid dysfunction, so levothyroxine is not indicated.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• PCOS requires hyperandrogenism plus either polycystic ovaries or ovulatory dysfunction, confirmed by clinical, lab, and ultrasound findings.
  - This patient has polycystic ovary syndrome, which is characterized by hyperandrogenism on clinical and laboratory evaluations, polycystic ovaries on pelvic ultrasonography, and ovulatory dysfunction.
  - Hyperandrogenism and either polycystic ovaries or ovulatory dysfunction are necessary to make the diagnosis.

**Treatment**
• In obese PCOS patients, lifestyle modification is first-line, metformin improves menstruation (SOR A), and OCPs reduce endometrial cancer risk from unopposed estrogen; levothyroxine is not indicated without thyroid dysfunction.
  - The first-line recommendation in obese patients is lifestyle modification, but metformin may improve abnormal menstruation (SOR A).
  - Low-dose combined oral contraceptives are more frequently used to reduce the risk of endometrial cancer in patients with chronic anovulation and the resulting unopposed estrogen secretion.
  - This patient does not have thyroid dysfunction, so levothyroxine is not indicated.

stem: A factory worker sustains a forced flexion injury of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint, resulting in a small bone fragment at the dorsal surface of the proximal distal phalanx (mallet fracture). Which one of the following is the most appropriate management strategy?

choices.A: Buddy taping and early range of motion
choices.B: Splinting the DIP joint in extension
choices.C: Splinting the DIP joint in flexion

correct_label: Splinting the DIP joint in extension

bullets.text: Mallet fractures are treated conservatively with DIP extension splinting for 8 weeks, as outcomes are similar to surgery, which is generally reserved for fractures involving >30% of the intra-articular surface.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The recommended treatment for a mallet fracture is splinting the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint in extension (SOR B). The usual duration of splinting is 8 weeks. It is important that extension be maintained throughout the duration of treatment because flexion can affect healing and prolong the time needed for treatment. If the finger fracture involves >30% of the intra-articular surface, referral to a hand or orthopedic surgeon can be considered. However, conservative therapy appears to have outcomes similar to those of surgical treatment and therefore is generally preferred.

explanation_raw:
**Treatment**
• Mallet fractures are treated conservatively with DIP extension splinting for 8 weeks, as outcomes are similar to surgery, which is generally reserved for fractures involving >30% of the intra-articular surface.
  - The recommended treatment for a mallet fracture is splinting the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint in extension (SOR B).
  - The usual duration of splinting is 8 weeks.
  - It is important that extension be maintained throughout the duration of treatment because flexion can affect healing and prolong the time needed for treatment.
  - If the finger fracture involves >30% of the intra-articular surface, referral to a hand or orthopedic surgeon can be considered.
  - However, conservative therapy appears to have outcomes similar to those of surgical treatment and therefore is generally preferred.

stem: A 30-year-old ill-appearing male presents with right hand and arm pain and a rapidly expanding area of redness. On examination he has a temperature of 38.9°C (102.0°F), a pulse rate of 120 beats/min, and a blood pressure of 116/74 mm Hg. He also has erythema from the dorsal hand to the elbow, violaceous bullae on the dorsal hand and wrist, and severe pain with dorsiflexion of the wrist or fingers. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient?

choices.A: Oral dicloxacillin and outpatient follow-up within the next 24 hours
choices.C: Consultation with an infectious disease specialist for antibiotic management
choices.D: Immediate surgical consultation for operative debridement
choices.E: Incision and drainage with wound cultures in the emergency department

correct_label: Immediate surgical consultation for operative debridement

bullets.text: This patient has physical findings consistent with a necrotizing skin and soft-tissue infection, or necrotizing fasciitis.
Severe pain and skin changes outside the realm of cellulitis, including bullae and deeper discoloration, are strong indications of necrotizing fasciitis.
Antimicrobial therapy is essential but is not sufficient by itself; aggressive surgical debridement within 12 hours reduces the risk of amputation and death.

stem: A mother brings her 2-year-old daughter to your office because the child is not using her left arm. Earlier in the day the mother left the toddler under the supervision of her 12-year-old sister while she went to the store. When she returned the toddler was playing with toys using only her right arm, and was holding the left arm slightly pronated, flexed, and close to her body. The older daughter was unaware of any injury to the girl’s arm, and the child does not seem distressed or traumatized. Physical examination of the child’s clavicle, shoulder, wrist, and hand do not elicit any signs of pain or change in function. She does seem to have some tenderness near the lateral elbow and resists your attempts to examine that area. There is no ecchymosis, swelling, or deformity of the elbow. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this point?

choices.A: Plain radiographs of the affected elbow
choices.C: Evaluation by an orthopedic surgeon within 24 hours
choices.D: Attempted reduction of the subluxed radial head
choices.E: Placement in a splint and follow-up in the office if there is no improvement in the next 1–2 weeks

correct_label: Attempted reduction of the subluxed radial head

bullets.text: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) is the most common pediatric elbow orthopedic condition in children 1–4 years, caused by axial traction on a pronated, extended arm, classically from a caregiver pulling the child's arm.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Radial head subluxation, or nursemaid's elbow, is the most common orthopedic condition of the elbow in children 1–4 years of age, although it can be encountered before 1 year of age and in children as old as 9 years of age. The mechanism of injury is partial displacement of the radial head when the child's arm undergoes axial traction while in a pronated and fully extended position. The classic history includes a caregiver picking up (or pulling) a toddler by the arm. In half of all cases, however, no inciting event is recalled.

bullets.text: Reduction (supination + full elbow flexion) should be attempted before imaging unless fracture or abuse is suspected, with imaging reserved for failed reduction or concerning signs.
bullets.sub_paragraph: As long as there are no outward signs of fracture or abuse it is considered safe and appropriate to attempt reduction of the radial head before moving on to imaging studies. With the child's elbow in 90° of flexion, the hand is fully supinated by the examiner and the elbow is then brought into full flexion. Usually the child will begin to use the affected arm again within a couple of minutes. If ecchymosis, significant swelling, or pain away from the joint is present, or if symptoms do not improve after attempts at reduction, then a plain radiograph is recommended.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis & Epidemiology**
• Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) is the most common pediatric elbow orthopedic condition in children 1–4 years, caused by axial traction on a pronated, extended arm, classically from a caregiver pulling the child's arm.
  - Radial head subluxation, or nursemaid's elbow, is the most common orthopedic condition of the elbow in children 1–4 years of age, although it can be encountered before 1 year of age and in children as old as 9 years of age.
  - The mechanism of injury is partial displacement of the radial head when the child's arm undergoes axial traction while in a pronated and fully extended position.
  - The classic history includes a caregiver picking up (or pulling) a toddler by the arm.
  - In half of all cases, however, no inciting event is recalled.

**Treatment**
• Reduction (supination + full elbow flexion) should be attempted before imaging unless fracture or abuse is suspected, with imaging reserved for failed reduction or concerning signs.
  - As long as there are no outward signs of fracture or abuse it is considered safe and appropriate to attempt reduction of the radial head before moving on to imaging studies.
  - With the child's elbow in 90° of flexion, the hand is fully supinated by the examiner and the elbow is then brought into full flexion.
  - Usually the child will begin to use the affected arm again within a couple of minutes.
  - If ecchymosis, significant swelling, or pain away from the joint is present, or if symptoms do not improve after attempts at reduction, then a plain radiograph is recommended.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea?

bullets.text: NSAIDs are the first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea, taken at menses onset and continued for 1–2 days.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea should be NSAIDs (SOR A). They should be started at the onset of menses and continued for the first 1–2 days of the menstrual cycle.

bullets.text: Combined oral contraceptives and progestin-only contraceptives are not first-line for primary dysmenorrhea, though COCs may help and are reasonable if contraception is also desired.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Combined oral contraceptives may be effective for primary dysmenorrhea, but there is a lack of high-quality randomized, controlled trials demonstrating pain improvement (SOR B). They may be a good choice if the patient also desires contraception. Although combined oral contraceptives and intramuscular and subcutaneous progestin-only contraceptives are effective treatments for dysmenorrhea caused by endometriosis, they are not first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea.

explanation_raw:
**Correct Answer**
• NSAIDs are the first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea, taken at menses onset and continued for 1–2 days.
  - The first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea should be NSAIDs (SOR A).
  - They should be started at the onset of menses and continued for the first 1–2 days of the menstrual cycle.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Combined oral contraceptives and progestin-only contraceptives are not first-line for primary dysmenorrhea, though COCs may help and are reasonable if contraception is also desired.
  - Combined oral contraceptives may be effective for primary dysmenorrhea, but there is a lack of high-quality randomized, controlled trials demonstrating pain improvement (SOR B).
  - They may be a good choice if the patient also desires contraception.
  - Although combined oral contraceptives and intramuscular and subcutaneous progestin-only contraceptives are effective treatments for dysmenorrhea caused by endometriosis, they are not first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea.

stem: Which one of the following medications should be started at a low dosage and titrated slowly to minimize the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

bullets.text: Lamotrigine is used in bipolar disorder but risks Stevens-Johnson syndrome, mitigated by slow dose titration starting at 25 mg daily.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Lamotrigine is an anti-epileptic medication that is often used in bipolar disorder.

bullets.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk is highest in children, with high initial dosing, or when combined with divalproex, and is reduced by slow titration starting at 25 mg daily.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which is a severe disorder of the skin and mucous membranes. This most commonly occurs in children or when the drug is initiated at a high dosage, and is also more likely to occur in patients taking divalproex. To decrease the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, it is recommended that lamotrigine therapy be started at a dosage of 25 mg daily and titrated every 2 weeks until the goal dosage is reached.

  - It can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which is a severe disorder of the skin and mucous membranes.
  - This most commonly occurs in children or when the drug is initiated at a high dosage, and is also more likely to occur in patients taking divalproex.

stem: A 70-year-old male with widespread metastatic prostate cancer is being cared for through a local hospice. Surgery, radiation, and hormonal therapy have failed to stop the cancer, and the goal of his care is now symptom relief. Over the past few days he has been experiencing respiratory distress. His oxygen saturation is 94% on room air and his lungs are clear to auscultation. His respiratory rate is 16/min. Which one of the following would be best at this point?

bullets.text: Dyspnea is a frequent, distressing symptom in terminally ill patients, with opiates as the mainstay of treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Dyspnea is a frequent and distressing symptom in terminally ill patients. Opiates are the mainstay of symptomatic treatment and other measures may be appropriate in specific circumstances.

bullets.text: Oxygen is not beneficial for non-hypoxemic patients, and evidence remains unclear even in hypoxemic patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In the absence of hypoxia, oxygen is not likely to be helpful. The evidence for oxygen in patients with hypoxemia is not clear, but there is no benefit from oxygen for nonhypoxemic patients.

bullets.text: Inhaled bronchodilators or glucocorticoids may help COPD patients, and diuresis may help those with heart failure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For example, inhaled bronchodilators or glucocorticoids may be helpful in patients with COPD, and diuresis may be helpful in patients with heart failure.

explanation_raw:

  - The evidence for oxygen in patients with hypoxemia is not clear, but there is no benefit from oxygen for nonhypoxemic patients.

**Condition-Specific Treatments**
• Inhaled bronchodilators or glucocorticoids may help COPD patients, and diuresis may help those with heart failure.

stem: A 56-year-old male complains of daily early awakening and low energy for the past 3 weeks. Six weeks ago he had a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary artery stent. stem: A 5-year-old white male is brought to your office with a chief complaint of chronic nocturnal limb pain. His mother states that his pain is often severe enough that it awakens him at night and she often gives him ibuprofen to help alleviate his calf pain, but she has never seen him limp or heard him complain of pain during the day. She also has not noticed any grossly swollen joints, fever, rash, or weight change. She is concerned because of a family history of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis in a distant cousin. The physical examination is within normal limits, as are a CBC and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this point?

choices.A: Bilateral plain radiographs of the lower extremities

bullets.text: Benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood (growing pains) present with nocturnal crampy pain in the thigh, calf, or shin in up to 35% of children ages 4–6, with unknown pathology and no signs of inflammation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood (previously known as "growing pains"). These crampy pains often occur in the thigh, calf, or shin, occur in up to 35% of children 4–6 years of age, and may continue up to age 19. The pathology of these pains is unknown. The pain is nocturnal, without limping or other signs of inflammatory processes.

bullets.text: Labs and imaging are not indicated for classic growing pains but are useful to rule out malignancy, infection, or inflammatory processes when clinical features warrant.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and CBC are normal in this condition but testing is indicated in patients with chronic joint pain to rule out malignancy or infection (SOR C). Rheumatoid factor and ANA have a low predictive value in primary care settings and are not indicated in the pediatric population without evidence of an inflammatory process (SOR C). Plain radiographs are more useful for excluding certain conditions such as cancer than for making a diagnosis of arthritis in children (SOR C).

bullets.text: Management consists of parental reassurance, supportive care, and OTC analgesics as needed.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Reassurance of the parents is indicated in this situation, along with instruction on supportive care and over-the-counter analgesics as necessary.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood (growing pains) present with nocturnal crampy pain in the thigh, calf, or shin in up to 35% of children ages 4–6, with unknown pathology and no signs of inflammation.
  - This patient has benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood (previously known as "growing pains").

stem: A 21-year old female comes to her family physician’s office with an unintended pregnancy and states that she wishes to have a medical abortion. bullets.sub_paragraph: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is now divided into five stages of progressively worsening function based on the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Stage 1 is defined as a GFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2, while the fifth stage, kidney failure, is defined as a GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anemia is associated with not only stage 5 disease, where it is universal, but also with earlier stages. The National Kidney Foundation Guidelines define anemia as a hemoglobin level ≤13.5 g/dL in men or ≤12.0 g/dL in women. Anemia due to CKD is diagnosed by excluding other etiologies. Usually the CBC will demonstrate a normochromic, normocytic anemia, but can show microcytosis (mean corpuscular volume <80). A serum ferritin level <25 ng/mL is indicative of low iron stores. Some patients have a combination of iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease due to the kidney disease.

stem: A 56-year-old female comes in for evaluation of gradually worsening right hip pain. She describes her pain as located in the groin and dull in nature, and with activity often notes a clicking sensation associated with sharp pain. On examination her hip range of motion is intact but pain is elicited with extremes of internal and external rotation and her groin pain is exacerbated with the FABER test (knee flexion, abduction and external rotation of the leg until the ankle rests proximal to the contralateral knee) and FADIR test (knee flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the leg). Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Hip labral tear presents with groin pain, mechanical symptoms, and insidious onset, diagnosed best with MR arthrography after physical exam findings on FADIR/FABER testing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has signs and symptoms of a hip labral tear. This causes dull or sharp groin pain, which in some patients radiates to the lateral hip, anterior thigh, or buttock. The pain usually has an insidious onset, but occasionally begins acutely after a traumatic event. Half of patients also have mechanical symptoms, such as catching or painful clicking with activity.

bullets.text: FADIR and FABER tests are sensitive but not specific for intra-articular pathology, and MR arthrography is the gold standard for labral tears, though less invasive imaging should be used first if the diagnosis is uncertain.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The FADIR and FABER tests are effective for detecting intra-articular pathology (the sensitivity is 75%–96% for the FADIR test and 88% for the FABER test), although neither test has high specificity. Magnetic resonance arthrography is considered the diagnostic test of choice for labral tears, as it has a sensitivity of 90% and an accuracy of 91%. However, if a labral tear is not suspected, less invasive imaging modalities such as plain radiography and conventional MRI should be used first to assess for other causes of hip and groin pain.

bullets.text: Fracture, femoral hernia, and trochanteric bursitis are excluded by this patient's presentation, which lacks trauma, a palpable bulge, or lateral hip tenderness over the greater trochanter.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has no history of trauma or risk factors to suggest a fracture. A femoral hernia would typically present as pain that is worse with straining or lifting, associated with a palpable bulge in the upper thigh. Trochanteric bursitis typically causes lateral hip pain with point tenderness over the greater trochanter of the femur.

stem: A 12-month-old male is brought to your office for a routine well child visit. His father has epilepsy and takes seizure medication. Which one of the following vaccines will slightly increase the child’s risk of a febrile seizure for up to 2 weeks after administration?

bullets.text: Children with personal or family history of seizures have higher postimmunization seizure risk, but vaccines remain recommended with parental counseling.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fever and febrile seizures may occur after administration of several vaccines. Postimmunization seizures, especially febrile seizures, occur at a higher rate in children who have a past history of seizures or a first-degree relative with a history of seizures. The benefits of the vaccines outweigh the risks, so they are not contraindicated in this situation, although the parents need to be cautioned about the increased risk of seizure.

bullets.text: The measles component of MMR causes fever ≥39.4°C in 5–15% of recipients at 6–12 days post-vaccination, lasting 1–5 days, making it the vaccine most likely to trigger seizure within 2 weeks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Of the vaccines listed, the only one likely to put the child at risk for a seizure up to 2 weeks after administration is the MMR vaccine. Specifically, it is the measles component of the vaccine that is the potential culprit. A temperature of 39.4°C (103°F) or higher develops in approximately 5%–15% of susceptible vaccine recipients, usually 6–12 days after receipt of MMR vaccine. The fever generally lasts 1–2 days but may last up to 5 days.

stem: A right-hand–dominant 38-year-old male comes to your office because of right elbow pain. He recently began participating in a highly competitive adult volleyball league, and 2 weeks after he first began playing he developed mild pain in the medial elbow of his right arm. While completing an overhead serve last night he felt an acute worsening of the elbow pain. After the match he noted bruising over his medial elbow. When you examine him you find bruising and pain to palpation around the medial elbow. With his shoulder in 90° of abduction and external rotation you rapidly flex and extend the elbow while maintaining valgus torque on the elbow (the moving valgus stress test). The patient reports pain between 70° and 120° of flexion. This clinical presentation is most consistent with which one of the following causes of elbow pain?

bullets.text: UCL injury is identified by mechanism (overhead throwing), presentation (pop, immediate medial elbow pain/bruising), anatomy (primary valgus restraint), and the moving valgus stress test (100% sensitivity, 75% specificity).
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has injured his ulnar collateral ligament (UCL). The UCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress on the elbow during overhead throwing. These injuries often occur in athletes participating in sports that require overhead throwing, such as baseball, javelin, and volleyball. Patients often report a pop followed by immediate pain and bruising around the medial elbow. The moving valgus stress test has 100% sensitivity and 75% specificity for diagnosing UCL injuries.

bullets.text: Medial epicondylitis, biceps tendinopathy, cubital tunnel syndrome, and triceps tendinopathy each have distinct insidious onsets, locations, and associated features that differentiate them from UCL injury.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Medial epicondylitis usually presents with an insidious onset of pain related to a recent increase in occupational or recreational activities. Patients also often report weakened grip strength. The point of maximal tenderness is 5–10 mm distal to and anterior to the medial epicondyle. It is most often a tendinopathy of the flexor carpi radialis and the pronator teres. Biceps tendinopathy usually presents with a history of vague anterior elbow pain and a history of repeated elbow flexion with forearm supination and pronation, such as dumbbell curls. Resisted supination produces pain deep in the antecubital fossa. Cubital tunnel syndrome is a neuropathy of the ulnar nerve caused by compression or traction as it passes through the cubital tunnel of the medial elbow. The onset of pain is more insidious than UCL injury, occurring with repetitive activity, and is usually accompanied by numbness and tingling in the ulnar border of the forearm and hand. If it has existed for some time, the intrinsic hand muscle may become weak. Tendinopathy of the triceps insertion is more common in weight lifters or athletes who repetitively extend their elbows against resistance. Pain occurs at the posterior elbow with resisted extension, and tenderness is located over the triceps insertion.

• UCL injury is identified by mechanism (overhead throwing), presentation (pop, immediate medial elbow pain/bruising), anatomy (primary valgus restraint), and the moving valgus stress test (100% sensitivity, 75% specificity).

  - Patients often report a pop followed by immediate pain and bruising around the medial elbow.

  - Patients also often report weakened grip strength.
  - The point of maximal tenderness is 5–10 mm distal to and anterior to the medial epicondyle.
  - It is most often a tendinopathy of the flexor carpi radialis and the pronator teres.
  - Biceps tendinopathy usually presents with a history of vague anterior elbow pain and a history of repeated elbow flexion with forearm supination and pronation, such as dumbbell curls.
  - Resisted supination produces pain deep in the antecubital fossa.
  - Cubital tunnel syndrome is a neuropathy of the ulnar nerve caused by compression or traction as it passes through the cubital tunnel of the medial elbow.
  - The onset of pain is more insidious than UCL injury, occurring with repetitive activity, and is usually accompanied by numbness and tingling in the ulnar border of the forearm and hand.
  - If it has existed for some time, the intrinsic hand muscle may become weak.
  - Tendinopathy of the triceps insertion is more common in weight lifters or athletes who repetitively extend their elbows against resistance.

explanation.heading: Why Cow's Milk Is Contraindicated Under 12 Months

bullets.text: Cow's milk (whole, skim, or low-fat) is inappropriate for infants under 12 months due to nutrient imbalances and inadequate calories for growth.

stem: A 68-year-old male with end-stage lung cancer is being treated for pain secondary to multiple visceral and skeletal metastases. He has been on oral ibuprofen and parenteral morphine. However, over the past few weeks he reports progressive worsening of his pain. In order to achieve better pain control his morphine dosage has been continuously titrated up. In spite of this increase he continues to report severe pain that is now diffuse and occurs even when his caregivers touch him. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: Increase the morphine dosage until continuous sedation is obtained
choices.B: Attempt a reduction in the morphine dosage
choices.C: Add an anxiolytic to help relieve anxiety
choices.D: Advise the family that nothing more can be done for his pain

correct_label: Attempt a reduction in the morphine dosage

bullets.text: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is a paradoxical pain sensitization seen with high-dose parenteral opioids, characterized by diffuse pain beyond the original site and allodynia.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is characterized by a paradoxical increase in sensitivity to pain despite an increase in the opioid dosage. It is seen in patients who are receiving high doses of parenteral opioids such as morphine. Patients report the development of diffuse pain away from the site of the original pain. Allodynia, a perception of pain in the absence of a painful stimulus, is also typical in opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

bullets.text: Management involves reducing or switching the opioid and adding non-opioid medications, while anxiolytics are not indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Strategies to manage this condition include reducing the current opioid dosage, and occasionally eliminating the current opioid and starting another opioid. The addition of non-opioid pain medications should also be considered. The addition of an anxiolytic is not likely to improve this patient's pain (SOR C).

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is a paradoxical pain sensitization seen with high-dose parenteral opioids, characterized by diffuse pain beyond the original site and allodynia.
  - Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is characterized by a paradoxical increase in sensitivity to pain despite an increase in the opioid dosage.
  - It is seen in patients who are receiving high doses of parenteral opioids such as morphine.

stem: A 24-year-old female presents to the emergency department because she thinks she is having an allergic reaction to her medication for depression. stem: A 30-year-old female reports that she and her husband have not been able to conceive after trying for 15 months. choices.B: TSH, free T , and prolactin levels

stem: Which one of the following conditions is the leading cause of death for patients with rheumatoid arthritis?

stem: A 67-year-old male presents with a persistent, intermittent cough. He says that his exercise tolerance has decreased, noting that he becomes short of breath more easily while playing tennis. He smoked briefly while in college but has not smoked for over 45 years, and reports no history of known pulmonary disease. You obtain pulmonary function testing in the office to help you diagnose and manage his respiratory symptoms. His FVC and FEV /FVC are both less than the lower limit of normal as defined by the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Repeat testing following administration of a bronchodilator does not correct these values. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this time?

choices.D: Testing for diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO)

correct_label: Testing for diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO)

bullets.text: A mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern exists when both FVC and FEV1/FVC fall below the LLN, as in this case.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An FVC that falls below the lower limit of normal (LLN), defined as the fifth percentile of spirometry data obtained from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, is consistent with a restrictive pattern of pulmonary function. bullets.text: This patient should be referred for full pulmonary function testing including DLCO, which measures gas transfer efficiency and is reduced when blood flow or alveolar integrity is compromised.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The patient should now be referred for full pulmonary function testing, including diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). DLCO is a quantitative measure of gas transfer in the lungs. Diseases that decrease blood flow to the lungs or that damage alveoli will lead to less efficient gas exchange and result in a lower DLCO value.

bullets.text: Bronchoprovocation testing is only indicated when pulmonary function tests are normal but exercise- or allergen-induced asthma is suspected, which is not the case here.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Bronchoprovocation (a methacholine challenge, a mannitol inhalation challenge, or exercise testing) should be performed if pulmonary function test results are normal but exercise- or allergen-induced asthma is suspected.

  - An FEV /FVC less than the LLN is consistent with an obstructive defect.1 A mixed pattern exists when both values are below the LLN, as in this case.

**Treatment**
• This patient should be referred for full pulmonary function testing including DLCO, which measures gas transfer efficiency and is reduced when blood flow or alveolar integrity is compromised.
  - The patient should now be referred for full pulmonary function testing, including diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
  - DLCO is a quantitative measure of gas transfer in the lungs.
  - Diseases that decrease blood flow to the lungs or that damage alveoli will lead to less efficient gas exchange and result in a lower DLCO value.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Bronchoprovocation testing is only indicated when pulmonary function tests are normal but exercise- or allergen-induced asthma is suspected, which is not the case here.

stem: A 42-year-old female presents with a cough productive of blood-streaked sputum for the past 3 days. Her hemoptysis was preceded by several days of rhinorrhea, congestion, and subjective fever. bullets.text: Chest radiograph is the first step in evaluating nonmassive hemoptysis, guiding all subsequent workup decisions.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The first step in the evaluation of nonmassive hemoptysis is to obtain a chest radiograph. If the chest radiograph is normal the patient is at low risk for malignancy, and if the history does not suggest lower respiratory infection and hemoptysis does not recur, observation can be considered. If a chest radiograph shows an infiltrate, treatment with antibiotics is warranted.

bullets.text: High-risk patients (age ≥40 with ≥30 pack-year history) with a normal chest radiograph require CT chest and consideration of bronchoscopy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: If this is normal and there is a high risk of malignancy (patient age 40 years or older with at least a 30-pack year smoking history), chest CT should be ordered. Bronchoscopy should also be considered in the workup of high-risk patients.

explanation_raw:
**Initial Evaluation**
• Chest radiograph is the first step in evaluating nonmassive hemoptysis, guiding all subsequent workup decisions.
  - The first step in the evaluation of nonmassive hemoptysis is to obtain a chest radiograph.
  - If the chest radiograph is normal the patient is at low risk for malignancy, and if the history does not suggest lower respiratory infection and hemoptysis does not recur, observation can be considered.
  - If a chest radiograph shows an infiltrate, treatment with antibiotics is warranted.

**High-Risk Malignancy Workup**
• High-risk patients (age ≥40 with ≥30 pack-year history) with a normal chest radiograph require CT chest and consideration of bronchoscopy.
  - If this is normal and there is a high risk of malignancy (patient age 40 years or older with at least a 30-pack year smoking history), chest CT should be ordered.

stem: While performing a digital rectal examination of the prostate on a 67-year-old patient with diabetes mellitus, you note the findings shown below. Of the following topical treatments, which one is most likely to provide significant improvement?

bullets.text: Inverse/flexural psoriasis presents in skin folds and genital regions with smooth, moist, minimally scaly lesions—distinct from classic plaque psoriasis—and can mimic intertrigo.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Plaque psoriasis is characterized by silvery-white scales adhered to well demarcated erythematous papules and/or plaques, typically on the scalp, extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, or buttocks, and often extending to other exposed areas of the body. When limited to skin folds or the genital region, psoriasis can easily be confused with other conditions such as bacterial or fungal intertrigo. The lesions in this variant, known as flexural or inverse psoriasis, usually appear smooth and moist to the point of maceration, often with minimal to no scaling. Affected patients may report significant pruritus and an unpleasant odor in the involved area.

bullets.text: First-line treatment uses mild corticosteroids, vitamin D preparations, or coal tar; higher-potency steroids are avoided due to atrophy risk in delicate, occlusive skin areas.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Evidence-based data for treatment options is limited but supports topical application of mild corticosteroid creams, vitamin D preparations, or coal tar products. Medium- or higher-potency corticosteroid creams are best avoided, as the affected areas are either delicate, occlusive, or both, and susceptible to corticosteroid-induced atrophy.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Inverse/flexural psoriasis presents in skin folds and genital regions with smooth, moist, minimally scaly lesions—distinct from classic plaque psoriasis—and can mimic intertrigo.
  - Plaque psoriasis is characterized by silvery-white scales adhered to well demarcated erythematous papules and/or plaques, typically on the scalp, extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, or buttocks, and often extending to other exposed areas of the body.
  - When limited to skin folds or the genital region, psoriasis can easily be confused with other conditions such as bacterial or fungal intertrigo.
  - The lesions in this variant, known as flexural or inverse psoriasis, usually appear smooth and moist to the point of maceration, often with minimal to no scaling.
  - Affected patients may report significant pruritus and an unpleasant odor in the involved area.

**Treatment**
• First-line treatment uses mild corticosteroids, vitamin D preparations, or coal tar; higher-potency steroids are avoided due to atrophy risk in delicate, occlusive skin areas.
  - Evidence-based data for treatment options is limited but supports topical application of mild corticosteroid creams, vitamin D preparations, or coal tar products.
  - Medium- or higher-potency corticosteroid creams are best avoided, as the affected areas are either delicate, occlusive, or both, and susceptible to corticosteroid-induced atrophy.

stem: Terminally ill cancer patients who receive palliative chemotherapy

choices.B: are less likely to die at home
choices.C: are less likely to undergo CPR
choices.D: are less likely to undergo mechanical ventilation
choices.E: are referred to hospice earlier in their disease course

correct_label: are less likely to die at home

bullets.text: Although family physicians do not prescribe chemotherapy, they are often called upon by families to help navigate the choices specialists offer.
Patients who receive palliative chemotherapy for end-stage cancers are less likely to die at home, more likely to undergo CPR, and more likely to undergo mechanical ventilation.
In addition, these patients are referred to hospice later and there is no survival benefit.

stem: A 14-year-old male presents to your office with a high fever that began suddenly. He has a diffuse petechial rash and some nuchal rigidity on examination. A lumbar puncture is performed, and gram-negative diplococci are found. You admit him to the hospital for treatment. Which one of the following would be most appropriate for prevention of secondary disease at this time?

choices.A: Immediate chemoprophylaxis for his entire school
choices.C: Chemoprophylaxis for family members and very close contacts only
choices.D: Isolation of all family members for 1 week
choices.E: No preventive measures until culture results are available

correct_label: Chemoprophylaxis for family members and very close contacts only

bullets.text: Meningococcal disease is a leading cause of sepsis/meningitis, with secondary cases rare but highest risk in the first few days after index case onset.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Meningococcal disease remains a leading cause of sepsis and meningitis. Those in close contact with patients who have presumptive meningococcal disease are at heightened risk. While secondary cases have been reported, they are rare because of prompt chemoprophylaxis of household members and anyone directly exposed to the index patient's oral secretions. The risk for secondary disease among close contacts is highest during the first few days after the onset of illness in the index patient, mandating immediate chemoprophylaxis of those exposed.

bullets.text: Immediate chemoprophylaxis is required for exposed contacts, while isolation of family members and reliance on vaccination are not appropriate preventive measures.
bullets.sub_paragraph: There is no need to isolate family members. The delay in immunity post vaccination makes it necessary to use other preventive measures instead.

explanation_raw:
**Epidemiology & Risk**
• Meningococcal disease is a leading cause of sepsis/meningitis, with secondary cases rare but highest risk in the first few days after index case onset.
  - Meningococcal disease remains a leading cause of sepsis and meningitis.
  - Those in close contact with patients who have presumptive meningococcal disease are at heightened risk.
  - While secondary cases have been reported, they are rare because of prompt chemoprophylaxis of household members and anyone directly exposed to the index patient's oral secretions.
  - The risk for secondary disease among close contacts is highest during the first few days after the onset of illness in the index patient, mandating immediate chemoprophylaxis of those exposed.

**Treatment & Prevention**
• Immediate chemoprophylaxis is required for exposed contacts, while isolation of family members and reliance on vaccination are not appropriate preventive measures.
  - There is no need to isolate family members.
  - The delay in immunity post vaccination makes it necessary to use other preventive measures instead.

stem: A 58-year-old male with COPD presents with a 5-day history of increased dyspnea and purulent sputum production. He is afebrile. His respiratory rate is 24/min, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 140/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Breath sounds are equal, and diffuse bilateral rhonchi are noted. He is currently using albuterol/ipratropium by metered-dose inhaler three times daily. In addition to antibiotics, which one of the following would be most appropriate for treating this exacerbation?

choices.A: A single dose of intramuscular dexamethasone
choices.D: Hospital admission for intravenous methylprednisolone sodium succinate (Solu-Medrol)

bullets.text: This mild-to-moderate COPD exacerbation can be managed outpatient with oral antibiotic and oral corticosteroid, as IV corticosteroids offer no advantage over oral therapy without GI limitations.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient most likely has a mild to moderate COPD exacerbation. His vital signs do not indicate a serious condition at this time, so he can be treated as an outpatient. Since he is already on a reasonable dose of an inhaled bronchodilator/anticholinergic combination, he should be treated with an oral antibiotic and an oral corticosteroid. Intravenous corticosteroids offer no advantages over oral therapy, provided there are no gastrointestinal tract limitations such as poor motility or absorption.

bullets.text: Oral corticosteroids (5–7 days) are the evidence-based choice for COPD exacerbations; inhaled corticosteroids and IM dexamethasone are ineffective in this setting.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Oral corticosteroid therapy initiated early in a COPD exacerbation reduces the rate of treatment failure, decreases hospitalization rates, improves hypoxia and pulmonary function, and shortens the length of stay for patients requiring hospitalization. Short courses of oral corticosteroids (5–7 days) are as effective as longer ones (SOR A). Inhaled corticosteroids are ineffective in the treatment of a COPD exacerbation. Intramuscular dexamethasone has no role in treating COPD.

explanation_raw:
**Correct Answer & Management**
• This mild-to-moderate COPD exacerbation can be managed outpatient with oral antibiotic and oral corticosteroid, as IV corticosteroids offer no advantage over oral therapy without GI limitations.
  - This patient most likely has a mild to moderate COPD exacerbation.
  - His vital signs do not indicate a serious condition at this time, so he can be treated as an outpatient.
  - Since he is already on a reasonable dose of an inhaled bronchodilator/anticholinergic combination, he should be treated with an oral antibiotic and an oral corticosteroid.
  - Intravenous corticosteroids offer no advantages over oral therapy, provided there are no gastrointestinal tract limitations such as poor motility or absorption.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Oral corticosteroids (5–7 days) are the evidence-based choice for COPD exacerbations; inhaled corticosteroids and IM dexamethasone are ineffective in this setting.
  - Oral corticosteroid therapy initiated early in a COPD exacerbation reduces the rate of treatment failure, decreases hospitalization rates, improves hypoxia and pulmonary function, and shortens the length of stay for patients requiring hospitalization.
  - Short courses of oral corticosteroids (5–7 days) are as effective as longer ones (SOR A).
  - Inhaled corticosteroids are ineffective in the treatment of a COPD exacerbation.
  - Intramuscular dexamethasone has no role in treating COPD.

stem: A 25-year-old male daycare worker presents with a 3-week history of bloating and foul-smelling stools. On examination the patient has mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness and increased bowel sounds. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's problem?

bullets.text: Diarrhea has multiple causes requiring careful identification, including viral/bacterial infections, C. difficile, travelers' diarrhea, Campylobacter, and giardiasis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diarrhea has several causes, requiring different management. In many cases the diarrhea is caused by a viral or bacterial infection that is self-limited and requires only supportive measures. In some cases, however, antibiotic treatment may be needed and it is important to determine the cause of the diarrhea. Patients who have recently been hospitalized for antibiotic treatment are susceptible to infection with Clostridium difficile, and should be treated with metronidazole. Travelers to less developed countries often develop travelers' diarrhea from ingesting contaminated food or water. This is most often due to enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, although travelers can also have Norovirus infections. Patients who become ill after an event where food is served and several attendees have similar symptoms should be suspected of having a Campylobacter infection if the symptoms include bloody diarrhea. Daycare workers are susceptible to giardiasis, with symptoms including bloating, flatulence, and foul-smelling stools.

bullets.text: Ciprofloxacin treats travelers' diarrhea and Campylobacter, while metronidazole treats C. difficile and giardiasis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The most appropriate antibiotic choice in this situation is ciprofloxacin. This should also be treated with ciprofloxacin. This can be treated with metronidazole.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Diarrhea has multiple causes requiring careful identification, including viral/bacterial infections, C. difficile, travelers' diarrhea, Campylobacter, and giardiasis.
  - Diarrhea has several causes, requiring different management.
  - In many cases the diarrhea is caused by a viral or bacterial infection that is self-limited and requires only supportive measures.
  - In some cases, however, antibiotic treatment may be needed and it is important to determine the cause of the diarrhea.
  - Patients who have recently been hospitalized for antibiotic treatment are susceptible to infection with Clostridium difficile, and should be treated with metronidazole.
  - Travelers to less developed countries often develop travelers' diarrhea from ingesting contaminated food or water.
  - This is most often due to enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, although travelers can also have Norovirus infections.
  - Patients who become ill after an event where food is served and several attendees have similar symptoms should be suspected of having a Campylobacter infection if the symptoms include bloody diarrhea.
  - Daycare workers are susceptible to giardiasis, with symptoms including bloating, flatulence, and foul-smelling stools.

**Treatment**
• Ciprofloxacin treats travelers' diarrhea and Campylobacter, while metronidazole treats C. difficile and giardiasis.
  - The most appropriate antibiotic choice in this situation is ciprofloxacin.
  - This should also be treated with ciprofloxacin.
  - This can be treated with metronidazole.

stem: A 60-year-old female has a strong family history of breast cancer and is considering tamoxifen (Soltamox) to reduce her risk. Which one of the following is an effect associated with this treatment that should be included in the shared decision-making discussion with the patient?

choices.A: An increased risk of bone fractures
choices.B: An increased risk of endometrial cancer
choices.D: A decreased risk of thromboembolic events

correct_label: An increased risk of endometrial cancer

bullets.text: The USPSTF (B recommendation) supports offering tamoxifen or raloxifene to high-risk, low-adverse-effect-risk women, reducing invasive breast cancer by 7–9 events per 1,000 women over 5 years, with tamoxifen being more beneficial than raloxifene.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that the selective estrogen receptor modulators tamoxifen and raloxifene be offered to women at high risk for breast cancer and low risk for adverse medication effects (B recommendation). This reduces the incidence of invasive breast cancer by 7–9 events per 1000 women over 5 years. Tamoxifen has been shown to be more beneficial than raloxifene.

bullets.text: Both agents increase venous thromboembolism risk (tamoxifen more so), and tamoxifen additionally raises endometrial cancer risk while causing leg cramps, bladder, vasomotor, and vaginal side effects, though it reduces bone fractures.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Potential harms include an increase of 4–7 events of venous thromboembolism per 1000 women over 5 years. Tamoxifen increases the risk more than raloxifene. Tamoxifen also reduces bone fractures but increases the incidence of endometrial cancer, leg cramps, bladder control issues, vasomotor symptoms, and vaginal dryness, itching, and discharge.

explanation_raw:
**USPSTF Recommendation**
• The USPSTF (B recommendation) supports offering tamoxifen or raloxifene to high-risk, low-adverse-effect-risk women, reducing invasive breast cancer by 7–9 events per 1,000 women over 5 years, with tamoxifen being more beneficial than raloxifene.
  - The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that the selective estrogen receptor modulators tamoxifen and raloxifene be offered to women at high risk for breast cancer and low risk for adverse medication effects (B recommendation).
  - This reduces the incidence of invasive breast cancer by 7–9 events per 1000 women over 5 years.
  - Tamoxifen has been shown to be more beneficial than raloxifene.

**Risks and Adverse Effects**
• Both agents increase venous thromboembolism risk (tamoxifen more so), and tamoxifen additionally raises endometrial cancer risk while causing leg cramps, bladder, vasomotor, and vaginal side effects, though it reduces bone fractures.
  - Potential harms include an increase of 4–7 events of venous thromboembolism per 1000 women over 5 years.
  - Tamoxifen increases the risk more than raloxifene.
  - Tamoxifen also reduces bone fractures but increases the incidence of endometrial cancer, leg cramps, bladder control issues, vasomotor symptoms, and vaginal dryness, itching, and discharge.

stem: A 57-year-old male presents to the emergency department complaining of dyspnea, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. A chest radiograph shows a large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis shows a pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio of 0.7 and a pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio of 0.8. Which one of the following causes of pleural effusion would be most consistent with these findings?

bullets.text: Pleural fluid protein and LDH levels, assessed via Light's criteria, differentiate transudative from exudative effusions with 99.5% sensitivity and 93–96% accuracy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The protein and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in pleural fluid can help differentiate between transudative and exudative effusions. Light's criteria (pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio >0.5, pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio >0.6, and/or pleural LDH >0.67 times the upper limit of normal for serum LDH) are 99.5% sensitive for diagnosing exudative effusions and differentiate exudative from transudative effusions in 93%–96% of cases.

bullets.text: Among the listed etiologies, only pulmonary embolism causes an exudative effusion; all others are transudative.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Of the listed pleural effusion etiologies, only pulmonary embolism is exudative. The remainder are all transudative.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Pleural fluid protein and LDH levels, assessed via Light's criteria, differentiate transudative from exudative effusions with 99.5% sensitivity and 93–96% accuracy.
  - The protein and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in pleural fluid can help differentiate between transudative and exudative effusions.
  - Light's criteria (pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio >0.5, pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio >0.6, and/or pleural LDH >0.67 times the upper limit of normal for serum LDH) are 99.5% sensitive for diagnosing exudative effusions and differentiate exudative from transudative effusions in 93%–96% of cases.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Among the listed etiologies, only pulmonary embolism causes an exudative effusion; all others are transudative.
  - Of the listed pleural effusion etiologies, only pulmonary embolism is exudative.
  - The remainder are all transudative.

stem: A copper T 380A intrauterine device (ParaGard) would be preferred over a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (Mirena) in a patient with a history of which one of the following?

bullets.text: IUDs are safe, effective contraceptives with two main classes—copper T 380A and levonorgestrel-releasing—with few contraindications overall.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The intrauterine device (IUD) is a safe and effective method of contraception. There are two main classes of IUDs: the copper T 380A IUD and the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (14 or 20 μg). There are few contraindications to their use but in certain conditions one class is preferred over the other (SOR C).

bullets.text: Severe liver disease, liver cancer, and breast cancer are contraindications to the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, with the copper T preferred in these cases.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Women with severe cirrhosis or liver cancer should not use the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, and the copper T is preferred. Hormonal contraceptives in general should be avoided in women with severe liver disease, as there is a known association between oral contraceptive use and the growth of hepatocellular adenoma, and this risk is thought to extend to other types of hormonal contraceptives (SOR C). Breast cancer is another contraindication to use of the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, and the copper T would be preferred.

explanation.heading: Conditions Where Either IUD Is Acceptable

bullets.text: Either IUD type is appropriate for women with DVT/PE risk, nulliparity, smoking history, heart failure, or controlled hypertension, with IUDs preferred over estrogen-containing contraceptives.
bullets.sub_paragraph: There is no difference in risk between the copper T and levonorgestrel-releasing IUD with regard to deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism. However, the IUD is preferable to contraceptives containing estrogen. IUDs can be used in nulliparous women and either type may be used, although there is some evidence that there are fewer complications with the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD. Smoking does not preclude the use of either type of IUD. Patients with heart failure may use either type of IUD as well. Women with controlled hypertension may use either form, but there is a slight risk from use of the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD in women with uncontrolled hypertension, although the benefits outweigh the risks.

explanation_raw:
**IUD Classes and General Safety**
• IUDs are safe, effective contraceptives with two main classes—copper T 380A and levonorgestrel-releasing—with few contraindications overall.
  - The intrauterine device (IUD) is a safe and effective method of contraception.
  - There are two main classes of IUDs: the copper T 380A IUD and the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (14 or 20 μg).
  - There are few contraindications to their use but in certain conditions one class is preferred over the other (SOR C).

**Contraindications to Levonorgestrel-Releasing IUD**
• Severe liver disease, liver cancer, and breast cancer are contraindications to the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, with the copper T preferred in these cases.
  - Women with severe cirrhosis or liver cancer should not use the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, and the copper T is preferred.
  - Hormonal contraceptives in general should be avoided in women with severe liver disease, as there is a known association between oral contraceptive use and the growth of hepatocellular adenoma, and this risk is thought to extend to other types of hormonal contraceptives (SOR C).
  - Breast cancer is another contraindication to use of the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, and the copper T would be preferred.

**Conditions Where Either IUD Is Acceptable**
• Either IUD type is appropriate for women with DVT/PE risk, nulliparity, smoking history, heart failure, or controlled hypertension, with IUDs preferred over estrogen-containing contraceptives.
  - There is no difference in risk between the copper T and levonorgestrel-releasing IUD with regard to deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism.
  - However, the IUD is preferable to contraceptives containing estrogen.
  - IUDs can be used in nulliparous women and either type may be used, although there is some evidence that there are fewer complications with the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD.
  - Smoking does not preclude the use of either type of IUD.
  - Patients with heart failure may use either type of IUD as well.
  - Women with controlled hypertension may use either form, but there is a slight risk from use of the levonorgestrel-releasing IUD in women with uncontrolled hypertension, although the benefits outweigh the risks.

stem: The mother of a 2-year-old calls you for advice because her child has an acute cough that is keeping him awake at night. Which one of the following has been shown in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study to decrease nighttime cough and improve sleep in children with this problem?

bullets.text: Honey given before bed reduces cough severity and frequency, improving sleep for both child and parents, though placebo also showed some effect in one study.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A teaspoon of honey, given alone or in a noncaffeinated liquid before bed, has been shown to reduce the severity and frequency of coughing. It improves the sleep of both the child and the parents. Placebo was also effective in one study, but not as effective as honey.

bullets.text: Honey is contraindicated in children under 12 months due to botulism risk, though the risk is very small.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Honey should not be given to children younger than 12 months of age because of the risk of botulism, although this risk is very small.

explanation_raw:
**Efficacy of Honey**
• Honey given before bed reduces cough severity and frequency, improving sleep for both child and parents, though placebo also showed some effect in one study.
  - A teaspoon of honey, given alone or in a noncaffeinated liquid before bed, has been shown to reduce the severity and frequency of coughing.
  - It improves the sleep of both the child and the parents.
  - Placebo was also effective in one study, but not as effective as honey.

**Safety Considerations**
• Honey is contraindicated in children under 12 months due to botulism risk, though the risk is very small.
  - Honey should not be given to children younger than 12 months of age because of the risk of botulism, although this risk is very small.

stem: Which one of the following is an effect of long-term treatment for narcotic addiction with methadone and buprenorphine?

choices.A: Greater success at producing minimal opiate use than detoxification programs

correct_label: Greater success at producing minimal opiate use than detoxification programs

bullets.text: Long-term medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine/naloxone) is strongly preferred over detoxification, with significantly better abstinence outcomes at 12 weeks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Long-term medication-assisted treatment for narcotic addiction is more successful than detoxification programs (SOR A). One study reported 49% of patients with minimal or no opiate use after 12 weeks of buprenorphine/naloxone treatment as opposed to only 7% of those undergoing a brief taper.

bullets.text: Methadone is safe and preferred in pregnancy, diversion is uncommon, and opioid agonists do not clearly reduce cocaine abuse.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Methadone is the drug of choice for pregnant women, with no long-term harmful effects noted. Diversion is reported but is not frequent. Treatment with opioid agonists does not clearly diminish cocaine abuse (SOR C).

explanation_raw:
**Treatment Efficacy**
• Long-term medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine/naloxone) is strongly preferred over detoxification, with significantly better abstinence outcomes at 12 weeks.
  - Long-term medication-assisted treatment for narcotic addiction is more successful than detoxification programs (SOR A).
  - One study reported 49% of patients with minimal or no opiate use after 12 weeks of buprenorphine/naloxone treatment as opposed to only 7% of those undergoing a brief taper.

**Special Populations & Limitations**
• Methadone is safe and preferred in pregnancy, diversion is uncommon, and opioid agonists do not clearly reduce cocaine abuse.
  - Methadone is the drug of choice for pregnant women, with no long-term harmful effects noted.
  - Diversion is reported but is not frequent.
  - Treatment with opioid agonists does not clearly diminish cocaine abuse (SOR C).

stem: A 12-month-old male is brought to your office by his mother because of concerns about his eating. She states that he throws tantrums while sitting in his high chair, dumps food on the floor, and refuses to eat. She has resorted to feeding him cookies, crackers, and juice, which are “all he will eat.” A complete physical examination, including a growth chart of weight, length, and head circumference, is normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.A: Use disciplinary measures to force the child to eat a healthy breakfast, lunch, and dinner
choices.B: Leave the child in the high chair until he has eaten all of the healthy food provided
choices.C: Play feeding games to encourage consumption of healthy meals or snacks
choices.D: Skip the next meal if the child refuses to eat
choices.E: Provide healthy foods for all meals and snacks, and end the meal if the child refuses to eat

correct_label: Provide healthy foods for all meals and snacks, and end the meal if the child refuses to eat

bullets.text: Food refusal affects 3%–10% of infants/toddlers, tends to persist without intervention, and warrants reassurance that healthy children will not self-starve.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It is estimated that 3%–10% of infants and toddlers refuse to eat, according to their caregivers. Unlike other feeding problems such as colic, this problem tends to persist without intervention. Parents can be reassured that a normal child will learn to eat enough to prevent starvation.

bullets.text: Management centers on consistent meal routines, appropriate division of feeding responsibility, and no food or rewards outside scheduled times.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It is recommended that caregivers establish routines for healthy scheduled meals and snacks, and follow them consistently. Parents should control what, when, and where children are being fed, whereas children should control how much they eat at any given time in accordance with physiologic signals of hunger and fullness. No food or drinks other than water should be offered between meals or snacks. Food should not be offered as a reward or present.

bullets.text: Malnutrition despite intervention should prompt evaluation for an underlying physical or mental abnormality.
bullets.sub_paragraph: If malnutrition does occur, a search for a physical or mental abnormality should be sought.

explanation_raw:
**Epidemiology**
• Food refusal affects 3%–10% of infants/toddlers, tends to persist without intervention, and warrants reassurance that healthy children will not self-starve.
  - It is estimated that 3%–10% of infants and toddlers refuse to eat, according to their caregivers.
  - Unlike other feeding problems such as colic, this problem tends to persist without intervention.
  - Parents can be reassured that a normal child will learn to eat enough to prevent starvation.

**Treatment**
• Management centers on consistent meal routines, appropriate division of feeding responsibility, and no food or rewards outside scheduled times.
  - It is recommended that caregivers establish routines for healthy scheduled meals and snacks, and follow them consistently.
  - Parents should control what, when, and where children are being fed, whereas children should control how much they eat at any given time in accordance with physiologic signals of hunger and fullness.
  - No food or drinks other than water should be offered between meals or snacks.
  - Food should not be offered as a reward or present.

**When to Investigate Further**
• Malnutrition despite intervention should prompt evaluation for an underlying physical or mental abnormality.
  - If malnutrition does occur, a search for a physical or mental abnormality should be sought.

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with lateral hip pain over the outer thigh. She has no history of injury, although she has just begun a walking program to lose weight. She has increased pain when she lies on that side at night. Her examination is unremarkable except that she is overweight and has tenderness over the greater trochanter. There is no pain with internal and external rotation of the hip. A radiograph reveals minimal osteoarthritic changes. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this point?

bullets.text: Trochanteric bursitis develops insidiously after repetitive use, and the patient may report morning stiffness and pain when lying on the affected side.
Palpation of the greater trochanter elicits tenderness, and occasionally swelling may be noted as well.
Early injection with a corticosteroid usually produces a satisfactory response.

explanation_raw:

• Palpation of the greater trochanter elicits tenderness, and occasionally swelling may be noted as well.

stem: A 70-year-old male who recently moved to your area sees you for the first time. He has a previous history of myocardial infarction, has a pacemaker, and has hypertension that had been well controlled on hydrochlorothiazide and atenolol (Tenormin) for several years. About 6 months ago his previous physician had to add amlodipine (Norvasc) to his regimen. On examination he has mild arteriolar narrowing in his fundi and there is a systolic bruit just to the right of his umbilicus. He has a log of home blood pressure readings that average 138/88 mm Hg for the past 2 months. His serum creatinine level has gone from 1.2 mg/dL to 1.4 mg/dL (N 0.6–1.2) in the past 2 months. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this time?

bullets.text: Renal artery stenosis affects ~5% of hypertensive patients and is associated with CAD/PVD, with clinical clues including resistant hypertension, abdominal bruits, and ACE inhibitor-induced hyperkalemia or renal insufficiency.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Renal artery stenosis may be present in as many as 5% of patients with hypertension. It is often seen in those who have coronary artery disease and/or peripheral vascular disease. bullets.text: Recommended screening includes duplex ultrasonography, CT angiography, or MR angiography (SOR B); captopril renography is no longer used; and no testing is needed in well-controlled patients beyond renal function monitoring.

stem: Many of the changes that occur as part of aging affect pharmacokinetics. Which one of the following is INCREASED in geriatric patients?

bullets.text: Aging causes predictable changes in body composition and renal function that significantly alter drug distribution and clearance, while absorption remains largely unaffected.

bullets.text: Increased body fat raises distribution and half-life of fat-soluble drugs, while decreased lean mass reduces the volume of distribution for water-soluble drugs, requiring lower doses.

bullets.text: Aging causes predictable reductions in glomerular filtration rate and tubular secretion, leading to decreased drug clearance in geriatric patients.

bullets.text: HSP is an immune-mediated vasculitis in children under 10, classically presenting with the triad of purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis.
