stem: A 72-year-old previously healthy female comes in for evaluation of recent headaches. She describes the pain as generalized all over her head and persisting over the past several months. She reports feeling more achy and fatigued in the past several weeks, with a decreased appetite and unintentional weight loss of 4 lb in the past 2 months. She denies any other symptoms including sinus congestion, nausea, vomiting, numbness, tingling, weakness, or vision changes. Acetaminophen has been minimally helpful for the pain. On examination you note a temperature of 37.9°C (100.2°F), normal cranial nerves, a normal eye examination, and no tenderness to palpation of the head. She is mildly tender to palpation of the shoulders and upper arms. Laboratory testing reveals an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/hr (N 1–25). Which one of the following is necessary to confirm the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a vasculitis most common in elderly women, presenting with systemic symptoms, jaw claudication, and temporal artery changes that can lead to blindness.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's clinical picture is most concerning for giant cell arteritis (also known as temporal arteritis). This condition is a type of vasculitis and in its most serious form can lead to blindness. It is most common in the elderly and is twice as common in women as in men. Because of its inflammatory nature, patients commonly have systemic symptoms, including fever. The temporal artery may be thickened, tender, or lacking pulsation, although a normal artery does not rule out the diagnosis. Jaw claudication is a fairly specific but nonsensitive finding.

explanation.heading: Workup and Why Other Options Are Wrong

bullets.text: GCA is classically associated with elevated ESR, confirmed by temporal artery biopsy before initiating high-dose corticosteroids, while MRI, CT, LP, and EEG evaluate other diagnoses.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The laboratory finding most classically associated with giant cell arteritis is an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Only 4% of patients with biopsy-proven giant cell arteritis have a normal ESR. However, a high ESR is nonspecific and may be caused by other conditions. Because the treatment for giant cell arteritis involves high-dose corticosteroids, which may cause significant morbidity, most clinicians favor confirmation of the diagnosis with a temporal artery biopsy prior to committing a patient to full treatment. MRI and CT would be used in the evaluation of other causes of headaches, including a cerebral hemorrhage or mass. A lumbar puncture would identify benign intracranial hypertension or meningitis, and an EEG would be helpful for evaluating seizures.

**Diagnosis**
• Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a vasculitis most common in elderly women, presenting with systemic symptoms, jaw claudication, and temporal artery changes that can lead to blindness.
  - This patient's clinical picture is most concerning for giant cell arteritis (also known as temporal arteritis).
  - This condition is a type of vasculitis and in its most serious form can lead to blindness.
  - It is most common in the elderly and is twice as common in women as in men.
  - Because of its inflammatory nature, patients commonly have systemic symptoms, including fever.
  - The temporal artery may be thickened, tender, or lacking pulsation, although a normal artery does not rule out the diagnosis.
  - Jaw claudication is a fairly specific but nonsensitive finding.

**Workup and Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• GCA is classically associated with elevated ESR, confirmed by temporal artery biopsy before initiating high-dose corticosteroids, while MRI, CT, LP, and EEG evaluate other diagnoses.

  - MRI and CT would be used in the evaluation of other causes of headaches, including a cerebral hemorrhage or mass.
  - A lumbar puncture would identify benign intracranial hypertension or meningitis, and an EEG would be helpful for evaluating seizures.

stem: A 52-year-old healthy male presents with a 2½-week history of diarrhea, consisting of 4–6 watery stools daily. He is afebrile and his examination is normal. You recommend symptomatic care. stem: Which one of the following has been shown to result from the use of continuous prophylactic antibiotics in patients with moderate COPD?

choices.B: A clinically significant improvement in quality-of-life scores
choices.C: A demonstrable decrease in the number of resistant organisms in the sputum
choices.D: The development of conduction defects, including prolonged QT intervals

correct_label: A clinically significant reduction in COPD exacerbations

bullets.text: A review of multiple studies has revealed that continuous daily macrolide antibiotic use for 1 year decreased the number of exacerbations in older patients with COPD (SOR A).
Quality of life did not show improvement, however, and resistance to macrolide and quinolone antibiotics rose.
There was no increase in conduction abnormalities or tinnitus, but the incidence of hearing loss increased with the use of azithromycin.

explanation_raw:
• A review of multiple studies has revealed that continuous daily macrolide antibiotic use for 1 year decreased the number of exacerbations in older patients with COPD (SOR A).
• Quality of life did not show improvement, however, and resistance to macrolide and quinolone antibiotics rose.
• There was no increase in conduction abnormalities or tinnitus, but the incidence of hearing loss increased with the use of azithromycin.

stem: A 65-year-old male has severe liver cirrhosis from a combination of hepatitis C infection and alcohol abuse. He previously underwent a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure. While the TIPS procedure reduces the likelihood of most complications of cirrhosis, it may increase the risk for which one of the following?

choices.D: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from esophageal varices
choices.E: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from portal hypertensive gastropathy

bullets.text: TIPS lowers portal pressure by shunting blood into systemic circulation, reducing variceal bleeding by up to 90%, and decreasing ascites, edema, and anasarca.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure, by shunting blood destined for the liver into the systemic circulation, lowers pressure in the portal veins, thereby decreasing portal system hypertension and making variceal bleeding and portal hypertensive gastropathy less likely. TIPS may decrease the likelihood of variceal bleeding by as much as 90%. TIPS also reduces the pressure that leads to ascites and lower extremity edema, or the massive edema of anasarca.

bullets.text: By diverting blood away from the liver, TIPS impairs toxin clearance including ammonia, increasing vulnerability to hepatic encephalopathy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The diversion of blood from the liver circulation compromises the liver's role in removing toxins, including the serum marker ammonia. This may make patients more vulnerable to episodes of hepatic encephalopathy.

explanation_raw:
**Mechanism and Benefits of TIPS**
• TIPS lowers portal pressure by shunting blood into systemic circulation, reducing variceal bleeding by up to 90%, and decreasing ascites, edema, and anasarca.
  - The transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure, by shunting blood destined for the liver into the systemic circulation, lowers pressure in the portal veins, thereby decreasing portal system hypertension and making variceal bleeding and portal hypertensive gastropathy less likely.
  - TIPS may decrease the likelihood of variceal bleeding by as much as 90%.
  - TIPS also reduces the pressure that leads to ascites and lower extremity edema, or the massive edema of anasarca.

**Risks and Complications of TIPS**
• By diverting blood away from the liver, TIPS impairs toxin clearance including ammonia, increasing vulnerability to hepatic encephalopathy.
  - The diversion of blood from the liver circulation compromises the liver's role in removing toxins, including the serum marker ammonia.
  - This may make patients more vulnerable to episodes of hepatic encephalopathy.

stem: A 33-year-old patient with allergic rhinitis tells you he feels drowsy when taking diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and asks if there is an alternative that will cause less sedation. You tell him that most second-generation antihistamines have a better adverse effect profile and cause less sedation than first-generation antihistamines. Which one of the following second-generation antihistamines would you advise the patient to avoid, however, because it is known to cause sedation?

Second-generation antihistamines have more complex chemical structures that decrease their movement across the blood-brain barrier, reducing central nervous system adverse effects such as sedation.
Although cetirizine is generally classified as a second-generation antihistamine and a more potent histamine antagonist, it is known to cause sedation (SOR A).

• Although cetirizine is generally classified as a second-generation antihistamine and a more potent histamine antagonist, it is known to cause sedation (SOR A).

stem: The mother of a 16-year-old male calls to report that her son has a severe sore throat and has been running a fever of 102°F. As you question the mother further, which one of the following would be most specific for peritonsillar abscess?

bullets.text: Trismus is the hallmark of peritonsillar abscess, which also features otalgia and odynophagia, though these symptoms overlap with pharyngotonsillitis and peritonsillar cellulitis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Trismus is almost universally present with peritonsillar abscess, while voice changes, otalgia, and odynophagia may or may not be present. Pharyngotonsillitis and peritonsillar cellulitis may also be associated with these complaints. Otalgia is common with peritonsillar abscess, otitis media, temporomandibular joint disorders, and a variety of other conditions.

bullets.text: Peritonsillar abscess is rarely diagnosed without at least a 3-day history of progressive sore throat.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Peritonsillar abscess is rarely found in patients who do not have at least a 3-day history of progressive sore throat.

  - Pharyngotonsillitis and peritonsillar cellulitis may also be associated with these complaints.
  - Otalgia is common with peritonsillar abscess, otitis media, temporomandibular joint disorders, and a variety of other conditions.

stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents to the labor suite with a complaint of painful uterine contractions every 3 minutes for the last 2 hours. A fetal monitor confirms the contraction pattern, and the fetal heart rate pattern is category 1. A fetal fibronectin test is ordered. Thirty minutes later the contractions have stopped, but results of the fetal fibronectin test are positive. A speculum examination shows no indication of ruptured membranes. The cervix is closed and thick to palpation. The positive result on this patient’s fetal fibronectin test

choices.A: has a low positive predictive value for preterm delivery
choices.B: indicates a high likelihood of delivery before term
choices.C: indicates a high likelihood of delivery within the next week
choices.D: indicates occult rupture of the membranes

correct_label: has a low positive predictive value for preterm delivery

bullets.text: Fetal fibronectin has a poor positive predictive value (<20%) but strong negative predictive value (>95%), limiting its usefulness to ruling out preterm delivery rather than confirming risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The fetal fibronectin test is used to help determine the risk of early delivery. Unfortunately, the positive predictive value for delivery within the next week is <20% in patients who have clinical indications of preterm labor. A negative result is reassuring, on the other hand, because the negative predictive value is >95%. In studies that tested gravidas every week, positive results had a mild correlation with preterm delivery, but not enough to guide management.

bullets.text: Fetal fibronectin does not affect management in asymptomatic patients, and false positives from blood or amniotic fluid do not indicate membrane rupture when other tests are negative.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In a patient who does not have any features of preterm labor, it does not affect management. False-positive test results can be caused by maternal blood or amniotic fluid, but fetal fibronectin does not indicate rupture of the membranes when other tests are negative.

explanation_raw:
**Clinical Utility and Predictive Value**
• Fetal fibronectin has a poor positive predictive value (<20%) but strong negative predictive value (>95%), limiting its usefulness to ruling out preterm delivery rather than confirming risk.
  - The fetal fibronectin test is used to help determine the risk of early delivery.
  - Unfortunately, the positive predictive value for delivery within the next week is <20% in patients who have clinical indications of preterm labor.
  - A negative result is reassuring, on the other hand, because the negative predictive value is >95%.
  - In studies that tested gravidas every week, positive results had a mild correlation with preterm delivery, but not enough to guide management.

**Limitations and Interpretation**
• Fetal fibronectin does not affect management in asymptomatic patients, and false positives from blood or amniotic fluid do not indicate membrane rupture when other tests are negative.
  - In a patient who does not have any features of preterm labor, it does not affect management.
  - False-positive test results can be caused by maternal blood or amniotic fluid, but fetal fibronectin does not indicate rupture of the membranes when other tests are negative.

stem: The rash associated with erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is characterized by which one of the following?

stem: A 66-year-old female with a history of shortness of breath returns to your office to review her pulmonary function test results. Her FEV /FVC ratio is 76%. You calculate that her FVC is below the normal range for an adult. Her DLCO is also low. Which one of the following is most consistent with her pulmonary function test results?

bullets.text: This patient's PFT findings show a restrictive defect with low DLCO, consistent with alveolar-damaging diseases like IPF, asbestosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and sarcoidosis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's pulmonary function test (PFT) findings are consistent with a restrictive defect with a low DLCO. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, asbestosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and sarcoidosis are restrictive lung diseases with a low diffusion capacity due to alveolar damage.

bullets.text: COPD/asthma are obstructive (not restrictive), morbid obesity is restrictive but with normal DLCO, and chronic PE causes low DLCO with normal PFTs — none match this restrictive + low DLCO pattern.
bullets.sub_paragraph: COPD and asthma are both obstructive lung diseases, but can be associated with an abnormal DLCO. Morbid obesity causes a restrictive lung disease associated with a normal DLCO. The presence of chronic pulmonary emboli is associated with a low DLCO due to pulmonary vascular disease, but PFTs are normal.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• This patient's PFT findings show a restrictive defect with low DLCO, consistent with alveolar-damaging diseases like IPF, asbestosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and sarcoidosis.
  - This patient's pulmonary function test (PFT) findings are consistent with a restrictive defect with a low DLCO.
  - Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, asbestosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and sarcoidosis are restrictive lung diseases with a low diffusion capacity due to alveolar damage.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• COPD/asthma are obstructive (not restrictive), morbid obesity is restrictive but with normal DLCO, and chronic PE causes low DLCO with normal PFTs — none match this restrictive + low DLCO pattern.
  - COPD and asthma are both obstructive lung diseases, but can be associated with an abnormal DLCO.
  - Morbid obesity causes a restrictive lung disease associated with a normal DLCO.
  - The presence of chronic pulmonary emboli is associated with a low DLCO due to pulmonary vascular disease, but PFTs are normal.

stem: Which one of the following is the recommended initial treatment for allergic rhinitis in a patient whose symptoms are affecting his quality of life?

bullets.text: Intranasal corticosteroids are the recommended first-line treatment for allergic rhinitis affecting quality of life, superior to antihistamines in efficacy and safety.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An intranasal corticosteroid alone should be the initial treatment for allergic rhinitis with symptoms affecting quality of life (SOR A). Intranasal corticosteroids act by decreasing the influx of inflammatory cells and inhibiting the release of cytokines, thereby reducing inflammation of the nasal mucosa. Intranasal corticosteroids are more effective than oral and intranasal antihistamines in the treatment of persistent or more severe allergic rhinitis (SOR A). Intranasal antihistamines also have more adverse effects than intranasal corticosteroids (SOR C).

bullets.text: Immunotherapy is not first-line but is appropriate for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic rhinitis unresponsive to standard treatments.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy are not considered first-line treatments but should be considered for moderate or severe persistent allergic rhinitis that is not responsive to usual treatments (SOR A).

explanation_raw:
**Correct Answer & Treatment**
• Intranasal corticosteroids are the recommended first-line treatment for allergic rhinitis affecting quality of life, superior to antihistamines in efficacy and safety.
  - An intranasal corticosteroid alone should be the initial treatment for allergic rhinitis with symptoms affecting quality of life (SOR A).
  - Intranasal corticosteroids act by decreasing the influx of inflammatory cells and inhibiting the release of cytokines, thereby reducing inflammation of the nasal mucosa.
  - Intranasal corticosteroids are more effective than oral and intranasal antihistamines in the treatment of persistent or more severe allergic rhinitis (SOR A).
  - Intranasal antihistamines also have more adverse effects than intranasal corticosteroids (SOR C).

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Immunotherapy is not first-line but is appropriate for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic rhinitis unresponsive to standard treatments.
  - Subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy are not considered first-line treatments but should be considered for moderate or severe persistent allergic rhinitis that is not responsive to usual treatments (SOR A).

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with an acute onset of chest pain. His EKG is shown on the page at right. Which one of the following agents would be most appropriate to relieve this patient’s chest pain?

bullets.text: Acute pericarditis is a common cause of chest pain in young adults, presenting with retrosternal/left precordial pain relieved by leaning forward and worsened supine, most often viral or idiopathic in etiology.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute pericarditis is a common cause of chest pain in young adults. It presents with an acute to subacute onset of severe retrosternal and left precordial chest pain that is characteristically alleviated by leaning forward or sitting up and worsened with lying supine. Viral and idiopathic acute pericarditis are most common and occur at all ages, but are more common in young adults.

bullets.text: Acute pericarditis responds to NSAIDs or high-dose aspirin, while other causes of chest pain require targeted therapies, and opioids lack anti-inflammatory benefit.

Patients with pain resulting from myocardial ischemia would benefit from nitroglycerin, while those with gastroesophageal reflux disease would benefit from a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole. Hydrocodone can be used to relieve moderate to severe pain but lacks anti-inflammatory properties (SOR C).

stem: A 40-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a fever and acute, severe abdominal pain. A complete history and careful physical examination fail to localize the source of his pain, and basic blood and urine tests also prove to be nondiagnostic. His pain is diffuse, and you are concerned about a potentially serious pathology. Which one of the following would be most appropriate to order next?

choices.B: An upper gastrointestinal series with small-bowel follow-through
choices.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

correct_label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

bullets.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the recommended imaging modality for acute nonlocalized abdominal pain when serious pathology is suspected or diagnosis remains unclear, and significantly impacts diagnosis and management.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The differential diagnosis of acute nonlocalized abdominal pain is broad. CT is typically the imaging modality of choice if there is significant concern about serious pathology or if the diagnosis is unclear from the history, physical examination, and laboratory testing. In this instance, the American College of Radiology recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis, preferably with contrast. One prospective study of patients with nontraumatic abdominal pain in an emergency department setting found that CT results changed the leading diagnosis in 49% of patients and the management plan in 42% of patients.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the recommended imaging modality for acute nonlocalized abdominal pain when serious pathology is suspected or diagnosis remains unclear, and significantly impacts diagnosis and management.
  - The differential diagnosis of acute nonlocalized abdominal pain is broad.
  - CT is typically the imaging modality of choice if there is significant concern about serious pathology or if the diagnosis is unclear from the history, physical examination, and laboratory testing.
  - In this instance, the American College of Radiology recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis, preferably with contrast.

stem: A 46-year-old male consults you because of chronic, moderate, nonradiating low back pain. The pain had a gradual onset and is partially relieved by rest; ibuprofen, 600 mg as needed; duloxetine (Cymbalta), 60 mg daily; and gabapentin (Neurontin), 300 mg 3 times/day. He denies weakness, changes in urination, or changes in sensation. His physical examination is notable for mild tenderness over the lumbar paraspinal muscles. A recent MRI of his lumbosacral spine showed mild degenerative disc disease. Which one of the following would you recommend as most likely to have long-term benefit?

choices.C: A series of epidural corticosteroid injections
choices.D: A transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) unit

bullets.text: Family physicians have many options for chronic low back pain, but evidence varies widely in quality and cost-effectiveness.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Family physicians are faced with many treatment options for managing chronic low back pain. Both supervised walking and physical therapy resulted in decreased disability and pain scores at 6 months in a 2015 randomized, controlled trial. A walking program is the best choice because it is much more affordable than physical therapy.

bullets.text: Epidural corticosteroids, TENS, and spinal manipulation lack evidence of sustained benefit, while spinal cord stimulators have insufficient evidence for widespread use.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cochrane reviews found that neither epidural corticosteroid injections nor transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation were better than placebo, and spinal manipulation showed no benefit after 6 months. Spinal cord stimulators may help patients with severe pain after failed back surgery, but lack moderate or better evidence to support their widespread use.

explanation_raw:
**Treatment Options Overview**
• Family physicians have many options for chronic low back pain, but evidence varies widely in quality and cost-effectiveness.
  - Family physicians are faced with many treatment options for managing chronic low back pain.
  - Both supervised walking and physical therapy resulted in decreased disability and pain scores at 6 months in a 2015 randomized, controlled trial.
  - A walking program is the best choice because it is much more affordable than physical therapy.

**Ineffective or Unsupported Treatments**
• Epidural corticosteroids, TENS, and spinal manipulation lack evidence of sustained benefit, while spinal cord stimulators have insufficient evidence for widespread use.
  - Cochrane reviews found that neither epidural corticosteroid injections nor transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation were better than placebo, and spinal manipulation showed no benefit after 6 months.
  - Spinal cord stimulators may help patients with severe pain after failed back surgery, but lack moderate or better evidence to support their widespread use.

stem: A 56-year-old male is hospitalized for workup of a syncopal episode. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia, which are well controlled with metformin (Glucophage) and atorvastatin (Lipitor). In addition, he takes a daily low-dose aspirin and a multivitamin. The cardiac examination reveals occasional skipped beats but the remainder of the physical examination is normal. While hospitalized he has another syncopal episode. His clinical examination and EKG post syncope are normal. A telemetry rhythm tracing captured during this syncopal episode is shown on the page at right. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his syncope?

choices.B: Mobitz type I second degree atrioventricular block
choices.C: Mobitz type II second degree atrioventricular block

bullets.text: Third degree AV block is identified by dissociated P waves and QRS complexes on EKG, distinguishing it from Mobitz I (progressive PR prolongation), Mobitz II (sudden dropped P wave), and atrial fibrillation (absent P waves, irregularly irregular QRS).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Third degree atrioventricular (AV) block is characterized by the inability of atrial impulses to reach the ventricles. Hence, the EKG will show both atrial activity (P waves) and ventricular "escape" activity (QRS complexes) with no correlation between them. With Mobitz type I AV block there is progressive PR interval prolongation preceding a nonconducted P wave. With Mobitz type II AV block the PR interval remains the same but there is a sudden dropped P wave. The EKG in atrial fibrillation lacks distinct P waves. Additionally, fibrillary waves and irregularly irregular intervals between QRS complexes are characteristic (SOR C).

bullets.text: Hemodynamically unstable third degree AV block requires emergent atropine and temporary pacing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Hemodynamically unstable patients with third degree AV block should be emergently treated with atropine and temporary pacing.

bullets.text: Second and third degree AV blocks occur in patients with advanced heart disease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Second and third degree AV blocks are seen in patients with advanced heart disease.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Third degree AV block is identified by dissociated P waves and QRS complexes on EKG, distinguishing it from Mobitz I (progressive PR prolongation), Mobitz II (sudden dropped P wave), and atrial fibrillation (absent P waves, irregularly irregular QRS).
  - Third degree atrioventricular (AV) block is characterized by the inability of atrial impulses to reach the ventricles.
  - Hence, the EKG will show both atrial activity (P waves) and ventricular "escape" activity (QRS complexes) with no correlation between them.
  - With Mobitz type I AV block there is progressive PR interval prolongation preceding a nonconducted P wave.
  - With Mobitz type II AV block the PR interval remains the same but there is a sudden dropped P wave.
  - The EKG in atrial fibrillation lacks distinct P waves.
  - Additionally, fibrillary waves and irregularly irregular intervals between QRS complexes are characteristic (SOR C).

**Treatment**
• Hemodynamically unstable third degree AV block requires emergent atropine and temporary pacing.
  - Hemodynamically unstable patients with third degree AV block should be emergently treated with atropine and temporary pacing.

**Epidemiology**
• Second and third degree AV blocks occur in patients with advanced heart disease.

stem: A 52-year-old healthy female nonsmoker who has a family history of coronary artery disease presents with episodes of left-sided chest pain that last 10–15 minutes but are unrelated to activity. bullets.sub_paragraph: Its recommendations focused on the level of pretest risk for ischemic heart disease (low, intermediate, and high), a normal or abnormal resting EKG, the ability of the subject to exercise, and potential risks of radiation exposure.

bullets.text: This low-to-intermediate risk patient with a normal resting EKG and good physical fitness should undergo an exercise treadmill test without imaging.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The patient in this scenario would be considered low to intermediate risk for ischemia due to her age and risk factors, along with a history of atypical chest pain. stem: A 90-year-old male with a history of metastatic lung cancer is admitted to hospice. You agree to follow the patient. choices.B: Albuterol in normal saline by nebulizer

bullets.text: Opioids (oral or IV) are first-line for dyspnea, proven effective and safe without causing respiratory depression when used carefully.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Opioids, given either orally or intravenously, are the treatment of choice for dyspnea and have been studied thoroughly in patients with COPD and patients with cancer. They have been found to be effective in alleviating dyspnea and, when used carefully, do not have serious side effects such as respiratory depression.

bullets.text: Benzodiazepines help anxiety associated with breathlessness but don't improve dyspnea; oxygen lacks benefit for non-hypoxemic cancer/heart failure patients but may help non-hypoxemic COPD patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: When the patient is experiencing anxiety, which regularly occurs in association with breathlessness, benzodiazepines can be added, although there is no evidence that they improve the dyspnea. Patients are regularly given supplemental oxygen for dyspnea, but systematic reviews have found no benefit for patients with cancer or heart failure who do not have hypoxemia. However, oxygen may provide some relief for patients with COPD who do not have hypoxemia.

bullets.text: Prednisone and albuterol are not indicated for this patient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prednisone and albuterol are not indicated for this patient.

stem: A 58-year-old minister comes to your office accompanied by his wife for a follow-up evaluation of personality changes. His wife says he has been making inappropriate comments to females in the church and has been more withdrawn at social gatherings. He has also not been preparing his sermons or balancing their checking account. These behaviors are uncharacteristic for him and his symptoms have been progressively worsening over the past 6–12 months. He is quiet during this discussion. He has been on an SSRI for 3 months with minimal to no improvement. The history is otherwise normal, as is a physical examination, including a focused neurologic examination. Short-term memory is intact. This presentation is most consistent with which one of the following diagnoses?

bullets.text: Behavioral variant FTD is characterized by insidious onset, early social/interpersonal decline, disinhibition, apathy, emotional blunting, and loss of insight, and is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Core features of the behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (FTD) include an insidious onset and gradual progression, an early decline in social and interpersonal conduct, early impairment in regulation of personal conduct, early emotional blunting, and early loss of insight. Common initial symptoms include apathy, lack of initiation, diminished interest, and inactivity. Common features also include disinhibition and impulsivity. Examples include socially inappropriate remarks, including sexual comments. These types of symptoms are less common in early phases of other types of dementia. FTD is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder such as depression.

bullets.text: Alzheimer's, Lewy body, vascular, and mixed dementias each have distinct clinical features that differentiate them from FTD.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Alzheimer's disease presents with memory and visuospatial loss. Lewy body dementia tends to cause memory loss, fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonian motor features. Vascular dementia patients usually have a history of cerebrovascular events. Mixed dementias generally are a combination of Alzheimer's and other types of dementias.

• Behavioral variant FTD is characterized by insidious onset, early social/interpersonal decline, disinhibition, apathy, emotional blunting, and loss of insight, and is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder.

  - Common features also include disinhibition and impulsivity.
  - Examples include socially inappropriate remarks, including sexual comments.
  - These types of symptoms are less common in early phases of other types of dementia.
  - FTD is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder such as depression.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Alzheimer's, Lewy body, vascular, and mixed dementias each have distinct clinical features that differentiate them from FTD.
  - Alzheimer's disease presents with memory and visuospatial loss.
  - Lewy body dementia tends to cause memory loss, fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonian motor features.
  - Vascular dementia patients usually have a history of cerebrovascular events.
  - Mixed dementias generally are a combination of Alzheimer's and other types of dementias.

stem: A 54-year-old male returns to your office for follow-up of chronic right knee pain that has worsened over the past month. On examination, range of motion of the knee is normal with no catching in the joint. There is a subtle effusion of the right knee and tenderness along the medial joint line. A radiograph shows medial joint space narrowing and subchondral sclerosis of the medial tibiofemoral joint. Which one of the following should you recommend at this point?

choices.A: Stretching and strengthening with physical therapy
choices.B: Taping and therapeutic ultrasound with physical therapy

correct_label: Stretching and strengthening with physical therapy

bullets.text: The mainstay of treatment for osteoarthritis of the knee is active rehabilitation and exercise (SOR A).
Active rehabilitation, such as stretching and strengthening, is more effective than passive rehabilitation, such as taping, heat, electrostimulation, or therapeutic ultrasound (SOR B).
Lateral wedge insoles and glucosamine and chondroitin supplements are unlikely to significantly improve pain in patients with knee arthritis (SOR B).

explanation_raw:
• The mainstay of treatment for osteoarthritis of the knee is active rehabilitation and exercise (SOR A).

stem: A 5-year-old male has a 10-day history of respiratory symptoms, including nasal congestion. He seemed to improve around day 5 but acutely worsened on day 7 with a new onset of fever, daytime cough, and persistent nasal drainage. On examination his oral temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and blood pressure 90/68 mm Hg. He has no sinus tenderness or cervical lymphadenopathy, and normal tympanic membranes bilaterally. You note nasal mucosal swelling and erythema, and mild pharyngeal erythema. Cardiac and lung examinations are normal. Which one of the following would you recommend?

choices.A: Saline nasal rinses, decongestants, fluids, and rest
choices.B: A laboratory workup including a CBC, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a C-reactive protein level

bullets.text: ABS is diagnosed clinically based on history alone, as physical exam, labs, and imaging do not reliably differentiate it from viral URI (CT reserved for complications).
bullets.sub_paragraph: The diagnosis of ABS is based on the history (SOR C). The physical examination is not particularly helpful and findings such as sinus tenderness, mucosal swelling, and transillumination of the sinuses do not help differentiate ABS from a viral URI. Laboratory studies are not indicated in the diagnosis. Imaging studies are likewise not indicated for the initial diagnosis, as they are often abnormal in both viral URIs and ABS. If complications such as orbital cellulitis or neurologic compromise are a concern, then CT may be indicated.

bullets.text: ABS is diagnosed by "double sickening," persistence of URI symptoms beyond 7–10 days without improvement, or severe onset with high fever and purulent discharge for ≥3 days.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This child meets the criteria for acute bacterial sinusitis (ABS) and should be treated with antibiotics. He exemplifies the concept of "double sickening," in which a child initially has typical symptoms of a viral upper respiratory infection and improves initially only to worsen later, with daytime cough, persistent nasal discharge, and/or new fever. Other criteria for ABS include persistence of URI symptoms without improvement after 7–10 days and "severe onset" ABS with a high fever and purulent nasal discharge for at least 3 days.

bullets.text: First-line treatment is amoxicillin ± clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day for high-risk) for 10–28 days; azithromycin and TMP/SMX should be avoided due to resistance, and cephalosporins used for penicillin-allergic patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Evidence shows that treatment with antibiotics in these situations improves outcomes (SOR B). The first-line antibiotic is amoxicillin with or without clavulanate. The length of treatment can range from 10 to 28 days. Depending on risks, patients may be treated with either high-dose amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanate, with an amoxicillin dosage of 90 mg/kg/day. Many of the bacteria causing ABS have been shown to be resistant to azithromycin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and these antibiotics should be avoided. For patients allergic to penicillins, cephalosporins should be used.

bullets.text: Saline irrigation, decongestants, and intranasal corticosteroids lack strong evidence and cannot replace antibiotics in children meeting ABS criteria.
bullets.sub_paragraph: There is no good evidence to support adjuvant care for ABS. Saline nasal irrigation, decongestants, or intranasal corticosteroids may be helpful but cannot replace antibiotic therapy in children who meet the criteria for ABS.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• ABS is diagnosed clinically based on history alone, as physical exam, labs, and imaging do not reliably differentiate it from viral URI (CT reserved for complications).
  - The diagnosis of ABS is based on the history (SOR C).
  - The physical examination is not particularly helpful and findings such as sinus tenderness, mucosal swelling, and transillumination of the sinuses do not help differentiate ABS from a viral URI.
  - Laboratory studies are not indicated in the diagnosis.
  - Imaging studies are likewise not indicated for the initial diagnosis, as they are often abnormal in both viral URIs and ABS.
  - If complications such as orbital cellulitis or neurologic compromise are a concern, then CT may be indicated.

**Diagnostic Criteria**
• ABS is diagnosed by "double sickening," persistence of URI symptoms beyond 7–10 days without improvement, or severe onset with high fever and purulent discharge for ≥3 days.
  - This child meets the criteria for acute bacterial sinusitis (ABS) and should be treated with antibiotics.
  - He exemplifies the concept of "double sickening," in which a child initially has typical symptoms of a viral upper respiratory infection and improves initially only to worsen later, with daytime cough, persistent nasal discharge, and/or new fever.
  - Other criteria for ABS include persistence of URI symptoms without improvement after 7–10 days and "severe onset" ABS with a high fever and purulent nasal discharge for at least 3 days.

**Treatment**
• First-line treatment is amoxicillin ± clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day for high-risk) for 10–28 days; azithromycin and TMP/SMX should be avoided due to resistance, and cephalosporins used for penicillin-allergic patients.
  - Evidence shows that treatment with antibiotics in these situations improves outcomes (SOR B).
  - The first-line antibiotic is amoxicillin with or without clavulanate.
  - The length of treatment can range from 10 to 28 days.
  - Depending on risks, patients may be treated with either high-dose amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanate, with an amoxicillin dosage of 90 mg/kg/day.
  - Many of the bacteria causing ABS have been shown to be resistant to azithromycin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and these antibiotics should be avoided.
  - For patients allergic to penicillins, cephalosporins should be used.

**Adjuvant Care**
• Saline irrigation, decongestants, and intranasal corticosteroids lack strong evidence and cannot replace antibiotics in children meeting ABS criteria.
  - There is no good evidence to support adjuvant care for ABS.
  - Saline nasal irrigation, decongestants, or intranasal corticosteroids may be helpful but cannot replace antibiotic therapy in children who meet the criteria for ABS.

stem: In an adult, the radiation exposure from a typical abdominal CT examination is approximately the same as how many posteroanterior chest radiographs?

bullets.text: Radiation exposure is measured in sieverts (Sv), with most diagnostic tests in the millisievert range and U.S. background averaging 3 mSv/year.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Radiation exposure in humans is quantified by the sievert (Sv), which equals 1 joule of radiation energy/kg of human tissue. Most clinical diagnostic test exposures measure in the millisievert (mSv) range. Natural background exposure in the United States averages 3 mSv/year.

bullets.text: Common radiographic studies vary widely in dose, from 0.02 mSv for a PA chest X-ray to 8 mSv for CT abdomen—a 400-fold difference.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Although exact exposures will vary according to patient size, type of equipment used, and operator expertise, typical radiation doses for common radiographic studies include the following: Posteroanterior chest—0.02 mSv Skull—0.1 mSv Lumbar spine—1.5 mSv CT head—2 mSv CT abdomen—8 mSv. This list shows that CT of the abdomen provides a radiation dose 400 times that of the typical posteroanterior chest radiograph.

bullets.text: Evidence of increased cancer mortality risk at diagnostic dose ranges supports careful risk/benefit assessment of radiographic studies.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A small increased relative risk of cancer mortality was demonstrated in Japanese survivors of atomic bombs receiving doses in the range of 5–20 mSv, suggesting that consideration of the risk/benefit ratio of some radiographic studies is warranted.

explanation_raw:

• Radiation exposure is measured in sieverts (Sv), with most diagnostic tests in the millisievert range and U.S. background averaging 3 mSv/year.
  - Radiation exposure in humans is quantified by the sievert (Sv), which equals 1 joule of radiation energy/kg of human tissue.
  - Most clinical diagnostic test exposures measure in the millisievert (mSv) range.
  - Natural background exposure in the United States averages 3 mSv/year.

**Typical Diagnostic Imaging Doses**
• Common radiographic studies vary widely in dose, from 0.02 mSv for a PA chest X-ray to 8 mSv for CT abdomen—a 400-fold difference.
  - Although exact exposures will vary according to patient size, type of equipment used, and operator expertise, typical radiation doses for common radiographic studies include the following: Posteroanterior chest—0.02 mSv Skull—0.1 mSv Lumbar spine—1.5 mSv CT head—2 mSv CT abdomen—8 mSv
  - This list shows that CT of the abdomen provides a radiation dose 400 times that of the typical posteroanterior chest radiograph.

**Clinical Risk Considerations**
• Evidence of increased cancer mortality risk at diagnostic dose ranges supports careful risk/benefit assessment of radiographic studies.
  - A small increased relative risk of cancer mortality was demonstrated in Japanese survivors of atomic bombs receiving doses in the range of 5–20 mSv, suggesting that consideration of the risk/benefit ratio of some radiographic studies is warranted.

stem: A 41-year-old male presents to your office for follow-up of recurrent nephrolithiasis. He currently follows a normal diet and does not drink soft drinks very often. Which one of the following would help prevent recurrent kidney stones?

choices.D: Two 12-oz cola-flavored soft drinks per day

bullets.text: Increasing fluid intake to achieve 2 L/day urine output is the primary intervention, reducing recurrence by at least 50%.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients with recurrent nephrolithiasis should first try to increase fluid intake to achieve a daily urine output 2 L. Increasing fluid intake decreases the recurrence of stones by at least 50%.

bullets.text: Reducing cola intake (acidified by phosphoric acid) may help, but citric acid–based drinks and general dietary changes show little benefit.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Reducing soft drink intake may also help but this seems to be limited to those who drink colas, which are acidified by phosphoric acid. Soft drinks acidified with citric acid, such as fruit-flavored drinks, do not appear to have the same effect. There is little evidence that dietary changes help significantly.

bullets.text: If fluid intake alone is insufficient, thiazide diuretics, citrate, or allopurinol are recommended (SOR C).
bullets.sub_paragraph: If a patient's fluid increase is not sufficient, treatment with a thiazide diuretic, citrate, or allopurinol is recommended (SOR C).

explanation_raw:
**First-Line Management**
• Increasing fluid intake to achieve 2 L/day urine output is the primary intervention, reducing recurrence by at least 50%.
  - Patients with recurrent nephrolithiasis should first try to increase fluid intake to achieve a daily urine output 2 L.
  - Increasing fluid intake decreases the recurrence of stones by at least 50%.

**Dietary Considerations**
• Reducing cola intake (acidified by phosphoric acid) may help, but citric acid–based drinks and general dietary changes show little benefit.
  - Reducing soft drink intake may also help but this seems to be limited to those who drink colas, which are acidified by phosphoric acid.
  - Soft drinks acidified with citric acid, such as fruit-flavored drinks, do not appear to have the same effect.
  - There is little evidence that dietary changes help significantly.

**Pharmacologic Treatment**
• If fluid intake alone is insufficient, thiazide diuretics, citrate, or allopurinol are recommended (SOR C).
  - If a patient's fluid increase is not sufficient, treatment with a thiazide diuretic, citrate, or allopurinol is recommended (SOR C).

stem: Acute altitude sickness consists of headache, nausea, dizziness, and sleep disturbance. Risk factors include which one of the following?

stem: A 70-year-old male presents to the emergency department with confusion and a fever of 38.9°C (102.0°F). He has a history of decreased mental status, feeling weak and confused, and low urinary output. On examination he has a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 100 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 24/min, and a temperature of 38.9°C (102.0°F). He has mottling of the skin, and his capillary refill time is 5 seconds. A CBC reveals a WBC count of 24,000/mm3 (N 4500–11,000) with 90% neutrophils. His urinalysis is remarkable for WBCs too numerous to count, with 4+ bacteria. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics are initiated but the patient remains hypotensive. Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this point?

bullets.text: Early recognition and aggressive fluid resuscitation are critical first steps in managing sepsis and septic shock.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prompt recognition and treatment of sepsis increases the chances of survival. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is the initial treatment for hypotension in patients in septic shock. Antibiotic therapy should be administered within 1 hour of suspecting sepsis.

bullets.text: Norepinephrine is the current first-line vasopressor, replacing dopamine, which has been shown ineffective for renal perfusion.
bullets.sub_paragraph: If fluid resuscitation is not successful in restoring blood pressure, norepinephrine is the currently recommended first-line vasopressor. Previously, dopamine was recommended, but low-dose dopamine for renal perfusion has now been shown to be ineffective.

bullets.text: Low-dose corticosteroids may be considered for vasopressor-dependent patients, while hydroxyethyl starch should be avoided due to increased mortality.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For patients who are vasopressor dependent, low-dose corticosteroids can be considered. The use of hydroxyethyl starch is not recommended because the mortality rate is higher in sepsis patients.

explanation_raw:
**Recognition and Initial Treatment**
• Early recognition and aggressive fluid resuscitation are critical first steps in managing sepsis and septic shock.
  - Prompt recognition and treatment of sepsis increases the chances of survival.
  - Aggressive fluid resuscitation is the initial treatment for hypotension in patients in septic shock.
  - Antibiotic therapy should be administered within 1 hour of suspecting sepsis.

**Vasopressor Management**
• Norepinephrine is the current first-line vasopressor, replacing dopamine, which has been shown ineffective for renal perfusion.
  - If fluid resuscitation is not successful in restoring blood pressure, norepinephrine is the currently recommended first-line vasopressor.
  - Previously, dopamine was recommended, but low-dose dopamine for renal perfusion has now been shown to be ineffective.

**Adjunct and Contraindicated Therapies**
• Low-dose corticosteroids may be considered for vasopressor-dependent patients, while hydroxyethyl starch should be avoided due to increased mortality.
  - For patients who are vasopressor dependent, low-dose corticosteroids can be considered.
  - The use of hydroxyethyl starch is not recommended because the mortality rate is higher in sepsis patients.

stem: Which one of the following is the most common cause of hearing loss in the newborn?

stem: An agitated 35-year-old male is brought to the urgent-care clinic by his wife. She reports that her husband has been restless and tremulous since early this morning. Further history reveals that he was seen 2 days ago for a work-related back injury and was given a prescription for cyclobenzaprine, 10 mg 3 times daily as needed. He reports improvement in his back pain but admits that last night he took an extra dose of a sleeping pill prescribed by his psychiatrist. His chronic medical conditions include controlled essential hypertension and depression. On examination the patient’s vital signs include a temperature of 38.1°C (100.6°F), a blood pressure of 124/82 mm Hg, a heart rate of 98 beats/min, and a respiratory rate of 12/min. The patient appears diaphoretic with a resting symmetrical tremor. He has a regular heart rate and rhythm and his lungs are clear. His abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. His strength is 5/5 bilaterally in the upper and lower extremities, and he has 4+ patellar and biceps reflexes bilaterally. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

bullets.text: Serotonin syndrome is a life-threatening condition from excessive serotonergic activity, diagnosed using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, and managed with discontinuation of the precipitating agent and supportive care.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity, and certain medications are more likely to precipitate it. Early recognition of symptoms is important, as most cases can be managed on an outpatient basis with discontinuation of the precipitating medication/agent and supportive care. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria can be used to diagnose serotonin syndrome (SOR C).

bullets.text: The differential diagnoses—anticholinergic syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and central cord syndrome—are distinguished by their distinct clinical features and precipitating causes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The differential diagnosis includes anticholinergic syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Anticholinergic syndrome is associated with tachycardia, tachypnea, and hyperthermia. Malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome are associated with hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hyperthermia. These conditions are precipitated by other classes of medications. Central cord syndrome is a spinal cord disease caused by spinal trauma, syringomyelia, and intrinsic cord tumors, and presents with arm weakness greater than leg weakness.

• Serotonin syndrome is a life-threatening condition from excessive serotonergic activity, diagnosed using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, and managed with discontinuation of the precipitating agent and supportive care.
  - Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity, and certain medications are more likely to precipitate it.
  - Early recognition of symptoms is important, as most cases can be managed on an outpatient basis with discontinuation of the precipitating medication/agent and supportive care.
  - The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria can be used to diagnose serotonin syndrome (SOR C).

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**

  - The differential diagnosis includes anticholinergic syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stem: A 68-year-old female sees you because she developed increased floaters followed by flashes of lights after a sneezing attack. She then noted a dark spot in the periphery of her right eye. Three weeks ago she underwent cataract removal with intraocular lens implantation in this eye. Her examination is notable for decreased visual acuity and a loss of peripheral field in the right eye. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Retinal detachment presents with progressive floaters, then light flashes, then vision loss, and must be distinguished from other acute eye conditions like central retinal artery occlusion and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Retinal detachments are often preceded by a posterior vitreous detachment, which can lead to a break in the retina, and patients may experience an increase in floaters but not light flashes or loss of vision. With a retinal detachment, patients typically experience floaters followed within 1 week by flashes of light as the retina tears. If the retinal tear becomes large enough vision is impaired. Central retinal artery occlusion is manifested by painless complete loss of vision in the affected eye. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is associated with eye pain, photophobia, headache, nausea and vomiting, and cloudy loss of vision, and the onset is not typically associated with coughing or sneezing.

bullets.text: Retinal detachments result from a break, exudate, or traction on the retina.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Retinal detachments can be caused by a break in the retina, exudate or leakage from beneath the retina, or traction on the retina.

bullets.text: Key risk factors include age 50–75, ocular trauma, prior cataract surgery, family history, previous retinal detachment (25% contralateral risk), and myopia >3 diopters (tenfold increased risk).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Risk factors for retinal detachment include age 50–75, ocular trauma, previous cataract surgery, family history, and a past history of retinal detachment. A patient with a previous retinal detachment has a 25% risk of developing a retinal detachment in the other eye. Myopia is the other significant risk factor, associated with a tenfold increased risk in patients with >3 diopters of refractive error.

bullets.text: Patients with typical history plus vision or visual field loss require urgent ophthalmology referral for possible surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Any patient with the typical history and loss of visual acuity or peripheral field should be urgently referred to an ophthalmologist, as urgent surgery may be required.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis & Presentation**
• Retinal detachment presents with progressive floaters, then light flashes, then vision loss, and must be distinguished from other acute eye conditions like central retinal artery occlusion and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
  - Retinal detachments are often preceded by a posterior vitreous detachment, which can lead to a break in the retina, and patients may experience an increase in floaters but not light flashes or loss of vision.
  - With a retinal detachment, patients typically experience floaters followed within 1 week by flashes of light as the retina tears.
  - If the retinal tear becomes large enough vision is impaired.
  - Central retinal artery occlusion is manifested by painless complete loss of vision in the affected eye.
  - Acute angle-closure glaucoma is associated with eye pain, photophobia, headache, nausea and vomiting, and cloudy loss of vision, and the onset is not typically associated with coughing or sneezing.

**Pathophysiology**
• Retinal detachments result from a break, exudate, or traction on the retina.
  - Retinal detachments can be caused by a break in the retina, exudate or leakage from beneath the retina, or traction on the retina.

**Risk Factors**
• Key risk factors include age 50–75, ocular trauma, prior cataract surgery, family history, previous retinal detachment (25% contralateral risk), and myopia >3 diopters (tenfold increased risk).
  - Risk factors for retinal detachment include age 50–75, ocular trauma, previous cataract surgery, family history, and a past history of retinal detachment.
  - A patient with a previous retinal detachment has a 25% risk of developing a retinal detachment in the other eye.
  - Myopia is the other significant risk factor, associated with a tenfold increased risk in patients with >3 diopters of refractive error.

**Treatment**
• Patients with typical history plus vision or visual field loss require urgent ophthalmology referral for possible surgery.
  - Any patient with the typical history and loss of visual acuity or peripheral field should be urgently referred to an ophthalmologist, as urgent surgery may be required.

stem: A 68-year-old female with well-controlled hypertension presents for a routine evaluation. The physical examination is significant for a BMI of 35.4 kg/m2. A comprehensive metabolic panel prior to the visit revealed the following: Serum calcium  9.2 mg/dL (N 8.5–10.2) Albumin  4.0 g/dL (N 3.5–5.4) Creatinine  0.6 mg/dL (N 0.6–1.1) 25-hydroxyvitamin D  9 ng/mL (N >20) Alkaline phosphatase  151 U/L (N 47–147) Which one of the following is true, based on these findings?

choices.C: She should take vitamin D supplements

correct_label: She should take vitamin D supplements

bullets.text: This patient's elevated alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D deficiency, and normal calcium are consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, putting her at risk for osteomalacia but not rickets.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has slight elevations of her alkaline phosphatase along with a deficiency of vitamin D and normal calcium levels. This constellation of findings is most consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism related to vitamin D deficiency. This would put the patient at risk for osteomalacia but not rickets, which is a clinical diagnosis based on the effects of insufficient bone mineralization secondary to low vitamin D activity before the closure of growth plates.

bullets.text: Vitamin D status is measured by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, with levels <10 ng/mL considered clearly deficient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Vitamin D storage is best reflected by the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level. While there is some disagreement regarding normal levels, a level <10 ng/mL is clearly deficient.

bullets.text: Standard vitamin D supplementation (not calcitriol) is appropriate here, as it will reduce PTH activity and normalize alkaline phosphatase; calcitriol is reserved for renal failure or impaired activation states.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Supplementation with activated vitamin D (calcitriol) is generally only necessary in patients with renal failure or other conditions associated with inadequate activation of the storage forms of vitamin D. Supplementation with vitamin D should decrease PTH activity and thus bone turnover in this patient, which would likely normalize the alkaline phosphatase.

**Diagnosis**
• This patient's elevated alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D deficiency, and normal calcium are consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, putting her at risk for osteomalacia but not rickets.
  - This patient has slight elevations of her alkaline phosphatase along with a deficiency of vitamin D and normal calcium levels.
  - This constellation of findings is most consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism related to vitamin D deficiency.
  - This would put the patient at risk for osteomalacia but not rickets, which is a clinical diagnosis based on the effects of insufficient bone mineralization secondary to low vitamin D activity before the closure of growth plates.

**Key Facts**
• Vitamin D status is measured by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, with levels <10 ng/mL considered clearly deficient.
  - Vitamin D storage is best reflected by the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level.
  - While there is some disagreement regarding normal levels, a level <10 ng/mL is clearly deficient.

**Treatment**
• Standard vitamin D supplementation (not calcitriol) is appropriate here, as it will reduce PTH activity and normalize alkaline phosphatase; calcitriol is reserved for renal failure or impaired activation states.
  - Supplementation with activated vitamin D (calcitriol) is generally only necessary in patients with renal failure or other conditions associated with inadequate activation of the storage forms of vitamin D.
  - Supplementation with vitamin D should decrease PTH activity and thus bone turnover in this patient, which would likely normalize the alkaline phosphatase.

stem: U.S. federal labor law requires companies with >50 employees to provide which one of the following benefits for employees who are nursing mothers?

choices.A: Extended Family and Medical Leave Act protection for a total of 6 months
choices.B: Reasonable unpaid break time to express milk
choices.C: Extended bathroom access time to express milk
choices.D: A refrigerator dedicated to storage of expressed milk

correct_label: Reasonable unpaid break time to express milk

bullets.text: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act amended the Federal Labor Standards Act of 1938 to require employers of >50 employees to provide nursing mothers reasonable break time to express milk for up to 1 year following the birth of their children.
The employer is not required to compensate nursing mothers during the breaks and is not required to provide refrigerated storage for the expressed milk.
The law also requires that the employer provide a place to express milk, other than a bathroom, that is shielded from view and free from intrusion from coworkers and the public.

explanation_raw:
• The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act amended the Federal Labor Standards Act of 1938 to require employers of >50 employees to provide nursing mothers reasonable break time to express milk for up to 1 year following the birth of their children.
• The employer is not required to compensate nursing mothers during the breaks and is not required to provide refrigerated storage for the expressed milk.
• The law also requires that the employer provide a place to express milk, other than a bathroom, that is shielded from view and free from intrusion from coworkers and the public.

stem: A 30-year-old ICU nurse has been caring for several patients infected with Clostridium difficile. She is asymptomatic but is worried that she may also be infected. Which one of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this nurse?

bullets.text: C. difficile infection requires symptomatic criteria plus positive stool/colonoscopic findings, and lab testing cannot distinguish colonization from infection.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Laboratory testing for Clostridium difficile should be done only on symptomatic patients. A diagnosis of C. difficile infection requires the presence of diarrhea (3 unformed stools in a 24-hour period) or radiographic evidence of ileus and toxic megacolon. In addition, the diagnosis requires a positive stool test for toxigenic C. difficile or its toxins, or colonoscopic or histopathologic findings showing pseudomembranous colitis. Laboratory testing cannot distinguish between asymptomatic colonization and symptomatic infection.

bullets.text: Test of cure is not recommended post-treatment, and probiotics are not specifically recommended for preventing or treating C. difficile infection despite some benefit for antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Test of cure is not recommended after C. difficile treatment. Probiotics may prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea and may also reduce C. difficile diarrhea in children and adults younger than 65, but are not specifically recommended for preventing or treating C. difficile infection.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• C. difficile infection requires symptomatic criteria plus positive stool/colonoscopic findings, and lab testing cannot distinguish colonization from infection.
  - Laboratory testing for Clostridium difficile should be done only on symptomatic patients.

stem: A homeless 47-year-old male visits the local health department and asks to be screened for tuberculosis. He is not aware of any definite exposure to tuberculosis and is asymptomatic. The nurse asks whether the patient should be screened with a tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA, QuantiFERON-TB Gold). Which one of the following would be an advantage of IGRA in this patient?

choices.A: It helps to distinguish latent tuberculosis from active tuberculosis
choices.B: The patient’s blood can be stored for up to 36 hours if needed, to allow transport to a qualified laboratory to run the test
choices.C: A follow-up visit is not required to obtain results
choices.D: The IGRA will be positive within 2 weeks of exposure to an individual with active tuberculosis
choices.E: The IGRA can simultaneously detect resistance to rifampin (Rifadin)

correct_label: A follow-up visit is not required to obtain results

bullets.text: Both TST and IGRA are used to screen for tuberculosis, but neither can distinguish latent from active TB, and both may miss conversion in the first 8–12 weeks post-exposure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It is important for health care professionals to be familiar with the various options for screening and testing for latent or active tuberculosis. In the United States the tuberculin skin test (TST) is the traditional screening test for tuberculosis. The interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test that can also aid in the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis. As with the TST, conversion (i.e., a positive test) of IGRA may not occur within the first 8–12 weeks following exposure to an individual with active tuberculosis. In addition, neither the TST nor the IGRA can distinguish between latent and active tuberculosis.

bullets.text: IGRA avoids false positives from BCG vaccination and requires no follow-up visit, but must be processed within 8–30 hours; a separate Xpert MTB/RIF assay is needed to detect MTBC and rifampin resistance.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Advantages of IGRA include the ability to get results without follow-up and the fact that prior bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination does not cause a false-positive test. With TST testing, prior BCG vaccination, especially if given within the last 10 years, can result in a false-positive test. There are two IGRA tests available for use in the United States and both tests need to be processed within 8–30 hours, depending on the specific test used. Although there is now a test available that can detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampin, it is a separate test called the Xpert MTB/RIF assay.

explanation_raw:
**TB Screening Tests Overview**
• Both TST and IGRA are used to screen for tuberculosis, but neither can distinguish latent from active TB, and both may miss conversion in the first 8–12 weeks post-exposure.
  - It is important for health care professionals to be familiar with the various options for screening and testing for latent or active tuberculosis.
  - In the United States the tuberculin skin test (TST) is the traditional screening test for tuberculosis.
  - The interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test that can also aid in the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis.
  - As with the TST, conversion (i.e., a positive test) of IGRA may not occur within the first 8–12 weeks following exposure to an individual with active tuberculosis.
  - In addition, neither the TST nor the IGRA can distinguish between latent and active tuberculosis.

**IGRA Advantages and Limitations**
• IGRA avoids false positives from BCG vaccination and requires no follow-up visit, but must be processed within 8–30 hours; a separate Xpert MTB/RIF assay is needed to detect MTBC and rifampin resistance.
  - Advantages of IGRA include the ability to get results without follow-up and the fact that prior bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination does not cause a false-positive test.
  - With TST testing, prior BCG vaccination, especially if given within the last 10 years, can result in a false-positive test.
  - There are two IGRA tests available for use in the United States and both tests need to be processed within 8–30 hours, depending on the specific test used.
  - Although there is now a test available that can detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampin, it is a separate test called the Xpert MTB/RIF assay.

stem: The preferred method for diagnosing psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (pseudoseizures) is

bullets.text: Inpatient vEEG is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES, combining extended EEG with time-locked video to capture clinical and electrographic features during an event.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Inpatient video-electroencephalography (vEEG) monitoring is the preferred test for the diagnosis of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES), and is considered the gold standard (SOR B). Video-EEG monitoring combines extended EEG monitoring with time-locked video acquisition that allows for analysis of clinical and electrographic features during a captured event.

bullets.text: Alternative diagnostic methods — including clinical features, suggestion, ambulatory EEG, prolactin, other serum markers, and MRI — are all unreliable or insufficient for diagnosing PNES.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Many other types of evidence have been used, including the presence or absence of self-injury and incontinence, the ability to induce seizures by suggestion, psychologic tests, and ambulatory EEG. While useful in some cases, these alternatives have been found to be insufficient for the diagnosis of PNES. Elevated postictal prolactin levels (at least two times the upper limit of normal) have been used to differentiate generalized and complex partial seizures from PNES but are not reliable (SOR B). While prolactin levels are often elevated after an epileptic seizure, they do not always rise, and the timing of measurement is crucial, making this a less sensitive test than was previously believed. Other serum markers have also been used to help distinguish PNES from epileptic seizures, including creatine phosphokinase, cortisol, WBC counts, lactate dehydrogenase, pCO , and neuron-specific enolase. These also are not2 reliable, as threshold levels for abnormality, sensitivity, and specificity have not been determined. MRI is not reliable because abnormal brain MRIs have been documented in as many as one-third of patients with PNES. In addition, patients with epileptic seizures often have normal brain MRIs.

stem: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Academy of Pediatrics support the advance provision of emergency contraception to sexually active women. Evidence shows that this practice

choices.A: decreases pregnancy rates on a population level
choices.B: decreases the time from unprotected sex to use of emergency contraception

choices.D: increases rates of sexually transmitted infection

correct_label: decreases the time from unprotected sex to use of emergency contraception

explanation.heading: Evidence on Advance Provision of EC

bullets.text: Multiple RCTs show advance provision increases EC use and reduces time-to-use, but does not improve STI rates, unprotected intercourse, routine contraceptive use, or pregnancy rates compared to standard access.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Multiple studies, including randomized, controlled trials, have compared standard access to emergency contraception (EC) with advance provision in which the patient is given a prescription for the EC and encouraged to have it filled in order to have it immediately available in case of unprotected intercourse. In multiple populations in the United States and Europe advance provision compared to standard access has been shown to increase the rate of use of EC and to reduce the interval between intercourse and use of EC. However, no change has been shown for several outcomes when advance provision was compared to standard access to EC. These include rates of sexually transmitted infections, unprotected intercourse, use of routine contraceptives prior to sexual activity, and pregnancy within the population studied.

stem: You see a 90-year-old patient with elevated blood pressure. Which one of the following is an expected physiologic change in elderly patients?

bullets.text: Elderly patients have distinct hemodynamic changes including wider pulse pressure, lower cardiac output, higher peripheral resistance, reduced intravascular volume, and lower renal blood flow compared to younger patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Age-related physiologic differences such as wider pulse pressure should be a consideration when treating hypertension in the elderly. These patients also have lower cardiac output, higher peripheral resistance, lower intravascular volume, and lower renal blood flow compared with younger patients.

explanation.heading: Pulse Pressure and Coronary Artery Disease Risk

bullets.text: Pulse pressure reflects age-related vascular stiffness and becomes the strongest predictor of CAD risk with advancing age, as systolic BP rises throughout life while diastolic BP peaks in middle age and then declines.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pulse pressure (the difference between systolic blood pressure and diastolic blood pressure) is a measure of the degree of age-related vascular stiffness and is a risk factor for coronary artery disease events. With increasing age the strongest predictor of coronary artery disease gradually shifts from diastolic blood pressure to systolic blood pressure, and then to pulse pressure. Systolic blood pressure rises gradually throughout adult life, whereas diastolic blood pressure peaks and plateaus in late middle age, and declines slightly thereafter. Diastolic hypertension occurs in <10% of all patients with hypertension after age 70.

stem: A 55-year-old female who works at a local day care center presents with a severe cough. Her illness began 10 days ago with malaise, a low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, tearing, and a mild cough. Over the past 3 days the cough has become much more severe and she coughs to the point that vomiting is induced. Which one of the following is most likely to lead to a definitive diagnosis?

choices.A: A Gram stain and culture of sputum

bullets.text: Pertussis is diagnosed clinically after ≥2 weeks of cough plus one classic sign, with PCR preferred over culture for confirmation due to faster results and higher sensitivity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pertussis can be diagnosed clinically if there is a coughing illness of 2 weeks' duration with one of the classic signs of pertussis (post-tussive emesis, respiratory whoop, or paroxysmal cough) and there is no other apparent cause. The CDC also recommends the use of both cultures and polymerase chain reaction testing to confirm the diagnosis. Culture is not the best choice, however, as it is often done improperly, and culture results may not be available for several days. Polymerase chain reaction has the advantage of providing results in 1–2 days. It has good specificity and the sensitivity is much higher than that of a culture; its sensitivity is highest during the first 2 weeks of symptoms.

bullets.text: Pertussis progresses through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, with increasing incidence and characteristic severe cough that can cause emesis and rib fractures.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pertussis has been increasing in incidence. The initial presentation usually involves nonspecific symptoms including malaise, lacrimation, and rhinorrhea, which is referred to as the catarrhal stage. The following stage, known as the paroxysmal stage, is manifested by severe coughing that may lead to the characteristic high-pitched whooping sound when the patient tries to catch his or her breath. Coughing to the point of emesis is also characteristic of pertussis, and the cough can be severe enough to actually result in rib fractures. The cough may last several weeks before it begins to wane during the convalescent phase, which usually lasts 2–3 weeks.

bullets.text: The CDC recommends azithromycin or clarithromycin for pertussis, primarily to reduce transmission rather than improve symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment with antibiotics usually does not improve clinical symptoms, although it does decrease transmission. The CDC continues to recommend antibiotics for pertussis. Either azithromycin or clarithromycin is currently recommended.
