  - Polymerase chain reaction has the advantage of providing results in 1–2 days.
  - It has good specificity and the sensitivity is much higher than that of a culture; its sensitivity is highest during the first 2 weeks of symptoms.

**Clinical Presentation**
• Pertussis progresses through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, with increasing incidence and characteristic severe cough that can cause emesis and rib fractures.
  - Pertussis has been increasing in incidence.
  - The initial presentation usually involves nonspecific symptoms including malaise, lacrimation, and rhinorrhea, which is referred to as the catarrhal stage.
  - The following stage, known as the paroxysmal stage, is manifested by severe coughing that may lead to the characteristic high-pitched whooping sound when the patient tries to catch his or her breath.

stem: A 6-month-old male is brought to your office for a well child check. He has been healthy except for mild eczema that resolved with about 7 days of a medium-potency corticosteroid when he was 4 months old. He is the only child of a single mother. However, she is concerned about introducing peanuts into her son’s diet. The mother’s brother suffers from a severe peanut allergy and was recently hospitalized after an accidental peanut ingestion. The mother herself does not eat nuts regularly because of her brother’s allergy but has had peanuts in small amounts without any trouble. Which one of the following would you recommend regarding the introduction of foods containing peanuts and other nuts into this child’s diet?

choices.B: Start introducing these foods once he has reached 12 months of age
choices.C: Wait until at least 5 years of age to introduce these foods
choices.D: Introduce these foods only after allergy testing of the child is performed
choices.E: Introduce these foods only after allergy testing of the mother is performed

stem: Which one of the following antidepressants can prolong the QT interval and should be avoided with concomitant QT-prolonging agents such as atypical antipsychotics?

bullets.text: QT prolongation is a critical, additive adverse effect of certain medications that can lead to life-threatening arrhythmias like torsades de pointes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prolongation of the QT interval is an important medication adverse effect to consider. This is particularly true in patients taking multiple medications, because this effect can be additive and increases the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes.

bullets.text: Among antidepressants, only citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT interval, while other SSRIs, bupropion, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine do not.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Among commonly used antidepressants, citalopram and escitalopram may prolong the QT interval. Other SSRIs, as well as bupropion, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine, do not have this effect.

bullets.text: Combined use of tricyclic antidepressants or antipsychotics with SSRIs is problematic due to additive QT prolongation risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Both tricyclic antidepressants and antipsychotics, commonly used in patients also taking SSRIs, can cause QT prolongation, making their combined use problematic.

explanation_raw:
**QT Prolongation Risk**
• QT prolongation is a critical, additive adverse effect of certain medications that can lead to life-threatening arrhythmias like torsades de pointes.
  - Prolongation of the QT interval is an important medication adverse effect to consider.
  - This is particularly true in patients taking multiple medications, because this effect can be additive and increases the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes.

**Antidepressants and QT Effects**
• Among antidepressants, only citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT interval, while other SSRIs, bupropion, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine do not.
  - Among commonly used antidepressants, citalopram and escitalopram may prolong the QT interval.
  - Other SSRIs, as well as bupropion, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine, do not have this effect.

**Drug Combinations**
• Combined use of tricyclic antidepressants or antipsychotics with SSRIs is problematic due to additive QT prolongation risk.

stem: A 6-month-old uncircumcised male is brought to your clinic by his parents, who are concerned because his foreskin remains “tight” and cannot be retracted when they bathe him. He has never been treated for a urinary tract infection or balanitis and his parents report he has a good urine stream. On examination the skin at the preputial outlet appears healthy with no scarring. Which one of the following is the most appropriate intervention?

choices.A: Reassurance and continued routine foreskin hygiene
choices.B: A short course of a topical corticosteroid twice daily to the foreskin
choices.C: Prophylactic topical antibacterial ointment twice daily
choices.D: Forceful retraction of the foreskin twice daily to reduce adhesions
choices.E: Referral to a pediatric urologist for circumcision

correct_label: Reassurance and continued routine foreskin hygiene

bullets.text: Phimosis can be physiologic (normal in young boys, resolves with development) or pathologic (distal scarring with white fibrotic ring), and this child's exam is consistent with physiologic phimosis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Phimosis is the inability of the foreskin (prepuce) to retract over the glans and it can be physiologic or pathologic. Nonretractile foreskin is very common in young boys, and is seen in up to 10% of uncircumcised 3-year-old boys. This physiologic phimosis is part of normal development and over time the foreskin will become retractile due to intermittent erections and keratinization of the inner foreskin. Pathologic phimosis is due to distal scarring and on examination typically appears as a white, contracted fibrotic ring around the preputial outlet. This child's examination is consistent with physiologic phimosis.

bullets.text: Pathologic phimosis, painful erections, recurrent balanitis, or recurrent UTIs with phimosis warrant urologic consultation and possible circumcision.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pathologic phimosis, painful erections with a tight foreskin, recurrent bouts of balanitis, and recurrent urinary tract infections in conjunction with phimosis are indications for urologic consultation and consideration of circumcision.

bullets.text: First-line management is reassurance and good foreskin hygiene; topical corticosteroids may accelerate resolution, but forcible retraction and empiric antimicrobials should be avoided.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A short course of a topical corticosteroid (2–8 weeks of 0.05% betamethasone twice daily) applied to the preputial outlet may result in accelerated resolution of physiologic phimosis. However, given this child's age and the absence of complications, reassurance and continued good foreskin hygiene are recommended. The foreskin should not be forcibly retracted, as this may lead to microtears and resultant scarring. In the absence of infection, neither antibacterial nor antifungal ointment is indicated.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Phimosis can be physiologic (normal in young boys, resolves with development) or pathologic (distal scarring with white fibrotic ring), and this child's exam is consistent with physiologic phimosis.
  - Phimosis is the inability of the foreskin (prepuce) to retract over the glans and it can be physiologic or pathologic.
  - Nonretractile foreskin is very common in young boys, and is seen in up to 10% of uncircumcised 3-year-old boys.
  - This physiologic phimosis is part of normal development and over time the foreskin will become retractile due to intermittent erections and keratinization of the inner foreskin.
  - Pathologic phimosis is due to distal scarring and on examination typically appears as a white, contracted fibrotic ring around the preputial outlet.
  - This child's examination is consistent with physiologic phimosis.

**Indications for Referral**
• Pathologic phimosis, painful erections, recurrent balanitis, or recurrent UTIs with phimosis warrant urologic consultation and possible circumcision.
  - Pathologic phimosis, painful erections with a tight foreskin, recurrent bouts of balanitis, and recurrent urinary tract infections in conjunction with phimosis are indications for urologic consultation and consideration of circumcision.

**Treatment**
• First-line management is reassurance and good foreskin hygiene; topical corticosteroids may accelerate resolution, but forcible retraction and empiric antimicrobials should be avoided.
  - A short course of a topical corticosteroid (2–8 weeks of 0.05% betamethasone twice daily) applied to the preputial outlet may result in accelerated resolution of physiologic phimosis.
  - However, given this child's age and the absence of complications, reassurance and continued good foreskin hygiene are recommended.
  - The foreskin should not be forcibly retracted, as this may lead to microtears and resultant scarring.
  - In the absence of infection, neither antibacterial nor antifungal ointment is indicated.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents to your office with a 3-month history of dyspnea. She does not smoke and has not had a productive cough. bullets.text: This patient has sarcoidosis, with erythema nodosum as a common cutaneous extrapulmonary manifestation.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Xerostomia suggests Sjögren's syndrome, while malar rash and alopecia point to lupus erythematosus, not sarcoidosis.
  - Xerostomia is associated with Sjögren's syndrome.
  - A malar rash and alopecia are dermatologic findings associated with lupus erythematosus.

stem: A 66-year-old male is diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. This patient will require regular follow-up visits because of the risk his condition will progress to

It is associated with a risk of progression to multiple myeloma at a rate of 1% per year.

Most patients diagnosed with MGUS should be reevaluated in 6 months with a medical history, physical examination, CBC, calcium and creatinine levels, and serum electrophoresis, and then annually thereafter.

stem: A 59-year-old female with hypertension takes hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine (Norvasc). A routine basic metabolic panel is normal except for a mildly elevated calcium level. Upon further questioning, she admits to a history of kidney stones in the past. After stopping her hydrochlorothiazide, which one of the following laboratory evaluations would be most appropriate?

choices.D: A repeat basic metabolic panel with ionized calcium

correct_label: A repeat basic metabolic panel with ionized calcium

bullets.text: Elevated calcium should be confirmed, then worked up with history, exam, and labs (25-OH vitamin D, magnesium, creatinine, PTH) before advanced imaging.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Isolated elevated calcium levels should be confirmed before pursuing further testing. After calcium elevation is confirmed, immediate treatment should be undertaken if hypercalcemia is severe. Otherwise, a history and physical examination would be appropriate, as well as 25-hydroxyvitamin D, magnesium, creatinine, and PTH levels.

bullets.text: PTH level guides further testing: normal/elevated PTH warrants 24-hour urine studies to distinguish primary hyperparathyroidism from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, while low PTH prompts evaluation of parathyroid-independent causes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In patients with a normal or elevated PTH level, 24-hour urine calcium and creatinine levels can help to differentiate between primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. If the PTH level is low, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and parathyroid hormone–related peptide levels should be checked to evaluate possible causes of hypercalcemia independent of the parathyroid.

bullets.text: Sestamibi scintigraphy is reserved for confirmed hyperparathyroidism when surgery is being considered.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Sestamibi scintigraphy is indicated only after confirmation of hyperparathyroidism, and typically in anticipation of surgical treatment.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Elevated calcium should be confirmed, then worked up with history, exam, and labs (25-OH vitamin D, magnesium, creatinine, PTH) before advanced imaging.
  - Isolated elevated calcium levels should be confirmed before pursuing further testing.
  - After calcium elevation is confirmed, immediate treatment should be undertaken if hypercalcemia is severe.
  - Otherwise, a history and physical examination would be appropriate, as well as 25-hydroxyvitamin D, magnesium, creatinine, and PTH levels.

**Workup Based on PTH Level**
• PTH level guides further testing: normal/elevated PTH warrants 24-hour urine studies to distinguish primary hyperparathyroidism from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, while low PTH prompts evaluation of parathyroid-independent causes.
  - In patients with a normal or elevated PTH level, 24-hour urine calcium and creatinine levels can help to differentiate between primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.
  - If the PTH level is low, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and parathyroid hormone–related peptide levels should be checked to evaluate possible causes of hypercalcemia independent of the parathyroid.

**Imaging**
• Sestamibi scintigraphy is reserved for confirmed hyperparathyroidism when surgery is being considered.
  - Sestamibi scintigraphy is indicated only after confirmation of hyperparathyroidism, and typically in anticipation of surgical treatment.

stem: A 10-year-old female is brought to your clinic complaining of toe pain after a playground injury. A radiograph reveals a displaced fracture involving half the joint surface of the first proximal phalanx. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management of this fracture?

choices.A: Buddy taping to the second phalanx for 6 weeks
choices.C: A short leg walking cast with a toe plate for 6 weeks
choices.D: A posterior splint with orthopedic referral at 1 week
choices.E: Prompt orthopedic referral for surgical fixation

correct_label: Prompt orthopedic referral for surgical fixation

bullets.text: Minor phalangeal fractures (2nd–5th toes) are managed with buddy taping and rigid-sole shoe, while displaced fractures may need closed reduction in the office.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Phalangeal fractures of the second to fifth toes can usually be managed with buddy taping and a rigid-sole shoe for 3 weeks followed by buddy taping for another 3 weeks. If the fracture is significantly displaced, closed reduction in the office using local anesthesia may be appropriate.

bullets.text: Hallux fractures carry higher risk due to weight-bearing importance and require nonsurgical management (short leg walking cast with toe plate, then rigid-sole shoe) only if non-displaced and involving less than 25% of the articular surface; otherwise, surgical referral is indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: However, because of its importance in weight bearing and balance, fractures of the first toe (hallux) have a higher potential for negative outcomes. Specifically, fractures of the hallux can be managed nonsurgically if they are not displaced and involve less than 25% of the articular surface of the joint. Nonsurgical management involves use of a short leg walking cast with a toe plate (extending past the end of the great toe) for 3 weeks and then progression to a rigid-sole shoe with buddy taping after that. Since this patient's fracture involves more than 25% of the articular surface of the joint of the first toe, early referral for surgical pinning by an orthopedic surgeon would lead to the best outcome.

explanation_raw:
**Treatment by Toe Type**
• Minor phalangeal fractures (2nd–5th toes) are managed with buddy taping and rigid-sole shoe, while displaced fractures may need closed reduction in the office.
  - Phalangeal fractures of the second to fifth toes can usually be managed with buddy taping and a rigid-sole shoe for 3 weeks followed by buddy taping for another 3 weeks.
  - If the fracture is significantly displaced, closed reduction in the office using local anesthesia may be appropriate.

**Hallux Fracture Management**
• Hallux fractures carry higher risk due to weight-bearing importance and require nonsurgical management (short leg walking cast with toe plate, then rigid-sole shoe) only if non-displaced and involving less than 25% of the articular surface; otherwise, surgical referral is indicated.
  - However, because of its importance in weight bearing and balance, fractures of the first toe (hallux) have a higher potential for negative outcomes.
  - Specifically, fractures of the hallux can be managed nonsurgically if they are not displaced and involve less than 25% of the articular surface of the joint.
  - Nonsurgical management involves use of a short leg walking cast with a toe plate (extending past the end of the great toe) for 3 weeks and then progression to a rigid-sole shoe with buddy taping after that.
  - Since this patient's fracture involves more than 25% of the articular surface of the joint of the first toe, early referral for surgical pinning by an orthopedic surgeon would lead to the best outcome.

stem: An 85-year-old female with hypertension and chronic kidney disease was admitted to the hospital for a total knee replacement. The next evening she becomes agitated and disoriented to place and time. Which one of the following interventions would be most appropriate in this patient’s management?

bullets.text: Delirium management prioritizes behavioral interventions first, reserves antipsychotics and restraints as last resorts, avoids sedative hypnotics, and carefully balances opioid use against untreated pain risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Behavioral interventions such as early and recurrent mobilization, continuous observation, improving sensory perception (such as with hearing aids), initial reorientation, and removal of unnecessary irritations such as intravenous lines and catheters have been shown to decrease symptoms of delirium (SOR B). Antipsychotic medications such as haloperidol, as well as physical restraints, should be used as last resorts and only after an appropriate medical evaluation (SOR A). Sedative hypnotics such as zolpidem are associated with increased delirium symptoms and should not be used as first-line therapy (SOR C). While opioids can affect mental status, untreated pain is also associated with delirium, and opioids are likely indicated in this postoperative patient.

explanation_raw:
**Treatment**
• Delirium management prioritizes behavioral interventions first, reserves antipsychotics and restraints as last resorts, avoids sedative hypnotics, and carefully balances opioid use against untreated pain risk.
  - Behavioral interventions such as early and recurrent mobilization, continuous observation, improving sensory perception (such as with hearing aids), initial reorientation, and removal of unnecessary irritations such as intravenous lines and catheters have been shown to decrease symptoms of delirium (SOR B).
  - Antipsychotic medications such as haloperidol, as well as physical restraints, should be used as last resorts and only after an appropriate medical evaluation (SOR A).
  - Sedative hypnotics such as zolpidem are associated with increased delirium symptoms and should not be used as first-line therapy (SOR C).
  - While opioids can affect mental status, untreated pain is also associated with delirium, and opioids are likely indicated in this postoperative patient.

stem: Which one of the following is the only intervention shown to be effective in the prevention and treatment of pressure ulcers?

bullets.text: ACP guidelines evaluated many pressure ulcer treatments but found good evidence for only a few modalities.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The American College of Physicians recently published clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of pressure ulcers. Many modalities were evaluated, but good studies and evidence were available only for a few treatments.

bullets.text: Protein supplementation is the notable evidence-based intervention, improving wound healing and aiding prevention.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Several good-quality studies indicate that protein supplementation improves wound healing and also appears to have some benefit in prevention as well.

bullets.text: Vitamin C, dextranomer paste, topical collagen dressings, and negative-pressure wound therapy either showed no benefit or worsened outcomes compared to standard care.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Vitamin C supplementation made no difference in wound healing. Dextranomer paste applied to wounds actually worsened wound healing compared to standard wound dressings. Topical collagen dressings and negative-pressure wound therapy yielded no improvement in wound healing compared to usual care.

stem: An 84-year-old female sees you for a follow-up visit for cardiovascular issues, including a previous myocardial infarction. Her current medication regimen consists of lisinopril (Prinivil, Zestril) and carvedilol (Coreg). While she is not dyspneic at rest, she now becomes short of breath after walking half a block. On examination her blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, pulse rate 72 beats/min, respirations 18/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She has no jugular venous distention and her lungs are clear. No edema is noted. A recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Adding which one of the following would help to decrease both mortality and the risk of hospitalization?

bullets.text: Systolic HF (EF <40%) requires ACE inhibitor + β-blocker as the foundation, with a diuretic added for volume overload, and an ARB substituted (never combined) if ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Systolic heart failure, or heart failure with a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (<40%), should be managed with an ACE inhibitor and a $-blocker. If there is volume overload, a diuretic should be added. For those who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker can be used. However, an ACE inhibitor should not be given with an angiotensin receptor blocker, as this combination increases mortality.

bullets.text: Digoxin reduces symptoms but not mortality; spironolactone reduces both; and hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate improves symptoms and mortality in African-Americans with NYHA class III–IV reduced EF.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Digoxin will decrease symptoms and lessen the chance of hospitalization, but mortality is not reduced. Mortality and hospitalization can be reduced by the addition of an aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone. In African-American patients, using a combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate improves both symptoms and mortality for those with New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction.

explanation_raw:
**First-Line Treatment**
• Systolic HF (EF <40%) requires ACE inhibitor + β-blocker as the foundation, with a diuretic added for volume overload, and an ARB substituted (never combined) if ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
  - Systolic heart failure, or heart failure with a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (<40%), should be managed with an ACE inhibitor and a $-blocker.
  - If there is volume overload, a diuretic should be added.
  - For those who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker can be used.
  - However, an ACE inhibitor should not be given with an angiotensin receptor blocker, as this combination increases mortality.

**Additional & Special Population Treatments**
• Digoxin reduces symptoms but not mortality; spironolactone reduces both; and hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate improves symptoms and mortality in African-Americans with NYHA class III–IV reduced EF.
  - Digoxin will decrease symptoms and lessen the chance of hospitalization, but mortality is not reduced.
  - Mortality and hospitalization can be reduced by the addition of an aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone.
  - In African-American patients, using a combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate improves both symptoms and mortality for those with New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction.

stem: A previously healthy 46-year-old female presents with a 1-month history of leg swelling and weight gain. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath. bullets.text: Diabetes mellitus is a secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome but is not a finding in primary nephrotic syndrome.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diabetes mellitus can be a secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome but is not a finding in primary nephrotic syndrome.

explanation_raw:

  - Nephrotic syndrome is associated with an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis but does not cause a coagulopathy.
  - Relative hypocalcemia may be found in patients with nephrotic syndrome due to low protein, but hypercalcemia is not associated with nephrotic syndrome.
  - Children and patients with relapses of nephrotic syndrome have an increased risk of infection.

**Evaluation**
• Initial workup should include testing for hyperlipidemia, which is commonly associated with nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 25-year-old gravida 1 para 0 presents for follow-up of gestational diabetes mellitus. stem: Which one of the following topical antibiotics used in the treatment of acne vulgaris is not known to increase bacterial resistance?

stem: Which one of the following therapies is most likely to reduce abdominal cramping in a patient with irritable bowel syndrome?

bullets.text: Peppermint oil, probiotics, and polyethylene glycol each have some evidence supporting their use in IBS, but with important limitations in scope.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Peppermint oil is an antispasmodic that has moderate evidence of benefit in the relief of abdominal cramping in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Probiotics as a group have some evidence of benefit in improving global IBS symptoms, but the studies have used different probiotic preparations so it is difficult to draw definite conclusions about their effectiveness or to recommend a specific preparation. Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that has evidence of benefit for bowel symptoms, including improvement in stool frequency and consistency, but it does not improve abdominal pain.

  - Probiotics as a group have some evidence of benefit in improving global IBS symptoms, but the studies have used different probiotic preparations so it is difficult to draw definite conclusions about their effectiveness or to recommend a specific preparation.
  - Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that has evidence of benefit for bowel symptoms, including improvement in stool frequency and consistency, but it does not improve abdominal pain.

stem: A drug available for over 20 years has been noted to have beneficial effects for a common disease. Because it is a cheap, generically available drug, no pharmaceutical firm is willing to fund a clinical trial. What type of study would be best suited to evaluate this treatment?

bullets.text: Non-inferiority trials rigorously demonstrate that a new treatment is at least almost as good as standard treatment, making them the preferred design for this comparison.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A non-inferiority trial rigorously evaluates a treatment against accepted and effective treatments, with the goal of demonstrating that it is at least almost as good. stem: While working yesterday, a 53-year-old roofer stepped on a nail that went through his shoe and penetrated the sole of his foot. He irrigated his foot thoroughly with water when he got home. stem: In an adult patient with significant depression and no other health problems, which one of the following is the best initial choice for pharmacotherapy?

  - Duloxetine is an SNRI that may lead to sweating, tachycardia, urinary retention, and elevation of blood pressure.

stem: A newborn male is brought to your office for his first examination after hospital discharge. He has been diagnosed with Down syndrome. Which one of the following is indicated for all newborns with Down syndrome?

bullets.text: Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal abnormality, with >90% 5-year survival and most individuals living past 60, with improving quality of life.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal abnormality. The 5-year survival rate is >90%, with most individuals living past 60 years of age, and there has been significant progress in improving quality of life for these patients. Infants with Down syndrome present with a wide variety of symptoms and signs, however, and there are certain health complications that can increase the risk of hospitalization.

bullets.text: All infants with Down syndrome require screening for cardiac, feeding, vision, hearing, thyroid, and hematologic abnormalities, with cardiology consultation, echocardiography, red reflex exam, thyroid screening, and CBC warranted.
bullets.sub_paragraph: All infants with Down syndrome should be screened for cardiac, feeding, vision, hearing, thyroid, and hematologic abnormalities. Up to 50% manifest congenital cardiac defects, and a cardiology consultation and echocardiography are warranted. Hypotonia may affect feeding and should be noted for assessment. Congenital cataracts are common, so a red reflex examination is imperative. Screening for subclinical thyroid disease should also be performed, as well as a CBC to evaluate for transient myeloproliferative disorder, leukemoid reaction, and polycythemia, which all occur more frequently in Down syndrome patients.

bullets.text: Cervical spine films, hip ultrasonography, and polysomnography are not recommended in newborns, but polysomnography should occur between ages 1–4, and parents should monitor for signs of atlantoaxial instability.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cervical spine films, hip ultrasonography, and polysomnography are not recommended in a newborn with Down syndrome. However, all children with Down syndrome should have polysomnography between the ages of 1 and 4 years. Due to concerns about atlantoaxial instability parents should be advised to monitor for any signs of spinal cord impingement.

bullets.text: Clinicians should congratulate parents, clearly explain all recommended tests and results, and implement an Individual Family Service Plan reviewed every 6 months.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It is important to congratulate the parents on their newborn and carefully explain the rationale for each recommended test and discuss results and their meaning clearly. An Individual Family Service Plan is also recommended, with a review every 6 months to evaluate specific measures indicated for each age group.

stem: A 2-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his frightened mother following the sudden onset of nasal stuffiness and a harsh, barking, nonproductive cough. The child does not appear significantly distressed. His temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F) orally. Mild nasal flaring is present. The nasopharyngeal mucus appears mildly edematous and injected, and upper airway noises are heard, but good air movement is evident on auscultation of his chest. choices.B: A single dose of oral dexamethasone

bullets.text: Croup is a clinical diagnosis in children 6 months–12 years presenting with barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever, and respiratory distress, while toxic appearance, wheezing, drooling, and dysphagia argue against it.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Croup is a common, self-limited illness caused by viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. The diagnosis is based primarily on the clinical history and examination findings. A history of the abrupt onset of a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness in a 2-year-old child is typical of croup, although it can present at any age between 6 months and 12 years. Low-grade fever, a barking cough, and varying degrees of respiratory distress (nasal flaring, retractions, or stridor) are typically present on examination. Findings such as a toxic appearance, wheezing, drooling, and difficulty swallowing are not consistent with the diagnosis.

bullets.text: Mild croup is treated with a single oral dose of dexamethasone (0.15–0.60 mg/kg); nebulized epinephrine benefits moderate-to-severe cases; humidification provides no benefit.

Nebulized epinephrine has been shown to improve outcomes in children with moderate to severe croup (SOR A). Humidification therapy in the emergency department setting provides no benefit (SOR A). This child has mild croup and a single dose of dexamethasone (0.15–0.60 mg/kg, usually given orally) followed by close observation is the most appropriate treatment.

stem: A 17-year-old high school football player presents to your office with right fourth finger pain that began suddenly after he made a tackle during last night’s game. Pain and tenderness are greatest at the flexor crease of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. He can fully flex the fourth metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. Flexion of the DIP is weak and cannot be held against applied resistance. Which one of the following is most likely?

choices.A: Rupture of the extensor tendon at the DIP
choices.B: Rupture of the extensor tendon’s central slip at the PIP

bullets.text: Jersey finger results from FDP tendon rupture when a sudden force is applied to the flexed distal phalanx, commonly during tackles when a finger catches an opponent's jersey.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has ruptured the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon as a result of a sudden force applied to the distal phalanx while in flexion. This happens when catching the finger in an opponent's jersey or belt loop while making a tackle, hence the name jersey finger. This injury is also seen in wrestlers.

bullets.text: The FDP attaches at the distal phalanx and FDS at the middle phalanx, allowing physical exam to distinguish which tendon is injured based on PIP and DIP flexion testing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The FDP attaches at the base of the distal phalanx while the flexor digitorum sublimis (FDS) attaches at the base of the middle phalanx. Thus, it can be determined by physical examination which tendon is injured, providing for early and accurate diagnosis and proper treatment. With the noninvolved fingers held in full extension, if the patient can flex the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint the FDS is intact. With rupture of the FDP, distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint flexion may still be weakly present, but the patient is unable to hold flexion against resistance and this maneuver elicits pain. With rupture of both flexor tendons, the patient is unable to flex either the PIP or the DIP joint. In the scenario presented, rupture of both flexor tendons is unlikely.

bullets.text: Extensor tendon rupture causes mallet finger or boutonnière deformity, not the flexion deficit seen here.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Rupture of the extensor digitorum tendons may cause mallet finger at the DIP joint, or a boutonnière deformity of the PIP joint.

bullets.text: Early orthopedic consultation is recommended as many flexor tendon injuries require surgical exploration and repair.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Since many of these flexor tendon injuries require surgical exploration and repair, early orthopedic consultation is recommended.

  - This happens when catching the finger in an opponent's jersey or belt loop while making a tackle, hence the name jersey finger.
  - This injury is also seen in wrestlers.

**Pathophysiology**
• The FDP attaches at the distal phalanx and FDS at the middle phalanx, allowing physical exam to distinguish which tendon is injured based on PIP and DIP flexion testing.
  - The FDP attaches at the base of the distal phalanx while the flexor digitorum sublimis (FDS) attaches at the base of the middle phalanx.
  - Thus, it can be determined by physical examination which tendon is injured, providing for early and accurate diagnosis and proper treatment.
  - With the noninvolved fingers held in full extension, if the patient can flex the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint the FDS is intact.
  - With rupture of the FDP, distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint flexion may still be weakly present, but the patient is unable to hold flexion against resistance and this maneuver elicits pain.
  - With rupture of both flexor tendons, the patient is unable to flex either the PIP or the DIP joint.
  - In the scenario presented, rupture of both flexor tendons is unlikely.

• Extensor tendon rupture causes mallet finger or boutonnière deformity, not the flexion deficit seen here.
  - Rupture of the extensor digitorum tendons may cause mallet finger at the DIP joint, or a boutonnière deformity of the PIP joint.

**Treatment**
• Early orthopedic consultation is recommended as many flexor tendon injuries require surgical exploration and repair.
  - Since many of these flexor tendon injuries require surgical exploration and repair, early orthopedic consultation is recommended.

stem: An 86-year-old female presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough. stem: A 52-year-old male runner with a long-standing history of essential hypertension presents for a follow-up visit. stem: A 32-year-old male with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to your office with a tender, scaly lesion on his anterior left shin. It is a 5-cm reddish-brown plaque with well-defined borders and what appears to be yellowish deposits in the center. You perform a punch biopsy of the lesion to confirm your diagnosis of

bullets.text: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is a rare diabetic skin condition presenting as sharply demarcated reddish-brown plaques with central yellow deposits in the pretibial area, which may precede diabetes diagnosis by years and is often diagnosable without biopsy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is seen in 0.3% of patients with diabetes mellitus or impaired glucose tolerance. The lesions may precede the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus by several years. The sharply demarcated reddish-brown plaque with central yellow deposits in the pretibial area is characteristic and a biopsy is not always necessary. Topical corticosteroids are sometimes helpful.

bullets.text: Granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis, and xanthomas are unlikely diagnoses here due to their typical locations and lack of the characteristic reddish-brown outer border seen in this case.

While xanthomas can be flat plaques up to several centimeters in size, they usually occur on flexor surfaces of the limbs along with the trunk and face. They lack the reddish-brown outer portion of the lesions described here.

stem: Pioglitazone (Actos) has been found to be associated with which one of the following adverse effects?

bullets.text: TZDs improve hyperglycemia by reducing insulin resistance and preserving β-cell secretory function.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) improve hyperglycemia by improving insulin resistance and by maintaining or improving $-cell secretory function.

bullets.text: TZDs cause fluid retention, weight gain, peripheral edema, and reduced bone mineral density, and are contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV heart failure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: One of the side effects of TZDs is that they can cause fluid retention, especially in patients with cardiac and renal disease. This may lead to weight gain and peripheral edema. Because of this effect, TZDs are contraindicated in patients with New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure. They can also reduce bone mineral density and are associated with a higher risk of non-osteoporotic bone fractures.

bullets.text: Beyond glucose lowering, TZDs reduce cardiovascular events, may prevent cognitive dysfunction, and are useful in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In addition to their ability to decrease glucose levels, however, there have been some other favorable effects noted with their use. Clinical trials have shown that treatment with pioglitazone resulted in a significant reduction in the composite outcome of nonfatal acute myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality. They may also help prevent central nervous system insulin resistance–related cognitive dysfunction. TZDs are also useful in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

explanation_raw:
**Mechanism of Action**
• TZDs improve hyperglycemia by reducing insulin resistance and preserving β-cell secretory function.
  - Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) improve hyperglycemia by improving insulin resistance and by maintaining or improving $-cell secretory function.

**Side Effects and Contraindications**
• TZDs cause fluid retention, weight gain, peripheral edema, and reduced bone mineral density, and are contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV heart failure.
  - One of the side effects of TZDs is that they can cause fluid retention, especially in patients with cardiac and renal disease.
  - This may lead to weight gain and peripheral edema.
  - Because of this effect, TZDs are contraindicated in patients with New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure.
  - They can also reduce bone mineral density and are associated with a higher risk of non-osteoporotic bone fractures.

**Additional Benefits**
• Beyond glucose lowering, TZDs reduce cardiovascular events, may prevent cognitive dysfunction, and are useful in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
  - In addition to their ability to decrease glucose levels, however, there have been some other favorable effects noted with their use.
  - Clinical trials have shown that treatment with pioglitazone resulted in a significant reduction in the composite outcome of nonfatal acute myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality.
  - They may also help prevent central nervous system insulin resistance–related cognitive dysfunction.
  - TZDs are also useful in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

stem: An asymptomatic 46-year-old male with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease sees you for a routine visit. His glomerular filtration rate is 49 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which one of the following is the preferred initial therapy for controlling this patient’s blood pressure?

bullets.text: ADPCKD is the most common genetic kidney disease, often presenting with flank pain, hematuria, or UTIs, and progresses to ESRD in ~80% of patients by age 70.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPCKD) is the most common genetic kidney disease and accounts for 4.7% of end-stage kidney disease cases in America. Many patients with ADPCKD are asymptomatic, but early symptoms can include flank pain, gross hematuria, or recurrent urinary tract infections. All ADPCKD patients eventually develop a loss of renal function, and approximately 80% develop end-stage renal disease by age 70.

bullets.text: Hypertension is the most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPCKD, requiring early management with a goal BP <140/90 mmHg; ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) are first-line, with ARBs as an alternative.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPCKD is hypertension, which can precipitate cardiovascular dysfunction, including left ventricular hypertrophy. Thus, early diagnosis and management of hypertension is crucial. The goal blood pressure should be <140/90 mm Hg in patients under the age of 60. An ACE inhibitor is the recommended first-line therapy (SOR C), so lisinopril is the best choice for this patient. Angiotensin receptor blockers are acceptable in patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors.

• ADPCKD is the most common genetic kidney disease, often presenting with flank pain, hematuria, or UTIs, and progresses to ESRD in ~80% of patients by age 70.

  - Many patients with ADPCKD are asymptomatic, but early symptoms can include flank pain, gross hematuria, or recurrent urinary tract infections.
  - All ADPCKD patients eventually develop a loss of renal function, and approximately 80% develop end-stage renal disease by age 70.

**Hypertension Management**
• Hypertension is the most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPCKD, requiring early management with a goal BP <140/90 mmHg; ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) are first-line, with ARBs as an alternative.
  - The most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPCKD is hypertension, which can precipitate cardiovascular dysfunction, including left ventricular hypertrophy.
  - Thus, early diagnosis and management of hypertension is crucial.
  - The goal blood pressure should be <140/90 mm Hg in patients under the age of 60.

stem: An active 76-year-old male presents to your office as a new patient. He recently fell while hiking and was diagnosed with rib fractures in the emergency department. stem: A 63-year-old female presents with a complaint of a painful, red right eye. She says that her vision has also been blurry. She has also noted a discharge. The patient wears contact lenses. When you examine the patient you note photophobia. The pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. You also note unilateral diffuse injection. Fluorescein staining reveals focal corneal uptake. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Red eye has many causes, each with distinct features including conjunctivitis (viral, bacterial, allergic), corneal abrasion, uveitis, and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Common causes of red eye include infectious conjunctivitis, allergies, corneal abrasion, keratoconjunctivitis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, uveitis, blepharitis, iritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

bullets.text: Viral, bacterial, and allergic conjunctivitis differ by laterality, discharge type, and associated symptoms, with adenovirus being the most common viral cause.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Viral infections typically cause conjunctivitis with mild pain and no loss of vision. The problem is usually unilateral in the beginning and a watery to serous discharge may be noted. Adenovirus is the most common cause. Acute bacterial conjunctivitis has a similar presentation and may include eyelid edema and a purulent discharge. Allergic conjunctivitis is usually bilateral and painless, with intense itching, and a stringy or ropy watery discharge. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is associated with a vesicular rash, keratitis, and uveitis. The rash is preceded by pain and a tingling sensation. Findings include conjunctivitis and dermatomal involvement, which are usually unilateral.

bullets.text: Corneal abrasion presents with severe eye pain, photophobia, and foreign body sensation after injury, with normal vision and reactive pupils; uveitis presents with red eye, vision loss, photophobia, and is linked to autoimmune diseases.
bullets.sub_paragraph: With corneal abrasion there is usually a history of an injury involving a foreign object. Signs and symptoms include severe eye pain; red, watery eyes; photophobia; and a foreign body sensation. Vision is usually normal and pupils are equal and reactive to light. Symptoms of uveitis include a red eye, loss of vision, and photophobia. It is associated with many autoimmune diseases, including reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

**Causes & Overview of Red Eye**
• Red eye has many causes, each with distinct features including conjunctivitis (viral, bacterial, allergic), corneal abrasion, uveitis, and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
  - Common causes of red eye include infectious conjunctivitis, allergies, corneal abrasion, keratoconjunctivitis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, uveitis, blepharitis, iritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

**Conjunctivitis Types**
• Viral, bacterial, and allergic conjunctivitis differ by laterality, discharge type, and associated symptoms, with adenovirus being the most common viral cause.
  - Viral infections typically cause conjunctivitis with mild pain and no loss of vision.
  - The problem is usually unilateral in the beginning and a watery to serous discharge may be noted.
  - Adenovirus is the most common cause.
  - Acute bacterial conjunctivitis has a similar presentation and may include eyelid edema and a purulent discharge.
  - Allergic conjunctivitis is usually bilateral and painless, with intense itching, and a stringy or ropy watery discharge.
  - Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is associated with a vesicular rash, keratitis, and uveitis.
  - The rash is preceded by pain and a tingling sensation.
  - Findings include conjunctivitis and dermatomal involvement, which are usually unilateral.

• Corneal abrasion presents with severe eye pain, photophobia, and foreign body sensation after injury, with normal vision and reactive pupils; uveitis presents with red eye, vision loss, photophobia, and is linked to autoimmune diseases.
  - With corneal abrasion there is usually a history of an injury involving a foreign object.
  - Signs and symptoms include severe eye pain; red, watery eyes; photophobia; and a foreign body sensation.
  - Vision is usually normal and pupils are equal and reactive to light.
  - Symptoms of uveitis include a red eye, loss of vision, and photophobia.
  - It is associated with many autoimmune diseases, including reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

**Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma**
• Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents suddenly with significant vision loss, dilated non-reactive pupils, severe pain, halos around lights, and possible nausea and vomiting.
  - Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a significant loss of vision, with dilated pupils that don't react normally to light.
  - Symptoms include severe pain and watery eyes, with halos around lights.
  - Patients may have nausea and vomiting.
  - This form of glaucoma often has an acute onset.

stem: A 19-year-old female high school student is brought to your office by a friend who is concerned about the patient cutting herself on the wrists. The patient denies that she was trying to kill herself, and states that she did this because she “just got so angry” at her boyfriend when she caught him sending a text message to another woman. She denies having a depressed mood or anhedonia, and blames her fluctuating mood on everyone who “keeps deserting her,” making her feel like she’s “nothing.” She admits that she has difficulty controlling her anger. Her sleep quality and pattern appear normal, as does her appetite. She denies hallucinations or delusions. The wounds on her wrists appear superficial and there is evidence of previous cutting behavior on her forearms. Her vital signs are stable. Which one of the following would be most beneficial for this patient?

bullets.text: Borderline personality disorder affects ~1% of the population equally by sex, is genetically predisposed, presents from a young age, and is characterized by emotional lability, unstable relationships, fear of abandonment, intense anger, and emptiness.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient displays most of the criteria for borderline personality disorder. This is a maladaptive personality type that is present from a young age, with a strong genetic predisposition. It is estimated to be present in 1% of the general population and involves equal numbers of men and women; women seek care more often, however, leading to a disproportionate number of women being identified by medical providers. Borderline personality disorder is defined by high emotional lability, intense anger, unstable relationships, frantic efforts to avoid a feeling of abandonment, and an internal sense of emptiness.

bullets.text: Nearly all patients engage in self-harm, with suicide attempts peaking in the early 20s, but completed suicide is most common after age 30 and in those who fail to recover; despite frequent threats, 90% of patients ultimately improve.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Nearly every patient with this disorder engages in self-injurious behavior (cutting, suicidal gestures and attempts), and about 1 in 10 patients eventually succeeds in committing suicide. However, 90% of patients improve despite having made numerous suicide threats. Suicidal gestures and attempts peak when patients are in their early 20s, but completed suicide is most common after age 30 and usually occurs in patients who fail to recover after many attempts at treatment. In contrast, suicidal actions such as impulsive overdoses or superficial cutting, most often seen in younger patients, do not usually carry a high short-term risk, and serve to communicate distress.

bullets.text: Psychotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, with hospitalization and pharmacotherapy reserved for select patients with more severe dysfunction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Inpatient hospitalization may be an appropriate treatment option if the person is experiencing extreme difficulties in living and daily functioning, and pharmacotherapy may offer a mild degree of symptom relief. While these modalities have a role in certain patients, psychotherapy is considered the mainstay of therapy, especially in a relatively stable patient such as the one described.

**Suicide Risk**
• Nearly all patients engage in self-harm, with suicide attempts peaking in the early 20s, but completed suicide is most common after age 30 and in those who fail to recover; despite frequent threats, 90% of patients ultimately improve.

  - However, 90% of patients improve despite having made numerous suicide threats.

stem: Long-term treatment with which one of the following is known to reduce serum vitamin D levels?

explanation.heading: Drugs That Increase Vitamin D Levels

bullets.text: Isoniazid, thiazide diuretics, and estrogen replacement therapy (diminished by progesterone) are known to increase vitamin D blood levels or activity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Isoniazid and thiazide diuretics can lead to increased blood levels or activity of vitamin D. Estrogen replacement therapy can also increase levels of vitamin D in the blood, although this potential benefit seems to diminish when progesterone is added.

explanation.heading: Drugs That Decrease Vitamin D Levels

bullets.text: Mineral oil, cholestyramine, certain antacids (reduced gut absorption), and anticonvulsants like phenobarbital and phenytoin (accelerated metabolism) can lower vitamin D levels.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Vitamin D absorption through the gut can be reduced by mineral oil, cholestyramine, and certain antacid preparations, leading to lower blood levels. The metabolism of vitamin D is accelerated by anticonvulsant drugs such as phenobarbital and phenytoin, which can also result in lower than desired levels of vitamin D.

explanation.heading: Drugs With No Effect & General Note

bullets.text: Vitamin D levels are affected by many drug interactions, though statins have no known effect.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Absorption and metabolism of vitamin D is known to be affected by interaction with other medications. Statins are not reported to have any known effect on vitamin D levels.

• Mineral oil, cholestyramine, certain antacids (reduced gut absorption), and anticonvulsants like phenobarbital and phenytoin (accelerated metabolism) can lower vitamin D levels.
  - Vitamin D absorption through the gut can be reduced by mineral oil, cholestyramine, and certain antacid preparations, leading to lower blood levels.

**Drugs With No Effect & General Note**
• Vitamin D levels are affected by many drug interactions, though statins have no known effect.
  - Absorption and metabolism of vitamin D is known to be affected by interaction with other medications.
  - Statins are not reported to have any known effect on vitamin D levels.

stem: A 6-year-old male is brought to your office by his parents. He describes pain in the right hip for the past month or two, and the parents report that for the past few weeks they have noticed intermittent limping. The history is negative for trauma, injury, and fever. On examination the patient indicates that the pain is over the anterior hip joint, with increased pain on internal rotation, which is limited to 90°. Of the options listed below, which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

choices.D: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease)

correct_label: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease)

bullets.text: This case of insidious hip pain with limited ROM in a child points to Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, affecting the femoroacetabular joint.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This case presents a child with an insidious onset of pain and mild limitation of range of motion of one hip joint. The case suggests involvement of the femoroacetabular joint, and all of the listed options can affect this joint. Idiopathic osteonecrosis of the hip (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease) occurs most commonly in children at 2–12 years of age and has a male predominance. bullets.text: The other diagnoses are excluded by age, acuity of onset, presence of fever, or typical demographic.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs much more commonly in adolescents. Transient synovitis and septic arthritis have a more acute onset, and typically cause fever. Osteoarthritis typically occurs in older adults.

stem: A 38-year-old female calls your office and reports nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after she ate some chicken salad that had been sitting outside at a picnic. Prior to that she was asymptomatic. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s foodborne illness?

bullets.text: Most of the symptoms of foodborne illness are not specific to the causative organism.

However, the onset of vomiting and diarrhea within hours of consumption of contaminated food results from the ingestion of preformed toxins, most often from Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus in the United States.
Campylobacter jejuni, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella species, and hepatitis A typically produce symptoms more than a day after ingestion.

stem: A 76-year-old nursing home resident complains of constipation. He has had minimal improvement with trials of scheduled toileting and increased fiber and fluids. A physical examination is normal. Which one of the following is the best intervention at this point?

bullets.text: Behavioral changes are the first-line management for functional constipation in older adults, including scheduled toileting, proper positioning, increased fiber and fluids, and avoiding bedpan use.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For functional constipation in older adults, behavioral changes should be first-line management. These include scheduled toileting with proper positioning, increased intake of fiber and fluids, and avoiding bedpan use.

bullets.text: When behavioral interventions fail, osmotic laxatives (preferably polyethylene glycol) are next, with stimulant laxatives reserved as a last resort and magnesium salts lacking strong evidence and posing toxicity risks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: If there is not an adequate response to behavioral interventions, osmotic laxatives should be initiated. Polyethylene glycol is more effective and has fewer side effects compared to lactulose. Magnesium salts, including magnesium citrate, do not have strong evidence for safety or efficacy, and magnesium toxicity is a concern with long-term use. Due to possible adverse effects of stimulant laxatives in the long term, particularly with older adults, these drugs should be used only if fiber and osmotic laxatives are unsuccessful.

explanation_raw:
**First-Line Treatment**
• Behavioral changes are the first-line management for functional constipation in older adults, including scheduled toileting, proper positioning, increased fiber and fluids, and avoiding bedpan use.
  - For functional constipation in older adults, behavioral changes should be first-line management.
  - These include scheduled toileting with proper positioning, increased intake of fiber and fluids, and avoiding bedpan use.

**Laxative Options and Sequencing**
• When behavioral interventions fail, osmotic laxatives (preferably polyethylene glycol) are next, with stimulant laxatives reserved as a last resort and magnesium salts lacking strong evidence and posing toxicity risks.
  - If there is not an adequate response to behavioral interventions, osmotic laxatives should be initiated.
  - Polyethylene glycol is more effective and has fewer side effects compared to lactulose.
  - Magnesium salts, including magnesium citrate, do not have strong evidence for safety or efficacy, and magnesium toxicity is a concern with long-term use.
  - Due to possible adverse effects of stimulant laxatives in the long term, particularly with older adults, these drugs should be used only if fiber and osmotic laxatives are unsuccessful.

stem: A 16-year-old male presents to your office with a 1-month history of paresthesias in the ring finger and little finger of his left hand. He is the catcher on his high school baseball team. The physical examination reveals no abnormalities of his neck, shoulder, or elbow. His hand grip is normal, but maximal flexion of the wrist elicits paresthesias in the fourth and fifth digits. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Ulnar neuropathy typically presents with sensory changes in digits 4–5 without grip weakness, often from repetitive wrist extension, and requires examination to rule out cervical or brachial plexus causes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An ulnar neuropathy most commonly presents with sensory changes in the fourth and fifth digits and usually does not involve weakness in hand grip. There is usually no specific injury, but any activity that results in repetitive or prolonged wrist extension, as with cycling or playing catcher, may increase the risk of this problem. It is important to examine the neck for cervical disc disease and to examine the shoulder to see if motion elicits the pain, which would indicate a brachial plexus problem.

bullets.text: Key clinical tests include Tinel sign over Guyon's canal, Phalen sign, and elbow compression to reproduce symptoms and localize the entrapment site.
bullets.sub_paragraph: If symptoms are reproduced by compressing the ulnar nerve at the elbow this could be the site of entrapment. Clinical tests may include a positive Tinel sign on percussion of the ulnar nerve over Guyon's canal. Also, there may be a positive Phalen sign, with maximum passive flexion of the wrist for 1 minute inducing paresthesias in the fourth and fifth fingers.

bullets.text: Plain radiographs are usually normal, but ultrasound and EMG/nerve conduction studies may be needed to identify the site of compression.
bullets.sub_paragraph: With ulnar neuropathy, plain radiographs are usually normal. Ultrasonography of the peripheral nerves may be helpful in identifying compression etiologies. However, electromyelography and nerve conduction velocities may be required to identify the area of entrapment.

explanation_raw:

• Ulnar neuropathy typically presents with sensory changes in digits 4–5 without grip weakness, often from repetitive wrist extension, and requires examination to rule out cervical or brachial plexus causes.
  - An ulnar neuropathy most commonly presents with sensory changes in the fourth and fifth digits and usually does not involve weakness in hand grip.
  - There is usually no specific injury, but any activity that results in repetitive or prolonged wrist extension, as with cycling or playing catcher, may increase the risk of this problem.
  - It is important to examine the neck for cervical disc disease and to examine the shoulder to see if motion elicits the pain, which would indicate a brachial plexus problem.

**Clinical Tests**
• Key clinical tests include Tinel sign over Guyon's canal, Phalen sign, and elbow compression to reproduce symptoms and localize the entrapment site.
  - If symptoms are reproduced by compressing the ulnar nerve at the elbow this could be the site of entrapment.
  - Clinical tests may include a positive Tinel sign on percussion of the ulnar nerve over Guyon's canal.
  - Also, there may be a positive Phalen sign, with maximum passive flexion of the wrist for 1 minute inducing paresthesias in the fourth and fifth fingers.

**Workup & Imaging**
• Plain radiographs are usually normal, but ultrasound and EMG/nerve conduction studies may be needed to identify the site of compression.
  - With ulnar neuropathy, plain radiographs are usually normal.
  - Ultrasonography of the peripheral nerves may be helpful in identifying compression etiologies.
  - However, electromyelography and nerve conduction velocities may be required to identify the area of entrapment.

stem: A 52-year-old male sees you at the request of his wife because of his snoring and her concerns that he has obstructive sleep apnea. Further evaluation with a sleep study is recommended if the patient reports which one of the following?

Other associated symptoms such as snoring, insomnia, and fatigue are either less clinically relevant or less responsive to treatment.

Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease are associated with OSA, but evidence is insufficient that continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) improves outcomes for these conditions, especially if they are not associated with daytime sleepiness.

stem: A full-term newborn female develops respiratory distress 1 hour after an uncomplicated caesarean delivery. She has a respiratory rate of 70/min, and mild grunting and intercostal retractions are noted on examination. The remainder of the examination is within normal limits. The chest radiograph typically shows fluffy densities with hyperinflation.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents to your office with a 2-week history of pain, mild swelling, and point tenderness in the midportion of her anterior tibia. She has recently increased her jogging from 6 miles per week to 30 miles per week. She is unable to hop on the involved leg, as this induces significant pain at the site. A plain radiograph reveals a faint lucency at the same location. This patient would most likely benefit from which one of the following?

bullets.text: Stress fractures from repetitive training are best initially evaluated with plain radiography, repeated in 2–3 weeks if negative, with MRI or bone scintigraphy used when urgent diagnosis is needed.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Repetitive high-intensity training places an individual at risk for developing a stress fracture. A plain radiograph is the best initial test for a suspected stress fracture. If this is negative, then the study should be repeated in 2–3 weeks. MRI is now considered the procedure of choice if there is an urgent need for a diagnosis, although triple-phase bone scintigraphy has a similar sensitivity.

bullets.text: Management centers on activity reduction or immobilization depending on fracture site, with walker boots, and avoidance of bone stimulators and NSAIDs, which may inhibit healing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment of stress fractures usually consists of decreasing activity or, in some instances, such as involvement of the anterior tibial cortex (where there is a risk of a complete fracture), non–weight bearing with immobilization. Using a walker boot for tibial stress fractures reduces the time to resumption of full activity. Most stress fractures should not be treated with a bone stimulator. NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated, as limited studies have shown that they may actually inhibit healing of traumatic fractures.

bullets.text: Vitamin D and calcium supplementation offers some preventive benefit, while bisphosphonates do not.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium has shown some benefit in prevention, whereas bisphosphonates have not.

explanation_raw:
**Diagnosis**
• Stress fractures from repetitive training are best initially evaluated with plain radiography, repeated in 2–3 weeks if negative, with MRI or bone scintigraphy used when urgent diagnosis is needed.
  - Repetitive high-intensity training places an individual at risk for developing a stress fracture.
  - A plain radiograph is the best initial test for a suspected stress fracture.
  - If this is negative, then the study should be repeated in 2–3 weeks.
  - MRI is now considered the procedure of choice if there is an urgent need for a diagnosis, although triple-phase bone scintigraphy has a similar sensitivity.

**Treatment**
• Management centers on activity reduction or immobilization depending on fracture site, with walker boots, and avoidance of bone stimulators and NSAIDs, which may inhibit healing.
  - Treatment of stress fractures usually consists of decreasing activity or, in some instances, such as involvement of the anterior tibial cortex (where there is a risk of a complete fracture), non–weight bearing with immobilization.
  - Using a walker boot for tibial stress fractures reduces the time to resumption of full activity.
  - Most stress fractures should not be treated with a bone stimulator.
  - NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated, as limited studies have shown that they may actually inhibit healing of traumatic fractures.

**Prevention**
• Vitamin D and calcium supplementation offers some preventive benefit, while bisphosphonates do not.
  - Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium has shown some benefit in prevention, whereas bisphosphonates have not.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with what he suspects is a dislocated finger. He was playing football with some friends 2 days ago and when he was trying to catch the ball it struck his finger. On examination the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the left fifth finger has full passive range of motion, but he cannot actively extend the joint. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment of this fracture?

choices.B: Immobilization of the DIP joint in extension for 6–8 weeks

Surgical pinning may be indicated in more complicated fractures or with failure of conservative therapy.

stem: Which one of the following descriptions of an injury by an athlete is most consistent with an isolated posterior cruciate ligament tear?

choices.A: Hearing a pop in the knee during a pivoting motion
choices.B: An immediate onset of pain after cutting on the knee
choices.C: A direct blow to the anterior tibia while the knee is in flexion
choices.E: An onset of pain after a running jump

correct_label: A direct blow to the anterior tibia while the knee is in flexion

bullets.text: The PCL connects the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibial intercondylar area, resists nearly all posterior tibial displacement, and is the strongest cruciate ligament.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An understanding of the anatomy and function of the components of the knee, coupled with a clear description of the traumatic event, is essential for making an accurate initial clinical assessment of sports-related knee injuries. The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) connects the medial femoral condyle to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and is affixed in such a way that the anterolateral section is taut in flexion and the posteromedial section is taut in extension, helping to maintain the correct anatomic relationship between the femur and tibia. The PCL alone provides almost all of the resistance to posterior displacement of the tibia and so is appropriately the strongest of the cruciate ligaments.

bullets.text: PCL tears most commonly result from a direct anterior tibial blow with the knee flexed, though hyperextension, hyperflexion, or rotation can also cause rupture, usually with concurrent knee injuries.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Tearing or rupture of the PCL can occur with hyperextension, hyperflexion, or rotation applied with a force that is so great that other knee components are also generally injured. The most common mechanism leading to an isolated injury of the PCL is a direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee in flexion, like that experienced when the proximal tibia impacts the dashboard in an automobile crash or when an athlete is hit or kicked in the proximal tibia while the knee is in flexion.

bullets.text: Isolated PCL injury presents with posterior knee pain and kneeling pain, and is strongly supported by painful flexion limitation and a positive posterior sag/drawer sign.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Athletes with a PCL injury frequently complain of posterior knee pain and pain when kneeling. The presence of painful limitation of flexion and a posterior sag sign (posterior drawer sign) on examination strongly supports a diagnosis of isolated PCL injury.

• The PCL connects the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibial intercondylar area, resists nearly all posterior tibial displacement, and is the strongest cruciate ligament.

  - The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) connects the medial femoral condyle to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and is affixed in such a way that the anterolateral section is taut in flexion and the posteromedial section is taut in extension, helping to maintain the correct anatomic relationship between the femur and tibia.
  - The PCL alone provides almost all of the resistance to posterior displacement of the tibia and so is appropriately the strongest of the cruciate ligaments.

**Mechanism of Injury**
• PCL tears most commonly result from a direct anterior tibial blow with the knee flexed, though hyperextension, hyperflexion, or rotation can also cause rupture, usually with concurrent knee injuries.
  - Tearing or rupture of the PCL can occur with hyperextension, hyperflexion, or rotation applied with a force that is so great that other knee components are also generally injured.
  - The most common mechanism leading to an isolated injury of the PCL is a direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee in flexion, like that experienced when the proximal tibia impacts the dashboard in an automobile crash or when an athlete is hit or kicked in the proximal tibia while the knee is in flexion.

**Diagnosis**
• Isolated PCL injury presents with posterior knee pain and kneeling pain, and is strongly supported by painful flexion limitation and a positive posterior sag/drawer sign.

  - The presence of painful limitation of flexion and a posterior sag sign (posterior drawer sign) on examination strongly supports a diagnosis of isolated PCL injury.

stem: A previously healthy 29-year-old pediatric nurse has a 3-day history of malaise, arthralgias, and a nonpruritic rash. The rash is a faint, maculopapular, irregular, reticulate exanthem that covers her thighs and the inner aspects of her upper arms. Symmetric synovitis is present in several distal and proximal interphalangeal joints and in her metacarpophalangeal joints. Small effusions, warmth, and tenderness are noted in her left wrist and right elbow. No other joints are affected. The most likely cause of this problem is

bullets.text: Parvovirus B19 (fifth disease/erythema infectiosum) is the likely diagnosis, suggested by the characteristic rash, joint involvement pattern, and occupational exposure in an otherwise healthy person.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Also known as erythema infectiosum or fifth disease, parvovirus B19 infection is a fairly common cause of an exanthematous rash and arthritis in younger women. This infection should be particularly suspected in health care workers who have frequent contact with children. The specific characteristics of the rash, the pattern of joint involvement, and the place of employment in an otherwise healthy person all offer clues suggesting parvovirus B19 as the infecting agent.

bullets.text: By age 15, ~50% of children have IgG antibodies to parvovirus B19, rising to 90% in the elderly, with a secondary infection rate approaching 50% in nonimmune household contacts.
bullets.sub_paragraph: By the age of 15 approximately 50% of children have detectable IgG antibodies to the virus, and this figure rises to 90% in the elderly. Within households and caregivers the secondary infection rate, especially among nonimmune children and young adults, approaches 50%.

bullets.text: Measles, adenovirus, and HIV rarely cause arthritis, and varicella-zoster causes large-joint arthritis but with a distinctively vesicular, pruritic rash unlike parvovirus B19.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Measles virus, adenovirus, and HIV rarely cause arthritis, although HIV infection can cause a musculoskeletal syndrome later in the disease. Varicella-zoster virus may cause large-joint arthritis, but the rash is distinctively vesicular and pruritic.

**Diagnosis**
• Parvovirus B19 (fifth disease/erythema infectiosum) is the likely diagnosis, suggested by the characteristic rash, joint involvement pattern, and occupational exposure in an otherwise healthy person.
