stem: A 36-year-old patient presents to the emergency department (ED) for the third time this month for fevers ≥101 °F. Extensive workups at past visits have not identified an etiology. The patient does not take any medications and has not traveled recently. Today a C-reactive protein level and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate are elevated, but a CBC, urinalysis, and chest x-ray are normal. Blood cultures are pending and prior cultures have been negative. A complete physical examination is unremarkable with no sign of localized infection or disease. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: Intravenous ceftriaxone, 1 g, plus intravenous azithromycin (Zithromax), 500 mg

bullets.text: FUO is defined as recurrent fever ≥38.3°C without clear diagnosis, most cases are due to common diseases, and ~75% resolve spontaneously.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fever of unknown origin (FUO) in adults is defined as a clinically documented fever ≥38.3 °C (101 °F) that occurs on multiple occasions without a clear diagnosis. Most cases of FUO are due to common diseases. About 75% of all cases of FUO in adults resolve spontaneously without a determined diagnosis.

bullets.text: FDG-PET/CT is the preferred next step when initial workup is unremarkable, while empiric antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, exploratory laparotomy, and bone marrow biopsy are not indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: When an initial workup is unremarkable, imaging with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)- PET/CT is helpful in identifying an inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic cause (SOR B) with sensitivities ranging from 86% to 98% and specificities from 52% to 85%. It is estimated that a diagnosis is found in >50% of patients using FDG-PET/CT. Patients who are neither neutropenic nor severely immunocompromised should not be started on empiric antibiotics (SOR C) or anti-inflammatories, as these have not been shown to effectively treat FUO. Previously, exploratory laparotomy was preferred in the workup of FUO but is now no longer indicated as the accuracy of less invasive diagnostic tests, such as CT, has increased. Bone marrow biopsy is not indicated in this patient with a normal CBC.

  - Previously, exploratory laparotomy was preferred in the workup of FUO but is now no longer indicated as the accuracy of less invasive diagnostic tests, such as CT, has increased.
  - Bone marrow biopsy is not indicated in this patient with a normal CBC.

stem: A 72-year-old male presents to the emergency department (ED) with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The symptoms developed after the recent repair of an inguinal hernia, and his surgeon advised him to come to the ED. The patient has a history of chronic heart disease, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus with kidney disease. His medications include atorvastatin (Lipitor), amlodipine (Norvasc), and dapagliflozin (Farxiga). He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. On presentation he is lucid and making jokes with the staff. His vital signs in the ED include a blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg, a heart rate of 110 beats/min, and an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Physical examination findings are unremarkable. He receives intravenous ondansetron, 4 mg, and laboratory studies are pending. Several hours later, the patient appears drowsy and has difficulty focusing. He fluctuates between lethargy and rambling about unrelated topics. Despite conservative treatment for the suspected condition, he starts displaying severe agitation, putting himself and the staff members at risk for harm. Which one of the following oral medications would be most appropriate for this patient?

bullets.text: Delirium meets DSM-5 criteria with acute, fluctuating cognitive disturbance, three subtypes, and symptoms that overlap with other diseases requiring comprehensive evaluation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's symptoms meet the DSM-5 criteria for delirium related to his emergency department visit. Delirium is characterized by an acute disturbance in cognition, awareness, and attention that deviates from the patient's baseline cognition, fluctuates in severity, and develops within hours to days. Delirium has 3 subtypes: hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed. Symptoms can overlap with other diseases and a comprehensive history and physical examination are essential for a timely diagnosis.

bullets.text: Delirium is common in hospitalized adults ≥65, carries increased mortality risk, and is associated with multiple independent risk factors including age, polypharmacy, and recent surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An accurate diagnosis is vital to prevent inappropriate treatments, increased morbidity and mortality, and prolonged hospitalization. It is among the most common complications in hospitalized adults age 65 and older, especially among those who have undergone surgery. Patients with delirium have an increased risk for death in the following year. While the pathophysiology of delirium is not well understood, multiple comorbidities, older age, poor functional status, polypharmacy, and recent surgery are all independent risk factors.

bullets.text: Management prioritizes nonpharmacologic, multidisciplinary prevention; when medications are needed, second-generation antipsychotics are preferred, benzodiazepines are limited to specific indications, and trazodone may be used as an alternative.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prevention using a multidisciplinary approach is the optimal management for delirium. Nonpharmacologic interventions are the foundation of delirium management, and no medications are approved by the FDA for its treatment. However, when indicated, second-generation antipsychotics such as risperidone, olanzapine, and quetiapine, are preferred over haloperidol because they have fewer side effects and a faster onset of action. The benzodiazepines lorazepam and midazolam may be given parenterally if delirium is attributed to alcohol consumption, uncontrollable seizure activity, or hypnotic drug withdrawal, but oral diazepam is not indicated. Trazodone may be used as an alternative treatment, but sertraline would not be appropriate.

stem: A 69-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease sees you for follow-up after hospitalization for new-onset atrial fibrillation. After some difficulty with low blood pressure with other rate control agents, he was discharged on amiodarone. This patient should be monitored for amiodarone toxicity with which one of the following?

bullets.text: Amiodarone requires baseline pulmonary function testing (including DLCO) and chest x-ray, with repeat testing if pulmonary toxicity is suspected.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients treated with amiodarone should be monitored with pulmonary function testing at baseline and if clinical suspicion of pulmonary toxicity develops. Amiodarone is associated with pulmonary fibrosis, and baseline assessment with pulmonary function tests including measurement of diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) and chest x-ray is recommended.

bullets.text: Amiodarone is used for ventricular arrhythmias and atrial fibrillation, and is associated with numerous systemic toxicities including thyroid, liver, neurologic, and dermatologic effects.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Amiodarone is commonly used to manage ventricular arrhythmias, and for rate and rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. Amiodarone is also associated with hypothyroidism and less commonly with hyperthyroidism, liver inflammation, peripheral neuropathies, optic neuritis and corneal microdeposits, and bluish skin discoloration.

bullets.text: Amiodarone plasma levels, blood glucose, CBC, and urinalysis are not routinely indicated for monitoring patients on amiodarone.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Amiodarone plasma levels, blood glucose monitoring, a CBC with differential, and urinalysis are not routinely indicated in patients taking amiodarone.

**Clinical Use & Adverse Effects**

stem: A 39-year-old female presents for a postpartum visit 2 months after a preterm delivery that was complicated by chronic hypertension and a bicornuate uterus. She does not smoke cigarettes. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate contraceptive for this patient?

bullets.text: This patient's uterine structural abnormality contraindicates IUDs, and well-controlled hypertension in a patient over 35 contraindicates estrogen-containing methods due to vascular risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has a structural abnormality of the uterus and IUDs are contraindicated. Furthermore, even well-controlled hypertension is a relative contraindication to estrogen-containing contraceptives such as combination pills and the vaginal ring, due to associated vascular risks in a patient older than 35 years.

bullets.text: Among remaining options (nonhormonal methods, progesterone-only pills, depot injections, and implants), the etonogestrel implant is the most effective.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Nonhormonal methods and progesterone-only contraceptive pills, depot injections, and implants remain options. The etonogestrel implant is the most effective of these options.

stem: A 77-year-old female with a medical history of atrial fibrillation, COPD, depression, and hypothyroidism presents for follow-up of a recent visit to the emergency department (ED) for a fall in which she hit her head on the edge of a dresser. Which one of the following medications in this patient's current regimen is most likely to increase her fall risk?

While anticoagulants such as apixaban increase the risk for bleeding from fall-related injuries, they are recommended to prevent stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation regardless of fall risk and have not been noted to increase the risk of falling.
Budesonide/formoterol, levothyroxine, and prednisone have not been associated with an increased fall risk.

stem: A 42-year-old female who has undergone a bilateral prophylactic mastectomy and a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy due to a known BRCA mutation sees you for follow-up. She is experiencing symptoms of vasomotor instability and dyspareunia. She asks about hormone replacement therapy. Which one of the following is the best evidence-based recommendation for this patient?

choices.C: Estrogen and progesterone therapy until age 50
choices.D: Estrogen and progesterone therapy after age 50

bullets.text: Hormone therapy until age 50 has been shown to mitigate some of the health outcomes of early menopause and is the most effective treatment for menopausal symptoms and improved quality of life.
Combined hormone replacement therapy with estrogen and progesterone is indicated for women with a uterus, while estrogen monotherapy is indicated for women without a uterus.
Hormone therapy does not seem to have a relevant effect on cancer risk in BRCA mutation carriers.

stem: A 5-month-old infant is brought to the urgent care clinic by her parent for evaluation of cough and fever. The parent reports that their 2 school-aged children came home with colds 5 days ago. Home tests were negative for COVID-19. Last night the 5-month-old infant developed a runny nose, sneezing, cough, and fever. The infant has also been sleeping more and nursing less. The infant’s vital signs are notable for a temperature of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), a pulse rate of 140 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 26/min, and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. On examination you note mild grunting but no nasal flaring or supraclavicular retractions. Auscultation of the lungs reveals a prolonged expiratory phase with diffuse wheezing and coarse breath sounds. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate intervention at this time?

bullets.text: RSV bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis presenting with respiratory and feeding symptoms, and does not require imaging or viral testing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with symptoms and findings consistent with uncomplicated respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis. Symptoms may include fever, lethargy, rhinorrhea, congestion, sneezing, cough, tachypnea, retractions, and difficulty feeding. The diagnosis of RSV bronchiolitis is clinical and does not require viral testing for confirmation. Because chest x-rays do not improve outcomes or reduce antibiotic use, they should only be obtained if there is concern for airway complications.

bullets.text: Management of uncomplicated RSV bronchiolitis is supportive, focused on hydration and nutrition, as antibiotics and corticosteroids are not indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Since this patient does not have any airway complications, concurrent bacterial infection, or need for hospitalization to manage oxygen therapy, treatment is primarily supportive. Ensuring adequate hydration and nutrition, with intravenous or nasogastric tube intervention if needed, is the most appropriate intervention at this time. Antibiotics such as azithromycin should not be used for the treatment of RSV bronchiolitis unless there is concern for a coexisting bacterial infection. Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone should not be used for the treatment of RSV bronchiolitis since they do not decrease the risk for hospital admission or duration of stay.

stem: A 27-year-old comatose female is brought to the emergency department. There is no history of trauma. An overdose of which one of the following would most likely account for a decreased respiratory rate of 10/min?

stem: A 65-year-old male sees you for an annual health maintenance examination. stem: Medicaid is the largest health insurance program in the United States based on its number of enrolled recipients. Which one of the following statements is true regarding Medicaid?

choices.A: Fewer than half of all states have participated in the Medicaid expansion associated with the Affordable Care Act
choices.B: Its federal funding decreased during the COVID-19 pandemic
choices.C: It is the predominant insurer for long-term care
choices.D: The racial and ethnic group distribution of Medicaid recipients reflects that of the U.S. population

correct_label: It is the predominant insurer for long-term care

Once older adults have exhausted their resources for long-term care, they can enroll in Medicaid. Sixty-two percent of nursing home residents are funded through Medicaid. As of 2022, 24% of all Americans were enrolled in Medicaid and almost 70% of enrollees participate in managed care programs.

bullets.sub_paragraph: Medicaid is a "countercyclical" program, meaning that as the economy worsens, enrollment increases. The federal government committed a 6.2% funding increase to states during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. The Affordable Care Act of 2010 expanded Medicaid coverage to a higher percentage of adults, with the federal government initially funding the expansion. As of 2022, 38 states and the District of Columbia had adopted the Medicaid expansion. The majority of Medicaid recipients (56%) are from racial and ethnic minorities, reflecting income inequality in the United States.

stem: A 40-year-old female presents to the urgent care clinic because of significant fatigue, malaise, nausea, and intermittent vomiting. She is also experiencing recurrent fever and abdominal pain and says that her symptoms started a couple of weeks ago while she was in South America. Now her urine is dark and her spouse has noted a yellow tinge to her skin and the white of her eyes, prompting today’s acute visit. Her vital signs are normal. A physical examination is unremarkable except for hepatomegaly and jaundice. Which one of the following test results would confirm the suspected diagnosis?

choices.D: A serum creatinine level of 2.5 mg/dL (N 0.6–1.1)

bullets.text: Hepatitis A is a common, vaccine-preventable RNA virus infection transmitted via fecal-oral route, with humans as the only host and an ~30-day incubation period.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Hepatitis A is a common cause of acute hepatic inflammation and jaundice. It was the most commonly reported type of hepatitis in the United States until 2004, when a combination of widespread vaccination and food safety practices decreased its incidence. Hepatitis A is caused by nonenveloped positive-strand RNA hepatitis A virus. Humans are the only natural host. Classified as a picornavirus, it is stable in many environments and is able to survive for multiple weeks on surfaces. It is transmitted through ingestion of infected stool particles. Consumption of contaminated water and food or close interpersonal or sexual contact with a person who is infected are common causes of infection, whereas drug use and blood transfusion are less common causes of infection. Incubation lasts approximately 30 days, followed by infectious symptoms, including nonspecific influenza-like symptoms, malaise, fever, nausea with vomiting, and abdominal pain. The classic findings are jaundice and dark urine.

bullets.text: Hepatitis A is self-limited and managed with supportive care, though fulminant hepatic failure may require liver transplant.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Most cases of acute hepatitis A are self-limited and there is no specific treatment. Supportive and symptomatic care should be utilized and hepatotoxins should be avoided. A liver transplant may be considered if fulminant hepatic failure develops.

bullets.text: Anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies (detectable 5–10 days before symptoms, persisting >6 months) confirm acute infection, unlike IgG antibodies which indicate past/convalescent immunity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Serologic testing is required for the diagnosis of hepatitis A. Anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies become detectable 5–10 days before the onset of symptoms, peak within a month, and can persist for >6 months. However, anti–hepatitis A IgG antibodies appear during the convalescent phase and remain elevated throughout the patient's lifetime. Therefore, anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies would confirm the diagnosis instead of anti-hepatitis A IgG antibodies.

bullets.text: Anti–hepatitis B surface antibodies, elevated transaminases, and serum creatinine are nonspecific or indicate other conditions and do not confirm hepatitis A.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Anti−hepatitis B surface antibodies indicate immunity to hepatitis B and would not be present in acute hepatitis B infection. A serum creatinine level >2 mg/dL is a positive predictor of fulminant hepatitis and death, but it is not diagnostic of hepatitis A. Although laboratory findings may include elevations of serum transaminase levels, it is not specific for hepatitis A.

• Hepatitis A is a common, vaccine-preventable RNA virus infection transmitted via fecal-oral route, with humans as the only host and an ~30-day incubation period.
  - Hepatitis A is a common cause of acute hepatic inflammation and jaundice.
  - It was the most commonly reported type of hepatitis in the United States until 2004, when a combination of widespread vaccination and food safety practices decreased its incidence.
  - Hepatitis A is caused by nonenveloped positive-strand RNA hepatitis A virus.
  - Humans are the only natural host.
  - Classified as a picornavirus, it is stable in many environments and is able to survive for multiple weeks on surfaces.
  - It is transmitted through ingestion of infected stool particles.
  - Consumption of contaminated water and food or close interpersonal or sexual contact with a person who is infected are common causes of infection, whereas drug use and blood transfusion are less common causes of infection.
  - Incubation lasts approximately 30 days, followed by infectious symptoms, including nonspecific influenza-like symptoms, malaise, fever, nausea with vomiting, and abdominal pain.
  - The classic findings are jaundice and dark urine.

**Treatment**
• Hepatitis A is self-limited and managed with supportive care, though fulminant hepatic failure may require liver transplant.
  - Most cases of acute hepatitis A are self-limited and there is no specific treatment.
  - Supportive and symptomatic care should be utilized and hepatotoxins should be avoided.
  - A liver transplant may be considered if fulminant hepatic failure develops.

**Diagnosis & Correct Answer**
• Anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies (detectable 5–10 days before symptoms, persisting >6 months) confirm acute infection, unlike IgG antibodies which indicate past/convalescent immunity.
  - Serologic testing is required for the diagnosis of hepatitis A.
  - Anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies become detectable 5–10 days before the onset of symptoms, peak within a month, and can persist for >6 months.
  - However, anti–hepatitis A IgG antibodies appear during the convalescent phase and remain elevated throughout the patient's lifetime.
  - Therefore, anti–hepatitis A IgM antibodies would confirm the diagnosis instead of anti-hepatitis A IgG antibodies.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Anti–hepatitis B surface antibodies, elevated transaminases, and serum creatinine are nonspecific or indicate other conditions and do not confirm hepatitis A.
  - Anti−hepatitis B surface antibodies indicate immunity to hepatitis B and would not be present in acute hepatitis B infection.
  - A serum creatinine level >2 mg/dL is a positive predictor of fulminant hepatitis and death, but it is not diagnostic of hepatitis A.
  - Although laboratory findings may include elevations of serum transaminase levels, it is not specific for hepatitis A.

stem: A healthy 15-year-old female is brought to your office for a well adolescent visit. She does not have any health concerns or preexisting medical conditions. Based on the guidelines from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which one of the following would be most appropriate for this patient?

bullets.text: USPSTF recommends depression screening for adolescents beginning at age 12 (B recommendation).
bullets.sub_paragraph: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends depression screening for adolescents beginning at age 12 (B recommendation).

bullets.text: Vision, iron, dyslipidemia, and cervical cancer screening recommendations do not support routine adolescent screening in the way depression screening does.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends routine vision screening from 12 months to 5 years of age and only risk-based vision screening in adolescents as vision conditions are less likely to begin in older children. The USPSTF recommends vision screening at least once in all children ages 3–5 (B recommendation). Iron deficiency screening is not recommended in adolescents; however, the AAP recommends universal hemoglobin or hematocrit screening at 12 months of age while the USPSTF states that there is insufficient evidence (I recommendation). While the AAP recommends dyslipidemia screening in children ages 9–11, the USPSTF currently states there is insufficient evidence for screening for ≤20 years of age (I recommendation). The USPSTF recommends against cervical cancer screening before age 21 (D recommendation). Furthermore, cytology is recommended for those age 21 and older while high-risk HPV testing is not recommended until age 30.

stem: A 64-year-old male with stage 3b chronic kidney disease (CKD) sees you for recommended follow- up screenings. Which one of the following is most likely to be found in a patient with chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)?

bullets.text: CKD-MBD screening via calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, and possibly 25-hydroxyvitamin D is recommended starting at stage 3 CKD.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Screening for signs of chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) through the monitoring of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and alkaline phosphatase, and possibly 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels is recommended beginning in stage 3 CKD.

bullets.text: CKD impairs phosphate excretion and vitamin D production, driving elevated phosphate and PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) and lowered calcium, ultimately causing CKD-MBD bone abnormalities.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Early changes include the kidneys' decreased ability to excrete phosphate. This can lead to elevated serum phosphate and PTH levels (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Decreased renal vitamin D production can lead to a lower calcium level, which also increases the PTH level. These changes can then lead to the abnormalities of bone strength and mineralization seen in CKD-MBD.

explanation_raw:
**Screening Recommendations**
• CKD-MBD screening via calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, and possibly 25-hydroxyvitamin D is recommended starting at stage 3 CKD.
  - Screening for signs of chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) through the monitoring of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and alkaline phosphatase, and possibly 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels is recommended beginning in stage 3 CKD.

**Pathophysiology**
• CKD impairs phosphate excretion and vitamin D production, driving elevated phosphate and PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) and lowered calcium, ultimately causing CKD-MBD bone abnormalities.
  - Early changes include the kidneys' decreased ability to excrete phosphate.
  - This can lead to elevated serum phosphate and PTH levels (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
  - Decreased renal vitamin D production can lead to a lower calcium level, which also increases the PTH level.
  - These changes can then lead to the abnormalities of bone strength and mineralization seen in CKD-MBD.

stem: A 62-year-old male who currently receives chemotherapy for colon cancer presents to the emergency department with a 1-week history of worsening nausea and vomiting. He has been vomiting all oral intake for the past day, and he has not had a bowel movement in the past week. He reports severe, diffuse, crampy, intermittent abdominal pain that improves after vomiting. He has not had any fevers or chills. The physical examination is significant for abdominal distention, minimal bowel sounds, and diffuse tenderness. Which one of the following studies would be the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.A: Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant
choices.B: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
choices.E: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) of the abdomen

correct_label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast

bullets.text: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast is the appropriate imaging choice for malignant bowel obstruction as it guides surgical decision-making.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's presentation is consistent with a malignant bowel obstruction, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast is useful for determining if any surgical interventions are warranted.

bullets.text: Ultrasonography, PET/CT, HIDA scan, and MRCP are all inappropriate for evaluating malignant bowel obstruction due to technical limitations or wrong indication.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Ultrasonography typically does not yield useful information due to the amount of bowel gas present during an obstruction. A PET/CT scan would not be indicated to evaluate for the etiology of a bowel obstruction in an acute situation. A HIDA scan or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) would be useful if biliary obstruction or gallbladder disease were suspected, but these are not helpful in the evaluation of a malignant bowel obstruction.

stem: A 3-year-old male with a peanut allergy is brought to your office by his parents for a well child visit. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate recommendation to decrease the risk for food allergies in children?

choices.B: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 3–4 months of life
choices.C: Regular antibiotics in the first 2 years of life
choices.D: Restricted cow's milk supplementation during the first 3 months of life

There is no supporting evidence that restricting the mother's diet during pregnancy and lactation reduces the risk for food allergies in children.

stem: A 30-year-old female comes to your office to establish care. She reports symptoms consistent with possible mild chronic malabsorption. stem: A 54-year-old postmenopausal female with a past medical history of hypertension, nicotine dependence, and obesity sees you to establish care. Her medications include hydrochlorothiazide, losartan (Cozaar), and metformin. She smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day and drinks 1 glass of wine each night. She returns 1 week later to discuss the results of laboratory studies. The laboratory studies demonstrate a positive hepatitis C antibody. Reflex testing reveals hepatitis C virus genotype and a hepatitis C viral load of 253,351 IU/mL. The AST level, ALT level, creatinine level, and INR are within normal limits. Tests for HIV, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B are negative. You calculate a Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score of 0.93, indicating a lack of advanced fibrosis. You initiate vaccination for hepatitis A and B. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate timing to initiate treatment with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret)?

choices.B: After she has abstained from alcohol for 3 months

While vaccinations are important, the hepatitis A and B series do not need to be completed prior to initiating treatment. Further imaging is not indicated for this patient given her low Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score, which indicates a very low likelihood of cirrhosis.

bullets.text: Delaying treatment for repeat viral load testing or requiring alcohol cessation are not necessary prior to initiating HCV therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Limiting alcohol use is important to decrease the risk for cirrhosis, but cessation is not necessary in those undergoing treatment for HCV infection. Further hepatitis C viral load testing in 3 months is not the most appropriate next step for this patient.

stem: A 63-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes mellitus presents to an urgent care clinic with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. After initiating intravenous fluids, you obtain an initial laboratory evaluation with the following results: Glucose 190 mg/dL Sodium 135 mEq/L (N 135–145) Potassium 5.1 mEq/L (N 3.5–5.2) Chloride 102 mEq/L (N 98–107) Creatinine 1.30 mg/dL (N 0.50–1.04) Osmolality 300 mOsm/kg H O (N 280–305) Bicarbonate 10 mEq/L (N 19–29) Anion gap 23 mEq/L (N <18) Urine ketones 4+ Urine glucose 4+ Which one of the following medications may be contributing to this clinical picture?

bullets.text: This is euglycemic DKA caused by a malfunctioning insulin pump in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor, which drives glycosuria and masks hyperglycemia while ketoacidosis progresses.

Glycosuria occurs and can even persist 10–14 days after discontinuation of an SGLT2 inhibitor. Further evaluation of this patient would reveal an elevated urine glucose level despite his relatively normal serum glucose level. With a high anion gap, a low arterial pH and a high serum β-hydroxybutyrate level should also be expected.

bullets.text: The other medications listed (atorvastatin, lisinopril, metformin, semaglutide) do not cause euglycemic DKA, each having distinct or absent metabolic risks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Atorvastatin is not implicated in acute metabolic problems. Lisinopril can cause hyperkalemia, but not DKA. Metformin can cause lactic acidosis in acutely ill patients, but the risk is low and lactic acid rather than ketone bodies would be high. GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide are not associated with an increased risk for euglycemic DKA.

stem: An 18-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents for a sports preparticipation evaluation prior to his high school senior football season. On cardiac auscultation, you detect a previously undocumented systolic murmur. Which one of the following additional characteristics of this murmur, if present, would raise concern for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and necessitate additional testing prior to clearing this patient for sports participation?

choices.A: Decreased intensity with an isometric handgrip
choices.B: Decreased intensity with the Valsalva maneuver
choices.C: Increased intensity with moving from squatting to standing
choices.D: Increased intensity with passive leg raise

correct_label: Increased intensity with moving from squatting to standing

bullets.text: The sports preparticipation evaluation screens for life-threatening cardiovascular conditions, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy being a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: One of the most important purposes of the sports preparticipation evaluation is to screen for potentially life-threatening cardiovascular conditions. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in younger athletes, and recognition of the typical pathologic murmur that occurs with this condition can identify people who are at risk.

bullets.text: HCM produces a harsh midsystolic ejection murmur from dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The characteristic harsh midsystolic ejection murmur results from a dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

bullets.text: Maneuvers that reduce preload or afterload (standing from squat, Valsalva, dehydration) increase relative obstruction and intensify the murmur.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The murmur intensifies with maneuvers that reduce preload or afterload, which increase the relative obstruction. Moving from squatting to standing, the Valsalva maneuver, and dehydration states all reduce preload and therefore cause the murmur to increase.

bullets.text: Maneuvers that increase preload (squatting, passive leg raise) or afterload (isometric handgrip) decrease relative obstruction and soften the murmur.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In contrast, maneuvers that increase preload or afterload cause the murmur to soften due to decrease in the relative obstruction. This includes moving from standing to squatting and passive leg raise, which increase preload, and isometric handgrip, which increases afterload.

**Maneuvers That Intensify the Murmur**
• Maneuvers that reduce preload or afterload (standing from squat, Valsalva, dehydration) increase relative obstruction and intensify the murmur.

  - Moving from squatting to standing, the Valsalva maneuver, and dehydration states all reduce preload and therefore cause the murmur to increase.

• Maneuvers that increase preload (squatting, passive leg raise) or afterload (isometric handgrip) decrease relative obstruction and soften the murmur.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents to your office for evaluation of acute penile pain. He has had painful erections for the past several days, and the current erection has lasted 5 hours. He has a history of sickle cell disease and diabetes mellitus. His only medication is daily metformin. On examination the patient appears quite uncomfortable and has a full erection with significant tenderness along the sides of the penile shaft. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

bullets.text: Priapism is defined as a non-sexual erection lasting ≥4 hours, classified as ischemic or nonischemic, with ischemic presenting as painful and fully erect with a history of painful erections preceding acute onset.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient is presenting with priapism, defined as an erection that is not associated with sexual activity and lasts ≥4 hours. Priapism may be ischemic or nonischemic. Nonischemic (high-flow) priapism is much rarer, stemming from an arterial fistula caused by trauma. Ischemic priapism typically presents with a painful, fully erect penis with a natural history of painful erections ranging from days to weeks preceding the acute presentation.

bullets.text: Ischemic priapism causes include sickle cell disease, leukemia, intracavernosal vasodilators, and antipsychotics — more so than PDE-5 inhibitors.

Intracavernosal vasodilator agents and antipsychotics are more likely causes than phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors. Intracavernosal alprostadil is a common cause of ischemic priapism.

bullets.text: Priapism is a urologic emergency requiring emergent urologic evaluation; analgesics and delayed workup are inappropriate, and intracavernosal phenylephrine is used only after urologist-performed aspiration restores oxygenated blood flow.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This is a urologic emergency that requires emergent evaluation and treatment by a urologist. Analgesic therapy is not the most appropriate next step for this patient. While a penile blood gas measurement can be used to distinguish between ischemic and nonischemic processes, urologic evaluation and treatment should not be delayed. Intracavernosal phenylephrine is used in the treatment of ischemic priapism after a urologist has performed several rounds of aspiration and reestablished oxygenated blood flow into the corpus cavernosum.

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with frequent episodes of palpitations, sweating, dizziness, and paresthesias associated with an impending sense of doom. These symptoms have occurred several times per week and have disrupted his performance at work. After an appropriate evaluation, you diagnose panic disorder. stem: A 40-year-old female presents with symptoms of heartburn and regurgitation of sour-tasting fluid into her throat after meals. stem: Bruising in which one of the following locations would most likely suggest a diagnosis of child abuse?

bullets.sub_paragraph: Bruises on the torso, ears, or neck in children ≤4 years of age are predictive of child abuse. "TEN 4" is a useful mnemonic for identifying child abuse: torso (T), ear (E), neck (N), and 4 (children ≤4 years of age and any infant <4 months of age). Bruising is the most common injury of physical abuse and may be the only external indicator of an internal injury. Bruises vary by age, location, and pattern. Any bruises identified in a nonambulatory infant require careful medical evaluation for possible abuse.

bullets.sub_paragraph: Bruising related to normal activity typically increases with age. The majority of preschool- and school-aged children have accidental bruises. stem: An 89-year-old female with end-stage, widely metastatic lung cancer is receiving hospice care. Her symptoms, including pain, have been well controlled until recently. bullets.text: Terminal secretions ("death rattle") cause noisy breathing distressing to families but not the patient, and suctioning is ineffective.
bullets.sub_paragraph: One of the common symptoms at the end of life is excessive oropharyngeal secretions. This can cause increased noisy breathing in the last hours to days of life, often referred to as a death rattle. stem: Which one of the following is a best practice strategy for avoiding the use of stigmatizing or judgmental language in the medical record?

choices.A: Attributing responsibility to patients for their condition
choices.B: Documenting when a patient “refuses” a recommendation
choices.C: Including socioeconomic status in the “one-liner” about the patient

bullets.text: Person-first language humanizes patients by focusing on the person rather than the condition, avoiding labels like "a diabetic" in favor of "a patient with diabetes."

bullets.text: Neutral language should be used in documentation, replacing terms like "refuses" with "chooses," and social identifiers should only appear in the social history when verified by the patient, not in the HPI or one-liner.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Documenting that a patient "refuses" a recommendation carries a negative connotation and it is preferable to use a neutral alternative such "chooses." Social identifiers such as race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status can be markers of marginalization and trigger unconscious bias. These identifiers should not be used to lead the history of present illness or included in a "one-liner." Instead, they can be included in the social history if verified by the patient.

stem: A 32-year-old male has presented to your office 4 times over the past several months because of periods of intractable nausea and vomiting lasting 1–2 days, with up to 14 episodes each day. He has also experienced moderate abdominal pain, flushing, sweating, and dry mouth during these episodes. On 2 occasions he has required brief admission to the hospital for fluid resuscitation. Promethazine, ondansetron, and metoclopramide (Reglan) have been ineffective in treating his symptoms, but hot showers provide him relief. His medical history is significant for allergic rhinitis and obesity. His social history includes episodes of binge drinking approximately twice monthly and daily marijuana use since age 21. He has no history of intravenous drug use or tobacco abuse. Physical findings are significant for a weight loss of 4.5 kg (10 lb) over the past 3 months and moderate tenderness to epigastric palpation. During acute episodes, laboratory evaluations have revealed only mild elevations in BUN and creatinine levels and hematocrit. Abdominal ultrasonography and CT scans have been normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: CHS is increasingly common with cannabis legalization and is distinguished by risk factors including long duration, high frequency, and high amounts of use, plus symptomatic relief with hot showers not seen in other conditions.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) has become more common with increased legalization and acceptance of cannabis use. Long duration, higher frequency of use, and higher amounts of cannabis use are all risk factors for CHS. Symptomatic relief with hot showers or baths is not found in abdominal migraines, carcinoid syndrome, or peptic ulcer disease.

bullets.text: Cannabis paradoxically promotes vomiting in susceptible individuals with significant use history despite its antiemetic properties.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While it can be used as an antiemetic, cannabis can also promote vomiting in susceptible individuals who have a significant history of cannabinoid use.

bullets.text: Pancreatitis, carcinoid syndrome, and other causes of nausea are ruled out by normal labs/imaging, distinct symptom profiles, and response to traditional antiemetics.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pancreatitis would cause elevations in lipase levels and some findings on imaging would be expected. Nausea from the other causes is generally relieved with traditional antiemetics. Carcinoid syndrome also causes episodic symptoms such as facial flushing, diarrhea, hypotension, and tachycardia, but not nausea or vomiting.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with an increased risk for venous thromboembolism?

stem: A 62-year-old female sees you for evaluation of pain and stiffness in her neck. For several years she has attributed these symptoms to the aging process, but she has recently developed a loss of dexterity in her hands that makes typing and knitting difficult. She does not have any loss of sensation or weakness in her extremities but has noticed some difficulties with balance in recent weeks. The pain does not radiate, and she does not have any history of recent trauma. She feels well otherwise and has not had any fevers, chills, bowel incontinence, or bladder incontinence. On examination you note mild tenderness of the spinous processes and paraspinous muscles of the cervical spine without focal tenderness. Her range of motion at the neck is limited due to pain. There are brisk reflexes in the bilateral upper and lower extremities and a positive Hoffman sign bilaterally with 4 beats of clonus on the right and 5 on the left. Her strength and sensation to light touch are intact in the bilateral upper extremities. Which one of the following cervical spine conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Degenerative cervical myelopathy presents with nonspecific symptoms progressing to upper motor neuron signs due to spinal cord compression from spondylosis, warranting urgent MRI.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The patient history and physical examination findings are most consistent with degenerative cervical myelopathy, a condition in which spinal cord dysfunction develops due to compression in the neck. Spinal cord compression can be due to disk herniation, ligament hypertrophy, or osteophyte formation, sometimes collectively called spondylosis. Symptoms can initially be nonspecific and subtle, and they can overlap with less serious conditions. Loss of hand dexterity, ataxia, and urinary urgency can be signs of spinal cord compression and warrant a comprehensive neurologic examination. The development of upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffmann sign (digital reflex of the fingers), and clonus are key findings that warrant urgent evaluation with MRI.

bullets.text: Facet arthropathy, cervical radiculopathy, vertebral compression fracture, and osteomyelitis each cause focal pain or dermatomal symptoms without the upper motor neuron or spinal cord compression findings seen here.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Facet joint arthropathy causes more focal pain and is not associated with neurologic symptoms. Cervical radiculopathy involves compression of the nerve root rather than the spinal cord. Symptoms include shooting pain with sensory changes and weakness in a dermatomal distribution. A vertebral compression fracture leads to focal pain in the neck at the site of the fracture without neurologic symptoms. Osteomyelitis also causes more focal pain in the setting of systemic symptoms such as malaise and fever.

  - The development of upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffmann sign (digital reflex of the fingers), and clonus are key findings that warrant urgent evaluation with MRI.

**Why Other Options Are Wrong**
• Facet arthropathy, cervical radiculopathy, vertebral compression fracture, and osteomyelitis each cause focal pain or dermatomal symptoms without the upper motor neuron or spinal cord compression findings seen here.
  - Facet joint arthropathy causes more focal pain and is not associated with neurologic symptoms.

stem: You see a 50-year-old female for a health maintenance examination. She is the primary caregiver for her father who has dementia, and she has heard that Alzheimer disease is genetic and asks if there is anything she can do to reduce her risk. She is in perimenopause and experiences severe hot flashes. She recently started a kickboxing class and drinks 1–2 beers per week. On examination her vital signs include a blood pressure of 138/80 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 63 beats/min, and a BMI of 30 kg/m2. Which one of the following should you recommend to decrease this patient’s risk for dementia?

choices.A: A memory training app on her smartphone
choices.C: Testing for biomarkers associated with Alzheimer disease
choices.D: A target systolic blood pressure ≤130 mm Hg
choices.E: Hormone therapy with estrogen and progesterone

correct_label: A target systolic blood pressure ≤130 mm Hg

bullets.text: Blood pressure control, moderate alcohol use, and avoiding hormone therapy (in older women) are key modifiable risk factors for dementia.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Maintaining a systolic blood pressure ≤130 mm Hg in midlife has been shown to reduce the risk for developing dementia. Extremes of alcohol use (both long-term abstinence and abuse) are associated with an increased risk for dementia. Hormone therapy with estrogen and progesterone is an effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms of menopause but is associated with an increased risk for dementia when administered in women ≥65 years of age.

bullets.text: Estrogen-only therapy in women aged 40s–50s significantly decreases dementia risk, while estrogen plus progesterone shows a nonsignificant decrease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For women in their 40s and 50s, hormone therapy with estrogen only has demonstrated a significant decrease in dementia, while estrogen plus progesterone therapy has demonstrated a nonsignificant decrease.

bullets.text: Computer-based memory games lack evidence for preventing cognitive decline, and presymptomatic Alzheimer biomarker identification has no proven benefit.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While reading, playing music, and speaking a foreign language have demonstrated benefits in maintaining cognition, there is no good-quality evidence to show that computer-based memory training games prevent cognitive decline. Most people who are positive for biomarkers associated with Alzheimer disease will not go on to develop the disease. Additionally, there is no evidence that presymptomatic identification of Alzheimer disease is beneficial.

explanation_raw:
**Dementia Risk Factors**
• Blood pressure control, moderate alcohol use, and avoiding hormone therapy (in older women) are key modifiable risk factors for dementia.
  - Maintaining a systolic blood pressure ≤130 mm Hg in midlife has been shown to reduce the risk for developing dementia.
  - Extremes of alcohol use (both long-term abstinence and abuse) are associated with an increased risk for dementia.
  - Hormone therapy with estrogen and progesterone is an effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms of menopause but is associated with an increased risk for dementia when administered in women ≥65 years of age.

**Hormone Therapy and Cognition**
• Estrogen-only therapy in women aged 40s–50s significantly decreases dementia risk, while estrogen plus progesterone shows a nonsignificant decrease.
  - For women in their 40s and 50s, hormone therapy with estrogen only has demonstrated a significant decrease in dementia, while estrogen plus progesterone therapy has demonstrated a nonsignificant decrease.

**Cognitive Training and Screening**
• Computer-based memory games lack evidence for preventing cognitive decline, and presymptomatic Alzheimer biomarker identification has no proven benefit.
  - While reading, playing music, and speaking a foreign language have demonstrated benefits in maintaining cognition, there is no good-quality evidence to show that computer-based memory training games prevent cognitive decline.
  - Most people who are positive for biomarkers associated with Alzheimer disease will not go on to develop the disease.
  - Additionally, there is no evidence that presymptomatic identification of Alzheimer disease is beneficial.

stem: Which one of the following attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medications is considered safest to take while breastfeeding?

bullets.text: Methylphenidate is considered safe in breastfeeding due to very low milk transfer, undetectable infant levels, and no developmental concerns, though it may reduce prolactin without clinical impact on milk supply.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Racemic methylphenidate has been studied in breastfeeding mothers and drug levels in breast milk were found to be about 0.2% of the adult dose. Drug levels were undetectable in breastfed infants and the infants had no long-term growth or developmental issues. Methylphenidate can reduce serum prolactin levels, but this has not been shown to have any clinical impact on milk supply.

bullets.text: Amphetamines, atomoxetine, guanfacine, and clonidine should be avoided during breastfeeding due to higher infant drug exposure or insufficient safety data.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Less is known about amphetamine in breastfeeding, but milk and infant serum levels are significantly higher than with methylphenidate. Atomoxetine and guanfacine have no reliable data in breastfeeding and should be avoided until more is known. Clonidine has been shown to be present in significant amounts in breast milk and serum from breastfed infants (up to 50% of the maternal serum levels). While no adverse effects have been shown, this high level of medication in the infant raises concerns, and experts recommend avoiding clonidine while breastfeeding.

explanation_raw:
**Methylphenidate in Breastfeeding**
• Methylphenidate is considered safe in breastfeeding due to very low milk transfer, undetectable infant levels, and no developmental concerns, though it may reduce prolactin without clinical impact on milk supply.
  - Racemic methylphenidate has been studied in breastfeeding mothers and drug levels in breast milk were found to be about 0.2% of the adult dose.
  - Drug levels were undetectable in breastfed infants and the infants had no long-term growth or developmental issues.
  - Methylphenidate can reduce serum prolactin levels, but this has not been shown to have any clinical impact on milk supply.

**Medications to Avoid While Breastfeeding**
• Amphetamines, atomoxetine, guanfacine, and clonidine should be avoided during breastfeeding due to higher infant drug exposure or insufficient safety data.
  - Less is known about amphetamine in breastfeeding, but milk and infant serum levels are significantly higher than with methylphenidate.
  - Atomoxetine and guanfacine have no reliable data in breastfeeding and should be avoided until more is known.
  - Clonidine has been shown to be present in significant amounts in breast milk and serum from breastfed infants (up to 50% of the maternal serum levels).
  - While no adverse effects have been shown, this high level of medication in the infant raises concerns, and experts recommend avoiding clonidine while breastfeeding.

stem: A 20-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after experiencing blunt abdominal trauma during a motor vehicle accident. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) examination is performed at the bedside and there are no signs of internal bleeding. Based on these results, which one of the following should be the next step in evaluation?

choices.A: No further imaging to evaluate for internal bleeding
choices.B: Additional imaging only if the patient develops signs of hemodynamic compromise
choices.C: Additional imaging to confirm the absence of bleeding

correct_label: Additional imaging to confirm the absence of bleeding

bullets.text: FAST is a rapid bedside ultrasound that evaluates the pericardium and three peritoneal spaces for hemoperitoneum/hemopericardium, replacing diagnostic peritoneal lavage in trauma settings.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) evaluates the pericardium and 3 potential spaces within the peritoneal cavity for hemoperitoneum and hemopericardium. This bedside examination can be completed in less than 5 minutes, so it is ideal for emergency department settings. FAST has replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavage as a bedside evaluation for bleeding.

bullets.text: FAST has high specificity (96%) but limited sensitivity (74% overall, 62% in children), meaning positive results are reliable but negative results require CT confirmation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A Cochrane review found that FAST has a 96% specificity but only a 74% sensitivity for detecting internal bleeding. The sensitivity in children was found to be even lower at 62%. Therefore, while a positive result will almost always be reliable and should prompt immediate bleeding control measures, a negative result carries the risk of being a false negative and must be confirmed by additional imaging such as CT.

explanation_raw:

stem: A 65-year-old male sees you for follow-up after he was hospitalized for pneumonia a few months ago. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 40 years. bullets.text: This patient meets criteria for Stage 2 COPD by GOLD spirometry, and with ≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalization, falls into a high-exacerbation risk category guiding therapy selection.

Initial inhaler pharmacotherapy can be guided by the GOLD ABCD assessment that integrates symptoms and exacerbations. Moderate exacerbations require either an oral antibiotic, an oral corticosteroid, or both, while a severe exacerbation results in an emergency department visit or hospitalization.

bullets.text: LAMA monotherapy is the first-line treatment for patients with 2+ moderate exacerbations or 1+ hospitalization, as it reduces symptoms, exacerbations, and hospitalizations.

bullets.sub_paragraph: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as fluticasone propionate are not recommended as monotherapy for COPD, particularly for those who have had pneumonia. Monotherapy with a LABA such as salmeterol reduces exacerbations requiring hospitalization, but symptoms are better controlled when a LABA is used in combination with a LAMA. Short-acting β-adrenergic agonists and short-acting muscarinic antagonists are appropriate for acute exacerbations rather than prevention.

stem: A 67-year-old male presents for an annual health maintenance visit. His medical conditions include hypertension, dyslipidemia, severe aortic stenosis, and osteoarthritis. He is under the care of a cardiologist and is scheduled for an annual echocardiogram next week. He reports that he generally feels well but “can’t keep up with the grandkids” anymore. choices.A: An elevated 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk
choices.B: A left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%–45%
choices.C: A need for an elective total knee replacement
choices.D: A normal exercise stress test result

bullets.text: AS results from age-related valve narrowing, and while asymptomatic AS carries normal survival, symptom onset dramatically worsens prognosis with no effective medical prevention of progression.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Aortic stenosis (AS) occurs primarily in older adults and is a result of narrowing of the aortic valve area due to damage from the aging process that involves lipid accumulation, calcification, and inflammation. While survival rates in patients with asymptomatic AS match those without AS, survival rates drop dramatically once symptoms develop. Because there is no effective medical management for preventing the progression of AS, recognizing indications for aortic valve replacement (AVR) results in improved survival and symptoms.

bullets.text: AVR is indicated in symptomatic severe AS, LVEF <50%, abnormal stress test, or need for concurrent cardiac surgery, but not for noncardiac elective surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Any symptomatic patient with severe AS (maximum transaortic velocity ≥4.0 m/s or mean pressure gradient ≥40 mm Hg) should undergo AVR. It is difficult to determine whether this patient is truly symptomatic from AS, but a left ventricular ejection fraction <50% would support a need for AVR in this patient. An abnormal exercise stress test, rather than a normal test, would also indicate a need for AVR. Finally, a need for other cardiac surgery, such as coronary artery bypass grafting, would also prompt AVR.

bullets.text: Elevated ASCVD risk and need for noncardiac elective surgery do not factor into AVR decision-making.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk should prompt consideration of statin and aspirin prophylaxis but does not play a role in deciding when to perform AVR. A need for a noncardiac, elective surgical intervention would not lead to a recommendation for AVR due to the high-risk nature of AVR.

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with low back pain that began after giving birth 3 months ago. She reports pain on her right side when climbing and descending stairs and when lying on her right side. On examination she has mild lumbar paraspinal muscle tightness on the left and moderate tenderness inferomedial to the posterior superior iliac spine on the right. bullets.text: Sacroiliac joint dysfunction is a common primary care condition often triggered by pregnancy/postpartum, trauma, or associated with spondyloarthropathies, presenting with SI joint pain worsened by specific activities and confirmed by provocation tests.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Sacroiliac joint dysfunction is commonly seen in primary care and is an important consideration in the evaluation of low back pain. It often occurs during pregnancy and post partum. Other inciting incidents include a motor vehicle accident or a mechanical fall onto the buttocks. It can be associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies; however, the etiology in this case is more likely to be childbirth. Symptoms often include pain at the sacroiliac joint that worsens with climbing stairs, lying on the affected side, prolonged standing and sitting, and weight-bearing on the leg of the affected side. Examination findings include tenderness that is inferomedial to the posterior superior iliac spine. A number of provocation tests for sacroiliac joint dysfunction can help to confirm the diagnosis.

bullets.text: First-line treatment includes NSAIDs, physical therapy, and joint manipulation, with pelvic belts, corticosteroid injections, and fusion reserved for refractory cases.

bullets.text: Lumbar strain, piriformis syndrome, pudendal nerve entrapment, and spondyloarthropathies are less likely given this postpartum patient's specific history, symptom location, and presentation.

choices.D: A pulsatile quality of the tinnitus

bullets.text: Tinnitus affects up to 25% of adults, with audiometry recommended for severe/persistent cases and imaging indicated for pulsatile tinnitus, unilateral tinnitus, asymmetric hearing loss, or focal neurologic findings.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Tinnitus is a common problem that is experienced by up to 25% of adults, although <10% of affected individuals report bothersome symptoms that impair sleep, focus, emotions, or general quality of life. Symptoms often persist for months to years; the duration of symptoms alone does not provide a reason to order head imaging.

stem: Your practice management team has reviewed the clinic-wide cancer screening rates and found that the frequency of cervical cancer screening appears to have fallen behind other cancer screenings. You are asked to lead a quality improvement project to increase rates of cervical cancer screening for appropriate patients. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate first step?

choices.A: Establishing a system for reviewing charts and contacting patients who are overdue for cervical cancer screening
choices.B: Evaluating barriers to cervical cancer screening and reporting
choices.C: Placing posters with information about cervical cancer screening inside the clinic
choices.D: Sending generalized reminders to patients who may qualify for cervical cancer screening
choices.E: Sending generalized reminders to all clinicians regarding cervical cancer screening guidelines

correct_label: Evaluating barriers to cervical cancer screening and reporting

bullets.text: The first step in any quality improvement project is identifying and evaluating current barriers before implementing interventions.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Quality improvement methodologies such as the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle require clear identification of existing problems before change can be effectively planned. If the root cause is a systemic data-capture issue rather than a clinician behavior issue, interventions targeting clinicians will be ineffective. Therefore, evaluating barriers to cervical cancer screening and reporting must precede any other action.

bullets.text: Patient-specific reminders and team-based care approaches are more effective at improving screening uptake than general clinic materials or broad reminders.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Once barriers are identified, targeted interventions should be implemented. Patient-specific reminders addressed at the point of care are more effective than generalized preventive care reminders, which may miss high-risk patients. General materials like clinic posters and broad mailings are less impactful than direct physician recommendations. Using the entire health care team as part of an organizational plan further improves screening rates.

explanation_raw: Quality improvement is a key area for clinical practice, but initiating these projects can be challenging. Many different methodologies have been used, including the Plan-Do-StudyAct cycle or Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, but clear identification of the current issues is critical in any framework. In order to plan appropriate interventions, it must first be determined what barriers are responsible for hindering performance in a certain area. If evaluation shows that there is a systemic issue in capturing data, rather than a clinician issue, no other interventions will be beneficial. When used as part of an organizational plan for staffing and clinical procedures, patient-specific reminders and use of the entire health care team are more likely to improve screening uptake than other methods, but the initial step should be delineating any current issues prior to implementing a change. Educating patients about preventive health care and screenings is essential and should be part of routine care. However, general materials such as clinic posters are less likely to increase screening rates than direct physician recommendations or conversations. Sending generalized reminders for preventive care may miss the patients in most critical need of services. General reminders that rely on clinician evaluation of every individual visit may be less effective than patient-specific reminders that can be addressed at the point of care.

stem: You are seeing a 32-year-old male in the office. His most recent hemoglobin A1c was 6.1%, indicating prediabetes. Which one of the following is most likely to prevent the development of diabetes?

choices.A: Intensive lifestyle and behavior change program
choices.C: Reduction in daily caloric intake by 250 kcal per day
choices.D: Strength training for 90 minutes per week

correct_label: Intensive lifestyle and behavior change program

bullets.text: Intensive lifestyle and behavior modification programs (e.g., National Diabetes Prevention Program) are the most effective intervention for preventing progression from prediabetes to diabetes, demonstrating a 27% reduction over 15 years in one U.S. study.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Intensive lifestyle and behavior modification programs, such as the National Diabetes Prevention Program, are low-cost and highly effective at preventing the development of diabetes. A key component is achieving weight loss ≥7% of baseline body weight, typically through a caloric reduction of 500–1000 kcal per day combined with physical activity goals of ≥150 minutes per week (including up to 75 minutes of strength training). While various dietary patterns—including low-carbohydrate diets—may support diabetes prevention, the evidence for structured intensive lifestyle programs is substantially stronger than for dietary changes alone.

explanation_raw: Given the growing prevalence of diabetes mellitus, clinicians should be familiar with effective prevention strategies. Intensive lifestyle and behavior modification programs, such as the National Diabetes Prevention Program, are low-cost and can reduce the development of diabetes, with one U.S. study demonstrating a 27% reduction over 15 years. These programs help patients set weight loss goals ≥7% of their baseline, which is thought to be a key component of diabetes prevention. This is typically achieved through a caloric reduction of 500–1000 kcal per day, with activity goals ≥150 minutes per week, including up to 75 minutes per week of strength training. While a variety of dietary patterns are thought to be effective for diabetes prevention, including low intake of carbohydrates, the evidence for changes in dietary patterns is not as strong as that of intensive lifestyle programs.

stem: An otherwise healthy 47-year-old male presents to the urgent care clinic with pain and swelling of his right foot after sustaining an injury during a game of ultimate frisbee. He jumped to catch the frisbee and landed on uneven ground. He is unsure of how he landed, but thinks he may have twisted his right foot, causing him to trip and fall. He has significant pain and swelling of his right foot but is weight-bearing. He rates the pain as 10 on a scale of 10. On examination, his vital signs are unremarkable. His right lateral foot shows significant bruising and swelling. The skin is intact. Range of movement is impaired due to the swelling and discomfort, and sensation and circulation are intact. An x-ray of the right foot is shown below. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Weight-bearing with a walking boot for 3–6 weeks
choices.B: Non–weight-bearing with a walking boot for 3–6 weeks
choices.C: Non–weight-bearing with a short leg cast for 6 weeks

correct_label: Weight-bearing with a walking boot for 3–6 weeks

bullets.text: Fifth metatarsal shaft fractures are managed with weight-bearing in a walking boot or hard-soled shoe for 3–6 weeks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fifth metatarsal shaft fractures should be treated conservatively with a walking boot or hard-soled shoe allowing weight-bearing as tolerated for 3–6 weeks. A short leg cast is reserved for proximal fifth metatarsal and tarsal bone fractures, not shaft fractures. Physical therapy is not first-line, and orthopedic referral is only indicated if reduction is needed or nonunion persists beyond 6 months.

bullets.text: Foot fractures typically result from axial, twisting, or crush forces and present with swelling and bony point tenderness; complications include nonunion, malunion, arthritis, infection, and compartment syndrome.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Foot fractures account for approximately one-third of lower extremity fractures in adults and are caused by axial or twisting forces or crush injuries. Patients present with localized swelling and bony point tenderness. The ability to bear weight varies with pain tolerance and fracture severity. Potential complications include infection, post-traumatic arthritis, nonunion, malunion, and compartment syndrome.

explanation_raw: This patient's imaging reveals a fifth metatarsal shaft fracture, which should be managed with a boot or hard-soled shoe for 3–6 weeks with weight-bearing. Foot fractures are typically caused by an axial or twisting force on the foot or a crush injury and account for about one-third of lower extremity fractures in adults. Patients present with swelling and bony point tenderness of the affected area, as seen in this patient. The ability to bear weight varies based on the patient's pain tolerance and the extent of the fracture. Complications of foot fractures include infection, arthritis, nonunion, malunion, and compartment syndrome. A short leg cast is not appropriate because it is used to treat proximal fifth metatarsal and tarsal bone fractures. Physical therapy is not first-line management for this patient's injury. If reduction is needed or if nonunion is present after 6 months, then referral to an orthopedic surgeon would be indicated.

stem: A 78-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of cough and fever and a 2-hour history of confusion. Her vital signs include a weight of 67 kg (148 lb), a temperature of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), a pulse rate of 122 beats/min, and a blood pressure of 72/44 mm Hg with a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 53 mm Hg. A chest x-ray shows left lower lobe pneumonia. She is given 2 L of lactated Ringer solution and started on broadspectrum antibiotics for sepsis secondary to pneumonia. Her blood pressure 3 hours later is 82/46 mm Hg with a MAP of 58 mm Hg. Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

bullets.text: In septic shock refractory to initial fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid), norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor per Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines when mean arterial pressure remains <65 mm Hg.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient is in septic shock secondary to pneumonia. After initial resuscitation with 30 mL/kg crystalloid and early antibiotics (within 1 hour), the next step is vasopressor therapy if the MAP remains below 65 mm Hg. Norepinephrine is the preferred first-line vasopressor because it is a more potent vasoconstrictor than dopamine. Vasopressin may be added if norepinephrine alone fails to achieve adequate MAP. Importantly, vasopressor therapy should not be delayed to await central line placement.

bullets.text: Additional large-volume fluid boluses are controversial and not the preferred next step once initial resuscitation has been completed; vasopressin is reserved as an add-on to norepinephrine, not a first-line agent.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Further fluid therapy beyond the initial 30 mL/kg is patient-specific and debated; some experts favor discrete 500 mL boluses with hemodynamic monitoring, and balanced crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer's) are preferred over normal saline. Vasopressin is indicated as a second agent for adults already on norepinephrine who still have inadequate MAP, not as the initial vasopressor. Dopamine is a less potent vasoconstrictor than norepinephrine and is associated with more adverse effects, making it a second-line choice.

explanation_raw: This patient is in septic shock secondary to pneumonia. Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) consisting of initial fluid resuscitation with 30 mL/kg of crystalloid solution within the first 3 hours and appropriate antibiotics within 1 hour of evaluation, which have already been done for this patient. The guidelines also recommend initiating vasopressor therapy with norepinephrine as the firstline agent if the mean arterial pressure remains <65 mm Hg after fluid resuscitation. Norepinephrine is a more potent vasoconstrictor than dopamine. Additional fluid therapy is controversial and patient-specific, with some experts recommending discrete 500-mL boluses with hemodynamic monitoring of response, and others recommending balanced crystalloids such as lactate Ringer solution over normal saline. Vasopressin should be added for adults with septic shock who are receiving norepinephrine but continue to have inadequate mean arterial pressure. Vasopressor therapy should not be delayed for placement of a central line.

bullets.text: Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the initial treatment of choice for thyroid storm, as it decreases circulating T3 levels more quickly than methimazole.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Thyroid storm is a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment. PTU is preferred as first-line therapy because it both blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis and inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Although PTU and methimazole show equal clinical efficacy overall, PTU's additional mechanism gives it an advantage in the acute setting.

bullets.text: Adjunct therapies include glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone or dexamethasone, not prednisone) and iodine, which must be given at least 1 hour after PTU initiation to prevent worsening hormone synthesis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Glucocorticoids such as hydrocortisone and dexamethasone can be added to further block T4-to-T3 conversion. Iodine is used to suppress new thyroid hormone synthesis but must be delayed at least 1 hour after PTU to avoid providing substrate for additional hormone production. Plasmapheresis is reserved for refractory cases that do not respond to pharmacologic treatment.

explanation_raw: Thyroid storm is a medical emergency that must be treated promptly. The initial treatment for thyroid storm is propylthiouracil (PTU). While PTU has been shown to decrease circulating T3 hormone levels more quickly than methimazole, they have both been shown to be equally effective clinically. Glucocorticoids can also be used to block the conversion of T4 to T3. Hydrocortisone and dexamethasone, not prednisone, are the preferred glucocorticoids if used in addition to PTU. While iodine is used to block the synthesis of new thyroid hormone, it should be started at least 1 hour after the initiation of PTU. Plasmapheresis is reserved for patients who do not respond to pharmacologic treatment.

stem: According to guidelines from the American Gastroenterological Association, which one of the following is recommended as the best pharmacologic treatment of typical symptoms in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome?

bullets.text: Rifaximin is the best-evidenced pharmacologic treatment for IBS-D per 2022 AGA guidelines, addressing diarrhea, bloating, discomfort, and abdominal pain with a 14-day course.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to the 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guidelines for diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D), the nonabsorbable antibiotic rifaximin has the strongest evidence for controlling diarrhea, discomfort, bloating, and abdominal pain. It has a broad spectrum with activity against gram-positive, gram-negative (including Clostridioides difficile), and anaerobic bacteria, and is thought to work by reducing bacterial byproducts and altering gut flora. It is prescribed as a 14-day course for acute and recurrent symptoms and has no significant adverse effects, though it is a high-cost medication.

bullets.text: Amitriptyline and dicyclomine may reduce IBS-D symptoms but lack the evidence strength of rifaximin; linaclotide and lubiprostone are indicated for IBS-C, not IBS-D.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Low-dose amitriptyline and dicyclomine are often effective in reducing IBS-D symptoms, but the evidence supporting their use is not as strong as that for rifaximin. Linaclotide is used for constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C), and its chief side effect of diarrhea causes many patients to discontinue it. Lubiprostone is similarly indicated for IBS-C and opioid-induced constipation, making it inappropriate for IBS-D.

explanation_raw: According to the 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guidelines for diarrheapredominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D), the nonabsorbable antibiotic rifaximin has the best evidence for controlling diarrhea, discomfort, bloating, and abdominal pain. It has a broad spectrum with activity against gram-positive, gram-negative (including Clostridioides difficile), and anaerobic bacteria. It is thought to work by reducing bacterial byproducts and altering the gut flora. It is prescribed as a 14-day course for acute and recurrent symptoms. Rifaximin does not have any significant adverse effects, but it is a high-cost medication. Low-dose amitriptyline and dicyclomine are often effective in reducing symptoms, but the evidence is not as strong as that of rifaximin. Linaclotide is used for constipationpredominant IBS (IBS-C), but its chief side effect of diarrhea results in many patients discontinuing the medication. Lubiprostone is another medication used for IBS-C and for opioid-induced constipation, not IBS-D.

stem: A 56-year-old female with moderately controlled type 2 diabetes presents with painful diabetic neuropathy in her feet. You address her diabetic control and other risk factors, but she says the pain continues and is affecting her life adversely. Which one of the following is considered a first-line treatment for pain relief in this condition?

bullets.text: First-line treatments for painful diabetic neuropathy include amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, and pregabalin; opioids should be avoided.
bullets.sub_paragraph: First-line treatments for the relief of painful diabetic neuropathy include amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, and pregabalin. Second-line treatments include topical lidocaine and capsaicin, which have less evidence of benefit. Opioids such as hydrocodone should be avoided in the treatment of neuropathic pain. Studies of peripheral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) have shown only modest benefit and it is not considered a first-line treatment.

explanation_raw: First-line treatments for the relief of painful diabetic neuropathy include amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, and pregabalin.
