Second-line treatments include topical lidocaine and capsaicin, with less evidence of benefit. Opioids such as hydrocodone should be avoided in the treatment of neuropathic pain. Studies of peripheral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation have shown modest benefit; however, it is not a first-line treatment.

stem: A generally healthy 60-year-old female presents to your office because she is concerned about urinary leakage. Her symptoms started a couple of years ago and have worsened. The leakage occurs when she coughs or laughs, but can also happen if she waits too long to urinate. She hydrates throughout the day. She does not take any medications and does not smoke. She has a remote surgical history of a hysterectomy after delivering her third child. She does not have any fever or abdominal pain and has not been exposed to any sexually transmitted infections. Recent laboratory studies, including a CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, TSH level, and hemoglobin A1c, were unremarkable. Today she has a blood pressure of 120/70 mm Hg and a BMI of 32 kg/m2. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the workup?

bullets.text: Urinalysis should be ordered for all patients with urinary incontinence as part of the initial evaluation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Urinary incontinence is common among women and can substantially diminish quality of life. The initial evaluation includes a thorough history to establish whether incontinence is transient or chronic, identify the subtype, and screen for red flags (e.g., pelvic organ prolapse, fistula) warranting subspecialist referral. Urinalysis is recommended for all patients. Additional helpful tools include an incontinence screening questionnaire, cough stress test (SOR C), postvoid residual measurement, and a 3-day voiding diary.

bullets.text: Renal and bladder ultrasonography, urodynamic testing, and cystoscopy are not recommended for the initial evaluation of uncomplicated urinary incontinence.
bullets.sub_paragraph: These more advanced studies are not indicated in the initial workup of uncomplicated urinary incontinence. They may be appropriate for complex or refractory cases or when subspecialist referral is warranted, but should not replace the basic initial evaluation anchored by history, physical examination, and urinalysis.

bullets.text: First-line treatments include weight loss, pelvic floor training, lifestyle modifications, smoking cessation, and pharmacologic therapy; refractory cases may require more invasive options.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Risk factors for urinary incontinence include obesity, parity, increasing age, and prior hysterectomy. Conservative management focuses on weight loss, pelvic floor muscle training, appropriate fluid intake, and smoking cessation. Pharmacologic therapy can be added as needed. Patients with refractory incontinence can be referred for invasive treatments such as mechanical devices, intravesical onabotulinumtoxinA injection, or surgical procedures.

explanation_raw: Urinary incontinence is common among women and can substantially diminish quality of life while contributing to increased financial strain. Risk factors include obesity, parity, increasing age, and a history of hysterectomy. The initial evaluation includes a thorough history and should establish whether the incontinence is transient or chronic. It should also identify the incontinence subtype as well as any red flags that would warrant subspecialist referral, such as pelvic organ prolapse or fistula. Urinalysis should be ordered for all patients with urinary incontinence. An incontinence screening questionnaire, cough stress test (SOR C), postvoid residual measurement, and a 3-day voiding diary are helpful tools. Renal and bladder ultrasonography, urodynamic testing, and cystoscopy are not recommended for the initial evaluation of uncomplicated urinary incontinence. Treatments include weight loss, pelvic floor training, lifestyle modifications including appropriate fluid intake, smoking cessation, and pharmacologic therapy. Patients with refractory urinary incontinence can be referred for more invasive treatments, such as mechanical devices, intravesical onabotulinumtoxinA injection, and surgical procedures.

stem: A 68-year-old female with previously diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia presents to your office to establish care. She has no current bleeding. A CBC is normal except for a platelet count of 47,000/mm3 (N 130,000–400,000). You refer her to a hematologist for long-term management. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's current thrombocytopenia?

bullets.text: Per American Society of Hematology guidelines, ITP does not require treatment unless there is active bleeding or a platelet count <30,000/mm³.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has a platelet count of 47,000/mm³ and no active bleeding, so no treatment is indicated at this time. The threshold for initiating therapy in ITP is active bleeding or a platelet count below 30,000/mm³. Corticosteroids, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin are all valid treatment options when therapy is needed, but hydroxychloroquine is not a recommended agent for ITP.

explanation_raw: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is caused by autoimmune destruction of platelets in the spleen and causes chronic thrombocytopenia of varying severity. Although hematologists typically oversee care for patients with ITP, family physicians may need to make acute treatment decisions in collaboration with these patients. The American Society of Hematology recommends not to treat ITP unless there is active bleeding or very low platelet counts, defined as <30,000/mm3. This patient does not require treatment at this time because she does not have any current bleeding and her platelet count is above the threshold for treatment. Corticosteroids and rituximab are both used to treat ITP, along with intravenous immunoglobulin. Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is not typically recommended in the treatment of ITP.

stem: A 45-year-old male who is living with HIV and has been on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for the past 10 years presents for routine follow-up. Which one of the following would be part of an appropriate screening strategy for long-term complications associated with HAART?

choices.A: Calculation of the Framingham Risk Score now, and a fasting lipid profile annually
choices.E: Urinalysis annually, and a glomerular filtration rate twice yearly

correct_label: Urinalysis annually, and a glomerular filtration rate twice yearly

bullets.text: The IDSA recommends urinalysis at least annually and GFR at least twice yearly in stable HAART patients to detect kidney function abnormalities and drug nephrotoxicity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends performing urinalysis at least once yearly and obtaining a glomerular filtration rate at least twice yearly in stable patients on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to detect kidney function abnormalities and drug nephrotoxicity. This reflects the nephrotoxic potential of certain antiretroviral agents (e.g., tenofovir) and the importance of early detection of renal complications in this population.

bullets.text: Framingham Risk Score is not well validated in HIV patients; neurocognitive, liver fibrosis, and bone density screenings are indication-based rather than routine annual screens for all HAART patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While cardiovascular risk assessment is important in persons living with HIV, the Framingham Risk Score is not well validated in this population; ACC/AHA recommend using traditional risk factors and clinical judgment instead. Neurocognitive screening is performed based on clinical indications, not as a routine annual screen. Liver fibrosis screening is appropriate only in patients coinfected with hepatitis B or C, not as universal annual screening. Bone mineral density screening is important in at-risk HIV patients but is not recommended annually for all patients on HAART.

explanation_raw: The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends performing urinalysis at least once yearly and obtaining a glomerular filtration rate at least twice yearly in stable patients on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to detect kidney function abnormalities and drug nephrotoxicity. While cardiovascular risk assessment is important in persons living with HIV, the Framingham Risk Score is not well validated in this population. The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association recommend using traditional risk factors and clinical judgment for cardiovascular risk assessment in this population. Neurocognitive screening is typically performed based on clinical indications rather than as an annual routine screening for all patients on HAART. Liver fibrosis screening is appropriate in patients with coinfection with hepatitis B or C, but it is not a routine annual screening. Although bone mineral density screening is important in persons living with HIV, especially those at risk for osteoporosis, it is not recommended annually for all patients on HAART.

stem: A 40-year-old male with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with chest pain and shortness of breath. The patient has normal vital signs. A physical examination and laboratory tests, including serial troponin levels, are normal. Outpatient records from about 6 months ago include a normal cardiac stress test that was negative for myocardial ischemia. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

bullets.text: For an intermediate-risk patient with suspected angina, negative ACS workup, and prior negative stress test within 1 year, coronary CT angiography is the next best step to evaluate for obstructive CAD or atherosclerotic plaques.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Coronary CT angiography is appropriate for intermediate-risk patients with no prior history of CAD who present with angina-like symptoms and have had a negative acute coronary syndrome workup (including serial troponins) along with a negative stress test within the past year. It provides anatomical detail to identify obstructive CAD or subclinical atherosclerotic plaques that functional testing may miss.

bullets.text: Repeat stress testing is not indicated given a recent negative result; fractional flow reserve-CT is reserved for guiding revascularization after an abnormal coronary CT angiogram; cardiac MRI is best used to evaluate structural or myocardial abnormalities.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A repeat stress test would be redundant given the documented negative stress test within the past 6 months. Fractional flow reserve derived from CT (FFR-CT) is a follow-up tool used when coronary CT angiography has already identified significant vessel stenosis, helping to guide decisions about revascularization. Cardiac MRI is most useful when structural heart disease, cardiomyopathy, or myocarditis is suspected, which is not the primary concern in this clinical scenario.

explanation_raw: For this intermediate-risk patient with no history of coronary artery disease (CAD) who presents with angina and a negative workup for acute coronary syndrome plus negative stress testing within 1 year, coronary CT angiography would be the next step to determine if he has obstructive CAD or atherosclerotic plaques. A repeat stress test would not be indicated. Fractional flow reserve with CT is useful to help guide revascularization after an abnormal coronary CT angiogram reveals vessel stenosis. Cardiac MRI would be useful to determine structural abnormalities.

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder presents to your office for help abstaining from alcohol. Until recently, he has been drinking at least 6 beers per day and often more on weekend days. He has 2 prior arrests for DUI, and his wife plans to file for divorce if he does not change. Over the past 2 weeks, he has been able to wean himself off alcohol and has joined a sobriety group. He requests medication to help him maintain his sobriety. Which one of the following medications should you recommend for this patient?

bullets.text: Acamprosate is the recommended first-line pharmacotherapy for patients with alcohol use disorder who have already achieved abstinence and wish to maintain it (SOR A).
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient meets criteria for moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD). Although AUD is a leading cause of preventable death, less than 2% of patients with AUD are prescribed medications. Acamprosate is recommended for patients who have achieved abstinence and desire to maintain it (SOR A). Gabapentin is useful for the prevention of withdrawal and is safe for those who are still drinking (SOR A). Topiramate is useful in decreasing heavy drinking (SOR B). There is insufficient evidence to recommend disulfiram.

explanation_raw: This patient meets criteria for moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD). Although AUD is a leading cause of preventable death, less than 2% of patients with AUD are prescribed medications. Acamprosate is recommended for patients who have achieved abstinence and desire to maintain it (SOR A). Gabapentin is useful for the prevention of withdrawal and is safe for those who are still drinking (SOR A). Topiramate is useful in decreasing heavy drinking (SOR B). There is insufficient evidence to recommend disulfiram.

stem: A 15-year-old male presents to your office with an intensely pruritic rash 2 days after returning from a camping trip in the woods. On examination you observe a rash on the hands, arms, face, and genitals with vesicles and a few bullae. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment option?

choices.A: Topical clobetasol, applied twice daily to affected areas until symptoms resolve
choices.B: Oral methylprednisolone, starting at 1 mg/kg and tapering over 5 days
choices.C: Oral prednisone, starting at 1 mg/kg and tapering over 15 days
choices.E: Draining the bullae and large vesicles

correct_label: Oral prednisone, starting at 1 mg/kg and tapering over 15 days

bullets.text: This presentation is classic for allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy (Toxicodendron species), a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction triggered by the oleoresin urushiol.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Poison ivy is the most common cause of allergic contact dermatitis in the US, affecting up to 10 million people annually. Caused by urushiol found in Toxicodendron species (poison ivy, sumac, oak), symptoms develop 12–72 hours after exposure and require prior sensitization. The rash can present as irregular erythematous patches, linear streaks of vesicles, or larger bullae. Importantly, blister fluid does NOT spread the rash — the apparent spreading is due to time variability in rash development based on the amount of resin contact.

bullets.text: Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 1 mg/kg, tapering over 15 days) are the most appropriate treatment when facial, genital, or significant vesiculobullous involvement is present.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In type IV hypersensitivity reactions, rebound inflammation occurs if corticosteroid treatment is insufficient in dose or duration. A 15-day prednisone taper starting at 1 mg/kg (maximum 60 mg) is the most effective approach. A common pitfall is prescribing a 5-day methylprednisolone dose pack, which provides only temporary relief and is frequently followed by rebound rash due to inadequate dose and duration. A single injection of triamcinolone has variable efficacy and slower onset than oral prednisone; if used, it must be given intramuscularly (never subcutaneously) to avoid lipoatrophy. Topical corticosteroids, even potent formulations, are ineffective on bullous lesions and are contraindicated on the face and genitals. There is no indication for draining vesicles or bullae.

explanation_raw: Poison ivy is perhaps the most common cause of allergic contact dermatitis in the United States, causing up to 10 million persons annually to seek medical care. Caused by the oleoresin urushiol that is present in Toxicodendron species (poison ivy, sumac, oak), allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Symptoms develop 12–72 hours after exposure. Prior sensitization is necessary. The rash has varying presentations, including irregular erythematous patches, linear streaks of vesicles, and larger fluid-filled bullae. The blister fluid does not cause the rash to spread. This illusion of spreading is due to the time variability in when the rash develops (hours to days) based on how much resin was in contact with the skin. Systemic corticosteroids are indicated for facial, genital, or significant vesiculobullous involvement. In type IV hypersensitivity reactions, rebound inflammation occurs if treatment with corticosteroids is insufficient in dose or duration. The most effective treatment in this patient would be a 15-day prednisone taper, starting with 1 mg/kg (60 mg at maximum). A single injection of triamcinolone has variable efficacy and often does not take effect as quickly as oral prednisone; however, if used, it should be administered intramuscularly, never subcutaneously, due to the likelihood of lipoatrophy. Topical corticosteroids, even the most potent formulations, do not work on bullous lesions and are contraindicated on the face and genitals. A common prescription for poison ivy dermatitis is a 5-day dose pack of methylprednisolone. This provides temporary improvement but is frequently followed by a rebound in rash, which indicates an insufficient dose and duration of the corticosteroid. There is no indication for draining the bullae or vesicles in this patient.

stem: A 50-year-old male sees you for follow-up of a pulmonary nodule. He recently presented to the emergency department (E

choices.D: Biopsy of the nodule to determine pathology
choices.B: A repeat CT scan in 6–12 months
choices.C: A repeat CT scan in 18–24 months

correct_label: A repeat CT scan in 6–12 months

bullets.text: A solid pulmonary nodule between 6–8 mm should be monitored with a repeat CT chest in 6–12 months.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Evaluation of a pulmonary nodule requires balancing minimal testing for likely benign nodules against the risk of missing malignancy. Solid nodules are classified by size: small solid nodules (6–8 mm) warrant repeat CT in 6–12 months, while larger solid nodules (8–30 mm) or subsolid nodules carry higher malignancy risk and should prompt pulmonology referral. A solid nodule unchanged over 2 or more years on CT is considered benign. Flexibility in follow-up intervals accommodates nodule features beyond size and patient/clinician preferences.

explanation_raw: Evaluation of a pulmonary nodule balances the benefits of minimal testing for benign nodules with the risks of malignant nodules. It requires knowledge of the factors associated with the probability that the nodule is malignant, the performance characteristics of additional testing, and the advantages and disadvantages of more or less intensive follow-up. The probability of malignancy and the effectiveness of diagnostic tests depend on the size and characteristics of the nodule, which can be classified into 3 categories: small solid nodules, larger solid nodules, and subsolid nodules. A solid nodule between 6 mm and 8 mm should be monitored with CT of the chest in 6–12 months. Flexibility in these time intervals (eg, 3–6 months, 6–12 months) is included in the guidelines to accommodate nodule features other than size, as well as clinician and patient preferences. A solid nodule that has remained unchanged in size on chest CT over a period of 2 years or longer is considered benign. Primary care physicians should consider referral to a pulmonologist for patients with a larger solid nodule (8–30 mm) or a subsolid nodule due to their higher risk of malignancy.

stem: On examination she is neurovascularly intact. Her vital signs are normal except for an elevated heart rate of 110 beats/min and a blood pressure of 150/92 mm Hg. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's injury?

choices.B: Observation in the ED, and acetaminophen
choices.C: Observation in the ED, and ibuprofen

bullets.text: The question stem describes a concussion/injury scenario, but the explanation addresses upper GI bleeding management — the core pearl is to initiate a proton pump inhibitor immediately on presentation regardless of endoscopy status.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient likely has an upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed from erosive gastritis or peptic ulcer disease, suggested by abdominal pain, nausea, consistent NSAID (ibuprofen) use with alcohol, elevated BUN, and anemia. Current guidelines recommend initiating a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) at presentation without delay, regardless of endoscopy timing or status.

bullets.text: Urgent endoscopy is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients; blood transfusion is indicated when hemoglobin is <7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL in high-risk cardiac patients); nasogastric lavage is not supported by guidelines.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Because this patient is hemodynamically stable and his hemoglobin is above the transfusion threshold (<7 g/dL for most patients, <8 g/dL for those with coronary artery disease, recent cardiac surgery, or hematologic malignancies), urgent endoscopy and blood transfusion are not yet indicated. Nasogastric lavage lacks randomized controlled trial or guideline support. Arterial embolization is only considered after endoscopy has failed to control bleeding.

explanation_raw: This patient likely has an upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed from erosive gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. This is suggested by a history of abdominal pain and nausea and the consistent use of ibuprofen with alcohol. The patient's BUN is elevated, and his hemoglobin level shows anemia. Given that the patient is hemodynamically stable and his hemoglobin level is above the transfusion threshold, he does not need excessive workup prior to treatment, but guidelines recommend initiating a proton pump inhibitor on presentation with no delay regardless of status for endoscopy. Urgent endoscopy is only indicated in patients with hemodynamic instability and signs of upper GI bleeding. There are no randomized, controlled trials or guidelines to support the use of nasogastric lavage. Current guidelines recommend blood transfusion for patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding when the hemoglobin level is <7 g/dL in most cases or <8 g/dL (80 g/L) in patients with coronary artery disease, recent cardiac surgery, or hematologic malignancies. Arterial embolization is only performed if endoscopy has failed to control bleeding.

stem: You see a 6-month-old infant for a routine visit. The child has started teething and the parents are concerned about preventing cavities, as their municipality does not fluoridate the water. In addition to providing daily oral fluoride supplementation, which one of the following should you recommend?

choices.A: Brushing the emerging teeth daily with a rice-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste
choices.B: Using mouthwash as an adjunct to toothbrushing until age 5
choices.C: Application of fluoride varnish to teeth annually, starting at age 1
choices.D: Application of fluoride varnish to teeth twice yearly, starting at age 3

correct_label: Brushing the emerging teeth daily with a rice-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste

bullets.text: Infants and toddlers should have their emerging teeth brushed once or twice daily with a rice-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste, increasing to a pea-sized amount at age 3.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fluoride is a key tool in preventing dental caries. When community water is not fluoridated, dietary fluoride supplements are recommended. Additionally, parents should brush their infant's teeth with a rice-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste starting at tooth emergence, increasing to a pea-sized amount at age 3. Fluoride varnish should be applied every 3–6 months depending on caries risk, starting with the first tooth.

bullets.text: Mouthwash (with or without fluoride) should not be used in children under age 6, and children may begin more independent toothbrushing around age 6, though some may still need assistance.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Children under age 6 are at risk of swallowing toothpaste or mouthwash, which can lead to dental fluorosis—permanent brownish staining of the teeth. Fluoride mouthwash can be introduced after age 6 only if the child can reliably spit rather than swallow. Toothbrushing independence may begin around age 6, but parental oversight is still often needed to ensure adequate technique.

explanation_raw: Fluoride is widely recognized for its role in preventing dental caries, and community water fluoridation remains a safe, effective, and evidence-based strategy for improving oral health. Dietary supplements are recommended for infants and children when the community water supply is nonfluoridated. It is also recommended for parents to brush the teeth of infants and toddlers once or twice daily with a rice-sized amount of fluoridated toothpaste, increasing to a pea-sized amount of toothpaste at age 3. At age 6, children are less likely to swallow toothpaste, which can lead to fluorosis (permanent brownish staining of teeth). Children may be more independent in toothbrushing starting at age 6, although some may still need assistance for adequate brushing. Mouthwash with or without fluoride should not be used in children younger than 6 years. It can be used after age 6 if the child can reliably spit out the mouthwash rather than swallow it. Starting at the emergence of the first tooth, fluoride varnish should be applied every 3 months for children at high risk of caries and every 6 months for all other children.

stem: A 75-year-old male presents to your office with his family. Although he is a long-term patient of yours, you have not seen him in more than 1 year. His family tells you that they have noticed a gradual progression of neurologic symptoms over the past 6 months, including a noticeably slower gait and a tremor of his right hand. The patient says that he has noticed worsening short-term memory loss. On examination, the patient has a flat affect and speaks slowly. You observe a shuffling gait and a resting pill-rolling tremor of his right hand. You also note cogwheel rigidity of his right arm. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial medication for the treatment of this patient's condition?

bullets.text: This patient's gradual progression of neurologic symptoms is consistent with Parkinson disease, making carbidopa/levodopa the appropriate first-line treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient likely presents with Parkinson disease based on hallmark symptoms and physical examination findings. First-line medications for Parkinson disease include carbidopa/levodopa, monoamine oxidase-B inhibitors, and nonergot dopamine agonists. It is important to distinguish Parkinson disease from essential tremor, as propranolol is effective for essential tremor but this patient's overall clinical picture is more indicative of Parkinson disease.

bullets.text: Amitriptyline, fluoxetine, gabapentin, and propranolol are not appropriate for this presentation—several are on the Beers Criteria list and none address the underlying dopaminergic deficit of Parkinson disease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant used for depression and neuropathic pain, but it is on the Beers Criteria list and must be used with great caution in older patients. Fluoxetine is prescribed for major depressive disorder, which is not the primary diagnosis here, and the Beers Criteria also cautions against its use in older patients. Gabapentin is typically used for partial seizures and postherpetic neuralgia and has no role in Parkinson disease management. Propranolol is effective for essential tremor but does not address the broader motor features characteristic of Parkinson disease.

explanation_raw: This patient likely presents with Parkinson disease based on the hallmark symptoms and physical examination findings. First-line medications for Parkinson disease are carbidopa/levodopa, monoamine oxidase-B inhibitors, and nonergot dopamine agonists. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant that is commonly used for treatment of depression and neuropathic pain. It is on the Beers Criteria list and must be used with great caution in older patients. Fluoxetine is typically prescribed for major depressive disorder, which is likely not the primary diagnosis in this patient. Furthermore, the Beers Criteria list cautions against prescribing fluoxetine in older patients. Gabapentin is typically used for partial seizures and postherpetic neuralgia. Propranolol hydrochloride is effective for management of essential tremor, but this patient's clinical picture is more indicative of Parkinson disease.

stem: A 26-year-old female presents to your clinic because of headache and vision changes. She has also noticed an increase in the size of her hands and feet, changes to her facial features, carpal tunnel symptoms, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and menstrual irregularities. MRI of the brain shows a 7-mm pituitary adenoma. Which one of the following diagnostic tests is most likely to be abnormal in this patient?

choices.D: A serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level

correct_label: A serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level

bullets.text: Acromegaly caused by a somatotroph adenoma is diagnosed by an elevated serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's presentation — enlarged hands and feet, facial feature changes, carpal tunnel symptoms, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and menstrual irregularities — is classic for acromegaly secondary to a growth hormone-secreting (somatotroph) pituitary adenoma. The initial diagnostic test of choice is a serum IGF-1 level, which reflects integrated GH secretion and is elevated in acromegaly.

bullets.text: Other pituitary adenoma subtypes present with distinct clinical syndromes and are confirmed by different laboratory tests.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Corticotroph adenomas (ACTH-secreting) cause Cushing disease and are diagnosed with a dexamethasone suppression test. Lactotroph adenomas (prolactin-secreting) cause galactorrhea, decreased libido, and amenorrhea, diagnosed with a serum prolactin level. Thyrotroph adenomas (TSH-secreting) cause hyperthyroidism symptoms such as weight loss, palpitations, and heat intolerance, diagnosed with elevated TSH and free T4 levels. None of these match this patient's acromegalic features.

explanation_raw: Pituitary adenomas are classified according to their primary cell origin and the specific hormones they produce. Somatotroph adenomas secrete growth hormone and cause symptoms consistent with acromegaly, including an increase in hand and foot size, enlargement of the mandible, carpal tunnel symptoms, fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, and menstrual irregularities. Somatotroph adenomas are diagnosed by a high serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level. Corticotroph adenomas secrete corticotropin (ACTH) and cause symptoms consistent with Cushing disease such as mood changes, weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, and menstrual irregularity. Corticotroph adenomas can be diagnosed by an abnormal result on a dexamethasone suppression test. Lactotroph adenomas secrete prolactin and cause symptoms consistent with hyperprolactinemia such as galactorrhea, decreased libido, and oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea. Lactotroph adenomas can be diagnosed with an elevated serum prolactin level. Thyrotroph adenomas secrete TSH and cause symptoms consistent with hyperthyroidism such as weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, and anxiety. Thyrotroph adenomas can be diagnosed with elevated TSH, free T4, and total T4 levels.

stem: An otherwise healthy 52-year-old female with a past surgical history of hysterectomy for the treatment of uterine fibroids presents with increasing episodes of hot flashes lasting 3–5 minutes and occurring 5–10 times per day over the past 5 months. She finds the symptoms highly disruptive and is interested in options for medical therapy. Which one of the following would be the most effective therapy for this patient's symptoms?

bullets.text: Oral or transdermal estrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms in menopausal women (SOR A), and is the preferred choice for a post-hysterectomy patient who needs no progestogen.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Oral or transdermal estrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms in menopausal women (SOR A). Because this patient has had a hysterectomy, she has no uterus and therefore does not require a progestogen to protect against endometrial hyperplasia, making estrogen-only therapy (e.g., a transdermal estradiol patch) the ideal choice. Vaginal estrogen cream is reserved for women whose primary complaint is vaginal atrophy rather than vasomotor symptoms.

bullets.text: SSRIs/SNRIs (e.g., paroxetine) are effective second-line alternatives, testosterone is not effective for vasomotor symptoms, and phytoestrogens such as soy have not been shown to consistently improve hot flashes (SOR B).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Antidepressants including SSRIs and SNRIs are effective alternatives to hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms (SOR A), with paroxetine being the only FDA-approved non-hormonal option for this indication; however, they are less effective than estrogen and are typically used when hormone therapy is contraindicated. Testosterone therapy has no established efficacy for vasomotor symptoms. Phytoestrogen supplements such as soy have not been shown to consistently improve menopausal vasomotor symptoms (SOR B) and are not recommended as primary therapy.

explanation_raw: Oral or transdermal estrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms in menopausal women (SOR A). Antidepressants, including SSRIs and SNRIs, are effective alternatives to hormone therapy for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms in menopause (SOR A). The SSRI paroxetine is FDA approved for this indication. Testosterone therapy is not effective for vasomotor symptoms. Vaginal estrogen cream is recommended for women whose primary symptoms are vaginal rather than vasomotor. Phytoestrogen supplements such as soy have not been shown to consistently improve vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause (SOR B).

stem: A 25-year-old male is brought to the level 1 trauma center with a gunshot wound. He is awake, alert, and oriented, and has full capacity for decision-making. The patient then becomes hemodynamically unstable with a blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg, a heart rate of 140 beats/min, and a hemoglobin level of 4.0 g/dL (N 14.0–18.0). Whole blood transfusion is indicated, but the patient refuses blood products as he is a practicing Jehovah's Witness. An advance directive on file at the hospital confirms this. He is aware that not administering blood will most likely cause his death. You disagree with the patient and would like to administer a whole blood transfusion as his condition is life-threatening. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Presenting the case to the ethics committee
choices.B: Respecting the patient's wishes by avoiding transfusion
choices.C: Consulting the patient's family and administering whole blood with their approval

correct_label: Respecting the patient's wishes by avoiding transfusion

bullets.text: A competent patient's autonomous refusal of treatment must be respected, even if it leads to adverse outcomes — blood refusal directives are legally binding and violating them can expose physicians to liability for infringing on religious freedom.
bullets.sub_paragraph: When a patient has either an advance directive or demonstrates decision-making capacity, their autonomous refusal of treatment must be respected, even if it leads to adverse medical outcomes or conflicts with the physician's values or ethical beliefs. Blood refusal directives are considered legally binding, and physicians have been found liable for violating religious freedom when overriding these directives. Transfusion of blood products may be permissible for patients who are Jehovah's Witnesses only if they are incapacitated, require transfusion, and do not have a blood refusal directive or a surrogate decision-maker available.

explanation_raw: When a patient has either an advance directive or demonstrates decision-making capacity, their autonomous refusal of treatment must be respected, even if it leads to adverse medical outcomes or conflicts with the physician's values or ethical beliefs. Blood refusal directives are considered legally binding and physicians have been found liable for violating religious freedom when violating these directives. Transfusion of blood products may be permissible for patients who are Jehovah's Witnesses if they are incapacitated and require transfusion but do not have a blood refusal directive or surrogate decision-maker.

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with a 45-minute history of persistent bleeding from his left nostril. He has a medical history of aortic stenosis with a mechanical aortic valve replacement, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. His medications include hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril (Zestril), metformin, and warfarin. A physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 170/100 mm Hg without orthostatic change and a heart rate of 90 beats/min. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate first step in the treatment of this patient's nosebleed?

choices.A: Digital compression of the lower nares for 20 minutes

correct_label: Digital compression of the lower nares for 20 minutes

bullets.text: The first-line treatment for a hemodynamically stable patient with epistaxis is digital compression (pinching the lower third of the nose) for 15–20 minutes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The initial treatment of a hemodynamically stable patient with epistaxis is to pinch the lower third of the nose for 15–20 minutes. If digital compression fails and an anterior bleeding site is visualized on rhinoscopy, the next step is to apply topical vasoconstrictors or perform chemical/electrical cautery. If local measures continue to fail, anterior nasal packing is indicated. Acute reversal of anticoagulation is reserved for patients with ongoing bleeding who are hemodynamically unstable.

explanation_raw: The initial treatment of a hemodynamically stable patient with epistaxis is to pinch the lower third of the nose for 15–20 minutes. If digital compression is not successful in stopping the bleeding and an anterior bleeding site is visualized on anterior rhinoscopy, then the next step would be to either apply topical vasoconstrictors or use chemical/electrical cautery. If bleeding continues after local measures fail, then anterior nasal packing would be indicated. Acute reversal of anticoagulation should be considered in a patient with ongoing bleeding who is hemodynamically unstable.

stem: An 80-year-old male presents to your office for follow-up of stable angina. He has a medical history of coronary artery disease with placement of a single drug-eluting stent, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertension. His most recent echocardiogram demonstrated a normal ejection fraction. He does not want additional cardiovascular intervention and prefers you to handle all of his care in the future. The patient’s current medications include the following: Aspirin, 81 mg daily Carvedilol (Coreg), 12.5 mg twice daily Empagliflozin (Jardiance), 10 mg daily Losartan (Cozaar), 50 mg daily On examination he has a blood pressure of 140/85 mm Hg, a heart rate of 52 beats/min, and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. A cardiopulmonary examination is within normal limits and an EKG is unchanged from past EKGs. Which one of the following changes to this patient’s medication regimen would be most appropriate to decrease his anginal symptoms?

bullets.text: When angina symptoms persist despite maximally tolerated doses of a single first-line agent, a medication from a different first-line class should be added; for this patient, isosorbide mononitrate is the most appropriate next step.
bullets.sub_paragraph: β-Blockers, calcium channel blockers, and long-acting nitrates are all first-line agents for symptomatic stable angina. If a patient remains symptomatic on a maximally tolerated dose of one agent, guidelines recommend adding a drug from a different first-line class. Adding isosorbide mononitrate is appropriate here, though it may lower blood pressure and warrants close monitoring at follow-up.

bullets.text: Increasing carvedilol is inappropriate given relative bradycardia; ranolazine is reserved for patients already on two other classes; empagliflozin and clopidogrel do not reduce anginal symptoms; ivabradine is contraindicated in chronic coronary disease with normal ejection fraction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Increasing carvedilol is unsafe because the patient already has relative bradycardia. Ranolazine is a reasonable option but is typically added only after two other anti-anginal classes are in use, and it is more costly. Neither increasing empagliflozin (an SGLT-2 inhibitor with cardiorenal benefits but no direct anti-anginal effect) nor adding clopidogrel (an antiplatelet agent) addresses anginal symptoms. Ivabradine reduces heart rate via HCN-channel inhibition and is contraindicated—and potentially harmful—in patients with chronic coronary artery disease who have a normal ejection fraction.

explanation_raw: β-Blockers, calcium channel blockers, and long-acting nitrates are first-line medications to decrease symptoms in patients with angina. If symptoms persist despite the use of a maximally tolerated dose of a single first-line medication, an additional drug from a different class should be introduced. Adding isosorbide mononitrate is the most appropriate option for this patient; however, it may decrease his blood pressure and will require close attention on follow-up. Ranolazine is another potential recommendation but is often more costly than alternatives. It is recommended in patients who are already taking medications from 2 other classes. Increasing the patient's carvedilol is not recommended due to his relative bradycardia. Neither increasing empagliflozin nor adding clopidogrel helps to decrease anginal symptoms. Ivabradine is contraindicated in patients with chronic coronary disease and normal ejection fraction and is potentially harmful.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents because of a 4-week history of difficulty sleeping following the death of her partner of 2 years. She has difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep and reports daytime sleepiness. Her symptoms have not improved despite attending grief counseling sessions. She requests nonpharmacologic treatment for her insomnia. Which one of the following is a component of sleep hygiene education for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia?

choices.C: Waking up at the same time every day
choices.D: Placing a digital clock next to the bed

correct_label: Waking up at the same time every day

bullets.text: Acute insomnia is defined as difficulty initiating and/or maintaining sleep occurring ≥3 days per week for 1 week to 3 months, often triggered by a precipitating life event or psychological distress.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute insomnia is a sleep continuity disturbance, defined as difficulty initiating and/or maintaining sleep, that occurs ≥3 days per week with a duration of 1 week to 3 months. It is often associated with a precipitating factor such as life events or psychological distress. The first step in management is identifying and treating the underlying cause.

bullets.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment, consisting of three categories: sleep hygiene education, sleep restriction, and stimulus control.
bullets.sub_paragraph: CBT-I is an effective, non-pharmacologic treatment for insomnia and is preferred as first-line therapy, especially for patients who wish to avoid medications. It encompasses three main categories: (1) Sleep hygiene education — includes waking up at the same time every day and avoiding daytime naps; (2) Stimulus control — going to bed only when sleepy and reserving the bedroom for sleep and sex; (3) Sleep restriction — reducing time in bed and gradually increasing it by 15 minutes per week once sleep efficiency reaches 90%.

bullets.text: Waking up at the same time every day is a sleep hygiene education component of CBT-I, distinct from stimulus control (e.g., going to bed only when sleepy) and sleep restriction techniques.
bullets.sub_paragraph: It is important to distinguish the three CBT-I categories on board exams. Waking up at the same time every day and not napping are sleep hygiene measures. Going to bed only when sleepy and reserving the bed for sleep/sex are stimulus control strategies. Limiting total time in bed and gradually extending it based on sleep efficiency is sleep restriction.

explanation_raw: Acute insomnia is a sleep continuity disturbance, defined as difficulty initiating and/or maintaining sleep, that occurs ≥3 days per week with a duration of 1 week to 3 months. It is often associated with a precipitating factor such as life events or psychological distress. The first step in the management of acute insomnia is identifying and treating the underlying cause. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is an effective treatment for insomnia and may be offered as first-line therapy, especially in patients who wish to avoid pharmacotherapy. CBT-I has 3 categories: sleep hygiene education, sleep restriction, and stimulus control. Waking up at the same time every day and not napping during the day are among the 8 components of sleep hygiene education. Stimulus control strategies include going to bed only when sleepy and reserving the bedroom for sleep and sex. Sleep restriction techniques involve reducing time spent in bed followed by gradually increasing it by 15 minutes each week once sleep efficiency reaches 90%.

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with classic symptoms of mild hypothyroidism including cold intolerance, mild fatigue, and constipation. Her TSH level is 6.0 μU/mL (N 0.4–4.2) and her free T4 level is within normal limits. A pregnancy test is negative. Which one of the following factors, if present, would be an indication for prescribing levothyroxine (Synthroid)?

choices.A: A repeat TSH level in 4–6 weeks remains at 6.0 μU/mL
choices.B: A repeat TSH level in 4–6 weeks increases to 8.0 μU/mL
choices.D: An elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody level

correct_label: An elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody level

bullets.text: This patient has subclinical hypothyroidism, defined as an elevated TSH (<10 μU/mL) with a normal free T4 level.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by a TSH level that is abnormal but less than 10 μU/mL while the free T4 level remains within the normal range. Because the signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism can be nonspecific, diagnosis is based on blood levels of TSH and free T4. Hypothyroidism affects approximately 1 in 300 individuals in the United States, with a higher prevalence among women and older adults.

bullets.text: Nonpregnant patients with subclinical hypothyroidism should only be treated with thyroid hormone replacement if the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody level is elevated or the TSH is >10 μU/mL (SOR A).
bullets.sub_paragraph: An elevated TPO antibody level indicates autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease) and significantly increases the risk of progression to overt hypothyroidism, justifying treatment initiation even when TSH is below 10 μU/mL. Additionally, treatment-resistant depression (but not treatment-resistant constipation) is a recognized indication for treating subclinical hypothyroidism. Evaluating total or free T3 levels is not routinely indicated in this setting.

bullets.text: Elevated T3 levels, treatment-resistant constipation, or a TSH that remains below 10 μU/mL without TPO antibodies do not independently justify initiating thyroid hormone replacement therapy in subclinical hypothyroidism.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Measuring total or free T3 is not routinely indicated in the workup of subclinical hypothyroidism and would not change the management decision. Treatment-resistant constipation alone is not a guideline-supported indication for treatment, unlike treatment-resistant depression. The threshold for treatment based on TSH alone is greater than 10 μU/mL; below that level, the presence of elevated TPO antibodies is the key factor that warrants initiating levothyroxine therapy.

explanation_raw: Hypothyroidism affects approximately 1 in 300 individuals in the United States, with a higher prevalence among women and older adults. Symptoms can range from mild to lifethreatening. Because the signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism can be nonspecific, diagnosis is based on blood levels of TSH and free T4. Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by a TSH level that is abnormal but <10 μU/mL while the free T4 level remains within the normal range. Nonpregnant patients with subclinical hypothyroidism should not be treated with thyroid hormone replacement therapy unless the thyroid peroxidase antibody level is elevated or the TSH level is >10 μU/mL (SOR A). Evaluating the total or free T3 level is not routinely indicated. Treatment-resistant depression is an indication for treating subclinical hypothyroidism; however, this is not the case for treatment-resistant constipation.

stem: A 44-year-old female presents to the emergency department for evaluation of heavy vaginal bleeding. She reports soaking a pad every hour for the past 6 hours and is feeling mildly short of breath and lightheaded. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, migraines, and breast cancer for which she underwent lumpectomy 6 months ago. The patient's only medication is hydrochlorothiazide, 25 mg. The patient's vital signs include a blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg, a heart rate of 80 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 16/min, and an oxygen saturation of 100% on room air. A prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and platelet count are all normal, and a urine pregnancy test is negative, but a hemoglobin level is 8.0 g/dL (N 12.0–16.0). Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

bullets.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid is the most appropriate next step for severe but hemodynamically stable abnormal uterine bleeding, particularly when hormonal therapies are contraindicated due to a history of breast cancer.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Abnormal uterine bleeding requires rapid assessment of hemodynamic stability. This patient is soaking a pad hourly and has symptoms of acute blood loss anemia, but her vital signs remain stable. IV tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic agent, is the preferred intervention in this scenario. IV estrogen, while effective, is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients due to its thrombotic risk. Hormonal options such as combined oral contraceptives or depot medroxyprogesterone acetate should be avoided in patients with a recent history of hormone-sensitive cancers like breast cancer. The levonorgestrel IUD is a viable long-term option but is impractical in the emergency setting and takes 3–6 months to reduce bleeding.

explanation_raw: Abnormal uterine bleeding is a common clinical entity with a broad differential diagnosis and can be grouped into structural and nonstructural causes. Clinicians should determine if the bleeding is severe or life-threatening and appropriately ensure stability with resuscitative measures. While this patient's bleeding is severe and she has symptoms of acute blood loss anemia, her vital signs indicate hemodynamic stability. The most appropriate next step is to administer intravenous tranexamic acid. Given this patient's recent cancer history, it is advisable to avoid therapies with estrogen or progesterone such as a high-dose combined oral contraceptive or depot medroxyprogesterone acetate if clinically appropriate. Intravenous estrogen should be reserved for patients who are hemodynamically unstable given the risk for clotting. While the levonorgestrel IUD is an effective long-term management for abnormal uterine bleeding, insertion in the emergency department is impractical, and it would not be anticipated to improve bleeding for 3–6 months.

stem: A 45-year-old female presents with a 1-year history of central facial erythema, telangiectasias, and inflammatory pustules and papules. The symptoms are worsened by alcohol and excessive sun exposure. You diagnose rosacea. She has not had any previous success with moisturizers, aggressive sun protection, or mild facial soap. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate first step in the management of this condition?

bullets.text: Topical metronidazole is the first-line treatment for rosacea, offering an favorable cost and side-effect profile compared to alternatives.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Topical metronidazole is a first-line treatment for rosacea with a favorable cost and side-effect profile. Topical azelaic acid is also a first-line option. Oral doxycycline is a reasonable next step if topical metronidazole fails, but its side-effect profile—particularly increased sun sensitivity—is problematic since rosacea typically worsens in warmer, sun-exposed months.

bullets.text: Laser therapy, brimonidine, and topical cyclosporine are all second-line options reserved for patients who have failed first-line topical treatments.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Laser and light-based therapies are second-line treatments appropriate only after failure of topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. Brimonidine, an α-2 agonist, is also second-line due to its higher cost and tendency to exacerbate skin irritation. Topical cyclosporine is similarly reserved for patients whose rosacea has been recalcitrant to first-line options.

explanation_raw: Topical metronidazole is a first-line treatment for rosacea. The cost and side-effect profile of topical metronidazole make it most appropriate. Topical azelaic acid is also a first-line treatment for rosacea. Oral doxycycline is a reasonable next step if topical metronidazole is not successful in managing symptoms. The side-effect profile of doxycycline makes it less desirable than topical metronidazole. Additionally, increased sun sensitivity is a common side effect of doxycycline that is problematic for management because rosacea is generally clinically worse in the warmer months. Laser and light-based therapies are second-line treatments for rosacea. They are reasonable options for patients who have not had success with topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. Brimonidine is an α-2 agonist that is another reasonable option in a patient who has not had success with topical metronidazole or topical azelaic acid. However, due to its cost and tendency to exacerbate skin irritation, it is considered a second-line treatment option. Topical cyclosporine is another second-line treatment that has been recalcitrant to first-line options.

stem: A 67-year-old female presents for a wellness examination. She has not been seen for medical care for several years and reports that her last Papanicolaou test was 15 years ago. She does not recall any medical problems and has no known history of abnormal cervical cytology in the past. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which one of the following should you recommend regarding further cervical cancer screening?

choices.A: No further screening due to the patient's age
choices.B: Cervical cytology alone now, with no further screening if the result is normal
choices.C: Cervical cytology alone now, then repeated in 3 years with no further screening if the results are normal
choices.D: Cervical cytology with HPV co-testing now, with no further screening if the results are normal
choices.E: Cervical cytology with HPV co-testing now, then repeated in 5 years with no further screening if the results are normal

correct_label: Cervical cytology with HPV co-testing now, then repeated in 5 years with no further screening if the results are normal

explanation.heading: Cervical Cancer Screening in Older Women

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends against cervical cancer screening in women over 65 only if they have had adequate prior screening; this patient has not, so screening must continue until adequacy criteria are met.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against cervical cancer screening in women older than 65 years only if they have had adequate prior screening. Adequate screening is defined as 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-testing results within the 10 years before stopping screening, with the most recent test occurring within 5 years. Because this patient's last Pap test was 15 years ago and she has no documented history of adequate prior screening, she does not meet the criteria to stop screening. She must therefore undergo either 2 consecutive negative co-testing results 5 years apart, or 3 consecutive negative cytology results 3 years apart, before screening can be discontinued. The correct next step is cervical cytology with HPV co-testing now, repeated in 5 years, with no further screening if both results are normal.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against cervical cancer screening in women older than 65 years only if they have had adequate prior screening. Adequate screening is defined as 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-testing results within 10 years before stopping screening, with the most recent test occurring within 5 years. Because this patient has not had adequate prior screening, she requires either 2 consecutive negative co-testing results that are 5 years apart or 3 consecutive negative cytology results that are 3 years apart before stopping screening.

stem: A 46-year-old male comes in for an acute visit for low back pain. During triage, a Patient Health Questionnaire–2 (PHQ-2) screen is positive. You then administer the PHQ-9. You ask, "Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself?" He responds, "Nearly every day." His total PHQ9 score is 19. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Suicidal ideation assessment and evaluation of risk factors for suicide completion
choices.C: Escitalopram plus lithium, and cognitive behavioral therapy

correct_label: Suicidal ideation assessment and evaluation of risk factors for suicide completion

bullets.text: A positive PHQ-9 suicidality item requires thorough individual risk assessment before any treatment is initiated, as up to half of patients classified as low risk ultimately complete suicide.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Suicidal ideation is far more common than suicide attempts or completions, but it must be taken seriously. Current recommendations emphasize individualized assessment, including asking whether the patient has a specific plan and means, and evaluating for underlying mental illness, substance use, and psychosocial stressors. This evaluation must precede any pharmacologic or other intervention.

bullets.text: SSRIs and CBT are first-line for depression with suicidality, but treatment should not be initiated until suicide risk is fully evaluated; inpatient transfer is indicated for high-risk patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: SSRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy are standard first-line treatments for depression and suicidality, but this patient has not yet had a formal risk stratification or diagnosis established. Lithium reduces suicide attempts and all-cause mortality in major depression and bipolar disorder but is premature here. Ketamine shows promise for rapid improvement in refractory depression and suicidality within 24 hours, but evidence quality is low, effects dissipate after ~2 weeks, and it is reserved for treatment-resistant cases. If the patient is found to be high risk, inpatient psychiatric transfer is warranted, often requiring stabilization in an emergency department while awaiting placement.

explanation_raw: Suicidal ideation is much more common than suicide attempts or suicide completions and should be carefully addressed; up to half of patients characterized as low risk ultimately complete suicide. Current recommendations for evaluating suicidal ideation suggest focusing on individual assessment and understanding certain risk factors that may exacerbate suicidal ideation for a given patient. This includes asking questions, such as whether the patient has a plan and means to complete the plan, as well as assessing for underlying mental illness, substance use, and life stressors. SSRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy are first-line treatments for the majority of people with depression and suicidality, but this patient requires further evaluation for suicide risk before initiating pharmacologic therapy. Lithium has been shown to decrease suicide attempts and all-cause mortality among patients with major depression and bipolar disorder, and SSRIs are often used in conjunction with lithium; however, an underlying diagnosis has not yet been established for this patient, so this treatment is not yet warranted. The use of ketamine for rapid improvement in depression has shown promise, with patients experiencing significant improvement in depression symptoms and suicidality within 24 hours, but the evidence quality is considered low, and effects dissipated after 2 weeks. Ketamine treatment is recommended only if depression is resistant to other medications. If the patient endorses suicide plans or any other factors that are consistent with high risk for suicide completion, transfer to an inpatient treatment facility may be indicated. Although, stabilization in a standard emergency department is often necessary while awaiting an inpatient bed due to facility limitations.

stem: A healthy 58-year-old patient presents for an annual health maintenance examination. They had an initial screening colonoscopy 3 years ago in which 2 polyps were removed. The polyps were found to be 6-mm and 8-mm tubular adenomas. The patient does not have a family history of colon cancer. Which one of the following is the most appropriate ongoing colon cancer screening for this patient?

choices.D: Repeat colonoscopy within the next 2 years
choices.E: Repeat colonoscopy 7–10 years after the initial colonoscopy

correct_label: Repeat colonoscopy 7–10 years after the initial colonoscopy

bullets.text: For average-risk patients with 1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm, the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer recommends repeat colonoscopy in 7–10 years.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The risk of small tubular adenomas progressing to malignancy is quite low and the rate of progression is slow, likely exceeding 10 years. Using GRADE criteria in its 2020 consensus guidelines, the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer recommends follow-up in 7–10 years for 1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm (moderate-quality evidence), 3–5 years for 3–4 tubular adenomas <10 mm (very low-quality evidence), 3 years for 5–10 tubular adenomas <10 mm (moderate-quality evidence), and yearly for >10 adenomas (very low-quality evidence). In the United States, only colonoscopy is recommended for polyp follow-up; international guidelines allow stool-based testing. Colon cancer screening should continue until at least age 75 (SOR A).

explanation_raw: For average-risk patients with 1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm in size found on screening colonoscopy, repeat colonoscopy in 7–10 years is recommended. The risk of small adenomas progressing to malignancy is quite low and the rate of progression is slow, likely >10 years. Using GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) criteria in its consensus guidelines from 2020, the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer recommends follow-up in 7–10 years for 1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm in size (moderate-quality evidence), 3–5 years for 3–4 tubular adenomas <10 mm in size (very low-quality evidence), 3 years for 5–10 tubular adenomas <10 mm in size (moderate-quality evidence), and yearly for >10 adenomas (very low-quality evidence). In the United States, only colonoscopy is recommended for follow-up of findings of colonic polyps. International guidelines allow for stool-based testing. This patient is healthy, and colon cancer screening should continue until at least age 75 (SOR A).

stem: A 27-year-old gravida 1 para 0 at 38 weeks' estimated gestation based on a first-trimester ultrasound presents for routine prenatal care. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. You discuss the potential risks and benefits of inducing labor at 39 weeks compared to expectant management. In this discussion, you should tell the patient that inducing labor at 39 weeks reduces

choices.A: the risk of low birth weight
choices.B: length of stay in the labor and delivery unit

bullets.text: The ARRIVE trial showed that elective induction of labor at 39 weeks in low-risk nulliparous patients significantly reduced the rate of cesarean delivery (18.6% vs. 22.2%) compared to expectant management.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The 2018 ARRIVE trial was a large randomized controlled trial of over 6,000 low-risk nulliparous patients at 41 U.S. sites. Patients were assigned to induction of labor (IOL) between 39 0/7 and 39 4/7 weeks or expectant management. The key finding was a significantly lower rate of cesarean delivery in the IOL group (18.6% vs. 22.2%, RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.76–0.93). There were no significant differences in the neonatal composite outcome (perinatal mortality and severe perinatal morbidity: 4.3% vs. 5.4%, RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.64–1.00), neonatal ICU admissions, or maternal postpartum hemorrhage.

bullets.text: Elective IOL at 39 weeks also reduced rates of gestational hypertension/preeclampsia and neonatal respiratory support needs, but increased labor and delivery length of stay.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Additional significant findings from the ARRIVE trial included lower rates of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia in the IOL group (9.1% vs. 14.1%, RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.56–0.74) and reduced need for neonatal respiratory support within 72 hours (3.0% vs. 4.2%, RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.93). The IOL group had a longer median stay in the labor and delivery unit (20 hours vs. 14 hours) and lower median birth weights (3300 g vs. 3380 g), though IOL did not increase the risk of low birth weight. These findings should be shared with patients as part of a shared decision-making discussion about timing of delivery.

explanation_raw: The 2018 ARRIVE (A Randomized Trial of Induction Versus Expectant Management) trial was a randomized, controlled trial that included more than 6000 low-risk nulliparous patients at 41 sites across the United States who were assigned to either induction of labor (IOL) between 39 weeks 0/7 days and 39 weeks 4/7 days or expectant management. The results showed no significant differences in a neonatal composite outcome, including perinatal mortality and severe perinatal morbidity between the intervention and control groups (4.3% compared to 5.4%, relative risk [RR] 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.00). A significantly lower rate of cesarean delivery was found in the intervention group than the control group (18.6% compared to 22.2%, RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.93). Other findings included: lower rates of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia (9.1% compared to 14.1%, RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.74), increased length of stay in the labor and delivery unit (a median duration of 20 hours with an interquartile range [IQR] of 13 to 28 compared to a median duration of 14 hours with an IQR of 9 to 20), and reduced need for neonatal respiratory support within the first 72 hours of life (3.0% compared to 4.2%, RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.93). The intervention group had significantly lower median birth weights than the control group (3300 g compared to 3380 g; P value <0.001); it did not reduce the risk of low infant birth weight. There were no significant differences in neonatal ICU admission and maternal risk of postpartum hemorrhage. This information should be shared with patients as part of a shared decision-making conversation regarding timing of delivery. Not all labor and delivery units can accommodate elective IOL at 39 weeks' gestation for all patients. It is important that clinicians and hospital systems assess their policies and procedures on a regular basis to ensure equitable access to IOL for those who choose this approach.

stem: A 75-year-old female presents to your office with a 1-year history of gradually worsening right-sided groin pain on standing. The pain improves with rest. These symptoms have been marginally relieved with ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but her use of these medications has been limited by gastric irritation. A physical examination is most notable for pain in the groin with passive flexion, adduction, and internal rotation (FADIR) testing. Which one of the following treatments would be most helpful in relieving her symptoms?

bullets.text: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are the preferred next step for hip osteoarthritis when oral analgesics are limited by side effects, providing pain relief for at least 4 months along with improved activity and quality of life.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has hip osteoarthritis with inadequate relief from NSAIDs and acetaminophen due to gastric intolerance. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections have demonstrated efficacy in relieving hip osteoarthritis pain for at least 4 months and can improve activity levels and quality of life, making them the most appropriate next intervention.

bullets.text: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid lacks substantial evidence for hip osteoarthritis; topical lidocaine is not effective for this condition; opioids (including tramadol and hydrocodone) are advised against for chronic osteoarthritis due to lack of long-term efficacy, significant side effects, and high addiction risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections have not been shown to be substantially beneficial for hip osteoarthritis symptoms. Topical lidocaine patches are neither effective nor a sustainable solution for hip osteoarthritis pain. Opioids such as hydrocodone are not recommended for chronic osteoarthritis management due to poor long-term effectiveness, significant adverse effects, and high risk of addiction and misuse. Tramadol similarly fails to provide meaningful pain relief or functional improvement in hip osteoarthritis and carries comparable risks to other opioids.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with hip osteoarthritis. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections have been shown to relieve hip and osteoarthritis pain for at least 4 months. In addition to pain relief, these injections may improve activity levels and quality of life. In contrast to intraarticular corticosteroid injections, intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections have not been shown to be substantially beneficial in relieving symptoms of hip osteoarthritis. Topical lidocaine patches have not been shown to be effective for management of pain due to hip osteoarthritis and are not a sustainable solution for this patient. Opioids such as hydrocodone are advised against for treatment of chronic osteoarthritis. They are not effective over the long term, have significant side effects, and carry a high risk of addiction and misuse. Tramadol is not effective for pain relief or functional improvement in hip osteoarthritis and carries similar risks as opioids.

stem: A 65-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his wife after developing confusion immediately after sexual intercourse. The wife reports that the patient does not remember anything from a few hours prior to the onset of symptoms. He repeatedly asks where he is, how he got here, and what time it is, despite having been given the answers to his questions. He is alert and knows his wife, his name, and his birth date. A neurologic examination is otherwise normal. A CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel are normal, an EKG is normal, and a CT scan of the head is unremarkable. It has now been 2 hours since the onset of his symptoms. Which one of the following would be most appropriate for treatment?

bullets.text: This patient has transient global amnesia (TGA), characterized by abrupt-onset anterograde amnesia without other neurologic deficits, often triggered by intense physical or psychological stress such as sexual intercourse.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Transient global amnesia (TGA) presents with the sudden onset of anterograde amnesia — the patient cannot form new memories and repeatedly asks the same questions — without accompanying neurologic deficits or cognitive impairment. Common triggers include intense physical exertion, sexual intercourse, emotional stress, or acute illness. Symptoms typically resolve within approximately 6 hours.

bullets.text: No specific intervention is required for TGA; observation and reassurance are the only indicated treatments, as the condition is self-limiting and unrelated to seizure, TIA, or stroke.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Because TGA is a benign, self-limited condition, the appropriate management is observation and reassurance. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, antiseizure medications, and thrombolytic therapy are not indicated. The etiology of TGA is distinct from that of seizure, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or ischemic stroke, so treatments targeting those conditions are inappropriate here.

explanation_raw: This patient has transient global amnesia (TGA), which is characterized by the abrupt onset of anterograde amnesia without other neurologic deficits or cognitive impairment. TGA can be triggered by intense physical or psychological stress such as sexual intercourse or acute illness. Symptoms usually resolve within approximately 6 hours. No intervention is indicated for TGA other than reassurance. The etiology of TGA is unrelated to seizure, TIA, or stroke. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet medications, antiseizure medications, and thrombolytic therapy are not indicated in the treatment of TGA.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the urgent care clinic with a 24-hour history of worsening fever, chills, and body aches. He tells you that he discovered a tick on his scalp during a camping trip last week. He does not have a rash, headache, or palpitations, and a neurologic examination is negative. A Lyme enzyme immunoassay and confirmatory Western blot are positive. When he has taken doxycycline in the past, he has developed headaches, severe nausea, and vomiting. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?

bullets.text: Tick-borne illness (likely Lyme disease) should be suspected in patients with influenza-like symptoms after outdoor exposure; without a rash, a 2-tiered serologic testing regimen is recommended.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In the United States, ticks can transmit Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, and Colorado tick fever. Tick-borne illnesses should be considered in patients presenting with influenza-like symptoms during spring and summer after outdoor exposure. Lyme disease can be diagnosed clinically when erythema migrans is present (SOR C), but in patients without a rash, a 2-tiered testing regimen is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

bullets.text: Doxycycline is the preferred first-line treatment for Lyme disease, but amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14–21 days is an appropriate alternative for patients who are pregnant or cannot tolerate doxycycline.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Doxycycline is the preferred first-line treatment for Lyme disease, but amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14–21 days is an appropriate alternative for patients who are pregnant or do not tolerate doxycycline. Cefuroxime axetil is another acceptable option. It is important to complete the full course of treatment, as partial treatment can lead to more serious complications. IV ceftriaxone is reserved for patients with late neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease, which this patient does not have. Chloramphenicol is used for Rocky Mountain spotted fever in patients with contraindications to doxycycline, not for Lyme disease.

explanation_raw: In the United States, multiple diseases are carried by ticks including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, and Colorado tick fever. Tick-borne illnesses should be considered in patients who present with influenza-like symptoms during the spring and summer months and who have spent time outdoors. Lyme disease can be diagnosed clinically in patients with erythema migrans (SOR C). In patients such as this who present without a rash, a 2-tiered testing regimen is recommended. Doxycycline is the preferred first-line treatment, but for patients who are pregnant or do not tolerate it, an appropriate alternative is amoxicillin, 500 mg 3 times daily for 14–21 days. It is important to prescribe a medication that the patient can tolerate for its full course, as partial treatment of the infection could lead to more serious complications. Cefuroxime axetil is another treatment option. Intravenous ceftriaxone is indicated for patients with Lyme disease who present with late neurologic manifestations, but that is not the case for this patient. Chloramphenicol is the preferred treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever in patients with contraindications to doxycycline therapy.

stem: A 66-year-old female asks about options for shingles vaccine. She received the live zoster vaccine (Zostavax) previously. She underwent urgent cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis 2 months ago and developed shingles in a dermatomal distribution soon after hospital discharge. She was given valacyclovir (Valtrex) and gabapentin (Neurontin) for treatment and symptom relief. The rash is gone but she still has mild postherpetic neuralgia. She would like to receive the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) as soon as it is safe to receive it. Which one of the following would be the earliest this patient can safely receive the first dose of recombinant zoster vaccine?

choices.B: After resolution of the postherpetic neuralgia
choices.C: 12 months after her episode of shingles

explanation.heading: Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV) Timing After Shingles Episode

bullets.text: The CDC recommends waiting until the zoster rash has resolved before receiving RZV, but postherpetic neuralgia does not need to resolve first — this patient's rash has resolved, so she can be vaccinated today.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV/Shingrix) is recommended for healthy adults ≥50 years of age, including those with a prior episode of shingles. The CDC advises waiting only until the acute zoster rash has resolved before administering RZV; resolution of postherpetic neuralgia is not required. Because recurrence risk remains after a prior shingles episode and RZV is safe and immunogenic, vaccination is still indicated.
