Additionally, patients who previously received the live zoster vaccine (Zostavax) should still receive RZV for superior and more durable protection.

explanation_raw: The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) is recommended for healthy adults ≥50 years of age, and this patient can receive it today. Because most studies of RZV effectiveness have excluded patients with a prior episode of shingles, direct evidence in this subgroup is limited; however, available data and expert reviews support vaccination after a prior episode because the risk for recurrence remains and RZV is safe and immunogenic. The CDC recommends that patients wait until the zoster rash has resolved prior to receiving RZV, but it is not necessary to wait until postherpetic neuralgia has resolved. Patients who have previously received live zoster vaccine should receive RZV as well.

stem: A 40-year-old male presents to the office with a 2-day history of right eye pain associated with redness and swelling. He does not wear contact lenses. Pertinent findings on a physical examination include a temperature of 37.3 °C (99.1 °F), visual acuity of 20/70 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, erythema and edema of the right eyelid, and pain with extraocular movements. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Frequent warm, moist compresses, and follow-up tomorrow
choices.B: Empiric treatment with an oral antibiotic
choices.C: A same-day evaluation with an ophthalmologist
choices.D: Noncontrast CT of the orbits and sinuses

bullets.text: Unilateral orbital swelling, erythema, pain with extraocular movements, and decreased visual acuity are hallmark features of orbital cellulitis, an ocular emergency requiring prompt recognition.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Unilateral orbital swelling, erythema, pain with extraocular movements, and decreased visual acuity are hallmark features of orbital cellulitis, an ocular emergency requiring prompt recognition. CT scan with intravenous contrast is the imaging modality of choice to confirm the diagnosis; noncontrast CT is less accurate and should be avoided when orbital cellulitis is suspected.

bullets.text: Patients with suspected orbital cellulitis presenting in an outpatient setting should be immediately transferred to the emergency department for urgent ophthalmology consultation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients with suspected orbital cellulitis presenting in an outpatient setting should be immediately transferred to the emergency department for urgent ophthalmology consultation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. Same-day outpatient ophthalmology referral, warm compresses with close follow-up, or empiric oral antibiotics are all inadequate responses that risk diagnostic and treatment delays, leading to potentially serious complications including vision loss or intracranial spread.

explanation_raw: This patient's unilateral orbital swelling, erythema, pain with extraocular movements, and decreased visual acuity are concerning for orbital cellulitis. Prompt recognition and early treatment are vital to avoid worsening outcomes associated with this ocular emergency. A patient who presents in the outpatient setting with clinical findings that are suspicious for orbital cellulitis should be promptly directed to the emergency department (ED) for expedited evaluation and anticipated hospitalization for urgent ophthalmology consultation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, if the diagnosis is confirmed. CT with intravenous contrast is the imaging modality of choice, although MRI is an alternative. Ordering noncontrast CT would potentially yield a less accurate diagnosis and could delay definitive treatment. Same-day outpatient evaluation by an ophthalmologist would cause a diagnostic delay, compared to transfer to the ED. Symptomatic treatment with warm compresses and close outpatient follow-up would cause a treatment delay with a risk of further clinical deterioration. Empiric treatment with an oral antibiotic would not provide adequate initial treatment of the infection compared to hospitalization for intravenous antibiotic treatment and closer clinical monitoring.

stem: A 63-year-old male presents with a 2-day history of right lower extremity edema and pain. He has a past medical history of hypertension, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes, for which he takes insulin. His last glomerular filtration rate was 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. He does not report any trauma, chest pain, or shortness of breath. On examination he has a weight of 70 kg (154 lb) and the remainder of his vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of his right lower extremity reveals erythema, tenderness, and 2+ edema at the back of the knee. A Doppler venous duplex ultrasound of the right thigh shows a noncompressible right femoral vein. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient’s condition?

choices.B: Oral rivaroxaban (Xarelto), 15 mg twice daily for 14 days, then 20 mg daily

bullets.text: This patient has an acute DVT without pulmonary embolism, making outpatient anticoagulation appropriate.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has an acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT) with no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Outpatient treatment is appropriate, and admission for intravenous heparin is generally not indicated for uncomplicated DVT.

bullets.text: Enoxaparin with renal dose adjustment (once daily instead of twice daily) is the preferred anticoagulant given his stage 4 CKD (GFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Low-molecular-weight heparin such as enoxaparin is a reasonable option for acute DVT. In patients with significant renal impairment, renal dosing (70 mg daily rather than twice daily) is required to avoid drug accumulation and bleeding risk.

bullets.text: DOACs such as rivaroxaban are contraindicated with GFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²; dabigatran carries higher bleeding risk; and warfarin is not recommended for acute-phase DVT treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Direct oral anticoagulants (e.g., rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are not appropriate when GFR is <30 mL/min/1.73 m². Additionally, the standard initial rivaroxaban dose of 15 mg twice daily must be given for 21 days, not 14 days. Dabigatran is avoided due to higher bleeding risk in renal impairment. Warfarin alone is not recommended for the acute phase of DVT treatment and requires bridging anticoagulation.

explanation_raw: This patient has an acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT) with no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Outpatient treatment would be appropriate and a low-molecular-weight heparin such as enoxaparin is a reasonable option in this patient. Renal dosing is the reason for daily, rather than twice-daily, dosing for enoxaparin. Dabigatran is not preferred due to a higher risk for bleeding. Direct oral anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban are not appropriate in this patient due to his glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Furthermore, the initial dose of rivaroxaban, 15 mg twice daily, should be 21 days, not 14 days. Warfarin is not recommended for the acute phase treatment of DVT in this patient. Admission for intravenous heparin is generally not indicated for uncomplicated DVT.

stem: A 65-year-old male presents to your office with a 4-month history of ill-defined lower pelvic pain. He is afebrile. An abdominal examination is unremarkable. A digital rectal examination yields a boggy prostate with moderate tenderness. Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and 10–20 WBCs/hpf, and testing for common sexually transmitted infections is negative. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

bullets.text: This patient's 4-month history of pelvic pain, boggy/tender prostate on DRE, and pyuria is consistent with chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Chronic bacterial prostatitis is characterized by recurrent or persistent pelvic/perineal pain lasting more than 3 months, often with lower urinary tract symptoms. Key findings include a boggy, tender prostate on digital rectal exam and evidence of urinary tract infection on urinalysis (leukocyte esterase positive, elevated WBCs). The diagnosis is clinical and does not require CT imaging.

bullets.text: Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) are the first-line treatment for chronic bacterial prostatitis due to excellent prostatic tissue penetration, high oral bioavailability, and broad coverage of common uropathogens.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fluoroquinolones are preferred for CBP because they achieve high concentrations within prostatic tissue, which is critical given the poor penetration of many other antibiotic classes into the prostate. Treatment courses are typically 4–6 weeks. Amoxicillin and ceftriaxone are not recommended due to poor prostatic penetration and inadequate coverage. Urology referral is not necessary for straightforward CBP, as its diagnosis and management fall within the scope of family medicine.

explanation_raw: This patient has chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) and should be treated with a fluoroquinolone. Fluoroquinolones are the first-line treatment for CBP because they favorably cover the common uropathogens that cause CBP, penetrate prostatic tissue well, and have high oral bioavailability. Amoxicillin and ceftriaxone are not preferred for the treatment of prostatitis. CT is not necessary to make the diagnosis. Referral to a urologist is unnecessary in this clinical scenario because the diagnosis and management of CBP is within the scope of family medicine.

stem: A 25-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of right-sided chest pain that started about 2 hours ago while he was resting and playing video games. He reports feeling slightly short of breath. He has no history of lung disease, and he smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day. On examination he has a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, a heart rate of 115 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 20/min, and an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. A chest x-ray reveals a pneumothorax involving <10% of the lung space. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance and discharge home with return precautions for worsening symptoms
choices.B: Initiation of oxygen via nasal cannula, and a repeat chest x-ray in 6 hours
choices.C: CT of the chest to verify x-ray findings
choices.D: Emergent needle decompression at the right second intercostal space in the anterior midclavicular line
choices.E: Placement of a chest tube at the right fourth or fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary to anterior axillary line

correct_label: Initiation of oxygen via nasal cannula, and a repeat chest x-ray in 6 hours

bullets.text: Stable patients with a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (<15% of hemithoracic cavity) should be managed conservatively with supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula and observation, followed by a repeat chest x-ray at 6 hours to assess stability.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For patients who are stable with a small (<15% of the hemithoracic cavity) primary pneumothorax, conservative management with initiation of oxygen via nasal cannula and observation for at least 6 hours is recommended, followed by a repeat chest x-ray to assess for stability in size of the pneumothorax. If stable at 6 hours, patients can return home with a repeat follow-up in 24 hours.

bullets.text: CT imaging is not required when chest x-ray is already diagnostic, and emergent needle decompression with tube thoracostomy is reserved for clinically unstable patients with large pneumothoraces or severe symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: CT imaging can aid in diagnosis if the initial chest x-ray is nondiagnostic or equivocal; however, it is not needed to confirm definitive findings of pneumothorax already visible on chest x-ray. Patients who are clinically unstable with a large pneumothorax or severe symptoms should receive emergent needle decompression, followed by an ipsilateral tube thoracostomy — interventions not warranted in this stable patient with a small pneumothorax.

explanation_raw: For patients who are stable with a small (<15% of the hemithoracic cavity) primary pneumothorax, conservative management with initiation of oxygen via nasal cannula and observation for at least 6 hours is recommended, followed by a repeat chest x-ray to assess for stability in size of the pneumothorax. If stable at 6 hours, patients can return home with a repeat follow-up in 24 hours. CT imaging can aid in diagnosis if the initial chest x-ray is nondiagnostic or equivocal; however, it is not needed to confirm definitive findings of pneumothorax on chest x-ray. Patients who are clinically unstable with a large pneumothorax or severe symptoms should receive emergent needle decompression, followed by an ipsilateral tube thoracostomy.

stem: A 17-year-old female with well-controlled diabetes mellitus is brought to your office by her mother for a sports preparticipation physical evaluation prior to playing soccer. She has intermittent knee pain when running but no other symptoms. Which one of the following, if present in this patient, would be a CONTRAINDICATION to playing soccer?

bullets.text: An acutely enlarged spleen (or liver) is a contraindication to contact sports participation due to the significantly increased risk of organ rupture.
bullets.sub_paragraph: During a sports preparticipation evaluation, an acutely enlarged spleen or liver represents a serious finding that warrants workup for the underlying cause and restriction from contact sports such as soccer until resolved. Organ rupture during contact or collision is a life-threatening risk in the setting of organomegaly.

bullets.text: Obesity, well-controlled diabetes, asymptomatic mild mitral valve prolapse, and tibial tubercle apophysitis are not contraindications to sports participation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Obesity increases the risk of heat-related illness but does not restrict play. Exercise is beneficial for adolescents with diabetes and may simply require adjustment of insulin and diet. Asymptomatic mild mitral valve prolapse is not a reason to deny participation. Tibial tubercle apophysitis (Osgood-Schlatter disease) is managed conservatively, and most experts encourage continued activity with appropriate modifications.

explanation_raw: A sports preparticipation evaluation is important for assessing health risks and ensuring an athlete is not unnecessarily restricted from play. An athlete with an acutely enlarged spleen or liver faces an increased risk of organ rupture during contact sports. This patient should be evaluated for a cause of the organomegaly, if present, prior to participation. Obesity in an athlete increases the risk for heat-related illness, but it is not an indication to restrict play. Exercise is beneficial for adolescents with diabetes mellitus and may require modification of insulin and eating regimens. Asymptomatic mild mitral valve prolapse is not a reason to deny participation. Tibial tubercle apophysitis is not a contraindication to play, and most experts encourage activity and conservative management.

stem: An otherwise healthy 26-year-old female presents to your clinic with a history of 3 episodes of vertigo occurring over the last week. Each episode lasts for several hours. During the episodes, she notes fullness in the right ear with tinnitus and hearing loss. She has not noticed anything specific that triggers the episodes, and reports consuming 1 glass of wine per night. She does not report headache, visual changes, fever, or upper respiratory symptoms. She is currently asymptomatic and a physical examination is unremarkable. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Recommending a reduction in alcohol intake
choices.E: Initiating oral prednisone, 20 mg daily for 5 days

bullets.text: Ménière disease presents with spontaneous recurring episodes of vertigo, unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness; audiometry is the appropriate next step in evaluation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Ménière disease is characterized by spontaneous recurring episodes of vertigo associated with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. While there are no pathognomonic diagnostic tests, audiometry should be performed in any patient suspected of having this condition to assess for sensorineural hearing loss, which may or may not be present on evaluation.

bullets.text: Acute attacks are managed with vestibular suppressants (e.g., promethazine, diazepam, prochlorperazine); lifestyle modifications are traditionally recommended but lack strong evidence.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute attacks of Ménière disease should be treated with vestibular suppressant medications such as promethazine, diazepam, or prochlorperazine. Lifestyle interventions including salt restriction and reduction of alcohol and caffeine intake have traditionally been recommended, but there is insufficient evidence to support these recommendations. Notably, there is also no good-quality evidence that diuretics, antivirals, or corticosteroids treat or prevent Ménière disease.

bullets.text: The Epley maneuver is specific to benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), not Ménière disease, which is distinguished by prolonged episodes with auditory symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The Epley maneuver is a canalith repositioning technique used for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), which features brief positional vertigo without auditory symptoms. It is not appropriate for Ménière disease. Similarly, diuretics, antivirals, and corticosteroids lack sufficient evidence for use in Ménière disease management and should not be routinely recommended.

explanation_raw: Meniere disease is characterized by spontaneous recurring episodes of vertigo with associated unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and nystagmus. Even though there are no specific diagnostic tests, audiometry should be performed in patients suspected of having this condition. Sensorineural hearing loss may or may not be present on audiometric evaluation. Acute attacks should be treated with medication such as promethazine, diazepam, or prochlorperazine to suppress vestibular function. Lifestyle interventions, including salt restriction and reduction in alcohol and caffeine intake, have traditionally been recommended. However, there is no sufficient evidence to support these recommendations. The Epley maneuver is a repositioning treatment used for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and not Meniere disease. There is no good-quality evidence that diuretics, antivirals, or corticosteroids treat or prevent Meniere disease.

stem: A new lipid-lowering drug is being evaluated for its cardioprotective effects. The event rate for acute myocardial infarction is 0.085 in the low-intensity treatment group and 0.045 in the high-intensity treatment group, yielding an absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 0.04. Which one of the following is the number needed to treat (NNT)?

bullets.text: The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is calculated as 1 divided by the Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR); here, 1 / 0.04 = 25.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The NNT represents how many patients must receive a treatment for one additional patient to benefit. It is derived by first calculating the ARR, which is the control event rate (CER) minus the experimental event rate (EER): 0.085 − 0.045 = 0.04. Dividing 1 by the ARR gives the NNT: 1 / 0.04 = 25. This means 25 patients would need to receive high-intensity treatment to prevent one additional myocardial infarction compared to low-intensity treatment.

explanation_raw: The number needed to treat (NNT) is the number of patients who need to receive a particular treatment in order for 1 patient to benefit. The NNT is the inverse of the absolute risk reduction (ARR), the amount by which a particular treatment reduces the risk of a negative outcome. The ARR must be calculated first in order to determine the NNT. To calculate the ARR, the experimental event rate (EER) is subtracted from the control event rate (CER). In this example, the low-intensity treatment group had a risk of acute myocardial infarction (bad outcome) of 0.085 (CER) whereas the high-intensity treatment group had a risk of 0.045 (EER). This would make the equation: 0.085 – 0.045 = an ARR of 0.04. The NNT is then calculated by dividing 1 by the ARR: 1 / 0.04 = 25. This means that 25 patients would need to receive the high-intensity treatment to prevent 1 additional myocardial infarction.

stem: A 75-year-old female presents to your office with a 3-month history of episodes of lightheadedness on standing. Orthostatic blood pressure testing in your office reveals an initial blood pressure of 134/76 mm Hg that drops to 104/46 mm Hg on standing. A laboratory evaluation is unremarkable and review of her medications does not show an obvious cause for her symptoms. Echocardiography and tilt table testing are unremarkable. You diagnose orthostatic hypotension. Monotherapy with which one of the following would be indicated for the management of this patient's neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?

bullets.text: Midodrine is the safest and best-tolerated first-line medication for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (SOR B).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Midodrine is considered the preferred monotherapy for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Atomoxetine can be used as an adjunctive agent alongside midodrine but is not effective as monotherapy. Fludrocortisone is sometimes used off-label but carries risks of left ventricular hypertrophy, renal failure, and hypokalemia. Methylphenidate has no established role in treating neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and sodium tablets are generally inadequate, fail to address the neurogenic mechanism, and significantly increase the risk of hypernatremia and renal injury.

explanation_raw: Midodrine has been found to be the safest and best-tolerated medication for the management of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (SOR B). Atomoxetine is an adjunctive treatment for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension that is generally successful when added to medication such as midodrine, but it is not effective as monotherapy. Although fludrocortisone is sometimes used off-label for this indication, it should be used with caution because of the risk of left ventricular hypertrophy, renal failure, and hypokalemia. Methylphenidate has not been shown to have a role in the successful treatment of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Treatment with sodium tablets is usually inadequate, does not correct the neurogenic issue, and substantially increases the risk of hypernatremia and resultant renal injury.

stem: A 22-year-old female with a past medical history of type 1 diabetes presents to the emergency department with multiple bouts of vomiting. She says that she is not consistently adherent to her insulin regimen. She has a plasma glucose level of 350 mg/dL, elevated ketones, and high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis is initiated with intravenous fluids and insulin therapy. Glucose should be added to this patient’s saline infusion when her plasma glucose levels reach which one of the following ranges?

bullets.text: In DKA, once plasma glucose reaches 201–250 mg/dL, dextrose should be added to the IV fluid infusion to maintain glucose in the 150–200 mg/dL range while continuing insulin therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The mainstay of treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis is intravenous fluid replacement and insulin therapy along with careful monitoring and frequent reassessment. Once plasma glucose levels reach 201–250 mg/dL, glucose should be added to the saline infusion to maintain plasma glucose levels in the 150–200 mg/dL range. Because acidosis and ketosis resolve more slowly than hyperglycemia, glucose needs to be added while insulin and saline therapy are continued — preventing hypoglycemia while allowing continued clearance of ketones and correction of the anion gap.

explanation_raw: The mainstay of treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis is intravenous fluid replacement and insulin therapy along with careful monitoring and frequent reassessment. Once plasma glucose levels reach 201–250 mg/dL, glucose should be added to the saline infusion to maintain plasma glucose levels in the 150–200 mg/dL range. Because acidosis and ketosis resolve more slowly than hyperglycemia, glucose needs to be added while insulin and saline therapy are continued.

stem: A 32-year-old female with a recent diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder presents to your clinic with difficulty sleeping. She recently left an abusive relationship and has been attending trauma-focused psychotherapy. She has found the psychotherapy helpful, but she continues to experience midsleep awakening due to hyperarousal and nightmares. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?

bullets.text: Prazosin is the preferred agent for PTSD-related sleep disturbances, particularly midsleep awakening and nightmares, due to its mechanism of reducing sympathetic tone during sleep.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist (often described as reducing central sympathetic activity) that decreases hyperarousal during sleep, making it effective for PTSD-associated nightmares and midsleep awakenings. It is considered a first-line pharmacologic option when sleep disturbance persists despite trauma-focused psychotherapy.

bullets.text: Amitriptyline, mirtazapine, and risperidone carry significant side-effect burdens and are not appropriate initial treatments; temazepam should be avoided due to its misuse potential and long-term adverse effects.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Amitriptyline has anticholinergic and cardiac side effects that limit its use. Mirtazapine and risperidone have significant metabolic and sedative side-effect profiles that make them poor first-line choices for sleep symptoms in PTSD. Temazepam is a benzodiazepine and should generally be avoided in PTSD patients because benzodiazepines carry a risk of dependence, misuse, and may worsen overall PTSD outcomes with chronic use.

explanation_raw: Prazosin is an α2-agonist that decreases sympathetic nervous tone during sleep and has been found to be helpful for midsleep awakening due to hyperarousal and nightmares in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder. Amitriptyline, mirtazapine, and risperidone have significant side-effect profiles and would not be appropriate initial treatments for this patient's sleep symptoms. Temazepam is a benzodiazepine and should be avoided if possible due to its potential for misuse and chronic long-term effects.

stem: A 58-year-old female with type 2 diabetes controlled on metformin recently underwent bariatric surgery. Today, she reports feeling off balance and having a burning sensation in her bilateral hands and feet that is worse at night. She reports difficulty ambulating and has fallen several times over the past few weeks. She has intermittent nausea, vomiting, and confusion, and reports aches and pains all over. A physical examination is significant for absent patellar and Achilles reflexes. Her strength is 4/5 in the bilateral lower extremities with decreased pinprick sensation. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: This patient's symmetric peripheral neuropathy with both sensory and motor components following bariatric surgery is characteristic of Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, or beriberi.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with a symmetrical peripheral neuropathy with sensory and motor components that are characteristic of beriberi caused by vitamin B1 deficiency. Risk factors include alcohol use, bariatric surgery, older age, diabetes mellitus, and HIV infection. Severe thiamine deficiency can lead to heart failure. Blood and urine tests for thiamine levels are recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

bullets.text: Diabetic neuropathy, Lyme disease, ME/CFS, and secondary syphilis do not adequately explain this clinical picture of combined sensory and motor polyneuropathy in the setting of recent bariatric surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy usually presents as a symmetric polyneuropathy, but it does not usually involve motor components, except in severe cases. Neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease include meningitis, facial nerve palsy, and radiculoneuritis, but peripheral neuropathy with Lyme disease is rare and typically presents as a mononeuropathy, not a polyneuropathy. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) typically occurs after an acute infection with fatigue, sleep changes, and cognitive symptoms, and is not associated with peripheral neuropathy. Secondary syphilis typically presents with a rash and constitutional symptoms; its neurologic manifestations include ocular symptoms and otosyphilis, but not peripheral neuropathy.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with a symmetrical peripheral neuropathy with sensory and motor components that are characteristic of beriberi caused by vitamin B1 deficiency. Risk factors include alcohol use, bariatric surgery, older age, diabetes mellitus, and HIV infection. Severe thiamine deficiency can lead to heart failure. Blood and urine tests for thiamine levels are recommended to confirm the diagnosis. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy usually presents as a symmetric polyneuropathy, but it does not usually involve motor components, except in severe cases. Neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease include meningitis, facial nerve palsy, radiculoneuritis with radicular pain in a dermatomal distribution with accompanied weakness, sensory deficits, abnormal reflexes, other cranial neuropathies, and Lyme encephalomyelitis. Peripheral neuropathy is rare with Lyme disease and typically presents as a mononeuropathy, not a polyneuropathy. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) typically occurs after an acute infection, presenting with symptoms such as severe fatigue, sleep changes, and cognitive changes that are exacerbated by physical activity. ME/CFS is not associated with peripheral neuropathy. Secondary syphilis typically presents with a rash and constitutional symptoms. Neurologic symptoms associated with secondary syphilis include ocular symptoms and otosyphilis with vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. Secondary syphilis is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 76-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension and major depressive disorder presents because of acute right knee pain that began after she sustained a mechanical fall and landed on her knee while taking a walk near her house yesterday. She was able to walk home without difficulty. She applied ice to the area after the fall, but her knee was more painful this morning. When asked to point to the pain, she points to an area lateral to the inferior patella. Examination of the knee reveals no redness or swelling but minor warmth over the anterior knee. Lower extremity sensation is intact. The patient has full range of motion with pain. There is no tenderness of the patella or the fibular head with palpation. Provocative testing including an Apley grind test, a McMurray test, a Lachman test, and anterior and posterior drawer tests is negative. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step to aid in diagnosis?

choices.E: Arthrocentesis with culture and Gram stain

bullets.text: The Ottawa Knee Rules indicate radiography for patients ≥55 years old with acute knee pain to rule out fracture, making plain x-ray the correct first-line imaging in this 76-year-old.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The Ottawa Knee Rules are a well-validated clinical decision tool designed to limit unnecessary radiography after knee injury. One of the criteria mandating an x-ray is patient age ≥55 years. In this case, the patient is 76 years old, so radiography is indicated. Plain radiography remains the preferred modality over ultrasonography for diagnosing fractures in adults.

bullets.text: MRI is not indicated because ligament and meniscal testing is negative; arthrocentesis with culture and Gram stain would only be appropriate if septic arthritis were suspected based on history and physical examination.
bullets.sub_paragraph: MRI is reserved for cases where ligamentous or meniscal injury is suspected based on physical examination findings; since those tests are negative here, MRI is not warranted. Arthrocentesis with culture and Gram stain is indicated when the clinical picture suggests an infectious process (e.g., septic arthritis), which is not supported by this patient's presentation of acute post-traumatic knee pain following a mechanical fall.

explanation_raw: According to the Ottawa knee rules, a well-validated tool used to limit unnecessary radiography, a knee x-ray is indicated in this patient to rule out fracture because she is ≥55 years of age. Radiography is currently the preferred modality over ultrasonography for diagnosing a fracture in an adult. Because ligament and meniscal testing is negative, MRI is not indicated. Arthrocentesis with culture and Gram stain would be indicated if the history and physical examination suggest an infection of the joint space.

stem: A 31-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 8 weeks' gestation presents to the urgent care clinic because of a 2-day history of headache and fever. This morning she removed an engorged tick from her leg. On examination she is ill appearing but alert and interactive. An HEENT examination is normal and there is no pain with neck flexion. A cardiopulmonary examination is normal. There is no rash. You suspect Rocky Mountain spotted fever. In addition to supportive care, which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?

bullets.text: Doxycycline is the recommended treatment for all individuals with presumed Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), including children and pregnant persons, as short courses (5–10 days) have been shown to be safe.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Doxycycline is the recommended treatment for all individuals with presumed Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF). RMSF can be fatal, so testing is not recommended as it would delay treatment. Short courses (5–10 days) of doxycycline have been shown to be safe in children and pregnant persons. Inpatient treatment with rapid desensitization is recommended for individuals with a true allergy to doxycycline.

bullets.text: Chloramphenicol is an alternative for RMSF but is associated with a higher risk of death than doxycycline; amoxicillin and erythromycin have no role in the treatment of RMSF.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Chloramphenicol is another treatment option for RMSF, but it is associated with a higher risk for death compared to doxycycline. There is no role for amoxicillin or erythromycin in the treatment of RMSF, making these incorrect choices even in a pregnant patient where providers might hesitate to use doxycycline.

explanation_raw: Doxycycline is the recommended treatment for all individuals with presumed Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF). RMSF can be fatal, so testing for the condition is not recommended because it would delay treatment. Short courses (5–10 days) of doxycycline have been shown to be safe in children and pregnant persons. Inpatient treatment with rapid desensitization is recommended for individuals with a true allergy to doxycycline. Chloramphenicol is another treatment option for RMSF, but it is associated with a higher risk for death than doxycycline. There is no role for amoxicillin or erythromycin in the treatment of RMSF.

stem: A 53-year-old female with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant discomfort. A physical examination reveals mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory Findings Alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L (N 44–147) AST 70 U/L (N 10–40) Total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL (N 0.1–1.2) Antimitochondrial antibodies positive Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is diagnosed when at least 2 of 3 criteria are met: elevated ALP (cholestasis), positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA), or histopathologic evidence of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis; AMA is present in >95% of cases.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Per AASLD guidelines, the diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis requires at least 2 of the following: biochemical evidence of cholestasis (elevated ALP), presence of antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and histopathologic evidence of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis. AMA is the most distinctive serologic marker, found in over 95% of PBC cases, making it highly sensitive and specific for this condition. The classic presentation includes fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant discomfort with a predominantly cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (markedly elevated ALP with only mildly elevated aminotransferases).

bullets.text: Autoimmune hepatitis, MASLD, drug-induced liver injury, and primary sclerosing cholangitis each have distinguishing features that separate them from PBC, particularly the absence of positive AMA and differing enzyme patterns.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Autoimmune hepatitis presents with elevated aminotransferases and autoantibodies such as ANA or anti-smooth muscle antibodies, not AMA, and is not primarily a cholestatic disease. MASLD (formerly NAFLD) is associated with metabolic syndrome and elevated aminotransferases, without cholestasis or AMA positivity. Drug-induced liver injury can mimic many patterns but the chronicity and positive AMA in this scenario make it unlikely. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) also causes cholestatic enzyme abnormalities but is typically associated with inflammatory bowel disease, diagnosed by characteristic bile duct strictures on MRI cholangiography or ERCP, and AMA is rarely positive in PSC.

explanation_raw: Primary biliary cholangitis is characterized by chronic cholestasis, positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP). The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) guidelines state that the diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis can be established with the presence of at least 2 of the following: biochemical evidence of cholestasis (elevated ALP), presence of AMA, and histopathologic evidence of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis. Elevated AMA is particularly helpful as it is found in >95% of cases of primary biliary cholangitis. Autoimmune hepatitis usually presents with elevated aminotransferases and positive autoantibodies such as antinuclear antibodies or anti–smooth muscle antibodies, rather than AMA. It is not primarily a cholestatic disease and elevated ALP is typically not the predominant finding. Depending on the instigating agent, drug-induced liver injury can present with a variety of liver enzyme abnormalities; however, the presence of positive AMA and the chronicity of symptoms make it less likely in this patient scenario. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) typically presents with elevated aminotransferases and is associated with metabolic syndrome. It is not characterized by cholestasis or positive AMA. Primary sclerosing cholangitis typically presents with cholestatic liver enzyme abnormalities and is often associated with inflammatory bowel disease. It is diagnosed based on characteristic imaging findings of bile duct strictures using MRI cholangiography or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. Positive AMA is rarely found in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem: A generally healthy 28-year-old female presents to your office because she is concerned about changes in her mood. For the last few months she has been intermittently irritable and unable to sit still. She has had some weight loss, is not sleeping well, and feels fatigued. She has been working extra hours to get ahead of her office deadlines. She has maxed out her credit card and repeatedly cheated on her husband, who filed for divorce 2 weeks ago. She now feels depressed and anxious, and has considered suicide but does not have suicidal ideations today. She says that she has had similar episodes in the past. Her father left when she was an infant and her mother is incarcerated, and the patient is unsure of their medical history. Today the patient's vital signs, a CBC, a comprehensive metabolic panel, and TSH and vitamin B12 levels are unremarkable. A urine pregnancy test and drug screen are negative. She is alert and oriented during the office visit. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate therapy at this time?

bullets.text: This patient's intermittent irritability, psychomotor agitation, insomnia, weight loss, and fatigue are consistent with bipolar disorder, which affects >1% of the population and carries a high suicide risk requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's intermittent irritability, psychomotor agitation, insomnia, weight loss, and fatigue are consistent with bipolar disorder, which affects >1% of the population and carries a high suicide risk requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment. DSM-5 criteria are used to determine episode type and severity. The risk of relapse increases significantly in untreated patients, making timely recognition and management essential.

bullets.text: FDA-approved first-line pharmacotherapy for bipolar disorder includes lithium, anticonvulsants, and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine; monotherapy with antidepressants is contraindicated in mixed features, manic episodes, or bipolar I disorder.
bullets.sub_paragraph: FDA-approved first-line pharmacotherapy for bipolar disorder includes lithium, anticonvulsants, and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine. Monotherapy with an antidepressant is contraindicated in patients with mixed features, manic episodes, or bipolar I disorder, as it can precipitate or worsen mania. Pharmacotherapy remains the cornerstone of treatment; augmenting strategies (omega-3 fatty acids, light therapy, ketamine, probiotics, CBT, exercise, nutrition) show some benefit but have insufficient evidence to replace medications. Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for psychotic depression, refractory illness, catatonia, acute psychosis, or suicidal behavior.

explanation_raw: This patient has features of bipolar disorder, a mental health condition affecting >1% of the world's population. The DSM-5 criteria can be used to suggest a prognosis and determine episode severity. Patients with bipolar disorder have a high suicide rate, so proper diagnosis and prompt treatment are important. The risk of relapse increases in patients who are untreated. Treatment improves prognosis and medications are the mainstay of therapy. FDA-approved medications for the treatment of bipolar disorder include lithium, anticonvulsants, and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine. Although this patient has symptoms of depression, monotherapy with an antidepressant is contraindicated in patients with mixed features, manic episodes, or bipolar I disorder. Augmenting therapies such as omega-3 fatty acids, light therapy, ketamine, and probiotics may be helpful but current evidence is insufficient. Cognitive behavioral therapy, exercise, and nutrition have been shown to be beneficial as well. Electroconvulsive therapy can be an effective treatment for psychotic depression, mania, refractory illness, catatonia, acute psychosis, and suicidal behavior. However, pharmacotherapy is the first-line treatment for bipolar disorder.

stem: A 23-year-old female presents for IUD removal because she wants to conceive. She has never been pregnant, is in good health, and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is normal and her BMI is 33 kg/m2. Which one of the following should you recommend regarding aspirin prophylaxis for preeclampsia?

choices.A: No aspirin as she does not meet criteria
choices.B: Aspirin for 1–3 months prior to conception
choices.D: Aspirin if her blood pressure during pregnancy is >135/80 mm Hg

bullets.text: Aspirin prophylaxis is recommended for patients with ≥1 high-risk factor or ≥2 moderate-risk factors for preeclampsia; this nulliparous patient with BMI >30 kg/m² has two moderate-risk factors.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF and ACOG recommend low-dose aspirin prophylaxis for pregnant patients at increased risk for preeclampsia. High-risk factors include prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, type 1 or 2 diabetes, and chronic hypertension. Moderate-risk factors include first pregnancy, maternal age ≥35, BMI >30 kg/m², family history of preeclampsia, and certain sociodemographic characteristics. This patient is nulliparous (first pregnancy) and has a pre-pregnancy BMI of 33 kg/m², conferring two moderate-risk factors and meeting the threshold for prophylaxis.

bullets.text: Low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) should be initiated at 12 weeks' gestation to reduce the risk of preeclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction, and preterm birth, with favorable fetal and maternal safety profiles.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The recommended regimen is aspirin 81 mg orally once daily, started at 12 weeks' gestation (and generally continued until delivery). Starting at this gestational age is critical, as earlier initiation during trophoblastic invasion is believed to optimize placental development. Low-dose aspirin has been shown to decrease the frequency of preeclampsia as well as other adverse pregnancy outcomes such as intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth, while maintaining a favorable safety profile for both mother and fetus.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend aspirin prophylaxis for pregnant patients who are at increased risk for preeclampsia. Indications include 1 or more high-risk factors or 2 or more moderate-risk factors. High-risk factors include a history of preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and chronic hypertension. Moderate-risk factors include first pregnancy, maternal age ≥35 years, BMI >30 kg/m2, family history of preeclampsia, sociodemographic characteristics, and personal history factors. This patient is nulliparous and has a pre-pregnancy BMI >30 kg/m2, giving her 2 moderaterisk factors. The recommended aspirin prophylaxis for preeclampsia is 81 mg per day and should be started at 12 weeks' gestation. Low-dose aspirin has been shown to decrease the frequency of preeclampsia as well as other adverse pregnancy outcomes such as intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth. It also has favorable fetal and maternal safety profiles.

stem: A 74-year-old female presents to your office for follow-up of cardioembolic stroke 1 day after being discharged from the hospital. She presented to the hospital with acute left-sided hand and face weakness. An evaluation in the hospital revealed new atrial fibrillation, mild mitral regurgitation, and a small right-sided cerebral infarction. Cardioembolic stroke was diagnosed. She was discharged 48 hours later after her left-sided weakness had almost completely resolved. Which one of the following therapeutic options is preferred for this patient?

bullets.text: In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with TIA or small cardioembolic stroke, guidelines recommend starting a direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban 2–14 days after the event, without antiplatelet agents.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with a recent cardioembolic stroke in the setting of newly diagnosed nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (defined by the absence of moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve). Guidelines recommend anticoagulation—preferring DOACs over warfarin—initiated 2–14 days after a TIA or small cardioembolic stroke. The 2024 OPTIMAS trial confirmed the safety of starting anticoagulation within 4 days of stroke onset. For larger strokes at higher risk of hemorrhagic conversion, initiation may be appropriately delayed up to 14 days.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with a recent history of cardioembolic stroke. In patients who have a TIA or small cardioembolic stroke and nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, guidelines recommend starting anticoagulation without antiplatelet agents 2–14 days after the event. Nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is defined by the lack of moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve; direct-acting oral anticoagulants are preferred to warfarin in these patients. The 2024 Optimal Timing of Anticoagulation After Acute Ischaemic Stroke (OPTIMAS) trial confirmed the safety of starting anticoagulation within 4 days of a stroke. In patients with larger strokes that may be at high risk for hemorrhagic conversion, initiating anticoagulation may be delayed to 14 days.

stem: A 75-year-old female with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) diagnosed in the emergency department has been admitted to your service. She underwent a percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent to the circumflex artery and had been recovering well until she developed acute shortness of breath on the fourth day of hospitalization. Today, her vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 91/55 mm Hg, a heart rate of 110 beats/min, and an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air. On physical examination, the patient appears moderately distressed and has no jugular venous pulse. Auscultation reveals a regular rate, normal S1 and S2, and a systolic murmur over the mitral post. Crackles are heard in all lung fields. There is no lower extremity edema. Which one of the following is the likely etiology of this condition?

bullets.text: Acute papillary muscle rupture occurs 3–5 days after a transmural infarction involving the right coronary artery or circumflex artery, leading to acute mitral regurgitation with flash pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Advances in angiography, pharmacology, and systems of care have reduced the incidence of mechanical complications of AMI, but hospital mortality for complications such as acute papillary muscle rupture remains high. Rupture of the papillary muscle typically occurs 3–5 days post-infarction and results in sudden, severe mitral regurgitation, manifesting as flash pulmonary edema and hemodynamic compromise as seen in this patient.

bullets.text: Cardiac tamponade, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, and atrial fibrillation are less likely given the clinical context of post-PCI recovery with acute pulmonary edema and shock without chest pain, neck vein distension, or absence of anticoagulation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cardiac tamponade from free wall rupture is rare and typically presents with chest pain, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins. Pericarditis features chest pain as a core symptom, which is absent here. Pulmonary embolism is less likely given that hospitalized post-PCI patients typically receive anticoagulation, and there is no peripheral edema suggesting venous thromboembolism. A supraventricular tachyarrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation at a ventricular rate of 110 beats/min is unlikely to produce the degree of hemodynamic compromise described in this case.

explanation_raw: Advances in angiography, pharmacology, and systems of care have improved morbidity and mortality for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) over the last several decades. This has reduced the incidence of mechanical complications of AMI; however, the hospital mortality for these complications, such as acute papillary muscle rupture, remains high. Acute papillary muscle rupture occurs 3–5 days after a transmural infarction involving the right coronary artery or circumflex artery, depending on coronary anatomy. This leads to acute mitral regurgitation, resulting in flash pulmonary edema and shock, as seen in this patient. Cardiac tamponade can occur after an AMI if the ventricular free wall ruptures, which is rare. Clinical clues include chest pain, shortness of breath, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins. Chest pain is also a core feature of pericarditis, making it an unlikely diagnosis in this patient. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common complication seen in immobile hospitalized patients and can be reduced with appropriate mechanical prophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis. While astute clinicians may rule out PE in this patient, her admission has likely included anticoagulation, and lack of edema makes a venous thromboembolism etiology for PE less likely. Arrhythmias can also occur after an AMI. Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation may present similarly to this patient, but a ventricular rate of 110 beats/min is unlikely to result in hemodynamic compromise as described in this case.

stem: A 14-year-old male sees you to establish care. He has a past medical history of asthma and uses an albuterol inhaler (Proventil, Ventolin) as needed. He normally has symptoms about 3–4 days per week. Recent pulmonary function tests showed mildly reduced lung function. Based on the Global Initiative for Asthma (GIN

choices.C: Switching to an as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plus formoterol
choices.D: Continuing as-needed albuterol, and adding a low-dose ICS for maintenance
choices.E: Continuing as-needed albuterol, and adding a low-dose ICS plus salmeterol for maintenance

correct_label: Switching to an as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plus formoterol

bullets.text: This patient meets GINA criteria for mild asthma, defined as symptoms occurring less than 3–5 days per week with normal or mildly reduced lung function.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to GINA guidelines, mild asthma is characterized by intermittent to mild persistent symptoms (fewer than 3–5 days per week) accompanied by normal or mildly reduced pulmonary function test results. This 14-year-old with symptoms 3–4 days per week and mildly reduced lung function fits this classification.

bullets.text: For patients 12 years and older with mild asthma, GINA recommends switching from as-needed SABA to as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus formoterol (ICS/formoterol), which reduces severe exacerbations by 60–64% compared to as-needed albuterol alone.
bullets.sub_paragraph: GINA guidelines recommend as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol as the preferred reliever therapy for mild asthma in patients aged 12 and older. This regimen significantly reduces the risk of severe asthma exacerbations by 60–64% compared to as-needed short-acting β-agonists (SABAs) such as albuterol, and also outperforms other regimens that use a SABA reliever. It is important to note that formoterol (a long-acting β-agonist) must always be used in combination with an ICS and should never be prescribed as monotherapy due to safety concerns.

explanation_raw: Based on the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guideline, patients who have symptoms <3–5 days per week with normal or mildly reduced lung function are classified as having mild asthma. For patients 12 years and older with mild asthma, the guidelines recommend treatment with as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus formoterol (ICS/formoterol). As-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol reduces the risk of severe asthma exacerbations by 60%–64% compared to as-needed short-acting β-agonists (SABAs) such as albuterol. ICS/formoterol also reduces the risk of severe exacerbations compared to other regimens that include a SABA reliever. Formoterol should not be used without an ICS.

stem: A 37-year-old male who recently returned from a trip to Vietnam presents for evaluation of an intensely pruritic rash on his feet. Physical examination findings are normal other than an erythematous, serpiginous rash on his feet and lower legs. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Cutaneous larva migrans presents as an intensely pruritic, erythematous, serpiginous rash on the feet and gluteal areas, diagnosed clinically without specific diagnostic tests, and is commonly acquired in Asia and Africa where macaque monkeys serve as the reservoir.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cutaneous larva migrans is the most likely diagnosis given the classic intensely pruritic, erythematous, serpiginous rash on the feet following travel to Vietnam. The infection is found mainly in Asia and Africa, has an incubation period of 1–5 days (up to 1 month), is diagnosed clinically, and is generally self-limited but can be treated with albendazole.

bullets.text: Cutaneous leishmaniasis causes painless nonhealing ulcers with raised borders; herpesvirus B causes vesicular lesions with flu-like symptoms; Neisseria meningitidis causes petechiae to severe systemic disease; and scabies presents with a pruritic rash along skinfolds rather than a serpiginous pattern on the feet.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cutaneous leishmaniasis presents with small papules that evolve into painless nonhealing open sores with raised borders and central ulceration — distinct from the serpiginous pattern here. Herpesvirus B produces vesicular lesions near the inoculation site with influenza-like symptoms. Neisseria meningitidis ranges from asymptomatic petechiae to severe systemic illness. Scabies is intensely pruritic but produces small red bumps along skinfolds, not a serpiginous tract on the feet.

explanation_raw: The most likely diagnosis is cutaneous larva migrans. The typical rash that occurs with this infection is an intensely pruritic, erythematous, serpiginous rash. It is typically seen on the feet and gluteal areas. There are no diagnostic tests for this infection and the diagnosis is made clinically. Infections are generally self-limited but can be treated with albendazole. Cutaneous larva migrans infections are mainly found in Asia and Africa where macaque monkeys are the reservoir. It has an incubation period of 1–5 days but can take up to 1 month. Cutaneous leishmaniasis generally presents with small papules that develop into nonhealing open sores with a raised border and central ulceration. The lesions are generally painless. Herpesvirus B presents with a vesicular rash near the site of inoculation and influenza-like symptoms. The clinical manifestations of Neisseria meningitidis range from asymptomatic dermatologic findings such as petechiae to severe systemic disease. Scabies presents with a very pruritic rash that is red with small bumps, typically appears along skinfolds, and often forms a line.

stem: A 10-year-old male is brought to your office by his mother for follow-up of treatment for a Cryptosporidium infection that he likely contracted during a camping trip after swimming in a freshwater lake. He has completed treatment and is asymptomatic. His mother asks when he is allowed to resume swimming. Because of concerns for ongoing asymptomatic shedding, you should recommend that the patient may return to swimming

bullets.text: Patients with Cryptosporidium infection should avoid swimming for 2 weeks after symptoms resolve, as oocyst shedding continues even after clinical recovery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cryptosporidium oocysts can survive up to 10 days in chlorinated/treated water, making post-symptomatic shedding a significant public health concern. Even after diarrhea resolves, patients continue to shed infectious oocysts in their stool. For this reason, the recommended guidance is to refrain from swimming for 2 weeks after resolution of symptoms to prevent transmission to others in recreational water settings.

bullets.text: Treatment for Cryptosporidium is primarily supportive with fluid and electrolyte replacement; nitazoxanide may be used for severe or prolonged disease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Most immunocompetent patients with Cryptosporidium infection recover with supportive care, including oral rehydration and electrolyte replacement. Nitazoxanide is an antiparasitic agent that can be used in cases of severe or prolonged infection, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or when symptoms do not resolve on their own. Diagnosis is confirmed via stool sample, typically with detection of oocysts using acid-fast staining or antigen testing.

explanation_raw: Infection with Cryptosporidium is caused by ingesting oocysts, which can survive for up to 10 days in treated water. Diarrhea is the predominant symptom, and a stool sample is used for diagnosis. Treatment for infection with Cryptosporidium is supportive with fluid and electrolyte replacement. Nitazoxanide can be used in cases of severe or prolonged disease. Because shedding of oocysts continues even after symptoms resolve, it is recommended that patients refrain from swimming for 2 weeks after resolution of symptoms.

stem: A previously healthy 27-year-old female at 36 weeks' gestation presents to the emergency department (E

bullets.text: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) should be suspected in pregnant women presenting with malaise, headache, hypertension, and proteinuria, and carries a 10–15% maternal morbidity and mortality rate.
bullets.sub_paragraph: HELLP syndrome should be suspected in pregnant women presenting with malaise, headache, hypertension, and proteinuria. Women with HELLP syndrome have 10%–15% maternal morbidity and mortality rates compared to those without, due to severe potential complications such as cerebral hemorrhage, cardiopulmonary arrest, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, renal failure, sepsis, and hepatic hemorrhage. Although this patient has been taking acetaminophen, the clinical picture is consistent with HELLP syndrome rather than acetaminophen toxicity.

bullets.text: Urgent delivery is the definitive treatment for HELLP syndrome in patients at or beyond 34 weeks' gestation and is critical to preventing maternal death.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Early diagnosis and management are critical in HELLP syndrome. Urgent delivery in patients over 34 weeks' gestation is the key intervention to avoid maternal deaths. Corticosteroids may be used to temporarily improve platelet counts but will not address hepatic failure. N-acetylcysteine is not warranted here, as the laboratory and clinical findings are consistent with HELLP rather than acetaminophen overdose.

explanation_raw: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome should be suspected in pregnant women presenting with malaise, headache, hypertension, and proteinuria. Women with HELLP syndrome have 10%–15% maternal morbidity and mortality rates compared to those without. The elevated risks are due to the potential of severe complications such as cerebral hemorrhage, cardiopulmonary arrest, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, renal failure, sepsis, and hepatic hemorrhage. Early diagnosis and management are critical. Quick and targeted evaluation with urgent delivery in patients over 34 weeks' gestation is key to avoiding maternal deaths. Corticosteroids can be used to treat low platelet count, but will not address the symptoms of liver failure. Acute liver failure due to HELLP is secondary to pregnancy. Although this patient has been taking acetaminophen, the examination and laboratory results are consistent with HELLP syndrome; therefore, treatment for acetaminophen overdose with N-acetylcysteine is not warranted.

stem: A 64-year-old female with a history of hypertension and no prior evidence of kidney disease presents for follow-up of a recent basic metabolic panel that showed an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 49 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which one of the following would confirm a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease?

choices.A: A urine albumin to creatinine ratio >30 mg/g at this time
choices.B: A urine albumin to creatinine ratio >300 mg/g at this time
choices.C: An additional eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 1 month
choices.D: An additional eGFR <90 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 2 months
choices.E: An additional eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 3 months

correct_label: An additional eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 3 months

bullets.text: A diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD) requires evidence of renal impairment or damage persisting for at least 3 months to differentiate it from acute kidney injury (AKI).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Before CKD can be diagnosed, evidence of renal impairment or damage must be present for at least 3 months. This is most commonly confirmed by a repeat eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² at least 3 months after the initial finding. However, per KDIGO guidelines, other markers of persistent renal damage — such as albuminuria, proteinuria, renal imaging abnormalities (e.g., decreased kidney volume, cortical thinning, or multiple cysts), or prior documentation of kidney damage — can also satisfy the chronicity requirement and confirm the diagnosis of CKD.

explanation_raw: Before a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease can be made, evidence of renal impairment or damage must be present for 3 months in order to differentiate the renal abnormalities from an acute kidney injury (AKI). This is most often an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m2; however, the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines do allow for other evidence of persistent renal damage or decreased function, such as albuminuria or proteinuria, that persists for at least 3 months. Previous documentation of kidney damage or impairment can also be sought. Renal imaging abnormalities such as decreased kidney volume, cortical thickening, or multiple cysts are also evidence of chronicity.

stem: A 4-year-old male presents with a 6-day history of fever, rash, and an enlarged lymph node. On examination, you note erythema of the lips, bilateral conjunctivitis, and a diffuse maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. The right anterior cervical lymph node is nontender and 2 cm in size. Which one of the following is the most serious complication of this patient's condition?

bullets.text: This patient meets criteria for Kawasaki disease, which classically presents in children <5 years with fever plus ≥4 of: oral mucous membrane changes, bilateral conjunctivitis, diffuse rash, hand/foot edema, and unilateral cervical adenopathy ≥1.5 cm.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Kawasaki disease is a systemic vasculitis most common in children under 5 years of age. The classic diagnostic criteria require fever plus at least 4 of the following features: oral mucous membrane changes (erythema/cracking of lips), bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, diffuse polymorphous rash, erythema/edema of the hands and feet, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy ≥1.5 cm. This patient demonstrates fever, lip erythema, bilateral conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, and cervical adenopathy — satisfying the diagnostic criteria.

bullets.text: The most serious complication of Kawasaki disease is cardiac: if untreated, 15–25% of patients develop cardiovascular abnormalities including coronary artery aneurysms, aortic root dilation, tachycardia, hypotension, and shock.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cardiac involvement is the most feared and serious complication of Kawasaki disease. Without treatment, 15–25% of patients will develop cardiovascular abnormalities such as coronary artery dilation, coronary artery aneurysms, aortic root dilation, tachycardia, hypotension, and shock. Echocardiography must be performed as soon as possible after diagnosis to assess for coronary artery involvement. Less serious complications include anemia, elevated liver function tests, sterile pyuria, and pulmonary edema. Treatment with high-dose aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms when initiated promptly.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with Kawasaki disease, which commonly occurs in children <5 years of age. Classic Kawasaki disease presents with 4 of the following features: oral mucous membrane changes, bilateral conjunctivitis, diffuse rash, hand and foot edema, and unilateral cervical adenopathy ≥1.5 cm. Inflammation occurs and can affect multiple organ systems. The most serious complication is cardiac. If untreated, 15%–25% of patients will develop cardiovascular abnormalities, including coronary artery dilation, aortic root dilation, cardiac aneurysms, tachycardia, hypotension, and shock. Echocardiography must be performed as soon as possible. Less serious complications of Kawasaki disease include anemia, elevated liver function test results, pyuria, and pulmonary edema.

stem: A 40-year-old female presents for a health maintenance examination. Her medical history is unremarkable, but her family history is significant for colorectal cancer in her father, thyroid cancer in her paternal aunt, and endometrial cancer in her maternal grandmother. The patient says that her friend was diagnosed with breast cancer 2 weeks ago and is BRCA2 positive. She is anxious about her risk of breast cancer and requests a mammogram and BRCA testing. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines, which one of the following would be most appropriate for this patient regarding genetic testing for BRCA1/2?

choices.B: Risk assessment using the 7-Question Family History Screening Tool

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends against routine BRCA1/2 screening in women without a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer (D recommendation).
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF gives a D recommendation against routine screening, risk assessment, counseling, and genetic testing for BRCA1/2 mutations in all women. Only women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer—or ancestry associated with BRCA susceptibility—should be formally evaluated using a validated risk assessment tool. This patient's family history (colorectal, thyroid, and endometrial cancers) does not meet the criteria that would trigger BRCA risk assessment, so reassurance only is appropriate.

bullets.text: Genetic testing for BRCA1/2 is indicated only after a positive risk assessment score and subsequent genetic counseling—not as a first-line step for all patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Even in patients who do meet criteria for BRCA risk assessment, the process is stepwise: first apply a validated risk assessment tool (e.g., Ontario Family History Assessment Tool, Manchester Scoring System), and only if the score is positive should genetic counseling and then testing be offered. Skipping directly to genetic testing without a qualifying family history or a positive risk assessment is not recommended practice.

explanation_raw: For this patient, reassurance only is indicated. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against routine screening, risk assessment, counseling, and testing in all women for BRCA1/2 mutations (D recommendation). Only women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneum cancer or specific susceptibility to BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations should be formally evaluated with a risk assessment tool. Furthermore, genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 is indicated only after a positive risk assessment score is calculated and subsequent genetic counseling is received.

stem: You are seeing a patient at 12 weeks' gestation for prenatal care. She has a family history of neural tube defects and is taking 4 mg of high-dose folic acid supplementation daily. Her pregnancy is progressing normally, and she has no concerns. Which one of the following should you recommend for this patient regarding ongoing folic acid supplementation?

choices.A: Continuing with 4 mg daily for the remainder of the pregnancy
choices.B: Decreasing the dosage to 1 mg daily for the remainder of the pregnancy
choices.C: Decreasing the dosage to 0.4 mg daily for the remainder of the pregnancy

correct_label: Decreasing the dosage to 0.4 mg daily for the remainder of the pregnancy

bullets.text: High-dose folic acid (4 mg/day) is recommended for high-risk pregnancies (e.g., family history of NTDs) from preconception through 12 weeks' gestation, after which the dose should be decreased to 0.4 mg/day for the remainder of the pregnancy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Supplementation with folic acid leading up to and during pregnancy significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs). Patients at higher risk — such as those with a personal or family history of NTDs — should take 4 mg per day, ideally starting 1–3 months prior to conception and continuing until 12 weeks after conception. After 12 weeks, organogenesis is largely complete, and there is theoretical concern for fetal toxicity with continued high-dose supplementation; therefore, the dose is reduced to the standard 0.4 mg per day for the remainder of the pregnancy. Folic acid supplementation is recommended in addition to usual dietary sources.

explanation_raw: Supplementation with folic acid leading up to and during pregnancy can significantly reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs). Ideally, supplementation should be started 1–3 months prior to conception. Those with pregnancies at higher risk of NTDs are candidates for high-dose folic acid supplementation, which is more effective at prevention. This patient is considered high risk as she has a family history of NTDs. The recommended dose of folic acid is 4 mg per day until 12 weeks after conception, and then 0.4 mg per day after 12 weeks. The rationale for decreasing the dose after 12 weeks is that organogenesis is largely complete by this stage and there is theoretical concern for fetal toxicity. Folic acid supplementation is recommended in addition to the usual dietary sources of folic acid.

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease presents for management of recurrent gout. He has had multiple attacks this year despite dietary changes. His uric acid level is 8.6 mg/dL (N 4.5–8.0) and he would like to start gout prophylaxis. Which one of the following would be most appropriate to initiate at this time?

bullets.text: Allopurinol is first-line urate-lowering therapy for gout (even in CKD), and the ACR strongly recommends co-initiating an anti-inflammatory such as colchicine to prevent acute flares when starting allopurinol.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Allopurinol is the preferred first-line urate-lowering agent for recurrent gout in all patients, including those with chronic kidney disease, with the dose titrated to achieve a target uric acid level below 6 mg/dL. The American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends concurrent use of an anti-inflammatory prophylactic agent—most commonly colchicine—at the time allopurinol is initiated, as mobilization of urate crystals during dose titration can precipitate acute flares. Colchicine alone is appropriate for managing acute attacks, as are NSAIDs or corticosteroids, but none of these lower uric acid levels.

bullets.text: Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor indicated for chronic gout but is not first-line; pegloticase is strongly discouraged as first-line therapy due to high cost, limited safety data, and less favorable benefit-to-harm ratio.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Febuxostat works by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, thereby reducing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, but it is not considered a first-line choice over allopurinol. Colchicine alone does not lower uric acid and is insufficient for long-term prophylaxis as monotherapy in a patient requiring urate-lowering therapy. Pegloticase, a recombinant uricase, is reserved for refractory cases and is strongly recommended against as a first-line option by the ACR due to its cost, infusion-related risks, immunogenicity concerns, and the availability of safer alternatives.

explanation_raw: Gout is a common crystalline arthropathy. Long-term treatment with urate-lowering medications is effective in preventing recurrent attacks and is generally well tolerated. Allopurinol is typically used as first-line treatment for gout in all patients, even in those with kidney disease. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) strongly recommends that an anti-inflammatory medication, such as colchicine, be given when allopurinol is initiated to prevent an acute flare. The allopurinol dosage should be adjusted to target a uric acid level <6 mg/dL. Colchicine alone is useful in the setting of an acute flare, as are NSAIDs or corticosteroids. Febuxostat is a urate-lowering medication that works by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, which interferes with the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid. While this medication is indicated for chronic gout, it is not a first-line choice. The ACR strongly recommends against pegloticase as a first-line therapy due to cost, lack of evidence regarding safety, and other options with more favorable benefit to harm ratios.

stem: In a patient with aortic stenosis, which one of the following is an indication for referral for possible valve replacement?

choices.A: Calcification of the valve on an echocardiogram
choices.B: Development of mitral insufficiency on an echocardiogram
choices.C: Left ventricular hypertrophy noted on a chest x-ray
choices.D: A systolic ejection murmur that has increased from grade 1/6 to grade 2/6

explanation.heading: Indications for Valve Replacement in Aortic Stenosis

bullets.text: New-onset angina in aortic stenosis is an indication for referral for valve replacement, as symptom onset marks a critical turning point with 2-year survival rates below 50% without intervention.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Once symptoms develop in aortic stenosis — including angina, syncope, or heart failure — the prognosis becomes extremely poor, with 2-year survival rates below 50%. Valve replacement reverses this prognosis, yielding postoperative survival rates comparable to age-matched normal adults with acceptable operative morbidity and mortality. New-onset angina specifically signals severe hemodynamic compromise and should also prompt evaluation for concurrent coronary artery disease.

explanation_raw: Once symptoms occur in patients with aortic stenosis, the clinical outcome is extremely poor, with 2-year survival rates below 50%. It is well established that this prognosis can be reversed by valve replacement, which has acceptable levels of operative morbidity and mortality, and postoperative survival rates similar to those of age-matched normal adults. Angina could be an indication of the seriousness of aortic valve stenosis. Patients should also be evaluated for coronary artery disease.

stem: A 23-year-old male presents on a spring day with a 2–3-day history of mild nasal congestion, sneezing, and slight watery discharge. He does not have a fever or other significant concerns. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?

bullets.text: Intranasal corticosteroids are first-line therapy for allergic rhinitis, even in mild cases, as they are more effective than antihistamines or cromolyn.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with classic mild allergic rhinitis (seasonal sneezing, nasal congestion, watery discharge, no fever). Intranasal corticosteroids are considered first-line therapy due to their superior efficacy. Intranasal or oral antihistamines may be considered for mild symptoms but are less effective overall.
