Intranasal cromolyn is less effective and requires multiple daily dosing. Oral antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of infection, and oral corticosteroids are not appropriate for mild allergic rhinitis. Nasal saline irrigation can help remove allergens but has limited evidence and should augment rather than replace pharmacotherapy.

explanation_raw: This patient has mild allergic rhinitis. Intranasal corticosteroids are considered first-line therapy. Intranasal or oral antihistamines may be considered given the patient's mild symptoms, but they are less effective. Intranasal cromolyn is less effective and requires multiple dosing. Since there is no apparent infection, oral antibiotics are not indicated. Oral corticosteroids are also not indicated at this time. Some experts recommend nasal saline irrigation to remove allergens from the nares, but this approach has limited evidence and would augment, not replace, pharmacotherapy.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents for follow-up of infertility. She and her husband have been trying to conceive for the past 12 months. She reports a history of irregular menstrual bleeding over the past several years. A physical examination is unremarkable except for a BMI of 29 kg/m2. You suspect polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and recommend diagnostic testing with fasting laboratory studies scheduled for 8:00 a.m. An elevation in which one of the following hormones would most strongly support a diagnosis of PCOS in this patient?

bullets.text: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria (at least 2 of 3): oligoanovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound; elevated free testosterone confirms biochemical hyperandrogenism.
bullets.sub_paragraph: There is no single test to diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The diagnosis is made when at least 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria are met: oligoanovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. Hyperandrogenism can be diagnosed clinically (hirsutism, androgenic alopecia, acne, seborrhea) or biochemically with elevated androgen levels, most importantly an elevated free testosterone level. Before confirming PCOS, other conditions must be excluded, including androgen-secreting tumors, Cushing syndrome, nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, thyroid disease, prolactin disorders, primary ovarian insufficiency, and acromegaly.

bullets.text: Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone suggests congenital adrenal hyperplasia; elevated cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome or adrenal tumor; elevated insulin or glucose reflect insulin resistance but are not part of the Rotterdam criteria.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level points toward nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which can mimic PCOS but is a separate diagnosis. An elevated cortisol level would suggest Cushing syndrome or an adrenal tumor, both of which share overlapping clinical features with PCOS but are distinct entities that must be excluded. Although insulin resistance is commonly part of PCOS pathophysiology, neither elevated insulin nor elevated fasting glucose levels are included in the Rotterdam diagnostic criteria and therefore would not be the best initial biochemical test to support a PCOS diagnosis.

explanation_raw: While there is no single test to diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the diagnosis can be made based on the presence of at least 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria: oligoanovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. Other conditions that may mimic PCOS must be excluded, including an androgen-secreting tumor, exogenous androgen exposure, Cushing syndrome, nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, primary hypothalamic amenorrhea, primary ovarian insufficiency, acromegaly, thyroid disease, prolactin disorders, and genetic disorders that impede insulin action. Hyperandrogenism may be diagnosed clinically with evidence of hirsutism, androgenic alopecia, acne, or seborrhea. Additionally, it may be diagnosed biochemically with elevated androgen levels, such as an elevated free testosterone level. An elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level would not suggest PCOS, but rather a possible diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which may share overlapping clinical features with PCOS. An elevated cortisol level would similarly suggest an etiology other than PCOS, such as Cushing syndrome or adrenal tumor, which may also share overlapping clinical features with PCOS. Although insulin resistance is often part of the complex pathophysiology of PCOS, neither elevated insulin nor glucose levels are part of the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS.

stem: A generally healthy 36-year-old male presents to your clinic with a 36-hour history of dizziness and nausea. He says he feels as though the world is spinning and he tends to fall to the left when he tries to walk. The episodes of dizziness occur spontaneously and can last from minutes to hours. He does not have any recent illness, hearing loss, or tinnitus, and he does not take any medications. An HEENT examination is normal. On neurologic testing, he exhibits horizontal nystagmus with left lateral gaze. Head-impulse testing reveals a rapid movement of both eyes. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Valacyclovir (Valtrex), 1000 mg twice daily for 7 days

bullets.text: This patient has vestibular neuritis, characterized by spontaneous rotatory vertigo, nausea, listing to the affected side, and a positive head-impulse test (saccade) with horizontal nystagmus on HINTS examination.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Vestibular neuritis most commonly affects patients aged 30–50 and is thought to have a viral etiology. It presents with prolonged, continuous vertigo — distinguishing it from BPPV, which causes brief, episodic vertigo triggered by head movements. The HINTS exam (Head-Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) is a key bedside tool; a positive head-impulse test with unidirectional horizontal nystagmus toward the affected side supports a peripheral (rather than central) cause.

bullets.text: The primary treatment for vestibular neuritis is reassurance, as it typically resolves within days; antiemetics may be used for symptomatic relief for up to 3 days.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Vestibular neuritis usually self-resolves, though some patients experience recurrent symptoms for months and may require vestibular rehabilitation. Antiemetics can be used short-term (up to 3 days) for nausea control. Corticosteroids and antiviral medications have not been shown to be effective. Home Epley maneuvers are appropriate only for BPPV and are neither indicated nor effective for vestibular neuritis (SOR A). MRI of the brain is reserved for patients with signs of central vertigo or hearing loss (SOR C).

bullets.text: Epley maneuvers, corticosteroids, antivirals, and MRI are not appropriate first-line interventions for vestibular neuritis without specific indications.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Epley maneuvers target canalith repositioning in BPPV and have no role in vestibular neuritis. Corticosteroids and antiviral agents have not demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials for this condition. MRI is indicated only when central causes of vertigo are suspected (e.g., stroke, tumor) or when hearing loss is present, neither of which applies here.

explanation_raw: This patient's vertigo is caused by vestibular neuritis, as evidenced by its spontaneity, rotatory vertigo, nausea, and listing to the affected side with walking. In this scenario, head-impulse testing shows saccade, and the head-impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (HINTS) examination is significant for horizontal nystagmus to the affected side. Vestibular neuritis is most often found in patients 30–50 years of age and is thought to have a viral etiology. It involves prolonged, continuous vertigo, while benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is characterized by brief, episodic vertigo associated with head movements. Vestibular neuritis usually resolves on its own within a few days, although some patients have recurrent symptoms for months. The treatment for vestibular neuritis is reassurance. Antiemetics can be used for up to 3 days. Patients with symptoms that last longer should be referred for vestibular rehabilitation. Home Epley maneuvers are appropriate for vertigo caused by BPPV, but are neither indicated nor effective for vestibular neuritis (SOR A). Corticosteroids and antiviral medications have not been shown to be effective in treating vestibular neuritis. MRI of the brain is indicated for patients who exhibit signs of central vertigo or those with hearing loss (SOR C).

stem: A 24-year-old gravida 2 para 2 presents to your office with melasma that has not resolved since she gave birth 6 months ago. She is eager to be treated. Which one of the following topical treatments would be the most effective for this patient's melasma?

choices.E: A combination of fluocinolone, hydroquinone, and tretinoin

correct_label: A combination of fluocinolone, hydroquinone, and tretinoin

bullets.text: The most effective topical treatment for melasma is the triple combination of fluocinolone (corticosteroid), hydroquinone, and tretinoin, which can be prescribed as a single formulation or as individual components.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Melasma is a common condition occurring in up to 75% of pregnancies, driven by elevated progesterone, estrogen, and melanocyte-stimulating hormone. Although it resolves in ~90% of postpartum cases, it can persist or recur with subsequent pregnancies or oral contraceptive use. When treatment is needed, the triple combination of a topical corticosteroid (fluocinolone), a depigmenting agent (hydroquinone), and a retinoid (tretinoin) has the highest evidence for efficacy and can be used as a single compounded formulation or as separate agents.

bullets.text: Azelaic acid and benzoyl peroxide target acne pathophysiology, not melanin overproduction, and imiquimod is an immunomodulator used for condyloma acuminata—none have a role in melasma treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Azelaic acid and benzoyl peroxide are indicated for acne and are not effective agents for reducing hyperpigmentation in melasma. Imiquimod works as a toll-like receptor agonist to stimulate local immune responses, making it useful for HPV-related lesions (condyloma acuminata) and certain skin cancers, but it has no established role in the management of melasma.

explanation_raw: Melasma is a common condition in pregnancy that occurs in up to 75% of patients. It is caused by increased levels of progesterone, estrogen, and melanocyte-stimulating hormone. While it resolves in 90% of cases during the postpartum period, it can persist and may recur in subsequent pregnancies or with the use of oral contraception. Topical tretinoin, hydroquinone, and a corticosteroid such as fluocinolone can all be used in the treatment of melasma, and a combination of the 3 is the most effective. These may be prescribed as a single formulation, which may be cost prohibitive, or as individual components. Azelaic acid and benzoyl peroxide are used to treat acne and are not effective for treating melasma. Imiquimod is an immunomodulator that is helpful in the treatment of condyloma acuminata but has no role in the treatment of melasma.

stem: You see a newborn for a routine wellness check. The parents tell you that there is a family history of allergies to eggs and peanuts, and they ask how to reduce their child's risk of developing these food allergies. Evidence supports exposing the patient to these potentially allergenic foods starting at which one of the following ages?

bullets.text: Early introduction of allergenic foods at 4–6 months of age is associated with the lowest risk of developing future food allergies, including to peanuts and eggs.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Evidence supports introducing potentially allergenic foods such as peanuts and eggs starting at 4–6 months of age to reduce the risk of developing allergies. Peanut butter should be thinned with water, breast milk, cow's milk, or formula before offering to infants, as whole peanuts pose a choking hazard. Eggs should be well-cooked prior to consumption. This early exposure strategy is recommended even in infants with a family history of food allergies.

explanation_raw: The lowest risk of developing future allergies to many foods, including peanuts and eggs, occurs with early exposure at 4–6 months of age. Peanut butter can be thinned with water, breast milk, cow’s milk, or formula. Peanuts should not be given in their original hard form because it is a choking hazard. Eggs should be cooked well prior to eating.

stem: A 23-year-old female presents after a sexual assault that occurred the prior evening. She reports nonconsensual penetrative vaginal intercourse. The assailant was an acquaintance with unknown medical history. The patient takes no medications and is up to date on vaccinations, including tetanus, HPV, and hepatitis B, although her hepatitis B serology status is unknown. She elects to undergo a medical forensic examination, which is completed with the help of a certified Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner. A urine pregnancy test is negative, and sexually transmitted infection testing is performed. Which one of the following would be most appropriate to offer at this time?

bullets.text: Empiric treatment for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis is recommended after sexual assault, using ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and metronidazole (or tinidazole).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Women who experience sexual assault should be offered empiric STI prophylaxis covering Neisseria gonorrhoeae (ceftriaxone), Chlamydia trachomatis (azithromycin), and Trichomonas vaginalis (metronidazole or tinidazole). This triple-regimen approach is standard of care alongside forensic examination, trauma-informed counseling, and emergency contraception.

explanation.heading: HIV and Hepatitis C Post-Exposure Considerations

bullets.text: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with triple antiretroviral therapy for 28 days should be offered, while routine post-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis C is not currently recommended.
bullets.sub_paragraph: HIV PEP should use a triple-therapy regimen (not the dual-therapy used for PrEP) initiated as soon as possible after exposure. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is a treatment for active hepatitis C infection but is not indicated for post-exposure prophylaxis, as routine HCV PEP is not recommended after sexual assault.

bullets.text: Effective emergency contraception (ulipristal, levonorgestrel, or copper IUD) should be offered promptly before considering long-term contraceptive methods.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients should first receive effective emergency contraception such as ulipristal acetate, levonorgestrel, or a copper IUD. While long-term contraception options may be discussed, they should not replace or delay the immediate provision of emergency contraception in the acute post-assault setting.

explanation_raw: In addition to trauma-informed evaluation and counseling, women who experience sexual assault should be offered forensic examination, emergency contraception, and screening and prevention for sexually transmitted infections. Empiric treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis is appropriate and should include ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and either metronidazole or tinidazole. Postexposure prophylaxis for HIV should be made available with triple therapy for 28 days, rather than the double therapy regimens used in pre-exposure prophylaxis. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is used to treat hepatitis C infection, but routine postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended. Long-term contraception may be offered, but patients should first be provided with effective emergency contraception, such as ulipristal, levonorgestrel, or the copper IUD.

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with a long-standing history of episodes of depressed mood, headaches, and irritability that occur in the 1–2 weeks preceding her menses. She has a history of anxiety that is well controlled on fluoxetine (Prozac), 60 mg daily. She has a copper IUD (Paragard) for contraception. She has tried combined oral contraceptives to control the premenstrual symptoms, but found that they worsened her irritability. Which one of the following treatments would be most effective for this patient's symptoms?

bullets.text: Calcium carbonate 1000–1200 mg daily is an evidence-based treatment (SOR B) for PMS symptoms, including mood instability, headaches, and irritability, likely related to cyclic changes in calcium levels.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients with PMS have been found to have cyclic changes in calcium levels that may account for their symptoms. Supplementing with calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily (1200 mg total) has been shown to reduce PMS symptoms. Other first-line treatments include all SSRIs (not bupropion) and continuous combined oral contraceptives (SOR A). In this patient already on fluoxetine 60 mg for anxiety, adding calcium carbonate is the most appropriate next step.

bullets.text: Bupropion is not effective for PMS/PMDD; high-dose dutasteride (2.5 mg) can worsen mood and is teratogenic; vitamin D supplementation has not been clearly shown to alleviate PMS symptoms; and evidence for acupuncture in PMS is insufficient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Bupropion, unlike SSRIs, has not been shown to be effective for PMS or PMDD symptoms. High-dose dutasteride (2.5 mg daily) has shown some benefit for PMDD but carries risks of mood deterioration and teratogenicity, making it inappropriate here. Low-dose dutasteride has not demonstrated benefit. Patients with PMS do not characteristically have low vitamin D levels, and cholecalciferol supplementation has not been clearly demonstrated to relieve PMS symptoms. There is also insufficient evidence to support acupuncture as a treatment for PMS.

explanation_raw: Symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS) with mood instability can be reduced with 1000–1200 mg of calcium carbonate daily (SOR B). Patients with PMS symptoms have been found to have cyclic changes in calcium levels that may account for the symptoms, but the mechanism of action is still unknown. All SSRIs are first-line treatments for symptoms of PMS and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), but bupropion has not been shown to be effective. Continuous combined oral contraceptives are also first-line treatment (SOR A). High-dose dutasteride (2.5 mg daily) has been shown to alleviate PMDD symptoms, but it can have a deleterious effect on mood and is teratogenic. Low-dose dutasteride has not demonstrated beneficial effect on PMDD symptoms. Patients with PMS have not been found to have low levels of vitamin D, and supplementing with vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) has not been clearly demonstrated to alleviate PMS symptoms. There is insufficient evidence to prove the benefit of acupuncture in reducing PMS symptoms.

stem: A 72-year-old female with osteoporosis (T-score –2.8) is seen in your office for the first time. She was prescribed alendronate (Fosamax), 70 mg weekly, by her previous physician. The patient took the medication but discontinued it after 4 weeks because of gastrointestinal symptoms. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate action at this time?

choices.B: Instructing the patient to take the medication before bed
choices.C: Instructing the patient to take the medication with food
choices.D: Discontinuing the medication and starting raloxifene (Evista)
choices.E: Discontinuing the medication and arranging for intravenous bisphosphonates

correct_label: Discontinuing the medication and arranging for intravenous bisphosphonates

bullets.text: Women ≥65 should be screened for osteoporosis; a T-score ≤–2.5 confirms osteoporosis and warrants pharmacologic treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Women aged 65 and older should be tested for osteoporosis per screening guidelines. A bone mineral density T-score of –2.5 or lower confirms the diagnosis of osteoporosis and indicates the need for treatment, as is the case with this 72-year-old patient whose T-score is –2.8.

bullets.text: Oral bisphosphonates are first-line for osteoporosis; if GI intolerance persists despite correct administration technique, transition to intravenous bisphosphonates is appropriate.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Oral bisphosphonates such as alendronate are considered first-line treatment for osteoporosis. To minimize gastrointestinal irritation, they must be taken on an empty stomach with 8 oz of water, with the patient remaining upright and avoiding food and all beverages except plain water for at least 30 minutes afterward. If GI symptoms persist despite correct administration, the patient should discontinue the oral agent and transition to intravenous bisphosphonate therapy. Raloxifene is not the preferred initial treatment in this clinical scenario.

explanation_raw: Women ≥65 years of age should be tested for osteoporosis. A bone mineral density score ≤–2.5 indicates the need for treatment, as seen in this patient. Oral bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, are considered first-line treatment. To minimize gastrointestinal irritation, oral bisphosphonates should be taken on an empty stomach with 8 oz of water, and the patient should remain upright and avoid food and beverages other than plain water for at least 30 minutes afterward. If oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated despite correct administration, intravenous bisphosphonates should be considered. In this case, the patient should discontinue alendronate and transition to intravenous bisphosphonate therapy. Raloxifene is not the preferred initial treatment.

stem: A 27-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a fever, headache, and stiff neck. You diagnose sepsis and perform a lumbar puncture. The results are consistent with bacterial meningitis. In addition to antibiotics, which one of the following intravenous therapies is most likely to improve mortality?

bullets.text: IV dexamethasone given shortly before or at the time of antibiotic administration improves mortality and reduces neurologic sequelae in bacterial meningitis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Despite optimal therapy, bacterial meningitis carries significant mortality and loss of quality-adjusted life-years. Empiric antibiotic therapy for adults includes vancomycin and ceftriaxone. IV dexamethasone, when administered shortly before or concurrent with antibiotics, has been shown to improve mortality (odds ratio 0.90) and reduce neurologic sequelae by dampening the inflammatory response triggered by bactericidal antibiotics.

bullets.text: Acyclovir is used for HSV encephalitis, furosemide is inappropriate in a septic patient needing fluid resuscitation, glycerol increases mortality risk in HIV-prevalent populations, and IV immunoglobulin has no recognized role in bacterial meningitis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acyclovir would only be indicated if there were clinical concern for herpes simplex virus encephalitis. IV furosemide is inappropriate here because this patient has concurrent sepsis and requires fluid resuscitation rather than diuresis. Glycerol, a hyperosmolar agent intended to reduce intracranial pressure, cannot be recommended due to an increased risk of death in adults with a high prevalence of HIV. IV immunoglobulin is not a recognized or evidence-based treatment for bacterial meningitis.

explanation_raw: Despite optimal therapy, the mortality and loss of quality-adjusted life-years from bacterial meningitis is significant. Empiric therapy for adults includes vancomycin and ceftriaxone. Intravenous (IV) dexamethasone, when given shortly before or at the time of administration of IV antibiotics, has been shown to improve mortality (odds ratio 0.90) and neurologic sequelae. Bactericidal antibiotics help to reduce inflammation. Acyclovir would be indicated if there is clinical concern for herpes simplex virus or symptoms of encephalitis. While optimal fluid management for meningitis should be tailored based on clinical evaluation, this patient has also been diagnosed with sepsis and should receive appropriate fluid resuscitation; therefore, IV furosemide would be inappropriate. Glycerol is a hyperosmolar agent intended to reduce intracranial pressure in bacterial meningitis, but it cannot be recommended for treatment due to an increased risk of death according to available data in adults with a high prevalence of HIV. IV immunoglobulin is not a recognized treatment for bacterial meningitis.

stem: A 33-year-old male presents for follow-up of long-standing heartburn. His symptoms have been present for 3 years and recent treatment for 1 month with pantoprazole (Protonix) has only provided partial relief. He has a history of allergic rhinitis that is treated with fluticasone propionate nasal spray (Flonase). He has had dysphagia with solids, and a food impaction 3 months ago that resolved spontaneously. Upper endoscopy reveals eosinophilic esophagitis. Which one of the following is most likely to improve this patient’s symptoms?

bullets.text: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) should be suspected in patients with heartburn and atopic history (allergic rhinitis, asthma, eczema) who fail PPI therapy; diagnosis is confirmed histologically with >15 eosinophils/hpf.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an inflammatory condition triggered by food antigens in sensitive individuals. Endoscopic findings of linear grooves, concentric rings, and whitish exudates may suggest its presence, but diagnosis is confirmed histologically based on >15 eosinophils/hpf and exclusion of other causes of eosinophilia. It is more common in men in their 20s and 30s, dysphagia may be present for 4 or more years before diagnosis, and more than half of patients may have a history of food impaction.

bullets.text: First-line pharmacologic treatment for eosinophilic esophagitis is oral budesonide suspension (Eohilia); swallowed topical corticosteroids are preferred over PPIs, which fail to provide complete relief in two-thirds of cases.
bullets.sub_paragraph: First-line pharmacologic treatment is oral budesonide suspension. Alternatively, inhalant corticosteroids may be sprayed into the oral cavity during a breath hold and then swallowed to minimize pulmonary deposition. PPIs may help but do not provide complete relief in two-thirds of cases. Dietary changes can be very helpful, but consultation with an allergist may be needed.

bullets.text: Fluconazole treats Candida esophagitis (not EoE), famotidine helps erosive esophagitis, metoclopramide is discouraged due to side effects, and montelukast is not effective for EoE.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Immunosuppressed individuals such as patients with HIV or diabetes mellitus may have Candida esophagitis, which is treated with fluconazole rather than clotrimazole. Adding an H2-blocker such as famotidine would help in cases of erosive esophagitis. Metoclopramide was previously used to treat severe GERD but is no longer encouraged due to side effects. While montelukast is used to treat asthma and allergic rhinitis, it is not as effective for eosinophilic esophagitis.

explanation_raw: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an inflammatory condition triggered by food antigens in sensitive individuals. Endoscopic findings of linear grooves, concentric rings, and whitish exudates may suggest its presence, but the diagnosis is confirmed histologically based on the presence of >15 eosinophils/hpf and the exclusion of other causes of eosinophilia. The diagnosis should be suspected in patients with heartburn who have atopic illnesses such as allergic rhinitis, asthma, or eczema and who do not respond to proton pump inhibitor therapy. Eosinophilic esophagitis is more common in men in their 20s and 30s, and dysphagia may be present for 4 or more years before diagnosis. More than half of patients with this condition may have a history of food impaction. First-line pharmacologic treatment is oral budesonide. Alternatively, inhalant corticosteroids may be sprayed into the oral cavity during a breath hold and then swallowed to minimize pulmonary deposition. Treatment with proton pump inhibitors may help, but they do not provide complete relief in two-thirds of cases. Dietary changes can be very helpful, but consultation with an allergist may be needed. Immunosuppressed individuals such as patients with HIV or diabetes mellitus may have Candida esophagitis, which is treated with fluconazole rather than clotrimazole. Adding an H2-blocker such as famotidine would help in cases of erosive esophagitis. Metoclopramide was previously used to treat severe GERD, but it is no longer encouraged due to side effects. While montelukast is used to treat asthma and allergic rhinitis, it is not as effective for eosinophilic esophagitis.

stem: A 45-year-old male with a recent diagnosis of Crohn disease presents to your office for a health maintenance examination. His gastroenterologist advised that he ask you about vaccine updates. He has not seen a primary care physician in over 15 years. His current medications include methotrexate and azathioprine (Imuran). He received a Tdap vaccine 6 years ago at an urgent care clinic and recently received a seasonal influenza vaccine and an updated COVID-19 vaccine at his gastroenterologist’s office. He is confident that he received all of his childhood vaccines. Which one of the following vaccines should you recommend today?

bullets.text: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) on immunosuppressive therapy should receive pneumococcal vaccination, with PCV20 (Prevnar 20) being the appropriate choice.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) should receive a pneumococcal vaccine. PCV20 (Prevnar 20) is recommended and provides broad serotype coverage in immunocompromised patients such as those on methotrexate.

bullets.text: MMR is contraindicated in patients already on immunosuppressive therapy; meningococcal vaccine is recommended for adolescents (not adults) with IBD; Tdap is not due if given within the last 10 years; and zoster vaccine is not recommended until age 50 regardless of IBD status.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The MMR vaccine is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in patients already on immunosuppressive treatment such as methotrexate. Meningococcal vaccine is currently recommended for adolescents with IBD, not adults. Because this patient's Tdap vaccine was administered less than 10 years ago, he is not due for another dose. Similarly, his next dose of zoster vaccine will be due when he is 50 years of age, and there is no recommendation to administer the zoster vaccine before age 50 in patients with IBD.

explanation_raw: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) should receive a pneumococcal vaccine. Meningococcal vaccine is currently recommended for adolescents with IBD. The MMR vaccine is contraindicated in patients already on immunosuppressive treatment. Because this patient's Tdap vaccine was administered <10 years ago, he is not due for another dose. Similarly, his next dose of zoster vaccine will be due when he is 50 years of age, and there is no recommendation to administer the next vaccine before the age of 50 in patients with IBD.

stem: A 19-year-old college student with a recent history of sinusitis and a past medical history of depression, adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism is brought to the urgent care clinic by her roommates after she experienced a syncopal episode. The patient reports progressive weakness and fatigue, increasingly severe abdominal pain, and repeated episodes of nausea and vomiting over the last few days. A review of her electronic health record shows the following medications: Amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) Escitalopram (Lexapro) Fludrocortisone Levothyroxine (Synthroid) Prednisolone Her vital signs at presentation include a blood pressure of 97/58 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 116 beats/min, and a temperature of 37.2 °C (99.0 °F). A basic metabolic panel is notable for the following results: Sodium 133 mEq/L (N 136–145) Potassium 5.8 mEq/L (N 3.4–4.4) Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (N 0.6–1.1) Glucose 60 mg/dL Which one of the following therapies should be started as soon as possible to prevent further worsening of this patient's acute condition?

bullets.text: This patient's chronic corticosteroid use, progressive weakness, fatigue, electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia), tachycardia, and hypotension are classic features of acute adrenal crisis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute illness, dehydration, severe physical stress, or nonadherence to treatment can all precipitate adrenal crisis in patients with known adrenal insufficiency. Presenting features include weakness, severe fatigue, abdominal pain, tachycardia, and hypotension, with laboratory findings of hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and sometimes hypoglycemia. If left untreated, adrenal crisis can be fatal.

bullets.text: The correct initial treatment for adrenal crisis is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, as recommended by Endocrine Society practice guidelines.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Intravenous hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef) 100 mg is the preferred therapy for acute adrenal crisis per Endocrine Society guidelines. Dexamethasone can be used as an alternative corticosteroid, but it is not the preferred agent, and a 1-mg dose would be subtherapeutic (that low dose is used for the dexamethasone suppression test to evaluate for primary hyperadrenalism, not to treat crisis).

bullets.text: Glucagon treats hypoglycemia but does not correct the cardiovascular collapse of adrenal crisis; levofloxacin and ondansetron do not address the underlying adrenal insufficiency.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Glucagon is primarily indicated for hypoglycemia in insulin-dependent diabetics and will not reverse the hemodynamic instability of adrenal crisis. Levofloxacin is an antibiotic with no role in treating adrenal crisis. Ondansetron may reduce vomiting symptomatically but does not correct the underlying hormonal deficiency causing this patient's life-threatening presentation.

explanation_raw: This patient's chronic corticosteroid use, symptoms, and electrolyte abnormalities suggest she is experiencing an adrenal crisis; the correct initial treatment of this is intravenous hydrocortisone. Acute illness, dehydration, severe physical stress, or nonadherence to treatment are all possible causes of acute adrenal crisis in patients with chronic adrenal insufficiency. These patients may present with weakness, severe fatigue, abdominal pain, tachycardia, and hypotension. Laboratory abnormalities can include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and, in some cases, hypoglycemia. If left untreated, adrenal crisis can be fatal. Glucagon is primarily used to treat hypoglycemia in patients with insulin-dependent diabetes, but it will not correct the cardiovascular abnormalities of adrenal crisis. Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid that can be used to treat adrenal crisis, but it is not the preferred therapy according to Endocrine Society practice guidelines. Additionally, a 1-mg dose is subtherapeutic for adrenal crisis. Dexamethasone is sometimes used at this dose to test for primary hyperadrenalism. Levofloxacin is not appropriate for treatment of this patient's adrenal crisis. Although ondansetron may help reduce vomiting, it will not correct the underlying cause of this patient's illness.

stem: A 37-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after collapsing while standing in line at a bookstore. Her friend witnessed the episode and describes it as "fainting." A history and physical examination were performed at the bedside while triaging the patient. The patient's past medical history and a physical examination, including vital signs and a neurologic assessment, are unremarkable. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this patient with suspected syncope?

bullets.text: EKG is a primary evaluation tool for syncope, along with a comprehensive history and physical examination, to investigate the etiology of a syncopal episode (SOR C).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Electrocardiography (EKG) is a primary evaluation tool, along with a comprehensive history and physical examination, to investigate the etiology of a syncopal episode (SOR C). Electroencephalography (EEG) is not recommended as a routine test. Carotid ultrasonography is not recommended for evaluation of syncope in patients with a normal physical examination (SOR B). Similarly, head CT and MRI are not recommended as neurologic imaging studies in patients with a normal neurologic examination after a syncopal episode (SOR B). If the patient were noted to experience syncope with exertion, an exercise stress test would be appropriate (SOR C); however, this patient was at rest when the episode occurred.

explanation_raw: Electrocardiography (EKG) is a primary evaluation tool, along with a comprehensive history and physical examination, to investigate the etiology of a syncopal episode (SOR C). Electroencephalography (EEG) is not recommended as a routine test. Carotid ultrasonography is not recommended for evaluation of syncope in patients with a normal physical examination (SOR B). Similarly, head CT and MRI are not recommended as neurologic imaging studies in patients with a normal neurologic examination after a syncopal episode (SOR B). If the patient were noted to experience syncope with exertion, an exercise stress test would be appropriate (SOR C). However, this patient was observed to be at rest when the "fainting" occurred.

stem: A 64-year-old male presents with urinary frequency. His symptoms have been ongoing for months, but he says they have acutely worsened in the last 6–8 weeks. His symptoms are predominantly storage-related with daytime frequency, nocturia, urgency, and even infrequent incontinence. He also reports difficulty voiding, noting a weak stream and hesitancy. He does not have erectile dysfunction. Urinalysis is negative. In addition to behavioral and lifestyle alterations, which one of the following medications should you recommend for initial therapy?

bullets.text: An α-blocker (e.g., tamsulosin, alfuzosin, terazosin) is the most appropriate initial treatment for male lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), regardless of whether storage or voiding symptoms predominate.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Men with LUTS may have overactive bladder, bladder outlet obstruction (most commonly from BPH), or both, with significant symptom overlap making differentiation difficult. An α-blocker is recommended as first-line therapy (Evidence Level A) for all LUTS presentations. 5-α-Reductase inhibitors are added when prostate volume is ≥30 mL, the prostate is enlarged on exam, or PSA exceeds 1.5 ng/mL, but can take up to a year for full effect. Anticholinergics (oxybutynin) or β3-agonists (mirabegron) may be added if α-blockers alone are insufficient for predominantly storage symptoms, ideally after assessing postvoid residual volume. Daily tadalafil (PDE-5 inhibitor) is an option for patients with concurrent erectile dysfunction but is not considered first-line.

explanation_raw: Men with lower urinary tract symptoms may have overactive bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, or both. Differentiating overactive bladder and bladder outlet obstruction can be difficult due to significant symptom overlap. Overactive bladder is most often due to detrusor overactivity, and bladder outlet obstruction is most often secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia. The most appropriate initial treatment for these symptoms is an αblocker, such as tamsulosin, alfuzosin, or terazosin (Evidence Level A), regardless of the predominance of storage symptoms (eg, daytime frequency, nocturia, urgency, incontinence) or voiding symptoms (eg, weak stream, hesitancy, straining, dribbling). The American Urological Association recommends 5-α-reductase inhibitors if prostate volume is ≥30 mL on imaging, the prostate is enlarged on examination, or PSA levels exceed 1.5 ng/mL. 5-α-Reductase inhibitors can take up to a year to take full effect. Anticholinergics (oxybutynin) and β3-agonists (mirabegron) may be used alone or in combination with α-blockers for patients with predominantly storage-related symptoms if α-blockers are not adequately effective. Some guidelines recommend assessing postvoid residual volume before initiating these agents. A daily phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (typically tadalafil) can be used as initial monotherapy or as combination therapy in patients with erectile dysfunction, although it is not generally recommended as first-line treatment. The mechanism of action is not fully understood.

stem: A 5-day-old male is brought to your office by his mother for an initial well child visit. After an uncomplicated, full-term pregnancy, the mother gave birth 102 hours ago through vaginal delivery and was discharged 48 hours ago. She shares that this is her first child, and she is concerned that he is not getting enough milk despite exclusively breastfeeding 10–12 times per day. Which one of the following factors, if present, would indicate inadequate breastfeeding at this time?

choices.C: Infant weight loss of 5% from birth weight
choices.D: Maternal breasts that appear small and not full
choices.E: Maternal nipple pain during the first 15 seconds of each feed

bullets.text: After 4 days of life, adequate newborn feeding is indicated by 6 or more wet diapers and 3 or more stools per day; only four wet diapers per day falls short of this threshold and suggests inadequate intake.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Recognition of adequate newborn feeding is critical during early well-child visits. After the first 4 days of life, an infant who is feeding adequately should produce 6 or more wet diapers and 3 or more stools per day. Four wet diapers per day at day 5 of life is therefore a concerning sign of insufficient feeding and warrants further evaluation and lactation support.

bullets.text: Smaller-appearing breasts, nipple pain in the first 30–60 seconds, and weight loss within the first 3 days are all normal findings that do not indicate a feeding problem on their own.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Maternal breasts that appear smaller or less full do not necessarily indicate poor milk supply, though lack of any breast changes or milk leaking by day 5 postpartum may be concerning. Maternal nipple pain is normal with breastfeeding, but pain persisting beyond the first 30–60 seconds should prompt evaluation. Infant weight loss is expected in the first 3 days of life; however, a loss exceeding 7% of birth weight or ongoing loss after day 3 is worrisome. These distinctions help clinicians differentiate normal postpartum and neonatal changes from true feeding problems.

explanation_raw: Recognition of adequate newborn feeding and parental lactation counseling is important in the care of mothers and infants. An infant who is feeding adequately should produce 6 or more wet diapers and 3 or more stools after 4 days of life. Infant weight loss is normal in the first 3 days of life, but a weight loss of more than 7% from birth weight or ongoing weight loss after 3 days of life should raise concern. Maternal breasts that appear smaller or less full do not necessarily indicate poor feeding; however, lack of any breast changes or leaking of milk by day 5 post partum may indicate a problem with milk supply. Maternal nipple pain is normal with breastfeeding, but pain that persists beyond the first 30–60 seconds should prompt evaluation and counseling. If supplementation with formula is deemed medically necessary, protocol from the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine should be followed.

stem: A 25-year-old male presents to the urgent care clinic with a 4-day history of fever, chills, myalgias, and cough. He lives with a roommate and works remotely from home. His last influenza vaccine was 5 years ago, and his most recent COVID-19 vaccine was 2 years ago. His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), and his heart rate and blood pressure are within the normal range. A physical examination is normal except for occasional rhonchi. Rapid antigen testing is positive for influenza B and negative for influenza A and COVID-19. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's influenza B?

bullets.text: For low-risk patients presenting more than 48 hours after influenza symptom onset, supportive therapy is the recommended approach; antivirals are not indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to the CDC, antiviral treatment for influenza is not recommended for non–high-risk individuals who present more than 48 hours after symptom onset. This patient has no underlying medical conditions, no known exposure to high-risk individuals, and presents 4 days into illness, making supportive care (rest, hydration, antipyretics) the most appropriate management.

bullets.text: Oseltamivir is reserved for high-risk patients or those presenting within 48 hours; methylprednisolone is not recommended for influenza; rimantadine lacks activity against influenza B and is not first-line therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Oseltamivir (a neuraminidase inhibitor) is first-line antiviral therapy for influenza but is only indicated for high-risk patients or those within 48 hours of symptom onset. Systematic and unpublished randomized clinical trials do not support a reduction in hospitalization or death with neuraminidase inhibitors in the outpatient setting for low-risk adults. Methylprednisolone is not recommended for influenza treatment. Rimantadine is an adamantane antiviral that has no activity against influenza B and is not considered first-line therapy even for susceptible strains.

explanation_raw: According to the CDC, antiviral treatment for influenza is not recommended for non–highrisk individuals who present more than 48 hours after symptom onset. Thus, supportive therapy is most important for this patient who is at low risk for hospitalization and death. Methylprednisolone is not recommended to treat influenza. The risk for hospitalization and death is not reduced in adults and children treated with a neuraminidase inhibitor in the outpatient setting, as supported by systematic and unpublished randomized clinical trials. While oseltamivir is recommended as first-line therapy for high-risk patients, it is not indicated for this patient, who has no underlying medical conditions or known exposure to high-risk individuals and presents more than 48 hours after symptom onset. Rimantadine is not active against influenza B and is also not considered first-line medical therapy for influenza.

stem: A 30-year-old male with a long-standing history of obsessive-compulsive disorder presents for follow-up to discuss potential pharmacotherapy due to an inadequate treatment response to psychotherapy. Which one of the following medications would be most likely to improve this patient’s symptoms while minimizing the risk of adverse side effects?

bullets.text: SSRIs are the first-line pharmacotherapy for OCD; fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, and paroxetine all carry FDA approval for this indication, often requiring higher-than-usual doses for symptom control.
bullets.sub_paragraph: SSRIs are the most effective and preferred pharmacotherapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, and paroxetine all have FDA approval specifically for OCD, and clinicians should be aware that doses higher than those used for depression are frequently necessary to achieve adequate symptom control. Clomipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant, also has FDA approval for OCD but carries a higher toxicity risk (including cardiac arrhythmias and seizures), making it a second-line option. Bupropion (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor), buspirone (atypical anxiolytic), and quetiapine (atypical antipsychotic) are not first-line treatments for OCD and lack robust evidence for this indication.

explanation_raw: The most effective medication therapy options for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) are SSRIs. Fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, and paroxetine all have approval from the FDA for the treatment of OCD. Dosages that are higher than usual are often required to achieve symptom control. Clomipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant, has an indication from the FDA for treatment of OCD, but a higher toxicity risk makes it less favorable for first-line treatment. Bupropion (a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor), buspirone (an atypical anxiolytic), and quetiapine (an atypical antipsychotic) are not first-line treatment for OCD.

stem: A 76-year-old female with hypertension sees you for a routine follow-up visit. She fell about 2 weeks ago while hurrying to answer her home telephone, and sustained bruising and swelling of the left lower leg. She does not recall feeling dizzy or lightheaded before the fall, and she did not hit her head or lose consciousness. She was able to get up and walk afterward without any limitations but developed a large bruise over the lateral hip. She has not had any previous falls and she feels well today. She lives alone and performs activities of daily living independently. Which one of the following has the best evidence to prevent future falls and associated serious injury?

choices.A: Patient education on fall harms and prevention
choices.B: Use of a cane while walking
choices.C: Referral to a group exercise program, including gait, balance, and functional training
choices.D: Referral to an ophthalmologist for a comprehensive vision assessment
choices.E: Referral to a podiatrist for footwear assessment

correct_label: Referral to a group exercise program, including gait, balance, and functional training

bullets.text: A history of falling is a key risk factor for future falls; in community-dwelling older adults at higher risk, exercise interventions are recommended by the USPSTF to lower fall risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Falls are a leading cause of injury-related death in older adults, with 27.5% of adults ≥65 reporting at least one fall in the past year. A prior fall is one of the strongest predictors of future falls, along with sensory/cognitive deficits, chronic conditions, and certain medications. The USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for community-dwelling older adults identified as higher risk, and both individual and group programs are beneficial — no single exercise type is preferred over others.

bullets.text: Multifactorial fall-prevention interventions assess modifiable risk factors (balance, gait, vision, cognition, postural BP, medications, home environment) and tailor interventions accordingly, though average net benefit is small.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Multifactorial interventions typically begin with a structured assessment of modifiable risk factors followed by a customized reduction plan. A 2023 Cochrane review found that home hazard reduction using a validated tool (usually via home visit) reduces falls. However, patient education alone, assistive devices, vision correction, and footwear selection were not found to be independently beneficial in reducing fall risk.

explanation_raw: Falls are a common cause of serious injury and death in older adults in the United States. A 2018 study found that 27.5% of adults ≥65 years of age had fallen at least once in the past year (714 falls per 1000 community-dwelling older adults). More than 300,000 older adults are hospitalized each year for hip fracture, which is one of the most serious potential complications from falls in older adults. Falls are also the leading cause of injury-related death in older adults. A history of a fall is a key risk factor for future falls. Other risks include sensory and cognitive deficits, acute and chronic health conditions, alcohol and drug use, and certain other medication use. In community-dwelling older adults who are identified as being at higher risk of falls, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found that exercise interventions lower the risk of falls and should be recommended. Both individual and group exercise programs are beneficial and there is no data to recommend any single type of exercise over others. Multifactorial interventions to reduce falls typically include an assessment of modifiable risk factors followed by a customized approach to reducing risk. Evaluations may include balance, gait, vision, cognition, postural blood pressure, medication use, and the home environment. This assessment differs from a focused diagnostic assessment of a patient with a specific concern such as vision change, dizziness, or numbness in the feet. Interventions to address risk factors identified in a multifactorial screening program may offer benefit to high-risk individuals, although studies have found a small net benefit on average. A 2023 Cochrane review comprising 22 studies on environmental interventions found evidence of benefit for reducing fall hazards at home by using a validated tool to identify and address hazards, usually via a home visit. Patient education, assistive devices, vision impairment correction, and footwear selection were not found to be beneficial.

stem: Which one of the following would be most appropriate for initial treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection?

choices.A: Dual therapy with vonoprazan (Voquezna) and amoxicillin
choices.B: Triple therapy with omeprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin
choices.C: Triple therapy with omeprazole, amoxicillin, and levofloxacin
choices.D: Quadruple therapy with bismuth, omeprazole, metronidazole, and tetracycline

correct_label: Quadruple therapy with bismuth, omeprazole, metronidazole, and tetracycline

bullets.text: Optimized quadruple therapy with bismuth, metronidazole, omeprazole, and tetracycline is the recommended first-line treatment for H. pylori, achieving approximately 91% eradication rates.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Current guidelines recommend optimized quadruple therapy with bismuth, metronidazole, omeprazole, and tetracycline as first-line treatment for H. pylori infection, with approximately 91% eradication efficacy. Dual therapy with vonoprazan and amoxicillin is an alternative for patients unable to tolerate quadruple therapy, but eradication rates are lower (70–80%). Regimens containing clarithromycin or levofloxacin should only be used when susceptibility to macrolides or fluoroquinolones, respectively, has been documented, due to rising resistance rates.

explanation_raw: Infection with Helicobacter pylori should be treated when it causes symptoms. Several regimens exist for the treatment of H pylori infection. Guidelines currently recommend optimized quadruple therapy with bismuth, metronidazole, omeprazole, and tetracycline. This combination is approximately 91% effective at eradicating H pylori infection. Dual therapy with vonoprazan and amoxicillin is an option for patients who are unable or unwilling to take quadruple therapy, but its eradiation rates only range from 70% to 80%. Regimens containing clarithromycin or levofloxacin should be limited to infections with documented susceptibility to macrolides or fluoroquinolones, respectively.

stem: The parent of a 5-year-old male calls your office after the child sustains burns to his arms and chest while helping his father boil pasta in the kitchen. The father tells you that the burned areas of skin are red without any open areas. He estimates the size of the burns on the arms at 2–3 cm in diameter and those on the chest at 5–6 cm. The child is crying in pain and the father asks what he should do. Which one of the following immediate interventions has the best evidence of reducing burn depth, improving healing time, and decreasing skin graft requirements?

choices.A: Cooling the burn surfaces with running tap water
choices.B: Applying ice to the burn surfaces
choices.C: Covering the burn surfaces with cool, wet gauze
choices.D: Applying aloe vera gel to the burn surfaces and leaving them uncovered
choices.E: Applying diclofenac gel to the burn surfaces and leaving them uncovered

correct_label: Cooling the burn surfaces with running tap water

bullets.text: The most effective first step for burn injuries is cooling the burn surface with running cool tap water for at least 20 minutes, ideally within 30 minutes of injury but potentially beneficial up to 3 hours post-injury.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The initial treatment goals for burn injuries include limiting the extent of injury, cleaning the area, and managing pain. Cooling the burn surface with running cool tap water for at least 20 minutes has been shown to reduce burn depth, improve healing time, and decrease skin graft requirements. Ideally this is done within the first 30 minutes of injury, but some evidence suggests benefit up to 3 hours after injury. Ice should be avoided due to risk of vasoconstriction and tissue damage, and wet dressings are not effective as a cooling strategy. After initial cooling, aloe vera and NSAIDs can address pain in superficial burns, but these are not the recommended first step.

bullets.text: Burns are classified by depth: superficial (first degree) burns appear red, blanchable, and intact without blistering; partial-thickness (second degree) burns involve the dermis and may blister; full-thickness (third degree) burns extend into fat and connective tissue, appearing white/waxy with less pain due to nerve destruction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Superficial burns are limited to the epidermal layer—they are painful, appear red and blanchable, with intact skin and no blistering. Partial-thickness burns involve the dermis: superficial partial-thickness burns may blister and be exudative, whereas deep partial-thickness burns are drier and do not blanch. Full-thickness burns involve the entire dermis and extend into fat and connective tissue; they appear white with a waxy, dry appearance and patients experience less pain due to destruction of nerve endings. Deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns should be evaluated and treated at a burn center.

explanation_raw: Burns are a common cause of injury in the United States, but most are minor and can be treated in the outpatient setting. The initial treatment goals for burn injuries include limiting the extent of the injury, cleaning the area, and managing pain. Removing clothing limits the injury related to scalding. The most effective way to limit the extent of injury is to cool the burn surface by running cool tap water over the burn surface for at least 20 minutes. This intervention has been shown to reduce burn depth, improve healing time, and decrease skin graft requirements. Ideally, burns should be cooled within the first 30 minutes of injury, but some evidence suggests benefit up to 3 hours after the initial injury. Applying ice to the burn surfaces is not recommended as a cooling strategy due to the risk of vasoconstriction, which can contribute to tissue damage. Wet dressings are not effective as a cooling strategy and are not recommended. For superficial burns such as those described in this patient, aloe vera and NSAIDs can be used to address pain after the initial cooling strategy, but these are not the recommended first step. Burns are classified by their depth: superficial (first degree), partial thickness (second degree), and full thickness (third degree). Superficial burns are limited to the epidermal layer. They are painful and appear red (blanchable), with intact skin and no blistering. Partial-thickness burns are deeper and involve injury to the dermis. Superficial partialthickness burns may blister and be exudative, whereas deep partial-thickness burns are drier and do not blanch. Full-thickness burns involve the entire dermis and extend into the fat and connective tissue layers. They appear white rather than red, and are dry with a waxy appearance. Patients often experience less pain due to the destruction of nerve endings. Deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns should be evaluated and treated at a burn center.

stem: A 45-year-old female with a past medical history of obesity and cigarette smoking presents with a popliteal deep vein thrombosis of the right leg, confirmed on ultrasonography. She has no prior history of venous thromboembolism and has not had any recent surgery, trauma, or immobilization. She does not take any medications. Which one of the following anticoagulation regimens would be the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.D: LMWH for 7 days, followed by warfarin
choices.E: Unfractionated heparin for 48 hours, followed by a DOAC

bullets.text: Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the preferred first-line monotherapy for outpatient management of DVT, offering rapid therapeutic onset without the need for bridging heparin and requiring less monitoring with fewer major bleeding events compared to warfarin.
bullets.sub_paragraph: DOACs reach therapeutic levels quickly, eliminating the need for concomitant unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) bridging. They have demonstrated less major bleeding and require less monitoring than warfarin, making them the preferred outpatient option. If a DOAC is unaffordable, subcutaneous LMWH can be initiated alongside warfarin as an outpatient, with LMWH continued until the goal INR is achieved — replacing the older practice of inpatient unfractionated heparin initiation during warfarin loading.

explanation_raw: Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are now recommended as monotherapy for outpatient management of deep vein thrombosis. DOACs reach therapeutic levels quickly; therefore, concomitant initiation of unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is not necessary. DOACs have less major bleeding and require less monitoring, making them preferred over warfarin. Previously, unfractionated heparin was administered during hospitalization while warfarin was simultaneously initiated; however, subcutaneous LMWH can now be started with warfarin as an outpatient and continued until the goal INR is reached if a DOAC is unaffordable.

stem: Which one of the following puts a patient at the highest risk of developing breast cancer?

choices.A: A first pregnancy at <30 years of age
choices.B: Onset of menopause at <50 years of age
choices.D: A grandmother with a history of breast cancer
choices.E: Chest radiation therapy as a child

correct_label: Chest radiation therapy as a child

bullets.text: Chest radiation therapy in childhood confers the highest risk for breast cancer, particularly whole lung radiation, making it a stronger risk factor than late menopause, late first pregnancy, first-degree family history, or dense breasts.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Women who received chest radiotherapy as children are at significantly increased risk for breast cancer as adults, with those who received whole lung radiation at especially high risk. While other factors such as menopause onset after age 55, first pregnancy after age 35, a first-degree relative with breast cancer, and dense breasts (which reflect higher glandular and stromal tissue compared to adipose tissue on mammography) all elevate breast cancer risk, childhood chest radiation represents the greatest individual risk factor among these options.

explanation_raw: Women who received chest radiotherapy as children are at increased risk for breast cancer as adults, with those who received whole lung radiation at especially high risk. Other risk factors for breast cancer include the onset of menopause at >55 years of age, a first pregnancy at >35 years of age, and a first-degree relative with breast cancer. Patients with dense breasts have a higher amount of glandular and stromal tissue compared with adipose tissue on mammography and are at higher risk for breast cancer.

stem: An 83-year-old female sees you for follow-up 2 weeks after being discharged home from an acute rehabilitation facility. She experienced an acute ischemic stroke 6 weeks ago and spent several weeks in the rehabilitation setting after an initial hospital stay. Home health services have been assisting her since she returned home. Today she reports improved mobility, speech, and swallowing, but persistent difficulties with low mood. She finds it difficult to enjoy hobbies and avoids visiting with family and friends. She has been sleeping more than usual and finds it difficult to get out of bed in the morning. You diagnose poststroke depression. In addition to talk therapy, which one of the following is recommended as first-line therapy for this condition?

bullets.text: SSRIs such as escitalopram are considered first-line therapy for poststroke depression (PSD), which affects 20–60% of stroke patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Poststroke depression (PSD) is a common complication occurring in 20–60% of stroke patients, with a complex, multifactorial pathophysiology involving abnormal neurotransmitter and inflammatory marker levels. SSRIs such as escitalopram are first-line therapy. Alternatives include SNRIs, newer multimodal agents like vortioxetine, and bupropion if SSRIs are ineffective or not tolerated.

bullets.text: TCAs are generally not preferred due to higher anticholinergic burden, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is not yet recommended as first-line treatment despite growing evidence.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Although nortriptyline (a TCA) has been shown effective in randomized controlled trials for PSD, TCAs as a class carry a higher anticholinergic effect than SSRIs, making them less preferred, especially in elderly patients. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation has an emerging evidence base but is not currently recommended as first-line treatment for PSD.

explanation_raw: Poststroke depression (PSD) is a common complication that occurs in 20%–60% of patients with stroke, depending on the definition used in diagnosis and the timing of symptom onset. The exact pathophysiology of PSD is unknown but appears complex and multifactorial. The incidence of PSD varies with the location of the stroke. Abnormal neurotransmitter and inflammatory marker levels have been associated with PSD. SSRIs such as escitalopram are considered first-line therapy for PSD. Other options include SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), and newer multimodal agents such as vortioxetine. Bupropion may be considered if SSRIs are ineffective or cannot be tolerated. As a class, TCAs have a higher anticholinergic effect than SSRIs and are therefore not preferred, although nortriptyline has been evaluated in randomized, controlled trials and found to be effective in treating PSD. There is a growing body of evidence to support the use of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, but it is not recommended as first-line treatment at this time.

stem: Patients with which one of the following should be provided opioid overdose education and a prescription for naloxone?

choices.A: A history of substance use disorder
choices.B: A prescription for alprazolam (Xanax), 1 mg nightly as needed
choices.C: A 3-day prescription for hydrocodone/acetaminophen, 5/325 mg twice daily
choices.D: A prescription through hospice treatment for morphine, 10 mg as needed

correct_label: A history of substance use disorder

bullets.text: The 2022 CDC guideline recommends offering naloxone to patients at increased risk of opioid overdose, including those with a history of substance use disorder.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The 2022 CDC clinical practice guideline for prescribing opioids recommends that clinicians offer naloxone to patients at increased risk of overdose, including patients with a history of substance use, overdose, and sleep-disordered breathing, as well as patients who take higher dosages of opioids (≥50 MME/day), take benzodiazepines concurrently with opioids, or are at risk of returning to higher opioid dosages with loss of tolerance, such as when tapering opioid dosages.

explanation_raw: The 2022 CDC clinical practice guideline for prescribing opioids recommends that clinicians offer naloxone to patients at increased risk of overdose, including patients with a history of substance use, overdose, and sleep-disordered breathing, as well as patients who take higher dosages of opioids (≥50 MME/day), take benzodiazepines with opioids, or are at risk of returning to higher opioid dosages with loss of tolerance, such as when tapering opioid dosages.

stem: A 55-year-old female with a medical history of hypothyroidism, hypertension, and morbid obesity with a recent gastric bypass surgery presents with a history of dizziness, sweating, shaking, fatigue, and occasional fainting, occurring 1–2 hours after consuming beverages containing dairy products or a high sugar content. Her blood glucose levels, measured with her husband's glucometer during each episode, range between 50 mg/dL and 55 mg/dL. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

bullets.text: Late dumping syndrome occurs 1–3 hours after eating due to rapid carbohydrate absorption causing exaggerated insulin secretion and chemical hypoglycemia, a common complication after bariatric surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Dumping syndrome affects approximately 40% of post-bariatric surgery patients and is divided into two types. Early dumping syndrome occurs within 30–60 minutes of eating, caused by rapid nutrient passage into the small bowel leading to intestinal hormonal release and fluid shifts; it presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, nausea, flushing, palpitations, sweating, tachycardia, hypotension, and syncope without chemical hypoglycemia. Late dumping syndrome occurs 1–3 hours after eating, caused by rapid carbohydrate absorption triggering exaggerated insulin secretion, resulting in measurable hypoglycemia with symptoms such as dizziness, sweating, shaking, fatigue, and syncope — matching this patient's presentation.

bullets.text: Gastroparesis, idiopathic postprandial syndrome, and insulinoma each have distinct features that differentiate them from late dumping syndrome.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Gastroparesis results from significantly delayed gastric emptying without hypoglycemia, most commonly a complication of diabetes mellitus. Idiopathic postprandial syndrome produces hypoglycemic-like symptoms after eating but lacks chemical (laboratory) evidence of true hypoglycemia, distinguishing it from late dumping syndrome. Insulinoma is a rare insulin-secreting pancreatic tumor that causes hypoglycemia independent of food intake timing — it is not triggered specifically by meals containing dairy or carbohydrates as seen in this patient.

explanation_raw: The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is late dumping syndrome. Dumping syndrome is a common postbariatric surgery complication occurring in about 40% of patients. There are 2 types of dumping syndrome: early dumping syndrome and late dumping syndrome. Early dumping syndrome is caused by the rapid passage of nutrients into the small bowel, resulting in intestinal hormonal release and fluid shift. Symptoms occur within 30–60 minutes of eating and include abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, nausea, flushing, palpitations, sweating, tachycardia, hypotension, and syncope without chemical evidence of hypoglycemia. Late dumping syndrome is caused by the rapid absorption of carbohydrates, leading to exaggerated insulin secretion, resulting in chemical evidence of hypoglycemia occurring 1–3 hours after eating. Gastroparesis, unlike dumping syndrome, results from significantly delayed gastric emptying without hypoglycemia, often due to complications of diabetes mellitus. Idiopathic postprandial syndrome describes hypoglycemic-like symptoms that occur after eating without chemical evidence of hypoglycemia. Insulinoma is a rare insulin-producing tumor of the pancreas that causes hypoglycemia regardless of food intake timing.

stem: A 10-month-old male is brought to your office with a 1-day history of fussiness and tugging at his ear. The child's mother says that he has had a fever this morning. He is up to date on all immunizations, and he does not have a history of previous ear infections or recent illness. He has a history of hives after being given amoxicillin. On examination the child has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F) but seems to be only slightly uncomfortable. When you examine his ears you note moderate bulging of the left tympanic membrane and normal findings in the right ear. All other findings are normal. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial management?

bullets.text: Children ≥6 months with severe AOM symptoms (moderate/severe otalgia, otalgia >48 hours, or temp ≥39°C) require antibiotic therapy regardless of laterality; children <24 months with bilateral AOM also require treatment even without severe symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends antibiotic therapy for children ≥6 months of age with severe signs and symptoms of acute otitis media (AOM), including moderate or severe otalgia, otalgia lasting longer than 48 hours, or a temperature ≥39°C (102°F), whether the AOM is unilateral or bilateral (SOR B). Children younger than 24 months without severe symptoms should receive antibiotic therapy for bilateral AOM, whereas older children or those with unilateral AOM can be offered the option of observation and follow-up.

bullets.text: First-line treatment for AOM is amoxicillin; penicillin-allergic patients should receive cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, or ceftriaxone as alternatives.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The usual treatment for AOM is amoxicillin, but an antibiotic with additional β-lactamase coverage, such as amoxicillin/clavulanate, should be given if the child has received amoxicillin within the past 30 days, has concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, or has a history of AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin (SOR C). Penicillin-allergic patients should be treated with an alternative antibiotic such as cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, or ceftriaxone. Ciprofloxacin should not be used in children, and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is no longer effective for AOM due to Streptococcus pneumoniae resistance.

explanation_raw: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends antibiotic therapy for children ≥6 months of age with severe signs and symptoms of acute otitis media (AOM), including moderate or severe otalgia, otalgia lasting longer than 48 hours, or a temperature ≥39 °C (102 °F), whether the AOM is unilateral or bilateral (SOR B). Children younger than 24 months without severe symptoms should receive antibiotic therapy for bilateral AOM, whereas older children or those with unilateral AOM can be offered the option of observation and follow-up. The usual treatment for AOM is amoxicillin, but an antibiotic with additional β-lactamase coverage, such as amoxicillin/clavulanate, should be given if the child has received amoxicillin within the past 30 days, has concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, or has a history of AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin (SOR C). Penicillin-allergic patients should be treated with an alternative antibiotic such as cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, or ceftriaxone. Ciprofloxacin should not be used in children. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is no longer effective for the treatment of acute otitis media due to evidence of Streptococcus pneumoniae resistance.

stem: A 5-year-old male is brought to the emergency department (E

choices.D: CT of the head and neck
choices.A: Providing reassurance and recommending outpatient follow-up
choices.B: Observation in the ED for worsening symptoms

correct_label: Providing reassurance and recommending outpatient follow-up

bullets.text: This child's presentation is consistent with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)/concussion based on mechanism and vomiting, without worsening symptoms or concerning exam findings.
bullets.sub_paragraph: mTBI (concussion) is classified as mild when there are no worsening symptoms and no additional concerning findings on examination, such as increased fussiness or signs of head or neck injury. The mechanism of injury combined with vomiting supports this diagnosis, but the overall clinical picture remains reassuring.

bullets.text: Routine imaging is not recommended for pediatric mTBI; reassurance and outpatient follow-up are the appropriate next steps.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For mild TBI in children, neither skull radiography nor CT of the head/neck is routinely indicated. CT would only be warranted if the patient had acutely worsening symptoms, significant headache, or suspected structural head or neck injury. Reassurance with outpatient observation and follow-up is the standard of care for uncomplicated pediatric concussion.

bullets.text: There is no role for skull X-ray in concussion management, CT is only indicated for worsening or high-risk features, and child protective services are not warranted without red flags for abuse.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Skull radiography has no utility in mTBI evaluation. CT imaging carries radiation risk and is reserved for high-risk presentations (e.g., worsening neurological status, severe or escalating headache, suspected cervical injury). Contacting child protective services is inappropriate here because there is no delay in seeking care, no unusual physical findings, and no concerning behaviors between the parents and child that would suggest non-accidental trauma.

explanation_raw: This patient likely has a mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), or concussion, based on the mechanism of injury and the presence of vomiting. This patient's TBI would be classified as mild due to the lack of worsening symptoms or additional concerning findings on examination, such as the child being fussier or holding his head. For these reasons, reassurance and outpatient observation with follow-up is the most appropriate next step. Routine imaging is not recommended for mTBI in children. There is no role for radiography of the skull in the management of mTBI or concussion. CT of the head or neck would only be indicated if the patient were experiencing acutely worsening symptoms, reporting or showing signs of headache, or had a suspected head or neck injury. There is no need to contact child protective services because there has been no delay in seeking care or the presence of other unusual physical findings or behaviors between the parents and child.

stem: A 32-year-old male presents for advice on smoking cessation. He has smoked 10 cigarettes per day for the past 10 years. His grandmother was recently diagnosed with lung cancer, and he is motivated to quit. You advise him that smoking cessation is the most important action that he can take for his health, and you counsel him about effective behavioral interventions. Which one of the following behavioral changes would improve this patient's chances of smoking cessation?

bullets.text: Creating a smoke-free home and car environment is a highly effective behavioral intervention for smoking cessation, forming a core part of the Ask-Advise-Assist/Connect brief intervention model.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Behavioral interventions are evidence-based treatments for smoking cessation. Advising patients to create a smoke-free home and car environment is an important component of the brief 3-step tobacco cessation model (Ask, Advise, Assist/Connect).
