The USPSTF recommends combining behavioral interventions with FDA-approved pharmacotherapy — such as nicotine replacement therapy, sustained-release bupropion hydrochloride, or varenicline — as combined interventions yield the highest tobacco-cessation rates.

bullets.text: Reducing caffeine intake, switching to menthol cigarettes, hypnotherapy, and acupuncture lack high- or moderate-quality evidence supporting their use in smoking cessation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Caffeine intake has no established role in smoking cessation. Switching to menthol cigarettes does not support cessation efforts. Neither hypnotherapy nor acupuncture has high- or moderate-quality evidence demonstrating effectiveness for smoking cessation, making these options less appropriate recommendations compared to evidence-based behavioral and pharmacologic strategies.

explanation_raw: Behavioral interventions are effective treatments for smoking cessation. Advising a patient who wishes to stop smoking to create a smoke-free home and car environment is a highly effective behavioral intervention. This advice is an important aspect of a brief 3-step tobacco cessation intervention model (Ask, Advise, Assist/Connect). Caffeine intake does not play a role in smoking cessation. Switching to menthol cigarettes does not have a role in supporting smoking cessation. There is no high- or moderate-quality evidence to support hypnotherapy or acupuncture for smoking cessation. In addition to behavioral interventions, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also recommends providing FDA-approved pharmacotherapy such as nicotine replacement therapy, sustained-release bupropion hydrochloride, or varenicline. Combined interventions result in increased tobacco-cessation rates.

stem: Which one of the following medications is the recommended initial management of COPD in patients who are classified as GOLD group A?

bullets.text: LAMAs (e.g., umeclidinium) are the preferred initial therapy for GOLD group A COPD; LABAs are an acceptable alternative.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) such as umeclidinium are recommended as the preferred initial management of COPD classified as GOLD group A. Long-acting β-agonists (LABAs) such as formoterol may be used as an alternative for these patients.

bullets.text: GOLD group B requires a LAMA/LABA combination, while GOLD group E can be managed with LAMA/LABA or ICS/LAMA/LABA, especially if blood eosinophils are ≥300 cells/μL.
bullets.sub_paragraph: LAMA/LABA combinations such as aclidinium bromide/formoterol are recommended as initial management for GOLD group B. For GOLD group E, LAMA/LABA combinations are standard, but ICS/LAMA/LABA combinations (e.g., fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol) can also be considered, particularly when blood eosinophil levels are ≥300 cells/μL.

explanation_raw: Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) such as umeclidinium are recommended as the preferred initial management of COPD that is classified as GOLD group A. Long-acting β-agonists (LABAs) such as formoterol may be used as an alternative for these patients. LAMA/LABA combinations such as aclidinium bromide/formoterol are recommended as initial management of COPD that is classified as GOLD group B. LAMA/LABA combinations are also recommended for management of COPD that is classified as GOLD group E. Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/LAMA/LABA combinations such as fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol can also be considered for initial management of COPD that is classified as GOLD group E, especially if blood eosinophil levels are ≥300 cells/μL.

stem: A 29-year-old female with type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department by her family, who state that she has grown increasingly confused over the last few days, with additional symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia. Her initial vital signs demonstrate hypotension and tachycardia. Laboratory Findings Serum glucose 750 mg/dL Serum osmolality 350 mOsm/kg H2O (N 275–295) Urine ketones trace Arterial pH 7.3 Anion gap normal Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.D: Intravenous isotonic fluid hydration with sodium bicarbonate

bullets.text: This patient presents with hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS), distinguished from DKA by the absence of significant ketonuria and acidosis, along with profound dehydration and altered mental status.
bullets.sub_paragraph: HHS is characterized by acute confusion, severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. The lack of ketonuria and acidosis differentiates it from DKA. Clinical clues include the markedly elevated serum osmolality and neurological changes such as confusion, which are more prominent in HHS than in DKA.

bullets.text: Initial treatment of HHS prioritizes aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid resuscitation (0.9% normal saline or lactated Ringer solution) to correct hypovolemia, followed by insulin infusion and potassium repletion.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The cornerstone of HHS management is IV isotonic fluid hydration to restore intravascular volume and correct hyperosmolality. Following the initial fluid bolus, a short-acting insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hr is initiated. Potassium chloride can be added to IV fluids after initial resuscitation to address total body potassium depletion. Sodium bicarbonate is reserved only for cases where arterial pH is less than 7.0, per American Diabetes Association guidelines.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with acute confusion, dehydration, hyperglycemia, and hyperosmolality. The appropriate diagnosis is hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS), rather than diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), given her lack of significant ketonuria and acidosis. She is hypovolemic and dehydrated as evidenced by her change in vital signs. Initial treatment consists of intravenous fluids with isotonic solutions, such as 0.9% normal saline or lactated Ringer solution. She will also need an intravenous insulin infusion of short-acting insulin at a dose of 0.05 units/kg/hr. After the initial fluid bolus, potassium chloride can be added to intravenous fluids to correct her total body potassium depletion. Sodium bicarbonate should only be considered if the arterial pH is <7.0 (see Figure 4 of the American Diabetes Association guideline for treatment pathways of DKA and HHS).

stem: A 65-year-old male with symptomatic heart failure presents for follow-up. He currently has no symptoms of dyspnea at rest, but has moderate to significant limitations with ordinary activity. His most recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38%. His last hemoglobin A1c was the highest it has ever been at 6.3%, and he does not take any glucose-lowering medications. His current medications include losartan (Cozaar), carvedilol (Coreg), furosemide (Lasix), and spironolactone (Aldactone). On examination he has a blood pressure of 120/75 mm Hg and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air, and there are no pulmonary crackles or peripheral edema. Adding which one of the following would be most likely to further reduce this patient’s mortality risk?

bullets.text: SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended to decrease all-cause mortality in HFrEF (EF <40%) regardless of whether the patient has diabetes mellitus.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to ACC/AHA guidelines, first-line medical management for symptomatic HFrEF includes ARNi therapy (or ACE inhibitor/ARB if ARNi is not feasible), a cardioselective β-blocker, a loop diuretic for congestion, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. SGLT2 inhibitors have demonstrated mortality benefit in HFrEF independent of glycemic control, making them a key component of guideline-directed medical therapy.

bullets.text: Calcium channel blockers may worsen cardiac outcomes in HFrEF; thiazide diuretics offer no mortality benefit; GLP-1 agonist mortality benefits in HFrEF remain investigational; and metformin's mortality benefit applies to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (EF >50%), not HFrEF.
bullets.sub_paragraph: CCBs are generally avoided in HFrEF because they can have negative inotropic effects and worsen outcomes. Thiazide diuretics may be used adjunctively for symptomatic congestion but do not improve mortality in HFrEF. GLP-1 receptor agonists are still under investigation for HFrEF mortality benefits. Metformin has shown mortality improvement specifically in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, not in reduced ejection fraction like this patient's EF of 38%.

explanation_raw: Treatment with an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended to decrease all-cause mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes mellitus. According to guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association, first-line medical management for symptomatic HFrEF is angiotensin receptor/neprilysin inhibitor (ARNi) therapy. If ARNi therapy is not feasible, an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is second-line therapy. These patients should also receive therapy with a cardioselective β-blocker, a loop diuretic (for pulmonary congestion or edema), and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Neither calcium channel blockers (CCBs) nor thiazide diuretics provide mortality benefits in HFrEF; although thiazide diuretics may be used for the adjunctive management of symptomatic congestion and edema, CCBs may lead to worse cardiac outcomes. The potential mortality benefits of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with HFrEF are still being investigated. Metformin has been shown to improve mortality in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction >50%).

stem: A 45-year-old male with a past medical history of hyperlipidemia and obesity presents with concerns of polydipsia and polyuria that have progressively worsened over the last 2 weeks. His older sister was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and your patient asks to be tested. Which one of the following test results would be sufficient to diagnose diabetes in this patient?

choices.B: A 1-hour plasma glucose level ≥140 mg/dL on 50-g oral glucose testing
choices.C: A fasting plasma glucose level ≥120 mg/dL
choices.D: A random blood glucose level ≥200 mg/dL

correct_label: A random blood glucose level ≥200 mg/dL

bullets.text: A random blood glucose ≥200 mg/dL in a patient with classic hyperglycemic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia) is sufficient to diagnose diabetes mellitus without confirmatory testing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to ADA guidelines, diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed with a random blood glucose level ≥200 mg/dL when classic symptoms of hyperglycemia are present, as seen in this patient with polydipsia and polyuria. Other diagnostic criteria—fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL on 75-g OGTT—are also valid but require a second confirmatory abnormal value in the absence of unequivocal symptoms.

bullets.text: Prediabetes thresholds (fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%) and gestational diabetes screening criteria (1-hour glucose ≥140 mg/dL on 50-g load) do not apply to this clinical scenario.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL or an HbA1c of 5.7–6.4% indicates prediabetes, not diabetes. The 1-hour plasma glucose ≥140 mg/dL on a 50-g oral glucose challenge is used as the first step in a two-step screening protocol for gestational diabetes in pregnant individuals, which is irrelevant here. While fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or a 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL can diagnose diabetes, they would each require confirmatory repeat testing unless the patient has unequivocal symptoms—making the random glucose ≥200 mg/dL the most direct answer given the symptomatic presentation.

explanation_raw: According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed with a random blood glucose level ≥200 mg/dL in patients with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia, such as polyuria and polydipsia, as seen in this patient. An 8hour fasting plasma glucose level ≥126 mg/dL, a hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5%, or a 2-hour plasma glucose level ≥200 mg/dL on 75-g oral glucose tolerance testing can also indicate diabetes but would require confirmatory testing with a second abnormal laboratory value to confirm the diagnosis. A fasting plasma glucose level 100–125 mg/dL or a hemoglobin A1c 5.7%–6.4% suggests a diagnosis of prediabetes. A 1-hour plasma glucose level ≥140 mg/dL on 50-g oral glucose testing is an abnormal first step in a 2-step screening approach for gestational diabetes mellitus in pregnant individuals.

stem: A 36-year-old male presents to your office with continued pain in his right arm after sustaining a right forearm fracture 6 weeks ago that was treated with cast immobilization. At the time of the injury, he noted a severe, throbbing pain in his right forearm that improved with NSAID therapy. Now, he feels a severe, sharp pain with burning and numbness throughout the arm and hand that worsens with any pressure, including clothing. He reports weakness in his right hand and notes that he drops objects such as cups. He is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. An examination reveals pain to light touch in the right arm. The right arm is warmer to the touch than the left arm with trace edema noted. The patient's right-hand grip is 4/5, and his left-hand grip is 5/5. You note 2+ radial and brachial pulses and normal bilateral reflexes. Which one of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient's pain?

bullets.text: This patient meets the Budapest criteria for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), which is a clinical diagnosis based on hyperalgesia, temperature asymmetry, edema, and motor weakness following limb trauma.
bullets.sub_paragraph: CRPS is diagnosed clinically using the Budapest criteria, which require continued pain disproportionate to the inciting event plus signs/symptoms in at least three of four categories: sensory (hyperalgesia/allodynia), vasomotor (temperature asymmetry, skin color changes), sudomotor/edema (sweating changes, edema), and motor/trophic (weakness, tremor, trophic changes). This patient demonstrates hyperalgesia, temperature asymmetry, edema, and motor weakness following a forearm fracture, satisfying the diagnostic threshold.

bullets.text: Cellulitis is excluded by the absence of fever or classic infection signs; peripheral neuropathy is unlikely without the characteristic stocking-glove pattern of sensory loss; factitious disorder and conversion disorder are inconsistent with the objective physical findings present.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cellulitis typically presents with warmth, erythema, and systemic signs of infection such as fever, which are absent here. Peripheral neuropathy classically produces a symmetric, stocking-glove distribution of altered sensation rather than the focal, post-traumatic presentation seen in CRPS. Factitious disorder involves intentional symptom production and conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder) is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring no better explanation—both are rendered unlikely by the objective examination findings including edema, temperature asymmetry, and motor weakness that align precisely with CRPS criteria.

explanation_raw: This patient meets the Budapest criteria for complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) including hyperalgesia, temperature asymmetry, evidence of edema, and motor weakness following trauma to the limb. CRPS is a clinical diagnosis. The absence of fever or other signs of infection makes cellulitis unlikely. The examination findings make factitious disorder and functional neurologic symptom disorder (conversion disorder) unlikely. The absence of the characteristic stocking-glove altered sensation makes peripheral neuropathy unlikely.

stem: A 28-year-old nulligravida has a 2- to 3-day history of severe lower abdominal pain. On examination the patient’s temperature is 37.7 °C (99.9 °F), bowel sounds are normal, and there is diffuse lower abdominal tenderness without rebound. On pelvic examination there is adnexal tenderness and pain on cervical motion. Vaginal discharge shows leukocytes. A pregnancy test is negative. In addition to sexually transmitted infection testing and empiric treatment, which one of the following should you recommend?

choices.B: A repeat pregnancy test in 7 days

bullets.text: PID can be diagnosed clinically; treatment should be initiated if cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness is present — no further testing is required in straightforward cases.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In women at risk for PID, the diagnosis is clinical and treatment should be initiated when any of the following minimum criteria are present: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. These criteria are intentionally sensitive to avoid missed diagnoses. No further testing is routinely required when the presentation is consistent with uncomplicated PID.

bullets.text: Additional imaging (ultrasound, MRI, CT) or laparoscopy is reserved for cases where complications such as tubo-ovarian abscess or alternative diagnoses like appendicitis are suspected based on history and exam findings.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pelvic ultrasound may reveal fluid-filled or thickened tubes in PID but is not routinely indicated for an uncomplicated presentation. Appendicitis typically causes unilateral pain, and a tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) often presents with unilateral pain and an adnexal mass — either finding would prompt imaging. MRI is reserved for cases where ultrasound suggests TOA or findings beyond simple PID. CT may evaluate complications above the pelvis. Laparoscopy is not the initial step, and delaying management to repeat a pregnancy test in one week is inappropriate in an acutely ill patient.

explanation_raw: This patient's likely diagnosis is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and the diagnosis can be made clinically in most cases. In women at risk of PID, treatment should be initiated if any of the following are present: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. These criteria are considered sensitive for the diagnosis, but the clinician should be mindful to evaluate for other causes, such as appendicitis or tuboovarian abscess (TOA) as indicated by the history and physical examination. Appendicitis would likely cause unilateral pain. TOA often presents acutely with unilateral pain on examination and an adnexal mass. These findings may prompt the clinician to pursue additional testing such as pelvic ultrasonography. A pelvic ultrasound may show fluid-filled or thickened tubes in the setting of PID, but it is not routinely indicated. MRI may be necessary if an ultrasound were to demonstrate TOA or findings other than simple PID. CT of the abdomen may be completed to evaluate complications above the pelvis. Laparoscopy would not be the initial evaluation. This patient is acutely ill and repeating a pregnancy test a week later would not be appropriate.

stem: A 65-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the urgent care clinic approximately 20 hours after experiencing an episode of sudden-onset right-hand weakness. He was suddenly unable to grasp his utensils while eating dinner. These symptoms resolved after about 20 minutes. His wife had encouraged him to seek urgent evaluation, but he declined because his symptoms had resolved. Today the patient's vital signs include a blood pressure of 124/72 mm Hg, a heart rate of 80 beats/min, and a respiratory rate of 12/min. The neurologic examination findings are normal. An EKG shows normal sinus rhythm. The ABCD2 score is 4. Further management includes which one of the following regimens?

choices.B: Clopidogrel (Plavix), 300 mg on day 1, followed by 75 mg daily
choices.C: Clopidogrel, 300 mg on day 1, followed by 75 mg daily on days 2–10; plus aspirin, 81 mg daily
choices.D: Clopidogrel, 300 mg on day 1, followed by 75 mg daily on days 2–21; plus aspirin, 81 mg daily

correct_label: Clopidogrel, 300 mg on day 1, followed by 75 mg daily on days 2–21; plus aspirin, 81 mg daily

bullets.text: For high-risk TIA or minor stroke presenting within 24 hours, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with clopidogrel loading dose plus aspirin for 21 days reduces 90-day stroke risk from 7.8% to 5.2% compared to aspirin alone.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In patients presenting with a moderate- to high-risk TIA or minor stroke within 24 hours of symptom onset, DAPT for 21 days prior to transitioning to a single antiplatelet agent significantly decreases 90-day stroke risk. Recommended management includes a loading dose of clopidogrel (300–600 mg) plus aspirin (50–325 mg) within 24 hours of symptom onset, followed by clopidogrel 75 mg and aspirin 81 mg daily for 21 days, after which the patient transitions to a single antiplatelet agent.

bullets.text: This patient's ABCD2 score of 4 (based on age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration, and diabetes history) classifies him as high-risk TIA, warranting prompt initiation of DAPT rather than single antiplatelet therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The ABCD2 score stratifies TIA patients by short-term stroke risk using age, blood pressure, clinical features of the TIA, duration of symptoms, and presence of diabetes mellitus. A score of 4 places this patient in the high-risk category. Single antiplatelet therapy alone or DAPT for fewer than 21 days does not provide equivalent stroke risk reduction compared to the full 21-day DAPT regimen, making clopidogrel 300 mg loading then 75 mg daily plus aspirin 81 mg daily for 21 days the correct choice.

explanation_raw: In patients presenting with a moderate- to high-risk TIA or minor stroke within 24 hours of symptom onset, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for 21 days prior to transitioning to a single antiplatelet agent decreases the 90-day stroke risk from 7.8% to 5.2% compared to aspirin alone. This patient has symptoms consistent with a high-risk TIA based on an ABCD2 score (age, blood pressure, clinical features of TIA, duration, and diabetes mellitus history) of 4. Recommended management includes loading doses of clopidogrel (300–600 mg) and aspirin (50–325 mg) within 24 hours of symptom onset followed by clopidogrel (75 mg) and aspirin (50–325 mg daily) for 21 days. The patient can then transition to a single antiplatelet agent. Initial treatment with a single antiplatelet agent or with DAPT for less than 21 days does not reduce stroke risk compared to DAPT for 21 days.

stem: A 55-year-old patient with a previous history of opioid use disorder and untreated hypertension presents to your office to establish care. They are now in recovery and would like to catch up on screening laboratory studies. Their blood pressure today is 160/90 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show elevated AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase levels and are positive for hepatitis C antibody and hepatitis C viral load. Testing for hepatitis B and HIV is negative. Lipids are elevated. You calculate an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 10-year risk score of 10%. A right upper quadrant ultrasound shows fibrotic changes of the liver. The patient is surprised that they have liver damage, as they feel well and have never consumed much alcohol. In addition to referring the patient to a gastroenterologist, which one of the following should you begin now to improve fibrotic changes?

choices.E: Upper endoscopy with banding of any varices

bullets.text: Treatment of hepatitis C can improve fibrotic changes in patients with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, as can bariatric surgery.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment of hepatitis C in patients with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (formerly known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis) can improve fibrotic changes, as can bariatric surgery. Coinfection with hepatitis C virus and HIV increases a patient's risk of fibrotic progression to cirrhosis, making treatment of hepatitis C especially important in this population. Offering treatment for viral hepatitis along with PrEP increases access for patients who are at risk of coinfection, though PrEP itself has not been shown to improve fibrotic changes.

bullets.text: Prophylactic antibiotics and nonselective β-blockers are indicated in specific cirrhosis scenarios, including prior SBP, significant varices, low ascitic fluid protein, and advanced hepatic or renal disease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prophylactic antibiotics should be initiated to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with a history of SBP; low ascitic fluid protein levels (<1.5 g/dL); advanced hepatic disease (Child-Pugh score ≥9 or bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL); or renal disease (creatinine ≥1.2 mg/dL, BUN ≥25 mg/dL, or sodium ≤130 mEq/L). Nonselective β-blockers should be started in patients with significant varices identified on upper endoscopy. In MASLD-related cirrhosis, antibiotic prophylaxis is also recommended during episodes of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

bullets.text: PrEP is beneficial for reducing HIV transmission risk but does not improve hepatic fibrosis; addressing both viral hepatitis treatment and PrEP together optimizes care for at-risk patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A conversation regarding the risks and benefits of initiating pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is beneficial for patients at risk of HIV coinfection; however, PrEP has not been shown to improve fibrotic changes in liver disease. Offering viral hepatitis treatment alongside PrEP improves overall access to care and addresses multiple overlapping risks in patients with a history of opioid use disorder.

explanation_raw: Treatment of hepatitis C in patients with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (formerly known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis) can improve fibrotic changes, as can bariatric surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics should be initiated to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with a history of SBP; low ascitic fluid protein levels (<1.5 g/dL); advanced hepatic disease as indicated by a Child-Pugh score ≥9 or a bilirubin level ≥3 mg/dL; or renal disease as indicated by a serum creatinine level ≥1.2 mg/dL or a serum sodium level ≤130 mEq/L. Nonselective β-blockers should be started in patients with significant varices seen on upper endoscopy. Coinfection with hepatitis C virus and HIV increases a patient's risk of fibrotic progression to cirrhosis. A conversation regarding risks and benefits of initiating pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) would be beneficial; however, PrEP has not been shown to improve fibrotic changes. Offering treatment for viral hepatitis along with PrEP increases access for patients who are at risk of coinfection. In individuals with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) and cirrhosis, antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended in specific scenarios: in patients with a history of SBP, during episodes of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and in select high-risk patients with low ascitic fluid protein levels (<1.5 g/dL) along with either advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh score ≥9 and a bilirubin level ≥3 mg/dL) or signs of renal impairment (a creatinine level ≥1.2 mg/dL, a BUN level ≥25 mg/dL, or a sodium level ≤130 mEq/L).

stem: A 46-year-old female sees you for an annual well woman visit. Her only concern is pelvic pressure that becomes more bothersome throughout the day. She notes occasional urinary incontinence of small amounts when coughing or running. She says these symptoms mildly bother her, and mostly wants to make sure there is not a more serious problem. On physical examination, using the lower half of a bivalve speculum, you note a prolapse of the anterior wall, 0.5 cm proximal to the hymenal ring. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step for this patient?

bullets.text: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is graded using the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system; grade 2 indicates prolapse extending within 1 cm above or below the hymenal ring.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pelvic organ prolapse can be described as apical, anterior wall, or posterior wall prolapse. The POP-Q system is used to evaluate and grade severity. A grade 2 prolapse indicates the leading edge extends within 1 cm above or below the hymenal ring. POP is generally progressive until menopause, after which it can alternate between regression and progression.

bullets.text: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is the first-line treatment for symptomatic POP, as it can reduce prolapse by 1–2 cm and provide subjective symptom improvement.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For patients who are only mildly bothered by their symptoms, conservative management with pelvic floor muscle training is the appropriate initial approach. PFMT has been shown to reduce prolapse by 1–2 cm and improve subjective symptoms. There is no clear evidence supporting estrogen alone for POP treatment. Surgical management is often the ultimate treatment but is not indicated when symptoms are minimal; additionally, urinary incontinence can worsen after surgical repair of prolapse, making conservative management even more preferable in this case.

explanation_raw: Pelvic organ prolapse is a common problem, and can be described as apical, of the anterior wall, or of the posterior wall. The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification system can be used to evaluate the prolapse and determine grading. A grade 2 prolapse indicates a prolapse that extends within 1 cm above or below the hymenal ring. Pelvic floor muscle training can reduce prolapse by 1–2 cm and provide subjective improvement in symptoms. There is no clear evidence of the benefit of estrogen alone for pelvic organ prolapse. Surgical management is often the ultimate treatment for pelvic organ prolapse, but it is important to note that urinary incontinence can worsen after repair. This patient is minimally bothered by her symptoms; therefore, surgical treatment would not be recommended at this time but may be indicated in the future. Pelvic organ prolapse is generally progressive until menopause, after which it can alternate between regression and progression.

stem: A 72-year-old male with a past medical history of coronary artery disease, COPD, and hyperlipidemia sees you because of an acute onset of left lower leg pain 1 hour ago. He was in his usual state of health when the pain occurred. His left foot is numb and cold, and he is having difficulty walking. He has a 60-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination findings include a mottled appearance of the left lower leg and foot. Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are absent. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate first step in management?

choices.D: Expedited outpatient referral to a vascular surgeon
choices.E: Transfer to the nearest emergency department with access to a vascular surgeon

correct_label: Transfer to the nearest emergency department with access to a vascular surgeon

bullets.text: This patient presents with acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency characterized by the 6 P's: pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute limb ischemia is identified by the classic 6 P's: pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis. Skeletal muscle can survive only 4–6 hours without blood flow, making rapid recognition critical. Imaging (duplex ultrasonography or CT angiography) can localize the obstruction but must not delay emergency transfer.

bullets.text: Immediate transfer to an emergency department with vascular surgery access is required; anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin should be initiated upon arrival.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The correct and immediate action is transfer to the nearest emergency facility with a vascular surgeon (SOR C). Unfractionated heparin anticoagulation should be started soon after arrival to prevent thrombus propagation. Outpatient referral to a vascular surgeon is inappropriate here as it would critically delay treatment; that approach is reserved for chronic peripheral artery disease (PAD) symptoms.

bullets.text: Direct-acting oral anticoagulants are used for symptomatic PAD management but are not appropriate for acute limb ischemia, and delaying transfer for imaging is dangerous.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have a role in managing symptomatic peripheral artery disease but are not indicated for the acute management of limb ischemia. While duplex ultrasonography or CT angiography can identify the location of the obstruction, obtaining imaging prior to transfer is inappropriate given the time-critical nature of the condition. Similarly, a routine vascular surgery referral would introduce unacceptable delays and is only suitable for chronic PAD presentations.

explanation_raw: This patient's presentation is concerning for acute limb ischemia and he requires immediate transfer to an emergency facility with vascular surgeon accessibility (SOR C). Anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin should be started soon after arrival. Acute limb ischemia is a vascular emergency as skeletal muscle can only survive 4–6 hours without blood flow. Acute limb ischemia is characterized by the 6 P’s: pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis. Direct-acting oral anticoagulants can be used to manage symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD), but not for acute management of limb ischemia. While duplex ultrasonography or CT angiography can be used to determine the presence and location of the obstructed vessel, transfer to an emergency facility should not be delayed for imaging. Referral to a vascular surgeon would delay treatment and would be more appropriate for chronic PAD symptoms.

stem: A 22-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of left lower leg pain over the midshaft of his tibia. Two months ago, he started training for a half marathon. Radiographs performed yesterday at an urgent care clinic were normal. You suspect a bone stress injury. Which one of the following is the preferred definitive imaging modality to evaluate for a bone stress injury?

bullets.text: When radiographs are negative but a bone stress injury is still suspected, MRI is the preferred next imaging study due to its high sensitivity and specificity without radiation exposure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Bone stress injuries are overuse injuries caused by accumulation of bone microdamage, often following an increase in training intensity, frequency, or duration. Radiography is the initial modality of choice because of its high specificity, but it has low sensitivity and is frequently negative in the first 2–3 weeks of symptoms. When radiographs are negative and the patient remains symptomatic, MRI is the preferred follow-up study for definitive diagnosis. It outperforms CT and nuclear bone scintigraphy by offering higher sensitivity and specificity while avoiding ionizing radiation. Point-of-care ultrasonography can serve as an adjunct in trained hands, but its sensitivity does not match that of MRI. Repeat radiography is not the preferred definitive modality given its well-known insensitivity early in the course of stress injuries.

explanation_raw: Bone stress injuries are typically overuse injuries that are caused by an accumulation of bone microdamage. They often occur after an increase in the intensity, frequency, or interval of training. They can also occur when there is structurally compromised bone (osteoporosis, tumors, infections) as normal physiologic loads can damage such compromised bone. Radiography is the initial imaging modality because of its high specificity, despite its low sensitivity. If the radiograph is negative and the patient remains symptomatic, then MRI is the preferred follow-up study for definitive diagnosis. It is preferred over CT and nuclear bone scintigraphy because it has higher sensitivity and specificity and avoids the use of radiation. Repeat radiography is not the preferred definitive imaging modality because radiographs are often negative when taken within the first 2–3 weeks of symptoms. Point-of-care ultrasonography can be used by trained clinicians as an adjunct modality, but its sensitivity is not as high as the sensitivity of MRI.

stem: A 32-year-old female presents to an urgent care clinic with a flare-up of her usually wellcontrolled chronic urticaria. She takes cetirizine (Zyrtec), 10 mg daily. Which one of the following should you recommend?

bullets.text: For chronic urticaria inadequately controlled on standard dosing of a second-generation H1-antihistamine, the recommended next step is to increase the dose up to 4 times the usual FDA-recommended amount before escalating to other therapies.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The first-line treatment of chronic urticaria is an oral second-generation H1-antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine). If standard dosing is ineffective, current guidelines support increasing the H1-antihistamine dose up to 4 times the usual FDA-recommended dosing as a reasonable next step. A short course of oral corticosteroids can address acute flares but is not recommended for chronic control. Cyclosporine is reserved for severe refractory cases unresponsive to high-dose antihistamines and H2-blockers, and omalizumab is indicated when aggressive antihistamine therapy fails.

bullets.text: Nasal corticosteroids are effective for allergic rhinitis but not chronic urticaria; pseudoallergen-free diets lack strong evidence; cyclosporine and omalizumab are reserved for refractory cases that have failed escalated antihistamine therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Nasal corticosteroids have not been shown to be useful for chronic urticaria. Current evidence does not strongly support a pseudoallergen-free diet in managing chronic urticaria. Cyclosporine is only recommended for patients with severe refractory symptoms that have not responded to increased dosages of second-generation antihistamines and a trial of H2-blockers. Omalizumab is effective for chronic urticaria but would only be indicated after aggressive antihistamine therapy has been unsuccessful.

explanation_raw: The first-line treatment of chronic urticaria is an oral second-generation H1-antihistamine. If that is not effective, a reasonable next step is to increase the H1-antihistamine, up to 4 times the usual FDA-recommended dosing. Current evidence does not strongly support the effectiveness of a pseudoallergen-free diet in managing chronic urticaria. Nasal corticosteroids are effective for allergic rhinitis but have not been found to be useful for chronic urticaria. A short course of oral corticosteroids, such as prednisone, can be effective as a short-term solution for a flare-up but is not recommended for chronic control. Cyclosporine is only recommended for patients with severe refractory symptoms that have not responded to increased dosages of second-generation antihistamines and a trial of H2-blockers. Omalizumab is effective for chronic urticaria and would be indicated if aggressive antihistamine therapy is unsuccessful.

stem: A 35-year-old female comes to your office with an 8-day history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and cough. Based on guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America, this patient should be treated with antibiotic therapy if she has which one of the following additional symptoms?

choices.C: An increase in nasal discharge after an initial improvement of symptoms

correct_label: An increase in nasal discharge after an initial improvement of symptoms

bullets.text: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is difficult to distinguish from viral sinusitis, but 'double sickening'—worsening or new symptoms after initial improvement—is a key indicator for immediate antibiotic therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Most cases of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis improve without antibiotics, and watchful waiting with symptomatic management is recommended for up to 10 days if follow-up can be ensured. However, per IDSA guidelines, two scenarios warrant immediate empiric antibiotic treatment: (1) severe symptoms such as fever ≥39°C accompanied by purulent nasal discharge and/or facial pain, and (2) 'double sickening,' defined as the return or worsening of symptoms (e.g., increased nasal discharge, congestion, or fever) after an initial period of improvement during an upper respiratory infection. Major symptoms of sinusitis include purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, decreased smell, and fever; minor symptoms include headache, cough, fatigue, ear pain, halitosis, and tooth pain.

explanation_raw: It is difficult to adequately distinguish between viral sinusitis and acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. However, most instances of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis improve without antibiotics. Major symptoms of sinusitis include purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, decreased smell, and fever. Minor symptoms include headaches, cough, fatigue, ear pain or pressure, halitosis, and tooth pain. If adequate follow-up can be ensured, watchful waiting and symptomatic management is recommended for up to 10 days. Patients with severe symptoms (fever ≥39 °C with purulent nasal discharge and/or facial pain) or those with double sickening (new symptoms following improvement of an upper respiratory infection) should be treated immediately with empiric antibiotics.

stem: You are seeing a 44-year-old female who has a 25-pack-year smoking history. She quit smoking 6 years ago after a friend received a diagnosis of lung cancer. According to U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations, lung cancer screening should be initiated at what age in this patient?

bullets.text: Per 2021 USPSTF guidelines, annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening begins at age 50 for adults with a ≥20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, with approximately 90% of cases linked to smoking. In 2021, the USPSTF updated its recommendation to initiate annual low-dose CT screening in adults aged 50–80 who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and either currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. This patient is 44 years old, smoked 25 pack-years, and quit 6 years ago—she meets the smoking history and recency criteria, so screening should begin when she turns 50.

explanation_raw: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, with approximately 90% of cases linked to smoking. In 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommended annual screening with low-dose CT in adults 50–80 years of age who have a 20-pack-year smoking history and either currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of dysuria and mucopurulent penile discharge. On examination the urethral meatus is erythematous and a small amount of discharge is noted. A urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and a nucleic acid amplification test is negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Gentamicin, 240 mg intramuscularly once, plus azithromycin, 2 g orally once
choices.E: Metronidazole, 2 g orally once, plus doxycycline, 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

bullets.text: This patient meets criteria for nongonococcal urethritis (NGU): dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, urethral erythema, and positive leukocyte esterase on first-void urine, with a negative NAAT for gonorrhea.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diagnostic criteria for urethritis include typical signs and symptoms plus at least one of the following: ≥10 WBCs/hpf on first-void urinalysis, ≥2 WBCs/oil immersion field on Gram stain of discharge, or a positive leukocyte esterase on first-void urine. At least half of NGU cases have no identified etiologic agent; of those with known causes, Mycoplasma genitalium accounts for 15–20% of cases.

bullets.text: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose is the preferred treatment for NGU, including cases caused by Mycoplasma genitalium.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment options for M. genitalium and NGU include azithromycin 1 g orally once, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, or moxifloxacin 400 mg orally for 7–14 days. If NAAT results for gonorrhea and chlamydia are unavailable, empiric therapy with IM ceftriaxone plus a 7-day course of oral doxycycline is appropriate while awaiting results.

bullets.text: The other answer choices are incorrect because they target different organisms or are not first-line for NGU in this clinical context.
bullets.sub_paragraph: IM gentamicin plus oral azithromycin is an alternative regimen for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, not NGU. Metronidazole is used for Trichomonas vaginalis, which accounts for only 1–8% of urethritis cases in men and requires confirmation with a molecular-based test. Levofloxacin is an option for chlamydial urethritis but is not first-line. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline would be appropriate empiric therapy if gonorrhea had not yet been ruled out, but since the NAAT for gonorrhea is negative here, it is unnecessary.

explanation_raw: This patient has nongonococcal urethritis, which should be treated with azithromycin. Symptoms of urethritis include dysuria, purulent or mucopurulent urethral discharge, and urethral discomfort and/or erythema. Diagnostic criteria include typical signs and symptoms or a history of exposure along with ≥10 WBCs/hpf on a first-void urinalysis, ≥2 WBCs/oil immersion field found on Gram stain of the discharge, or a positive leukocyte esterase with first-void urine. At least half of nongonococcal urethritis cases have no known etiologic agent. Of the cases with known etiologies, Mycoplasma genitalium is responsible for 15%–20%. Treatment options for M genitalium include azithromycin, 1 g orally; doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 1 week; or moxifloxacin, 400 mg orally for 7–14 days. If the results of nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia are unavailable, then intramuscular ceftriaxone plus a 7-day course of oral doxycycline would be appropriate and can be used for empiric therapy while awaiting results. Intramuscular gentamicin plus oral azithromycin is used as an alternative treatment regimen for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Metronidazole is used to treat Trichomonas, which represents 1%– 8% of cases in men and should be diagnosed using a molecular-based test. Levofloxacin is a treatment option for chlamydia and is not first line.

stem: A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department with what she describes as the worst headache of her life that began suddenly 1 hour ago. Her medical history is significant for tobacco use and uncontrolled hypertension. She indicates that she has had a few headaches over the last month, but today's headache came on suddenly and is extremely intense, unlike the previous headaches. There is no history of head trauma. Her accompanying relative adds that the patient has been experiencing waxing and waning levels of consciousness since the sudden onset of the headache. She has vomited several times, secondary to pain from the headache. Which one of the following is the most important, immediate next step in management?

bullets.text: A sudden-onset 'worst headache of life' is the classic presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and non-contrast head CT is the immediate first-line diagnostic test due to its speed and high sensitivity in the acute setting.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's presentation — sudden thunderclap headache, history of tobacco use, and uncontrolled hypertension — is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Non-contrast head CT is the most immediate and appropriate next step because it can rapidly confirm the diagnosis and guide urgent neurosurgical consultation. Time-sensitive management makes CT the preferred modality over MRI, which offers no diagnostic advantage for SAH and takes longer to obtain.

bullets.text: Brain MRI is not preferred over CT in acute SAH due to longer acquisition time and no added diagnostic benefit; lumbar puncture is reserved for cases where CT is negative but clinical suspicion remains high (especially >6 hours after onset).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Brain MRI takes longer to obtain and is not diagnostically superior to head CT for acute SAH, making it a less appropriate immediate choice. Pain and nausea control are reasonable supportive measures but should not precede the critical diagnostic workup. Lumbar puncture is an important secondary step — it should be performed if the head CT is negative but clinical suspicion for SAH remains high, particularly when presentation occurs more than 6 hours after headache onset, as xanthochromia in the CSF would support the diagnosis.

explanation_raw: This patient's clinical picture is most consistent with a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Patients typically describe this as a sudden onset of the worst headache they have experienced. The most immediate and meaningful next step is to order a CT scan of the head to verify the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage. The diagnosis and management of subarachnoid hemorrhage is time sensitive. Neurosurgery should be consulted immediately if subarachnoid hemorrhage is verified. Brain MRI would likely take longer to obtain than head CT and is not diagnostically advantageous in subarachnoid hemorrhage compared to a head CT. Pain and nausea control are reasonable, but a CT scan of the head should take precedence because of the time sensitivity of diagnosis and management. A lumbar puncture should be considered if the head CT scan is negative but clinical suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage remains high, especially if the presentation occurs >6 hours after onset.

stem: A 28-year-old male who uses cannabis daily presents with a 2-week history of persistent nausea and vomiting. He notes little relief from previously prescribed ondansetron but does feel better during a hot shower. While tapering his cannabis use, which one of the following would be most likely to improve this patient's nausea?

bullets.text: This patient has cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), characterized by heavy chronic cannabis use, cyclic nausea/vomiting, and relief with hot showers or baths.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome should be suspected in any chronic daily cannabis user presenting with refractory nausea and vomiting, particularly when standard antiemetics like ondansetron fail and hot water bathing provides symptomatic relief. Cessation of cannabis use is the only definitive treatment.

bullets.text: Haloperidol is more effective than traditional antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) or corticosteroids for acute management of CHS; topical capsaicin applied to the upper abdomen is also effective via TRPV1 receptor desensitization.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Current evidence supports haloperidol as the preferred acute antiemetic in CHS, outperforming traditionally used agents. Topical capsaicin activates transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) receptors, leading to desensitization of sensory nerve fibers and symptom relief. Benzodiazepines may help acutely, and tricyclic antidepressants may offer benefit for longer-term management. Diclofenac gel has no established role in CHS.

explanation_raw: This patient has cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, characterized by heavy chronic cannabis use and nausea that improves with hot baths or showers. Current evidence suggests that haloperidol is more effective than more traditionally used antiemetics, such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, or corticosteroids in managing nausea associated with this syndrome. Topical capsaicin has also been shown to be effective. Topical capsaicin, when applied to the upper abdomen, may help alleviate symptoms by activating transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) receptors. This mechanism can lead to desensitization of sensory nerve fibers, potentially reducing the need for antiemetic medications. Benzodiazepines may help acutely, and tricyclic antidepressants may have efficacy for longer-term management. Cessation of cannabis use is necessary for definitive treatment. Diclofenac gel is not appropriate pharmacotherapy for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome.

stem: A 30-year-old female with fibromyalgia sees you for follow-up. Her symptoms include widespread pain and prominent fatigue. At your advice, she has engaged in a trial of multidisciplinary, nonpharmacologic treatment including structured exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, and therapeutic massage, and has experienced only partial improvement in her symptoms. She expresses interest in trying a medication to treat her pain. Which one of the following medications would be most likely to improve this patient's pain?

bullets.text: Duloxetine (SNRI) has Level A evidence for treating fibromyalgia pain and is a first-line pharmacologic option after nonpharmacologic therapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Duloxetine is an SNRI with strong (SOR A) evidence for reducing fibromyalgia-related pain. Other medications with Level A evidence include amitriptyline, cyclobenzaprine, pregabalin, and the SNRI milnacipran (which also reduces fatigue and improves cognition). Venlafaxine has not been studied as extensively. Acetaminophen and gabapentin lack sufficient evidence for fibromyalgia pain. Opioids such as hydrocodone are not recommended due to risks of dependence, misuse, and worsening hyperalgesia. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen perform no better than placebo and carry significant adverse effect risks.

explanation_raw: Duloxetine is an SNRI that is effective for treating fibromyalgia pain (SOR A). Other medications with level A evidence of effectiveness in reducing fibromyalgia-related pain include amitriptyline, cyclobenzaprine, and pregabalin. The SNRI milnacipran also has level A evidence for reducing fibromyalgia-related pain and has evidence for reducing fatigue and improving cognition in patients with fibromyalgia. Other SNRIs, including venlafaxine, have not been studied as extensively. Current evidence is insufficient to support acetaminophen or gabapentin use to treat fibromyalgia pain. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of opioids such as hydrocodone, which are associated with a significant risk of adverse effects, dependence, misuse, and worsening hyperalgesia. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are no better than placebo and introduce significant risk of adverse effects.

stem: An 8-year-old male is brought to your office by his parents because of concerns about ongoing nocturnal enuresis. He wets his bed several nights per week despite behavioral interventions. He has no daytime urinary symptoms. Physical examination findings and urinalysis are normal. You discuss treatment options and the parents indicate a preference for medication, as the patient will be attending an overnight summer camp in several weeks. Which one of the following would be the preferred pharmacologic treatment for this child’s nocturnal enuresis?

bullets.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is the preferred pharmacologic agent for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis when behavioral interventions have failed.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Behavioral methods and enuresis alarms are considered first-line treatments for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis. When pharmacotherapy is needed, intranasal or oral desmopressin is the preferred first choice. If desmopressin fails, secondary options include imipramine or oxybutynin. Tamsulosin is not indicated for nocturnal enuresis in children.

explanation_raw: Behavioral methods and enuresis alarms are first-line treatments for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis without an identifiable cause. If pharmacotherapy is initiated, intranasal or oral desmopressin is acceptable. Imipramine and oxybutynin are additional options if there is no response to oral desmopressin. Tamsulosin is not recommended for this indication.

stem: A 25-year-old male with a childhood diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADH

bullets.text: When stimulants are not tolerated in adult ADHD, atomoxetine (an SNRI) is the preferred second-line pharmacotherapy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Stimulants are first-line pharmacotherapy for adults with ADHD given extensive data supporting their effectiveness. However, adverse effects such as headaches, insomnia, poor appetite, weight loss, anxiety, depression, elevated heart rate, and elevated blood pressure can prevent patients from taking them. When stimulants are not tolerated or do not provide an adequate response, the second-line therapy is an SNRI such as atomoxetine or viloxazine.

bullets.text: Clonidine and guanfacine are only FDA-approved for ADHD in children and adolescents, tricyclic antidepressants like nortriptyline have limited evidence and no ADHD approval, and escitalopram is not effective for ADHD.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Clonidine and guanfacine are only approved for the treatment of ADHD in children and adolescents; although sometimes used off-label in adults, there is limited evidence to support such use. Tricyclic antidepressants such as nortriptyline have limited evidence and are not approved for ADHD treatment. Escitalopram (an SSRI) is not effective for treating ADHD and has no role in its management.

explanation_raw: Stimulants are first-line pharmacotherapy for adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) given the extensive data supporting their effectiveness. However, there are potential adverse effects that can prevent patients from taking them, such as headaches, insomnia, poor appetite, weight loss, anxiety, depression, elevated heart rate, and elevated blood pressure. When stimulants are not tolerated or do not provide an adequate response, the second-line therapy would be an SNRI such as atomoxetine or viloxazine. Clonidine and guanfacine are only approved for the treatment of ADHD in children and adolescents. Although they are sometimes used off-label in adults, there is limited evidence to support such use. Tricyclic antidepressants such as nortriptyline have limited evidence and are not approved for ADHD treatment. Escitalopram is not effective for treating ADHD.

stem: A 19-year-old college basketball player consults you for follow-up after sustaining an anterior shoulder dislocation for the first time. He initially presented to the emergency department where his shoulder was reduced and immobilized in a sling. Which one of the following is most likely to decrease the risk of future recurrence?

choices.B: Completion of a course of physical therapy
choices.C: Administration of an intra-articular corticosteroid injection

bullets.text: Surgical repair is most likely to decrease recurrence of anterior shoulder dislocation in young, active patients under 25 years of age.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Anterior shoulder dislocations carry a recurrence rate of up to 90%. Evidence from cohort studies consistently shows that surgical repair significantly reduces recurrence in active patients younger than 25. Given this patient's age and high activity level as a college basketball player, referral for surgical repair is the most appropriate recommendation.

bullets.text: Non-surgical management includes sling immobilization for 2–4 weeks followed by graduated rehabilitation; athletes may return to play when pain-free with symmetric range of motion, sometimes as early as 2–3 weeks.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For patients who do not undergo surgery, conservative management consists of sling use for 2–4 weeks with progressive passive then active range-of-motion rehabilitation. Return to sport is permitted when the athlete is pain-free, has symmetrical shoulder range of motion, and can perform sport-specific movements. Intra-articular corticosteroids are not recommended following a shoulder dislocation.

explanation_raw: Although anterior shoulder dislocations have a high rate of recurrence (up to 90%), evidence from cohort studies has consistently found a lower rate of recurrence in active patients <25 years of age who have received surgical treatment for first-time dislocations. Because of this patient's age and activity level, referral for surgical repair would be appropriate. Other treatment options for anterior shoulder dislocation include the use of a sling for 2–4 weeks with graduated rehabilitation of passive and active range of motion. If no surgery is warranted, athletes can return to play when they are pain free with symmetrical shoulder range of motion and able to perform sport-specific motions, which can be as early as 2–3 weeks after injury. Intra-articular corticosteroids are not advised after a shoulder dislocation.

stem: A 32-year-old gravida 2 para 2 female who is 3 weeks post partum presents to the local urgent care center for left breast pain, swelling, and redness that started a few hours ago. She does not have fever or chills. A breast examination is significant for warm, tender, and mildly erythematous nodules localized to the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. In addition to initiating NSAIDs, which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Applying cold compresses to the affected breast
choices.B: Applying warm compresses to the affected breast
choices.C: Using a manual breast pump on the affected breast for complete breast emptying
choices.D: Obtaining a CBC and C-reactive protein levels

correct_label: Applying cold compresses to the affected breast

bullets.text: Inflammatory mastitis presents with unilateral breast erythema, swelling, and pain, and is diagnosed clinically without need for laboratory testing or imaging.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Mastitis is a spectrum of inflammatory breast conditions including lactational/inflammatory mastitis, bacterial mastitis, and breast abscess. Inflammatory mastitis presents with unilateral breast erythema, swelling, and pain, and may include systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, or headache. It is a clinical diagnosis — CBC, C-reactive protein, and breast milk cultures are not routinely helpful, as inflammatory markers can be elevated in both inflammatory and bacterial mastitis, and milk cultures may yield false positives from normal skin flora colonization.

bullets.text: Initial management of inflammatory mastitis is supportive care with NSAIDs and cold compresses; antibiotics are reserved for cases that fail to improve within 24–48 hours.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The first-line treatment for inflammatory mastitis is supportive care: NSAIDs for pain and inflammation, and cold compresses to the affected breast. Warm compresses and frequent breast pumping to avoid milk stasis are no longer recommended. If symptoms worsen or do not improve within 24–48 hours of conservative management, narrow-spectrum antibiotics empirically targeting Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species should be initiated for presumed bacterial mastitis.

explanation_raw: Mastitis is a spectrum of inflammatory breast conditions, which includes lactational or inflammatory mastitis, bacterial mastitis, breast abscess, postpartum breast engorgement, and more. Patients with inflammatory mastitis exhibit unilateral breast erythema, swelling, and pain and may experience systemic inflammatory responses such as fever, malaise, or headache. The initial steps in managing inflammatory mastitis are supportive care with NSAIDs, cold compresses, and watchful waiting. Inflammatory mastitis is diagnosed clinically and does not require laboratory testing or imaging. If a patient's symptoms worsen or do not improve within 24–48 hours with conservative measures, narrow-spectrum antibiotics targeting the most common organisms (Staphylococcus species and Streptococcus species) should be empirically initiated for bacterial mastitis. Warm compresses and frequent breast pumping for complete breast emptying to avoid milk stasis are no longer recommended. CBC and C-reactive protein testing are not helpful as these levels can be elevated in both inflammatory and bacterial mastitis. Breast milk cultures are seldom necessary because they may produce falsepositive results caused by normal skin bacteria colonization.

stem: A young couple in your practice presents for preconception counseling. Both partners are known carriers of cystic fibrosis (CF). They ask what risk this poses to their future children. Which one of the following accurately reflects the risk of CF disease transmission to any potential offspring of this couple?

choices.A: 25% risk of being affected and 25% risk of being a carrier
choices.B: 25% risk of being affected and 50% risk of being a carrier
choices.C: 50% risk of being affected and 25% risk of being a carrier
choices.D: 50% risk of being affected and 50% risk of being a carrier

correct_label: 25% risk of being affected and 50% risk of being a carrier

explanation.heading: Autosomal Recessive Inheritance in Cystic Fibrosis

bullets.text: When both parents are carriers (heterozygous) for cystic fibrosis, each pregnancy carries a 25% chance of being affected, 50% chance of being an unaffected carrier, and 25% chance of being an unaffected noncarrier.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cystic fibrosis follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Affected individuals are homozygous for the CFTR mutation (two mutated copies), while carriers are heterozygous (one mutated, one normal copy). When two carriers reproduce, a Punnett square analysis reveals four equally probable outcomes: 25% homozygous affected (disease), 50% heterozygous carrier (unaffected), and 25% homozygous normal (unaffected noncarrier). This makes the risk of an affected child 1 in 4 per pregnancy.

explanation_raw: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder with an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. People who are affected by the disease are homozygous for the condition, with 2 copies of the mutated gene. Carriers are heterozygous for the condition with 1 mutated gene and 1 normal gene. When both partners in a couple are carriers, any potential offspring has a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an unaffected carrier, and a 25% chance of being an unaffected noncarrier.

stem: A 47-year-old nurse presents with a 9-month history of fatigue and brain fog that has kept them from working. Their symptoms began after a confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19. They report sleeping at least 7 hours per night but wake unrefreshed and experience lightheadedness throughout the day. They used to run 4 miles 5 days per week but now report feeling exhausted and experience energy crashes after showering and getting dressed. The patient's vital signs and BMI are normal. A physical examination is unremarkable. Their Patient Health Questionnaire–9 (PHQ-9) score is 3. A CBC, TSH level, basic metabolic panel, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are within the normal range. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: This patient meets National Academy of Medicine criteria for ME/CFS: ≥6 months of new-onset fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, postexertional malaise, cognitive impairment (brain fog), and orthostatic intolerance (lightheadedness), with symptom onset following confirmed COVID-19.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The National Academy of Medicine criteria for ME/CFS require at least 6 months of substantially reduced functioning accompanied by three core symptoms: unrefreshing sleep, new-onset fatigue with postexertional malaise, and either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance. This patient fulfills all criteria. COVID-19 is a well-recognized trigger for post-infectious ME/CFS, making it a key consideration in patients with prolonged post-COVID symptoms.

bullets.text: Depression (PHQ-9 of 3, indicating minimal/no depression), fibromyalgia, SLE, and obstructive sleep apnea do not fully account for this clinical picture—particularly the hallmark postexertional malaise, which worsens with exercise rather than improving.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A PHQ-9 score of 3 indicates no or minimal depression, making major depressive disorder an unlikely explanation for the severity of fatigue and energy crashes. Importantly, exercise typically improves depression but can worsen ME/CFS due to postexertional malaise. Secondary causes of fatigue such as fibromyalgia and systemic lupus erythematosus generally improve with exercise, distinguishing them from ME/CFS. Obstructive sleep apnea may cause unrefreshing sleep but does not characteristically produce the profound postexertional malaise seen in this patient.

explanation_raw: Based on the National Academy of Medicine criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), this patient has demonstrated the core symptoms of ME/CFS (unrefreshing sleep, new-onset fatigue, and postexertional malaise) for at least 6 months, in addition to brain fog and lightheadedness. Notably, their symptoms developed after a previous COVID-19 infection, an illness that is commonly associated with ME/CFS. A Patient Health Questionnaire–9 (PHQ-9) score of 3 indicates no or minimal depression, which would not account for severe fatigue or energy crashes after minimal exertion. Exercise may actually improve depression. Secondary causes of fatigue, such as fibromyalgia and systemic lupus erythematosus, typically improve with exercise. Although obstructive sleep apnea may cause unrefreshing sleep, it is not associated with profound fatigue and postexertional malaise.

stem: A 62-year-old male is brought to the clinic by his wife for fatigue. His wife says he has been sleeping in the recliner rather than in bed and has been less active over the last several weeks. He reports that his clothes have been fitting tightly and he has gained weight despite feeling full early in a meal. He also notes difficulty bending over to tie his shoes and pet the dog. He has no chest pain or pressure and has not traveled recently. His past medical history is notable for a myocardial infarction 5 years ago treated with a stent, and elevated cholesterol. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history but quit 20 years ago. His medications include aspirin, 81 mg daily; lisinopril (Zestril), 20 mg daily; and metoprolol succinate (Toprol-XL), 50 mg daily. On examination he has a blood pressure of 110/65 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 89 beats/min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. You also note mildly increased work of breathing, a regular heart rate, and a laterally displaced apical impulse. Which one of the following tests would most likely confirm this patient’s underlying diagnosis?

bullets.text: Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosing heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), confirming left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40% along with elevated BNP.
bullets.sub_paragraph: HFrEF affects more than 6.5 million U.S. adults and presents with symptoms including dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea (sleeping reclined rather than supine), and right-sided heart failure symptoms such as early satiety, abdominal bloating, and ill-fitting clothes. Physical exam may reveal elevated jugular venous pressure, S3 gallop, or laterally displaced apical impulse. The definitive diagnosis requires echocardiographic documentation of left ventricular systolic dysfunction with EF ≤40% and an elevated BNP level.

bullets.text: EKG helps evaluate contributing factors like arrhythmia or MI but does not diagnose HFrEF; chest X-ray is limited as it is normal in ~20% of acute HFrEF cases; CT angiography is inappropriate here as it is reserved for low-risk coronary artery disease evaluation or pulmonary embolism workup.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While an EKG is an important part of the workup to assess for arrhythmia or acute MI, it does not establish the diagnosis of HFrEF. Chest X-ray may show cardiomegaly or vascular congestion but has limited diagnostic utility given its ~20% false-negative rate in acute HFrEF. CT angiography would be inappropriate in this patient with a prior MI history and is typically used for evaluating coronary artery disease in low-risk patients or for suspected pulmonary embolism—a less likely diagnosis given the absence of immobility, prolonged travel, or other PE risk factors, and a clinical picture more consistent with heart failure.

explanation_raw: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is a major public health concern affecting more than 6.5 million U.S. adults. Family physicians should be familiar with its typical clinical presentations and diagnosis, which is best established using echocardiography. Symptoms vary and may include dyspnea, ankle edema, and fatigue. Orthopnea, as evident by modification of sleeping from supine to reclined or semireclined, is also common. Symptoms of right-sided heart failure, such as early satiety, abdominal bloating, ill-fitting clothes, and shortness of breath when bent forward, are also frequently encountered, but are less specific. Physical examination may reveal signs of congestion such as elevated jugular venous pressure, S3 gallop, or a laterally displaced apical impulse. Some predictors of HFrEF include increased heart rate, coronary artery disease (hazard ratio [HR] 1.73), and previous myocardial infarction (MI) (HR 3.49). The diagnosis is made by documenting left ventricular systolic dysfunction with a left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40% and an elevated BNP level. An EKG is a key component of the workup and evaluation of contributing factors, such as arrhythmia or acute MI, but not diagnosis. A chest x-ray, while quick and readily available, may identify cardiomegaly or vascular congestion but is normal in approximately 20% of those with acute HFrEF, limiting diagnostic utility. Given this patient's history of MI, CT angiography would be inappropriate and is typically reserved for evaluating coronary artery disease in low-risk patients. CT angiography is used to evaluate for pulmonary embolism, which is less likely, given this patient's lack of immobility, prolonged travel, or other risk factors, as well as a history and physical examination that favor heart failure (displaced apical impulse, orthopnea, abdominal distention/weight gain).

stem: A 3-year-old male is brought to your office by his parents for a routine well child visit. He is up to date on vaccines and the parents have no concerns to discuss today. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, this child should be screened for which one of the following conditions?

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends vision screening at least once in all children ages 3–5 years to detect amblyopia or its risk factors (Grade B recommendation).
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF recommends vision screening at least once in all children ages 3–5 years to detect amblyopia or its risk factors (Grade B recommendation). Screening methods include visual acuity testing with picture identification, Snellen or 'tumbling E' charts, or automated devices. Early identification can prevent permanent vision loss due to amblyopia.

bullets.text: Anemia screening (AAP recommends at 1 year), autism screening (AAP recommends at 18 and 24 months), dental caries screening (<5 years), and universal hearing screening (recommended for newborns only) all have insufficient evidence per USPSTF at this age and are not universally recommended by the USPSTF for a 3-year-old.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Anemia screening is recommended by the AAP at 1 year of age, but the USPSTF found insufficient evidence of benefit (I recommendation). Autism spectrum disorder screening is recommended by the AAP at 18 and 24 months, but the USPSTF found insufficient evidence that universal screening improves outcomes when families have no developmental concerns (I recommendation). The USPSTF found insufficient evidence for dental caries screening in children under 5, though it does recommend fluoride varnish application every 3–6 months for children ages 6 months to 5 years (B recommendation) and oral fluoride supplements for those without adequate fluoride in their water supply (B recommendation). Universal hearing screening is recommended for newborns, not for children at age 3.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends vision screening at least once in all children 3–5 years of age to detect amblyopia or its risk factors (B recommendation). Screening may be performed using visual acuity testing with picture identification, Snellen or "tumbling E," or by an automated device that assesses visual acuity. Early identification of vision disorders can help prevent permanent vision loss due to amblyopia. Anemia screening is recommended for all children at 1 year of age by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), but this approach was found to have insufficient evidence of benefit by the USPSTF (I recommendation). Screening for autism spectrum disorder is recommended by the AAP at 18 and 24 months of age, but the USPSTF found insufficient evidence that universal screening results in improved care in families without concerns about their child's development (I recommendation). The USPSTF found insufficient evidence of benefit of screening for dental caries in children <5 years of age (I recommendation). Instead, it recommends that fluoride varnish be applied every 3–6 months in all children 6 months to 5 years of age to prevent dental caries (B recommendation). This should be performed in the family physician's office if it has not been applied by a dentist. Additionally, an oral fluoride supplement is recommended to prevent dental caries in children without adequate fluoride in their water supply (B recommendation). Universal hearing screening is recommended for newborns, but screening at this age is not recommended.

stem: A 50-year-old female comes to your clinic for an annual wellness examination. Her past medical history is notable for dermatomyositis diagnosed 2 years ago. She is otherwise healthy and her BMI is normal. Patients with dermatomyositis are at increased risk of which one of the following conditions?

bullets.text: Dermatomyositis diagnosed after age 40 carries up to a 25% risk of associated malignancy within 3 years of diagnosis, making malignancy screening the highest priority in this patient's wellness visit.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cancer is a leading cause of death in patients with dermatomyositis, and malignancy is diagnosed in up to 25% of these patients within 3 years of their dermatomyositis diagnosis. The most commonly associated cancers are adenocarcinomas of the ovary, lung, pancreas, stomach, and colon, as well as non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Standard population-level cancer screening is generally insufficient for this population, and advanced modalities such as CT and PET scans may be warranted based on individual risk factors.

bullets.text: Chronic kidney disease and obesity have not been shown to occur at increased rates in patients with dermatomyositis, and while screening for diabetes and hyperlipidemia remains important, it is not the most critical concern specific to this diagnosis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Chronic kidney disease and obesity are not established complications or associations of dermatomyositis.
