Counseling on diet, exercise, and screening for diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia are all important components of a wellness visit but are not unique to or disproportionately elevated in dermatomyositis patients. The defining clinical concern specific to dermatomyositis, particularly in patients diagnosed after age 40, is the markedly elevated risk of underlying or subsequent malignancy.

explanation_raw: While counseling on diet and exercise and screening for diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia are important, malignancy screening is the most important component of the wellness visit in this patient with dermatomyositis diagnosed after the age of 40. Cancer is a leading cause of death in this patient population and is diagnosed in up to 25% of these patients within 3 years of their dermatomyositis diagnosis. The most likely cancers in this population include adenocarcinomas of the ovary, lung, pancreas, stomach, and colon as well as non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Population-level cancer screening recommendations are generally insufficient for this population, and advanced cancer screening modalities, including CT scans and PET scans, may be recommended based on the patient's individual risk factors to target these types of cancers. Chronic kidney disease and obesity have not been observed to have an increased risk in patients with dermatomyositis.

stem: Of the following cognitive biases, which one best describes the practice of prioritizing data that supports an initial impression, even when the initial impression is incorrect?

bullets.text: Anchoring bias occurs when a physician over-relies on their initial clinical impression and prioritizes supporting data while discounting contradictory information, even when that first impression is wrong.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Anchoring bias describes the tendency of physicians to 'anchor' to their first impression of a diagnosis and selectively prioritize information that supports it, even in the face of contradicting evidence. This is distinct from availability bias (linking diagnoses to easily recalled examples), implicit bias (unconscious attitudes related to race, gender, age, etc.), and outcomes bias (attributing all results to prior decisions regardless of actual causation). Recognizing anchoring bias is critical to avoiding diagnostic errors in clinical practice.

explanation_raw: Anchoring bias describes the practice of physicians prioritizing information and data that supports their initial impressions, even when these impressions are incorrect. In other words, it is when physicians are biased toward their first impression. Availability bias describes the likelihood of a diagnosis being erroneously linked to how easy it is to think of examples. Implicit bias is defined as attitudes and beliefs about race, ethnicity, age, ability, gender, or other characteristics. Implicit bias operates on an unconscious level and can only be measured indirectly. Outcomes bias refers to the attribution of all results to prior decisions, regardless of whether there is a reason to do so.

stem: An otherwise healthy 15-year-old female presents for evaluation of a 7-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding. Her periods are 10 days long, irregular, and require 10 tampons per day. She sometimes passes large clots. Other than some fatigue, she feels well today and her vital signs are normal. A point-of-care hemoglobin level is 10.2 g/dL (N 12.0–16.0). Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

bullets.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding in adolescents warrants evaluation for an underlying bleeding disorder, as prevalence rises to ~20% in this population (vs. 1–2% general population), with von Willebrand disease and platelet dysfunction being most common.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is very common in adolescents and may signal an underlying bleeding disorder. While bleeding disorders affect only 1–2% of the general population, prevalence increases to approximately 20% among adolescent girls with HMB. Von Willebrand disease and platelet dysfunction are the most commonly identified conditions. Evaluation is indicated when there is frequent pad/tampon use (>1 every 1–2 hours), bleeding lasting >7 days, passage of clots >1 inch in diameter, personal history of anemia treatment or excessive bleeding with procedures, or a family history of a bleeding disorder.

bullets.text: The initial workup for HMB in an adolescent includes CBC, PT/PTT/INR, von Willebrand panel, hCG, ferritin, fibrinogen, and TSH; hormonal contraceptives and tranexamic acid may treat HMB but workup comes first.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The initial laboratory workup for HMB in an adolescent includes a CBC; prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and INR; a von Willebrand panel; and hCG, ferritin, fibrinogen, and TSH levels. Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea should be considered in sexually active patients. Testosterone, prolactin, and DHEA levels are obtained if signs of PCOS or other endocrine disorders are present. FSH, LH, estrogen, and progesterone levels are not helpful in evaluating excessive uterine bleeding. Pelvic imaging is not routinely necessary but should be considered for HMB not responding to initial management. Hormonal contraceptives and tranexamic acid can treat HMB, but workup for a bleeding disorder is the most important first step.

explanation_raw: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is very common in adolescents and may be a sign of an underlying bleeding disorder. Although bleeding disorders affect 1%–2% of the general population, the prevalence increases to 20% among adolescent girls with heavy menstrual bleeding. Platelet dysfunction and von Willebrand disease are most commonly identified. Evaluation for bleeding disorders is indicated when there is frequent pad or tampon use (>1 every 1–2 hours); menstrual bleeding lasting longer than 7 days; passage of clots larger than 1 inch in diameter; a personal history of anemia treatment, excessive bleeding with tooth extraction or surgery, or excessive bruising; or a family history of a bleeding disorder. The initial workup for HMB in an adolescent includes a CBC; a prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and INR; a von Willebrand panel; and hCG, ferritin, fibrinogen, and TSH levels. Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea should be considered in sexually active patients. Testosterone, prolactin, and DHEA levels should be obtained if there are signs of polycystic ovary syndrome or other endocrine disorders. Levels of FSH, LH, estrogen, and progesterone are not helpful in the evaluation of excessive uterine bleeding. Pelvic imaging is not routinely necessary but should be considered for HMB that does not respond to initial management. Hormonal contraceptives and tranexamic acid may be used for the treatment of HMB, but workup for a bleeding disorder is the most important first step.

stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with a 6-month history of epigastric burning pain that occurs several days per week. The pain does not seem to have a clear correlation to eating. There has been no substernal pain or regurgitation and no weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, fever, night sweats, or fatigue. The patient has no prior medical history and takes no medications, but has tried calcium carbonate occasionally without benefit. A physical examination reveals normal vital signs and no abdominal abnormalities or enlarged lymph nodes. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: Stool antigen testing for Helicobacter pylori

correct_label: Stool antigen testing for Helicobacter pylori

bullets.text: This patient has dyspepsia, defined by symptoms including epigastric pain/burning, early satiety, or postprandial fullness, and testing for H. pylori is the recommended first step.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Dyspepsia is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring at least one of the following: early satiety, epigastric pain, epigastric burning, or postprandial fullness. The majority of patients have functional dyspepsia with no organic disease found on endoscopy. Testing for and treating H. pylori is recommended in dyspepsia patients, with evidence showing symptom improvement at 1 year post-treatment. The preferred noninvasive tests are the stool antigen test and the urea breath test; serum H. pylori testing is not recommended due to lower sensitivity and specificity.

bullets.text: Sucralfate lacks evidence for dyspepsia; abdominal ultrasound is not useful for dyspepsia investigation; and endoscopy is reserved for patients over 60 or those with alarm features.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Sucralfate has not been shown to be effective for dyspepsia and is not a recommended treatment. Abdominal ultrasonography is indicated for evaluating liver or gallbladder pathology, not dyspepsia. Endoscopy is recommended for patients >60 years of age with new dyspepsia, or for patients <60 years with multiple or severe alarm symptoms such as marked weight loss, rapidly progressive dysphagia, an epigastric mass, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy — none of which are present in this 45-year-old patient.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with symptoms of dyspepsia. Dyspepsia is a diagnosis of exclusion and should be considered if at least 1 of the following symptoms is present: early satiety, epigastric pain, epigastric burning, and postprandial fullness. The majority of patients diagnosed with dyspepsia have functional dyspepsia with no evidence of organic disease on endoscopy. Testing for and treating Helicobacter pylori infection is recommended in patients with dyspepsia, with evidence of improvement 1 year after treatment. The stool antigen test and the urea breath test are the preferred noninvasive options for detecting H pylori. Serum testing for H pylori is not recommended because it has lower sensitivity and specificity than other noninvasive tests. Sucralfate has not been shown to be effective for dyspepsia. Abdominal ultrasonography, particularly of the upper abdomen, is indicated when evaluating for liver pathology or gallbladder disease but is not useful for investigating dyspepsia. Endoscopy is recommended for patients >60 years of age with new dyspepsia, and for patients <60 years of age with multiple or severe alarm symptoms, such as marked weight loss, rapidly progressive dysphagia, an epigastric mass, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

stem: A 48-year-old female comes to your office for a health maintenance examination. She is currently asymptomatic but has a medical history of renal calculi. Laboratory studies reveal a serum calcium level of 12.1 mg/dL (N 8.7–10.2), confirmed by an ionized calcium level. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step at this time?

choices.D: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

bullets.text: After confirming hypercalcemia, the initial diagnostic test should be a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level, as primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Hypercalcemia identified on a metabolic panel should be confirmed with a corrected or ionized calcium level. Once confirmed, the first step is to measure PTH, since primary hyperparathyroidism is the leading etiology. An elevated PTH warrants further workup including 25-hydroxyvitamin D, creatinine, 24-hour urinary calcium, and bone density testing. A low PTH level raises concern for malignancy and may prompt CT imaging. Parathyroid gland imaging is not required for diagnosis but is useful when surgical management is being considered.

bullets.text: A thorough history for hypercalcemia should include symptoms (nephrolithiasis, arrhythmias, bone pain, mental status changes), dietary calcium/phosphorus intake, medication use (e.g., lithium), and family history of MEN syndromes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Clinical evaluation of hypercalcemia must include assessment for classic manifestations such as renal calculi (as seen in this patient), hypertension, abdominal pain, arthralgias, fractures, anxiety, depression, and altered mental status. Additionally, dietary habits, lithium use, and a family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) are important contextual factors that help guide the diagnostic workup and identify the underlying etiology.

explanation_raw: Hypercalcemia is commonly identified through a metabolic panel and should be confirmed with a corrected or ionized calcium level. The most common cause of hypercalcemia is primary hyperparathyroidism, but any underlying malignancy should be ruled out. A thorough history should assess for symptoms such as arrhythmias, hypertension, abdominal pain, arthralgias, fractures, mental status changes, anxiety, depression, and nephrolithiasis. Dietary intake of calcium and phosphorus, use of medications such as lithium, and a family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia are also important to evaluate. After confirming hypercalcemia, the initial test should be a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. If the PTH level is elevated, then 25-hydroxyvitamin D, creatinine, and 24-hour urinary calcium levels should be measured in addition to ordering a bone density test. Imaging of the parathyroid glands is not necessary for diagnosis, but is useful if surgical management is indicated. A low PTH level could suggest malignancy and may indicate the need for a CT scan.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents to your office with a 3-day history of right-sided facial weakness. She has flattening of the nasolabial fold and is unable to elevate the right corner of her mouth. She is able to close her right eye and raise her eyebrows. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

bullets.text: Forehead-sparing facial weakness indicates a supranuclear (central) lesion, not peripheral nerve palsy, because the forehead receives bilateral cortical input.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The nucleus of cranial nerve VII receives corticobulbar fibers from both hemispheres for the upper face (forehead and eye closure), so a unilateral central lesion spares the forehead. In contrast, Bell palsy (peripheral CN VII lesion) affects the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead. This patient's ability to raise her eyebrows and close her eye points to a supranuclear etiology requiring urgent central nervous system evaluation.

bullets.text: MRI of the brain is the appropriate next step to identify a central cause such as stroke or intracranial tumor in a patient with forehead-sparing facial weakness.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Because forehead sparing is inconsistent with Bell palsy and instead suggests a cortical or subcortical lesion, brain MRI is warranted to evaluate for ischemic stroke, hemorrhage, or mass lesion. This presentation should not be attributed to Bell palsy and should not be treated empirically with prednisone or valacyclovir.

bullets.text: Prednisone, valacyclovir, plasmapheresis, and surgical decompression are all inappropriate because they address peripheral CN VII palsy (Bell palsy), not a central lesion.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prednisone and valacyclovir are standard treatments for Bell palsy, which presents with complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including forehead involvement. Plasmapheresis has no role in Bell palsy, stroke, or tumor management. Surgical decompression is not indicated in this clinical scenario. Since the presentation is inconsistent with Bell palsy, none of these interventions are appropriate before central pathology is excluded.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with a relatively acute onset of facial weakness affecting only the right side of the face, but she is able to close her right eye and raise her eyebrows. Sparing of the forehead muscles is consistent with a supranuclear lesion because the nucleus of cranial nerve VII receives fibers from both sides of the cortex for the upper face, meaning the forehead would be unaffected. Cranial nerve VII includes visceral efferent fibers (facial muscles and stapedius), visceral motor fibers (salivary and lacrimal glands), and special sensory fibers (taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue). In Bell palsy, which involves edema of this cranial nerve, the entire side of the face is affected, including the forehead. Therefore, this presentation is not consistent with Bell palsy and warrants further evaluation, including brain MRI, to assess for a central cause. Prednisone and valacyclovir are not appropriate for this patient, as they are treatments used for Bell palsy. Plasmapheresis is not indicated for Bell palsy, stroke, or tumor. Surgical decompression is not indicated.

She was slightly confused after the injury, but was able to stand and describe the incident. On initial assessment in the ED, she is holding her head in obvious discomfort and a hematoma is developing on her forehead. She is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of

She was slightly confused after the injury, but was able to stand and describe the incident. On initial assessment in the ED, she is holding her head in obvious discomfort and a hematoma is developing on her forehead. She is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of

bullets.text: In older adults (≥65 years), head trauma with loss of consciousness, vomiting, anterograde amnesia, or prior head trauma warrants CT imaging of the head, as age itself is an independent risk factor for significant intracranial injury.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In an older adult, head trauma accompanied by loss of consciousness, vomiting, anterograde amnesia, or a previous history of head trauma requires CT of the head. Being older than 65 years is considered an independent risk factor for serious head trauma outcomes. Even patients with minor mechanisms of injury and a normal neurologic examination may harbor subdural or epidural bleeding due to age-related physiological changes.

bullets.text: Age-related vascular fragility and white matter vulnerability make older adults disproportionately susceptible to intracranial hemorrhage and shear injury, resulting in higher morbidity and mortality from traumatic brain injury compared to younger patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Older adults with traumatic brain injury experience higher morbidity and mortality due to age-related changes in vasculature that leave vessels more vulnerable to rupture, and changes in white matter that render white matter tracts more susceptible to shear injury. As a result of these physiological changes, older patients are more susceptible to significant injury even from seemingly minor trauma.

bullets.text: NSAIDs should be avoided following traumatic brain injury due to their bleeding risk; alternative analgesics that do not impair hemostasis should be used for pain management.
bullets.sub_paragraph: NSAIDs carry a risk of bleeding through platelet inhibition and should be avoided following a traumatic brain injury. Clinicians should select analgesic agents that do not further compromise hemostasis in the setting of potential intracranial or extracranial bleeding.

explanation_raw: In an older adult, head trauma with a loss of consciousness, vomiting, anterograde amnesia, or a previous history of head trauma requires CT of the head. Being older than 65 years is considered an independent risk factor for head trauma. Older adults with a traumatic brain injury experience higher morbidity and mortality due to age-related changes in vasculature that leave vessels more vulnerable to rupture and changes in white matter that render white matter tracts more susceptible to shear injury. As a result of these physiological changes, older patients are more susceptible to injury, and even those with minor mechanisms of injury and no abnormalities on a neurologic examination may still have subdural or epidural bleeding. NSAIDs carry a risk of bleeding and should be avoided following a traumatic brain injury.

stem: A 3-day-old infant presents to your clinic for a routine check-up. The parents report that the infant has been feeding well but has had fewer wet diapers than expected. On examination, the infant appears slightly lethargic with dry skin. You need to assess the hydration status of the infant. Which one of the following would be the most reliable clinical sign for assessing dehydration in this 3-day-old infant?

bullets.text: Capillary refill time (>2 seconds) is the most reliable clinical sign for assessing dehydration in infants, with a high likelihood ratio for predicting dehydration in children.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Capillary refill time is the most reliable clinical sign for assessing dehydration in infants. An abnormal capillary refill time (>2 seconds) is a strong indicator of dehydration and has been shown to have a high likelihood ratio for predicting dehydration in children.

bullets.text: Decreased urine output, dry mucous membranes, abnormal skin turgor, and sunken fontanelle are all less reliable indicators of dehydration in neonates compared to capillary refill time.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Decreased urine output is sensitive but not specific, as it can be influenced by feeding patterns and ambient temperature. Dry mucous membranes are subjective and less reliable. Abnormal skin turgor is more commonly used in older children and is less reliable in neonates due to their higher skin elasticity. A sunken fontanelle can indicate dehydration but is less specific and can be affected by the patient's position during examination.

explanation_raw: Capillary refill time is the most reliable clinical sign for assessing dehydration in infants. An abnormal capillary refill time (>2 seconds) is a strong indicator of dehydration and has been shown to have a high likelihood ratio for predicting dehydration in children. While decreased urine output is a sensitive indicator of dehydration, it is not specific and can be influenced by other factors such as feeding patterns and ambient temperature. Dry mucous membranes are a useful sign but can be subjective and less reliable compared to capillary refill time. Abnormal skin turgor is more commonly used in older children and is less reliable in neonates due to their higher skin elasticity. A sunken fontanelle can indicate dehydration, but it is less specific and can be influenced by other factors, such as the patient's position during the examination.

stem: A 16-year-old female presents with her parents because she has been experiencing a loss of interest in her usual activities, trouble sleeping, difficulty concentrating, and low energy over the last month. After a discussion with the patient and her parents, you refer her for cognitive behavioral therapy and start an antidepressant. Which one of the following medications is approved by the FDA to treat depression in patients such as this?

bullets.text: Only fluoxetine and escitalopram are FDA-approved SSRIs for treating depression in adolescents.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Two SSRIs — fluoxetine and escitalopram — have received FDA approval for the treatment of depression in adolescents. Other antidepressants such as sertraline (SSRI), bupropion (NDRI), and venlafaxine (SNRI) are frequently used off-label in this population but lack FDA approval for this indication. Esketamine (a ketamine-derived nasal spray) is reserved for treatment-resistant depression in adults and is not appropriate for adolescent use.

explanation_raw: Two SSRIs, fluoxetine and escitalopram, have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of depression in adolescents. Other SSRIs such as sertraline, NDRIs such as bupropion, and SNRIs such as venlafaxine are often used off-label for this purpose but have not been approved by the FDA for use in adolescents. Esketamine is a ketamine nasal spray used in conjunction with an oral antidepressant for treatment-resistant depression in adults.

stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with a 14-day history of a productive cough and green sputum. They report they initially had a fever but that it resolved after a few days. The cough is interfering with their sleep and daily activity, and they have tried cough drops without relief. They have a history of hypothyroidism for which they take levothyroxine (Synthroid), and do not have a history of asthma. They do not smoke, and their immunizations are up to date. On examination, the patient is afebrile and has an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, a heart rate of 82 beats/min, and a blood pressure of 120/82 mm Hg. A lung examination reveals mild rhonchi that clear with cough, and you do not note any wheezing or egophony. Which one of the following treatments would be the most effective in reducing this patient's cough?

bullets.text: Acute bronchitis is a self-limited, usually viral lower respiratory tract infection lasting 2–3 weeks; patients may have purulent sputum, rhonchi, and wheezing but are typically afebrile with normal oxygen saturation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute bronchitis is most commonly caused by a virus and is a self-limited illness lasting 2–3 weeks. Despite the presence of purulent sputum and occasionally rhonchi or wheezing, patients are typically afebrile with normal oxygen saturation, which helps distinguish it from pneumonia.

bullets.text: Supportive care with dextromethorphan, guaifenesin, or honey is recommended for cough suppression (SOR B); antibiotics offer negligible net benefit and are not routinely indicated (SOR A).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment of acute bronchitis is generally supportive. Dextromethorphan (Delsym), guaifenesin, and honey have evidence supporting reduction in cough frequency (SOR B). While 90% of cases are viral, antibiotics are frequently overprescribed; they reduce cough duration by only 0.46 days and their minimal benefit is outweighed by potential side effects (SOR A). β2-agonists such as albuterol are not recommended unless wheezing is present (SOR B), and codeine has no demonstrated benefit and carries significant side effect risks.

explanation_raw: Acute bronchitis is a lower respiratory tract infection that is most commonly caused by a virus. Treatment is generally supportive as it is a self-limited illness. Guaifenesin, honey, and dextromethorphan have been shown to decrease the frequency of cough (SOR B). In otherwise healthy patients without evidence of pneumonia, acute bronchitis can last 2–3 weeks. Patients may exhibit purulent sputum, rhonchi, and wheezing with acute bronchitis but are typically afebrile with normal oxygen saturation. β2-Agonists such as albuterol are not recommended for the treatment of acute bronchitis unless wheezing is present (SOR B). While 90% of acute bronchitis cases are caused by viruses, a significant percentage are treated inappropriately with antibiotics. Antibiotics can decrease the duration of cough by 0.46 days, but the overall net benefit of antibiotics is negligible and often outweighed by potential side effects (SOR A). Studies show codeine has no benefit in the treatment of acute bronchitis and has rather significant side effects.

stem: A 20-year-old male presents to the urgent care center for left ankle pain and swelling following an ankle inversion injury that occurred a few hours earlier. A physical examination reveals mild swelling of the left ankle joint. Using the Ottawa foot and ankle rules, which one of the following findings, if present, would be an indication for radiography for an acute ankle inversion injury?

choices.A: Bone tenderness at the anterior edge of the lateral malleolus
choices.B: Bone tenderness at the anterior edge of the medial malleolus
choices.C: Bone tenderness at the base of the fourth metatarsal
choices.D: Bone tenderness of the navicular bone
choices.E: Inability to bear weight on the left foot for at least 10 steps after the injury

correct_label: Bone tenderness of the navicular bone

bullets.text: The Ottawa foot and ankle rules specify indications for x-ray after acute ankle inversion injury, including bone tenderness at the navicular bone.
bullets.sub_paragraph: According to the Ottawa foot and ankle rules, a foot x-ray should be obtained if any of the following are present: bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or navicular bone, or inability to bear weight on the affected leg or foot for at least 4 steps after the injury. Bone tenderness of the navicular bone (answer D) is therefore a specific indication for obtaining a foot x-ray, making it the correct answer among the choices provided.

explanation_raw: When a foot or ankle fracture is suspected, a weight-bearing foot and ankle x-ray should be obtained. The Ottawa foot and ankle rules are a useful tool for determining the need for an x-ray for an acute ankle inversion injury. According to the Ottawa foot and ankle rules, a foot x-ray should be obtained if any of the following requirements are met: bone tenderness at the posterior edge or the tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or navicular bone, or inability to bear weight on the affected leg or foot for at least 4 steps after the injury.

stem: A generally healthy 13-year-old male presents with his parents because they are concerned that he has very large-volume stools that clog the toilet. The patient says that he averages fewer than 2 bowel movements per week and they are sometimes painful. He does not have any abdominal pain and has not seen any blood in his stools. Examination findings are unremarkable. His height, weight, and BMI percentiles have remained steady for years. A CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin level, and TSH level are all normal. An abdominal x-ray is normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

bullets.text: This patient meets Rome IV criteria for functional constipation: ≤2 bowel movements per week, painful/hard stools, and large stools that clog the toilet.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The Rome IV criteria for functional constipation require at least 2 of the following occurring at least once per week for a minimum of 1 month: ≤2 defecations per week, at least one episode of fecal incontinence per week, history of retentive posturing or excessive volitional stool retention, history of painful or hard bowel movements, presence of a large fecal mass in the rectum, and history of large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet. This patient satisfies at least 3 of these criteria.

bullets.text: Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX) is the first-line treatment for functional constipation in children and adolescents, with strong evidence supporting its efficacy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is an osmotic laxative with robust evidence for effectiveness in pediatric functional constipation. It is well-tolerated, tasteless, and can be mixed into beverages, making it practical for daily use. Probiotics lack evidence of benefit for functional constipation. In the absence of red flag symptoms (rectal bleeding, weight loss, fever, family history of IBD or colorectal cancer), advanced imaging such as MR enterography or colonoscopy is not indicated.

bullets.text: Probiotics lack evidence for functional constipation, and there are no red flag symptoms to justify colonoscopy or MR enterography in this patient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Probiotics have not been shown in clinical trials to be effective for functional constipation in children. Magnetic resonance enterography is used to evaluate for inflammatory bowel disease when red flag features are present (e.g., rectal bleeding, weight loss, elevated inflammatory markers), none of which are described here. Colonoscopy would be appropriate if a structural lesion or mucosal disease were suspected, but this patient's presentation is entirely consistent with functional constipation without any alarming features.

explanation_raw: This patient meets 3 of the Rome IV diagnostic criteria for functional constipation (≤2 bowel movements per week, painful hard stools, and stools that clog the toilet). There is good evidence that polyethylene glycol is effective for treating functional constipation in children and adolescents. There is no evidence that probiotics are effective. This patient does not have any red flag symptoms that would prompt a need for either magnetic resonance enterography to evaluate for inflammatory bowel disease or a colonoscopy to evaluate for a structural lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old male sees you for routine follow-up of diabetes mellitus. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day and does not have any other medical conditions. His diabetes is well controlled on liraglutide (Victoza) and metformin. He has an LDL-cholesterol level of 120 mg/dL, an HDL-cholesterol level of 55 mg/dL, and a triglyceride level of 300 mg/dL. His 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk is 8.2%. According to 2018 guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association, the most appropriate recommendation for this patient would be

bullets.text: Diabetic patients aged 40–75 with LDL ≥70 mg/dL and elevated cardiovascular risk factors (e.g., smoking) should receive high-intensity statin therapy, making atorvastatin 40–80 mg daily the correct choice.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients 40–75 years of age with diabetes mellitus and an LDL-cholesterol level ≥70 mg/dL should receive at least moderate-intensity statin therapy without needing to calculate a 10-year ASCVD risk score. However, high-intensity statin therapy (targeting ≥50% LDL reduction) is preferred for those at elevated risk, particularly patients aged 50–75 or those with multiple cardiovascular risk factors such as smoking. Atorvastatin 40–80 mg daily is the only high-intensity statin option among the choices listed.

bullets.text: Pravastatin 20 mg is low-intensity, simvastatin 20–40 mg is moderate-intensity, and ezetimibe or fenofibrate are not recommended first-line agents for cardiovascular risk reduction in diabetes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Pravastatin 20 mg daily is classified as low-intensity statin therapy and is insufficient for this high-risk patient. Simvastatin 20–40 mg daily is moderate-intensity and is not recommended at doses above 40 mg due to increased myopathy risk. Ezetimibe and fenofibrate are not first-line recommended therapies for hyperlipidemia management or primary cardiovascular disease prevention in diabetic patients per current guidelines.

explanation_raw: Patients 40–75 years of age with diabetes mellitus and an LDL-cholesterol level ≥70 mg/dL should be treated with a moderate-intensity statin without calculating a 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. However, high-intensity statin therapy should be considered to lower the LDL-cholesterol level by at least 50% for patients such as this one who are at elevated risk, especially those 50–75 years of age or with multiple risk factors. Of the options listed, atorvastatin, 40–80 mg daily, is the only therapy that is considered high-intensity statin therapy. Pravastatin, 20 mg daily, is low-intensity statin therapy. Simvastatin, 20–40 mg daily, is considered moderate-intensity therapy and is not recommended at doses >40 mg daily. Ezetimibe and fenofibrate are not recommended first-line medications for the treatment of hyperlipidemia and the prevention of cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 37-year-old male comes to the primary care clinic with a several-month history of worsening paresthesia in his right foot. He says that he sometimes has numbness and a hot sensation in his feet and has difficulty using the pedals of his car. Sometimes, he has pain that wakes him up at night but eases when he walks around the room. He has no significant past medical history but did sustain a severe right ankle sprain about 1 year ago. His vital signs are unremarkable. Examination of the ankle reveals pain along the medial malleolus and a positive Tinel sign at the ankle. An x-ray of the ankle is unremarkable. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy caused by compression of the tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum, presenting with paresthesias, medial ankle pain, and plantar sensory loss; the most helpful clinical sign is a positive Tinel sign at the ankle.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy of the foot caused by compression of the tibial nerve or one of its branches in the fibro-osseous tunnel under the flexor retinaculum and within the abductor hallucis muscle. It may occur following ankle fracture or sprain. Patients present with paresthesias, local pain behind the medial malleolus, and loss of sensation in the sole; paresis of small foot muscles can impair abduction. There is no criterion standard for diagnosis, but a positive Tinel sign at the ankle is the most helpful clinical finding. Electrophysiologic studies aid diagnosis, and MRI is useful when a mass lesion is suspected. Conservative management is tried initially, with surgery reserved for advanced cases.

bullets.text: Achilles tendinopathy, Haglund deformity, heel pad syndrome, and plantar fasciitis each have distinct clinical features that differentiate them from tarsal tunnel syndrome.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Achilles tendinopathy causes posterior heel pain localized at the tendon insertion, worsening with activity or pressure. Haglund deformity presents with pain at the upper posterior calcaneus, more common in middle-aged women wearing ill-fitting shoes, with a characteristic finding on X-ray at the superior posterior calcaneus. Heel pad syndrome causes deep, bruise-like pain in the middle of the heel reproducible on palpation, typically from prolonged barefoot walking. Plantar fasciitis causes tenderness along the medial calcaneal tuberosity and plantar fascia, classically worse with the first steps in the morning — none of these match the nocturnal paresthesias and diffuse sensory symptoms seen in this patient.

explanation_raw: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy of the foot caused by compression of the tibial nerve or one of its branches in the fibro-osseous tunnel under the flexor retinaculum and within the abductor hallucis muscle of the foot. It may occur following an injury, such as a fracture or sprain of the ankle. Patients can present with paresthesias, local pain behind the medial malleolus, and loss of sensation in the sole. Paresis of the small muscle of the foot can lead to impaired abduction. There is no criterion standard for the diagnosis of tarsal tunnel syndrome. The most helpful clinical diagnostic sign is a positive Tinel sign at the ankle, and electrophysiologic studies can help in making the diagnosis. MRI can be useful in cases of compression due to a mass lesion. Patients can begin a trial of conservative management, but advanced cases are better treated surgically. Achilles tendinopathy causes posterior heel pain that is localized at the site of insertion of the Achilles tendon and worsens with increased activity or pressure on the area. Haglund deformity presents with pain in the upper part of the posterior calcaneus and is more common in middle-aged women who repeatedly wear ill-fitting shoes. X-rays demonstrate the deformity on the superior aspect of the posterior calcaneus. Patients with heel pad syndrome report a deep-seated pain that feels like a bruise in the middle of the heel. The pain can be reproduced by palpating the area. It is typically an inflammatory response to damage of the heel pad secondary to walking barefoot for prolonged periods of time. Plantar fasciitis causes tenderness along the medial calcaneal tuberosity and along the plantar fascia. Patients typically report pain with their first steps after getting out of bed in the morning.

stem: A 36-year-old female comes to your office for a health maintenance examination. She mentions that she engages in amateur rifle target shooting matches. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate advice concerning this patient’s physical safety?

choices.A: She should wear electronic hearing protection that amplifies quiet sounds
choices.D: She should wear her regular glasses so that she has eye protection

correct_label: She should wear electronic hearing protection that amplifies quiet sounds

bullets.text: Electronic hearing protection is the best choice for shooters because it amplifies quiet sounds (e.g., range officer instructions) while automatically dampening dangerously loud gunshot noise exceeding 140 dB.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Firearm noise routinely exceeds 140 dB, and even a single gunshot can cause permanent sensorineural hearing loss. Standard earmuffs or earplugs with a noise reduction rating of 28–31 dB are protective but do not allow normal communication. Electronic hearing protection solves this by amplifying ambient sounds at safe levels while compressing loud impulse noise, making it the preferred option at shooting ranges—many of which mandate its use. Noise-canceling headphones, by contrast, do not provide adequate impulse-noise attenuation for firearms.

bullets.text: Loose-fitting clothing risks trapping ejected hot brass casings, leading to unsafe gun handling; regular glasses lack the impact resistance needed to protect against bullet fragmentation or firearm malfunctions.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Loose clothing around the neckline or collar can catch ejected brass casings, causing burns and reflexive unsafe gun movement. Certified ballistic or shooting safety eyewear (meeting ANSI Z87.1 or equivalent standards) is required to protect against shrapnel from bullet strikes on targets or from firearm malfunctions; ordinary prescription glasses do not meet this standard and should not be substituted.

explanation_raw: Hearing protection is essential while shooting firearms because noise exposure often exceeds 140 dB. Even a single gunshot can cause permanent hearing loss. Earmuffs and earplugs with a noise reduction rate of 28–31 dB are common and inexpensive protective devices. Electronic hearing protection can amplify quiet sounds such as a range safety officer's instructions, but also safely protect against loud sounds. Many ranges require their use. Noise-canceling headphones do not provide enough noise reduction for gunshots. Wearing loose-fitting clothing can trap the ejected hot brass casings, leading to unsafe gun handling. Safety eyeglasses that meet the necessary certifications can protect against shrapnel from the bullet striking the target or a malfunction. Regular glasses do not provide sufficient eye protection.

stem: A 66-year-old male presents to your office with a 2-hour history of discomfort in the midsternal area that began while taking a walk earlier today. He says that he feels 90% better. He had a Welcome to Medicare visit 1 year ago, in which an EKG was normal. You order an EKG today. Which one of the following EKG findings, if present in this patient, should prompt urgent transport to the emergency department?

choices.E: Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy

bullets.text: New-onset left bundle branch block on EKG is a high-risk finding that increases the likelihood of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and warrants immediate transfer to the emergency department.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Approximately 1% of primary care office visits involve chest pain evaluation, and 2–4% of those patients have unstable angina or myocardial infarction. A 12-lead EKG is recommended to look for ST-segment changes, new-onset left bundle branch block, Q waves, and new T-wave inversions. New-onset LBBB is particularly significant because it increases the likelihood of ACS and acute MI, mandating immediate emergency department transfer.

bullets.text: First-degree AV block, frequent PVCs, sinus tachycardia, and voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy do not increase the likelihood of ACS and are not indications for emergent transfer.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While these EKG findings may be clinically relevant in other contexts, none of them independently raise suspicion for acute coronary syndrome in the way that new-onset LBBB does. In a patient presenting with chest discomfort, only findings such as ST-segment changes, new LBBB, pathologic Q waves, or new T-wave inversions should prompt emergent evaluation and transport to the ED.

explanation_raw: Approximately 1% of primary care office visits are for evaluation of chest pain, in which 2%–4% of these patients have unstable angina or myocardial infarction. Twelve-lead EKG is recommended to look for ST-segment changes, new-onset left bundle branch block, presence of Q waves, and new T-wave inversions. The presence of new-onset left bundle branch block increases the likelihood of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and acute myocardial infarction. Patients with suspected ACS or the aforementioned changes on EKG should be transported immediately to the emergency department. The presence of first-degree atrioventricular block, frequent PVCs, sinus tachycardia, or voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy does not increase the likelihood of ACS.

stem: A generally healthy 56-year-old female sees you for follow-up of pneumonia diagnosed in the emergency department (ED). A chest x-ray performed in the ED showed a left lower lobe infiltrate and several compression fractures involving the thoracic vertebrae. A DXA scan performed 7 months ago showed a T-score of –1.9. Her daily medications include a multivitamin; calcium, 1000 mg; and vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), 800 IU. Today she feels well and has no concerns. This patient would be most likely to benefit from therapy for which one of the following conditions?

bullets.text: Postmenopausal osteoporosis can be diagnosed by the presence of a fragility fracture even when the T-score is better than –2.5 (osteopenia range).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Although this patient's T-score indicates osteopenia (between –1.0 and –2.49), the presence of compression fractures of the thoracic vertebrae qualifies as fragility fractures — fractures occurring with no associated trauma or after a fall from standing height or lower. Postmenopausal osteoporosis may therefore be diagnosed by bone mineral density (T-score ≤ –2.5) OR by the presence of a fragility fracture, making osteoporosis the correct diagnosis here despite a T-score above –2.5.

bullets.text: Osteopenia alone does not account for the fragility fractures, and spondylolisthesis/spondylolysis describe distinct vertebral conditions unrelated to this presentation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Osteopenia (T-score between –1.0 and –2.49) would be incorrect because the compression fractures upgrade the diagnosis to osteoporosis. Spondylolisthesis is the acquired anterior displacement of one vertebral body over another, typically associated with degenerative changes, and is not suggested here. Spondylolysis refers to a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis of the lumbar vertebra, most commonly seen in young athletes, which does not apply to this clinical scenario.

explanation_raw: Although this patient's T-score indicates osteopenia, the presence of fragility fractures indicates osteoporosis. The T-score is obtained by measuring bone mineral density using DXA at the spine, total hip, or femoral neck. A T-score between –1.0 and –2.49 indicates osteopenia, whereas a T-score of ≤–2.5 denotes osteoporosis. However, postmenopausal osteoporosis may be diagnosed by bone mineral density or by the presence of a fragility fracture, which is a fracture that occurs with no associated trauma or after a fall from standing height or lower. Hence, osteoporosis can be diagnosed and the patient further evaluated and treated even though her T-score is >–2.5. Spondylolisthesis is the acquired anterior displacement of one vertebral body over another and is typically associated with degenerative changes. Spondylolysis is a cause of acute back pain resulting from a stress fracture involving the pars interarticularis of the lumbar vertebral body. It is typically found in young athletes.

stem: A gravida 2 para 1 at 28 weeks' gestation presents with an episode of second-trimester bleeding that spontaneously resolved. She has not had any prenatal laboratory studies during either of her pregnancies. Ultrasonography today shows a healthy fetus and a small placental abruption. Which one of the following would be most important to order at this time?

choices.E: A urine toxicology screen for cocaine

bullets.text: Rh factor testing is the most time-sensitive test when evaluating second-trimester bleeding, as Rh-negative patients require Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) to prevent isoimmunization from fetal-maternal blood mixing.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In any pregnant patient presenting with second-trimester bleeding, Rh factor status must be determined promptly. If the patient is Rh negative, Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) must be administered to prevent maternal sensitization from fetal red blood cell exposure. This is especially critical here because the patient had no prior prenatal labs (possibly an unattended home birth), meaning her Rh status is unknown and prior sensitization from her first delivery is possible. The placental abruption further increases the risk of fetomaternal hemorrhage, making this the most urgent and clinically impactful test.

bullets.text: Antiphospholipid antibody profile, HIV testing, toxoplasmosis antibody, and urine toxicology for cocaine are each appropriate in specific clinical contexts but are not the most urgent test in this acute bleeding scenario.
bullets.sub_paragraph: An antiphospholipid antibody profile is indicated for recurrent pregnancy loss (>2 losses <10 weeks, or any loss >10 weeks), certain preterm deliveries, or thrombosis—not acute second-trimester bleeding alone. HIV testing is an important prenatal screening test but does not affect immediate management of this bleeding episode. Toxoplasmosis antibody testing is only relevant with signs or exposure history suggesting infection. While cocaine use is a risk factor for placental abruption, a urine toxicology screen would not change the immediate management priority of determining Rh status.

explanation_raw: Blood type/Rh factor testing should be ordered when evaluating second-trimester bleeding. This patient would require a dose of Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) if found to be Rh negative. Therefore, of all the tests listed, an Rh factor test is the most time sensitive and affects the plan of care. Patients may have had unattended home births with prior pregnancies or refused laboratory tests altogether. With the potential exposure to mixing of maternal and fetal blood during the patient's first delivery, it is crucial during this pregnancy to ensure maternal and fetal blood are compatible because there is a high risk of contact between maternal and fetal blood. An antiphospholipid antibody profile would be appropriate for evaluation of an underlying hypercoagulable disorder, such as in cases of late pregnancy loss (>10 weeks), recurrent early pregnancy loss (<10 weeks), certain preterm deliveries, or thrombosis. Although HIV testing is an important component of prenatal laboratory studies, it would not be the most important test to order at this time. A toxoplasmosis antibody test may be considered if there are signs of infection or exposure to toxoplasmosis. While cocaine use can cause placental abruption, a urine toxicology screen for cocaine is not the most pressing laboratory study to order at this time.

stem: A generally healthy 50-year-old nurse presents to your clinic 1 day after sustaining an accidental needlestick containing the blood of a person with active hepatitis B virus infection who has not yet begun treatment. Your patient completed the hepatitis B (Hep

choices.D: Both HBIG and recombinant HepB vaccine

bullets.text: Patients who have completed the hepatitis B vaccine series and demonstrate proven immunity (hepatitis B surface antibody titer >10 mIU/mL) do not require additional vaccination or hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) after a needlestick exposure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Post-exposure prophylaxis with HBIG or hepatitis B vaccine is not recommended when a patient has documented immunity to hepatitis B virus. A hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) titer >10 mIU/mL confirms protective immunity, whether from prior vaccination or prior infection (in which case both anti-HBs and hepatitis B core antibody would be reactive). HBIG would only be indicated in a patient with negative hepatitis B serology or a known non-responder to the vaccine series.

explanation_raw: Postexposure prophylaxis with hepatitis B immune globulin or hepatitis B vaccine is not recommended in those who have completed the hepatitis B vaccine series and have proven immunity to hepatitis B virus. The presence of hepatitis B surface antibody titers of >10 mIU/mL are indicative of immunity either from previous vaccination or from previous infection with hepatitis B (both hepatitis B core and surface antibodies are reactive). Hepatitis B immune globulin would be recommended in a patient with negative hepatitis B serology testing.

stem: A 20-year-old female presents for a routine health maintenance examination and has no medical concerns today. She does not have a history of sexual activity, and screenings for alcohol and substance use, intimate partner violence, anxiety, depression, and suicidality are negative. An examination reveals fair skin, an elevated BMI of 31 kg/m2, and normal blood pressure. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, you should recommend screening for which one of the following?

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends HIV screening for all persons aged 15–65 years regardless of risk factors (Grade A recommendation).
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient is a healthy 20-year-old female with no identified risk factors beyond an elevated BMI. Despite the absence of sexual activity or other risk factors, the USPSTF gives a Grade A recommendation for HIV screening for all individuals aged 15–65, making it the appropriate screening to offer at this visit.

bullets.text: Cervical cancer screening is not recommended before age 21, chlamydia screening requires sexual activity, and diabetes screening applies to those aged 35–70 with overweight/obesity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cervical cancer screening carries a Grade D recommendation before age 21, so it is not indicated. Chlamydia screening is recommended only for sexually active females under 25 (Grade B), and this patient has no history of sexual activity. Diabetes mellitus screening is recommended for persons aged 35–70 who are overweight or obese (Grade B), so this patient's age precludes it, though she should receive intensive behavioral counseling for weight loss. Skin cancer preventive counseling (not screening exams) applies to fair-skinned individuals aged 6 months to 24 years (Grade B for counseling; Grade I for screening examinations). Hepatitis C screening should also be offered to this patient.

explanation_raw: This patient is a healthy young adult female who presents with an elevated BMI but no other identified risk factors. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends HIV screening for all persons 15–65 years of age (A recommendation). Cervical cancer screening is not recommended in women before age 21 (D recommendation), thus precluding the patient from screening. Chlamydia screening is recommended for all sexually active females under 25 years of age (B recommendation), but this patient has no history of sexual activity. Diabetes mellitus screening is recommended for persons 35–70 years of age with overweight or obesity (B recommendation). While the patient's age precludes her from this screening, she should be offered intensive multicomponent behavioral intervention for weight loss. Preventive counseling for skin cancer is recommended for persons with fair skin types who are 6 months to 24 years of age (B recommendation), but screening examinations are not recommended (I recommendation). This patient should also be offered screening for hepatitis C.

stem: A 65-year-old male presents to your clinic with symptoms of flashing lights and increased floaters in his left eye. He does not have any pain, and he has no past medical history. His vital signs are normal. His visual acuity is at baseline when wearing his glasses, and you note a visual field defect on the left. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Peripheral flashing lights, new floaters, and a visual field defect in the absence of pain are classic signs of retinal detachment, requiring urgent ophthalmologic referral for dilated fundoscopic examination.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Retinal detachment presents with peripheral flashing lights (photopsia) and floaters due to vitreous traction on the retina, followed by a visual field defect as the retina separates. It is painless and constitutes an ophthalmologic emergency. Family physicians must recognize this presentation and refer urgently, as delayed treatment can result in permanent vision loss.

bullets.text: Migraine with aura causes transient visual phenomena followed by headache; central retinal artery occlusion causes rapid painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot and afferent pupillary defect; globe rupture requires trauma; and ischemic stroke does not typically cause floaters or photopsia.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Migraine with aura can cause visual disturbances but these are transient and followed by a typical migraine headache — new-onset migraine at age 65 is also uncommon and warrants further workup. Central retinal artery occlusion is ischemic or thromboembolic, occurs in patients with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, tobacco use), and presents with sudden painless vision loss, an afferent pupillary defect, and a cherry-red spot on fundoscopy. Globe rupture requires a history of significant ocular trauma. Acute ischemic stroke may impair vision but does not characteristically produce floaters or flashing lights.

explanation_raw: Family physicians frequently evaluate ophthalmologic symptoms and should be familiar with conditions requiring emergent evaluation. Peripheral flashing lights and floaters are common symptoms of retinal detachment. This patient should be referred for urgent ophthalmologic evaluation including a dilated fundoscopic examination. While positive and negative visual features are seen with migraine with aura, these features should be transient and followed by a headache typical of migraine. New-onset migraine in a 65-year-old is also uncommon and would require further evaluation. Central retinal artery occlusion, often ischemic or thromboembolic, typically occurs in those with risk factors such as diabetes mellitus, vascular disease, and tobacco use. Rapid, painless vision loss is often accompanied by afferent pupillary defect and the lesion can be visualized on a dilated fundoscopic examination as a cherry-red spot. Globe rupture is unlikely to occur without a history of trauma. Acute ischemic stroke may cause vision loss but is unlikely to cause ocular symptoms of flashing lights and floaters.

stem: A 46-year-old male presents for an acute visit due to a 2-week history of low back pain. He was moving furniture when the pain started, and he felt a pop in his right lower back area. The pain is severe enough that it keeps him from standing up straight and is causing him trouble with sleeping. He does not have fever or chills, numbness, paresthesia, or weakness in his lower extremities. He has no radicular pain on a straight leg–raising test. He went to a chiropractor who did x-rays and told him he needed to get an MRI. Which one of the following, if present, would be an indication for advanced imaging?

choices.C: Disrupted sleep due to nocturnal pain

bullets.text: Early advanced imaging for low back pain is associated with increased surgery rates, higher opioid use, higher costs, worse pain scores, and more work absenteeism — it should be reserved for true red flags.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Early advanced imaging for low back pain increases the probability of surgery and is associated with a higher use of opioids, a higher cost of care, higher pain scores, and more work absenteeism. Therefore, imaging should only be pursued when genuine red flag findings are present.

bullets.text: New urinary retention is a red flag for cauda equina syndrome and warrants immediate advanced imaging; other cauda equina features include bladder fullness and saddle anesthesia.
bullets.sub_paragraph: New urinary retention is concerning for cauda equina syndrome, which requires urgent evaluation. Other associated symptoms include bladder fullness and saddle anesthesia. While cigarette use raises the risk of underlying malignancy and IV drug use raises the risk of epidural abscess, neither alone — without additional signs of infection, known cancer history, or other supporting features — constitutes a sole indication for advanced imaging. Nocturnal pain is not uncommon in benign low back pain and is only more specifically concerning if it occurs in the early morning hours. Severity of pain alone does not correlate clearly with pathologic back pain.

explanation_raw: Early advanced imaging for low back pain increases the probability of surgery and is associated with a higher use of opioids, a higher cost of care, higher pain scores, and more work absenteeism. While there is no consensus on what constitutes red flags for low back pain, new urinary retention is concerning for cauda equina syndrome. Other symptoms associated with cauda equina syndrome are bladder fullness and saddle anesthesia. The severity of pain does not correlate clearly with pathologic back pain. While cigarette use increases the chance of an underlying cancer, without a known history of cancer or other signs, it is not an indication for advanced imaging. While intravenous drug use increases the risk of epidural abscess, with no other signs of infection or history of infection, it is not solitarily an indication for advanced imaging. Nocturnal pain is not uncommon in benign low back pain and may be associated with a more specific underlying cause if the pain occurs in the second part of the night (early morning).

stem: How long after intranasal administration does naloxone (Narcan) reach peak plasma concentrations?

bullets.text: After intranasal administration, naloxone reaches peak plasma concentrations within 15–30 minutes, though clinical effects (reversal of opioid toxicity) may be observed sooner.
bullets.sub_paragraph: After intranasal administration, naloxone reaches peak plasma concentrations within 15–30 minutes, though clinical effects may be seen sooner. Absorption can be affected by conditions altering nasal mucosal function or blood flow. The half-life of naloxone is approximately 2 hours, which is shorter than many long-acting opioids, making ongoing monitoring essential even after successful reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression.

explanation_raw: After intranasal administration of naloxone, peak plasma concentrations are attained within 15–30 minutes, although its effect on the patient may be seen sooner. Absorption may be affected by substances or conditions that impact the nasal mucosa function or its blood flow. The half-life of naloxone is 2 hours, which is shorter than many long-acting opioids. Ongoing monitoring is important even after reversal of opioid respiratory depression is achieved.

stem: A 24-year-old male presents for evaluation of a bulge in his groin. He reports that it is larger at the end of the day and with straining but says it often goes away when he lies down. He reports a mild dull ache that limits his ability to lift lumber at work. On examination there is no obvious bulge in the inguinal area. When the patient bears down, a bulge becomes apparent. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

bullets.text: Inguinal hernia can be diagnosed clinically when apparent on examination; no further imaging is needed.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with classic features of an inguinal hernia: a groin bulge that enlarges with straining and at end of day, reduces when supine, and is confirmed on physical examination. When the hernia is apparent on exam, imaging is unnecessary. Recent studies have found that nearly 50% of patients sent for inguinal imaging have been unnecessarily referred, highlighting the importance of clinical diagnosis.

bullets.text: Symptomatic inguinal hernias that limit function warrant surgical referral; watchful waiting is reserved for truly asymptomatic hernias.
bullets.sub_paragraph: When an inguinal hernia is symptomatic or limits the patient's functional capacity—as in this case where the patient cannot lift lumber at work—surgical referral is the appropriate next step. Watchful waiting is a viable option only for asymptomatic hernias. Physical therapy has no role in the management of a symptomatic inguinal hernia and would not address the underlying anatomical defect.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with an inguinal hernia that is apparent on examination. When the hernia is apparent, no further imaging is needed. Recent studies have found that nearly 50% of patients sent for inguinal imaging have been unnecessarily referred. When the hernia is symptomatic or limits function, surgical referral is appropriate. If the hernia is asymptomatic, then watchful waiting would be a viable option. Physical therapy would not be appropriate for this patient with a symptomatic inguinal hernia.

stem: A 72-year-old male presents to your office with his daughter who is concerned about her father's recent decline in memory. His history is notable for hypertension, urinary urgency with occasional incontinence, and GERD. On examination, you notice a slow, wide-based gait. A Mini-Mental State Examination (MMS

bullets.text: This patient presents with the classic triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH): gait disturbance (wide-based, shuffling), urinary incontinence, and dementia. MRI will demonstrate hydrocephalus, and gait often improves with high-volume CSF removal (large-volume lumbar puncture).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is characterized by the classic triad of gait apraxia (wide-based, magnetic gait), urinary urgency/incontinence, and cognitive decline. MRI of the brain will show ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cortical atrophy. A diagnostic and therapeutic clue is improvement in gait after large-volume lumbar puncture (removing 30–50 mL of CSF), which supports the diagnosis and predicts shunt responsiveness.

bullets.text: Definitive treatment of NPH is placement of a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt to continuously divert CSF and relieve elevated ventricular pressure, often leading to improvement in gait and urinary symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The definitive treatment for normal-pressure hydrocephalus is ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, which diverts excess CSF from the ventricles to the peritoneal cavity. This can lead to significant improvement—particularly in gait and urinary incontinence—and to a lesser extent in cognitive function. Early diagnosis and shunting before severe dementia sets in is associated with better outcomes.

bullets.text: Carbidopa/levodopa treats Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia; donepezil treats Alzheimer dementia; levothyroxine treats hypothyroid-related cognitive decline; and surgery with chemotherapy is used for brain neoplasms—none of these address NPH.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Other answer choices correspond to treatments for different causes of dementia or cognitive impairment: carbidopa/levodopa is used for Parkinson disease (which can present with Lewy body dementia and gait changes but lacks the full NPH triad); donepezil (a cholinesterase inhibitor) is a mainstay of Alzheimer disease management; levothyroxine corrects hypothyroidism, a reversible cause of cognitive decline; and surgical resection with chemotherapy addresses primary or metastatic brain tumors. None of these are appropriate for NPH, making ventriculoperitoneal shunt the correct answer.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with the classic triad symptoms associated with normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait change, urinary incontinence, and dementia. MRI will show evidence of hydrocephalus, and gait changes will often improve with high-volume removal of cerebrospinal fluid. Treatment involves placing a ventriculoperitoneal shunt to relieve hydrocephalus. Carbidopa/levodopa, donepezil, levothyroxine, and surgery with chemotherapy are all treatments for other causes of dementia including Parkinson disease with Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer dementia, hypothyroidism, and brain tumor or neoplasm, respectively.

stem: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with an acute onset of bloody urine confirmed to be hematuria on urinalysis. He does not have any pain, fever, or recent trauma. His medical history is significant for hypertension that is managed with lisinopril (Zestril). A physical examination is unremarkable. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.B: Initiating empiric antibiotic therapy and re-evaluating in 1 week
choices.D: Referring the patient for immediate cystoscopy and imaging studies

correct_label: Referring the patient for immediate cystoscopy and imaging studies

bullets.text: All adults with gross hematuria should be referred for urologic evaluation including cystoscopy and imaging due to high association with malignancy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The American College of Physicians recommends that all adults with gross hematuria undergo prompt urologic evaluation with cystoscopy and imaging studies. Cystoscopy has a sensitivity of 87–100% and specificity of 64–100% for detecting bladder cancer, and the positive predictive value of gross hematuria for urologic malignancy is particularly high in older men. Delaying evaluation with a repeat urinalysis in one month is inappropriate given the urgency of ruling out malignancy.

bullets.text: Empiric antibiotics, repeat urinalysis, and urine cytology alone are insufficient and inappropriate initial approaches for gross hematuria.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Initiating empiric antibiotic therapy without evidence of infection is not warranted and delays necessary workup. Repeating urinalysis in one month is inappropriate because gross hematuria requires immediate investigation. Urine cytology has limited sensitivity and specificity and should not replace cystoscopy and imaging as the initial evaluation strategy for gross hematuria.

explanation_raw: The American College of Physicians recommends that all adults with gross hematuria be referred for further urologic evaluation, including cystoscopy and imaging, due to the high association with malignancy. The sensitivity and specificity of cystoscopy for detecting bladder cancer are high, with a sensitivity ranging from 87% to 100% and a specificity of 64% to 100%. The positive predictive value of gross hematuria for urologic malignancy in older men is high. Gross hematuria warrants immediate investigation to rule out serious underlying conditions; thus a repeat urinalysis in 1 month would not be appropriate. Initiating empiric antibiotic therapy and re-evaluating in 1 week would not be appropriate without evidence of infection. Urine cytology has limited sensitivity and specificity and should not replace cystoscopy and imaging for the initial evaluation of hematuria.

stem: A 40-year-old male presents to establish care. He smokes 1½ packs of cigarettes per day and is uncertain about cutting back or quitting. While planning to enact a patient-centered strategy to help him overcome his reluctance, you recall that evidence supports the application of a counseling technique that uses open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summary statements to help foster a sense of patient autonomy and effect positive behavioral change. Which one of the following counseling strategies best fits this description?

choices.B: The five A’s (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange)

bullets.text: Motivational interviewing (MI) is an evidence-based counseling strategy particularly effective for patients who are ambivalent about behavior change, using open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries (OARS).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Motivational interviewing (MI) is the counseling strategy that best fits a patient-centered approach to ambivalence. In primary care settings, MI has been shown to help people achieve weight loss, improve blood pressure, and reduce alcohol use (SOR A). The key elements are captured by the acronym OARS: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, and Summaries. These components work together to elicit the patient's own values and motivation for change rather than imposing directive recommendations.

bullets.text: BATHE, the Five A's, and the transtheoretical model each serve different purposes and use more targeted or directive questioning, making them less suited for addressing pure ambivalence toward change.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The BATHE model (Background, Affect, Troubles, Handling, Empathy) addresses psychosocial problems with targeted lines of questioning, contrasting with MI's open-ended approach. The Five A's (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) provide a stepwise guide for health-behavior counseling but lead to more directive recommendations rather than reflective dialogue. The transtheoretical (stages of change) model is useful for identifying a patient's readiness to change—with stages of precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance—but focuses on stage identification rather than resolving ambivalence; it can, however, serve as a framework to select MI as a next step.

explanation_raw: Motivational interviewing (MI) is the counseling strategy that best fits the described approach. MI is an evidence-proven strategy that is particularly helpful in situations of ambivalence toward change. In primary care settings, MI has been shown to help people achieve weight loss, improve blood pressure, and reduce alcohol use (SOR A). The key elements of MI include establishing rapport, eliciting the patient's values, asking openended questions, offering affirmations, practicing reflective listening, and recapping discussions with summarizing statements. The acronym OARS (open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries) serves as a reminder of these 4 MI components. The BATHE (background, affect, troubles, handling, empathy) model provides a structure for addressing various psychosocial problems. BATHE uses more targeted lines of questioning, in contrast to the MI approach of asking open-ended questions that give way to affirming, reflective, and summarizing statements. The five A's (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange) approach provides a stepwise guide for assessing and counseling on health-related behaviors. In this strategy, the lines of questioning are targeted, rather than open-ended, leading to more directive recommendations and focused follow-up questions. The transtheoretical (stages of change) model can be helpful when patients are ambivalent, but this approach focuses more on identifying the patient's current level of readiness to modify a particular health behavior. The stages are precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance. Identifying a patient's current stage can facilitate movement to the next stage of change and can provide a helpful framework to select another counseling strategy, such as MI.

stem: A 35-year-old female with type 1 diabetes presents with a skin lesion on her leg. The lesion began as a small, dusky red, elevated nodule with a sharply circumscribed border, and slowly enlarged to become the lesion shown below. The most likely diagnosis is

bullets.text: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum presents as dusky red nodules on the lower legs that enlarge, flatten, and develop a brownish-yellow center with a reddened border.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is a skin condition associated with type 1 diabetes whose pathophysiology is poorly understood. Lesions characteristically occur on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the lower legs. They begin as small, dusky red, elevated nodules with sharply circumscribed borders, then slowly enlarge, develop an irregular outline, flatten, and acquire a brownish-yellow center, often with a reddened border.

bullets.text: Other diabetic skin conditions have distinct features: dermopathy presents as crops of brownish atrophic lesions; lipoatrophy shows skin depression; rubeosis is facial/extremity reddening; and eruptive xanthomas are small reddish-yellow clustered nodules on extensor surfaces.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diabetic dermopathy characteristically occurs as crops of brownish atrophic lesions, not nodules with a yellow center. Diabetic lipoatrophy causes skin depression with an otherwise normal appearance. Diabetic rubeosis refers to reddening of the face and extremities in longstanding diabetes mellitus. Eruptive xanthomas are typically small (up to 0.5 cm), reddish-yellow nodules appearing in clusters on extensor surfaces and buttocks, distinguishing them from the enlarging, flattening lesions of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum.

explanation_raw: This patient's most likely diagnosis is necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. Its pathophysiology is poorly understood, but lesions are commonly found on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the lower legs. Lesions may begin as a small, dusky red, elevated nodule with a sharply circumscribed border. The nodule slowly enlarges, develops an irregular outline, and flattens, and has a brownish-yellow center. A reddened border may be present. Diabetic dermopathy characteristically occurs as crops of brownish atrophic lesions. In diabetic lipoatrophy the skin is depressed but otherwise normal. Diabetic rubeosis is described as reddening of the face and extremities in patients with longstanding diabetes mellitus. Eruptive xanthomas from diabetes are typically small, reddishyellow nodules up to 0.5 cm in diameter that appear in clusters on the extensor surfaces and buttocks.

stem: Metformin can cause which one of the following?

bullets.text: Metformin is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency, with patients showing a 19% decrease in B12 levels and a 7% absolute increase in risk of deficiency compared to placebo.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Asymptomatic vitamin B12 deficiency has been reported in a significant proportion of patients taking metformin (SOR A). A randomized, placebo-controlled trial demonstrated that metformin use leads to a 19% decrease in vitamin B12 levels and a 7% absolute increase in the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency compared to the placebo group. Clinicians should monitor B12 levels periodically in patients on long-term metformin therapy.

bullets.text: Chromatopsia is linked to PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil), not metformin; metformin does not cause ileus, renal failure, or weight gain.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Chromatopsia (a visual disturbance of color perception) is associated with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil, not metformin. While metformin is contraindicated in patients with impaired renal function, it does not itself cause renal failure. Metformin does not cause ileus.
