Because diarrhea is a relatively common side effect of metformin, weight gain is not typically associated with its use.

explanation_raw: Asymptomatic vitamin B12 deficiency has been reported in a significant proportion of patients taking metformin (SOR A). A randomized, placebo-controlled trial showed that patients taking metformin had a 19% decrease in vitamin B12 levels and a 7% increase in absolute risk of vitamin B12 deficiency compared to the placebo group. Chromatopsia, which is a visual disturbance of color perception, is associated with use of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, such as sildenafil. Metformin use is not associated with ileus. Although metformin use is contraindicated in patients with impaired renal function, metformin itself does not cause renal failure. Because diarrhea occurs relatively frequently with metformin therapy, metformin use is not commonly associated with weight gain.

stem: A 3-year-old female is brought to your office by her parents with fever, cough, and decreased appetite. On examination you hear crackles in the left upper lobe and a chest x-ray confirms a left upper lobe consolidation. She appears well hydrated and her vital signs are normal. On examination she is drinking water and interacting normally. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate antibiotic for this patient's condition?

bullets.text: Amoxicillin is the first-line antibiotic for typical bacterial community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children, targeting pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In children with CAP presenting with focal consolidation, the most likely causative organisms are typical bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Amoxicillin for 7 days is the first-line treatment. Azithromycin is reserved for atypical pneumonia. Cefdinir, while covering typical CAP pathogens, is not recommended first-line due to its broader spectrum. Doxycycline is contraindicated in children under 8 years old. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim has no role in CAP treatment.

explanation_raw: The majority of cases of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children are caused by viruses. If bacterial pneumonia were suspected, then antibiotics would be warranted. Given this patient's focal lung examination and x-ray findings, the most likely causative bacteria would be a typical pathogen such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae. The first-line choice of antibiotics would be amoxicillin for 7 days. Azithromycin is appropriate for treatment of atypical pneumonia. While cefdinir does treat the typical pathogens seen in CAP, it would not be recommended for first-line treatment due to its broader spectrum. Doxycycline is used to treat CAP but should not be used in a 3-year-old. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is not indicated for CAP treatment.

stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the urgent care clinic with pain in his right index finger after jamming it during basketball practice. An examination demonstrates a gross deformity of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the affected finger. There is dorsal angulation of the proximal phalanx. Capillary refill, sensation, and pulses are all intact. Because the patient has pain with attempted movement of the finger, a digital block using 1% lidocaine without epinephrine is used to complete the examination. Complete x-rays, including true lateral films, reveal a very small fracture of the middle phalanx involving a minimal (<20%) area of the articular surface. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the treatment of this patient's finger dislocation?

choices.A: Discharging home, and repeating x-rays in 1 week
choices.B: Reduction, followed by splinting in a flexed position and buddy taping
choices.D: Referral for physical therapy with instructions to start early range-of-motion exercises
choices.E: Urgent referral to an orthopedist for hand surgery

correct_label: Reduction, followed by splinting in a flexed position and buddy taping

bullets.text: This patient has a dorsal dislocation of the PIP joint, the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, presenting with dorsal angulation and gross deformity after axial load injury.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has a dorsal dislocation of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the finger, which is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body. The mechanism — jamming during basketball — combined with dorsal angulation of the proximal phalanx and gross deformity at the PIP joint is classic for this injury.

bullets.text: Stable dorsal PIP dislocations with intact neurovascular findings are managed conservatively with in-office reduction, splinting in ~30° of flexion for 2–4 weeks, and buddy taping to prevent hyperextension.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Conservative management is indicated given limited articular surface involvement and intact neurovascular findings. A simple, stable dorsal PIP dislocation can be managed with in-office reduction, followed by splinting in approximately 30° of flexion for 2–4 weeks. Buddy taping is also recommended to prevent hyperextension deformities. X-rays should be repeated directly after reduction and again in 1 week. Neither MRI nor physical therapy are immediately indicated.

bullets.text: Immediate surgical referral is reserved for irreducible or unstable dislocations, fractures involving >30% of the articular surface, significant displacement/angulation >15°, malrotation, open fractures, or neurovascular compromise — none of which are present here.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Immediate surgical referral is necessary for finger fracture-dislocations that are irreducible, unstable after reduction, or involve significant soft tissue, tendon, or neurovascular injury. Additional indications include fractures involving a large portion of the articular surface (typically >30%), significant displacement or angulation (>15°), malrotation, comminution, persistent subluxation or dislocation on imaging, open fractures, and injuries with vascular compromise or loss of function. Since none of these high-risk features are present in this case, surgical referral is not warranted.

explanation_raw: This patient has a dorsal dislocation of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the finger, which is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body. Examination of the patient's finger reveals intact neurovascular findings. Conservative management is indicated given the limited articular surface involvement. A simple, stable dorsal PIP dislocation can be managed with in-office reduction, followed by splinting in approximately 30° of flexion for 2–4 weeks. Buddy taping is also recommended to prevent hyperextension deformities. Xrays should be repeated directly after reduction, and again in 1 week. Neither MRI nor physical therapy are indicated. Immediate surgical referral is necessary for finger fracture-dislocations that are irreducible, unstable after reduction, or involve significant soft tissue, tendon, or neurovascular injury. Additional indications include fractures involving a large portion of the articular surface (typically >30%), significant displacement or angulation (>15°), malrotation, comminution, and persistent subluxation or dislocation on imaging. Open fractures (exposed bone or joint) and injuries with vascular compromise or loss of function also require urgent surgical evaluation.

stem: A 27-year-old female comes to your office because she is having moderately severe, diffuse abdominal pain with nausea and approximately 5 loose, greasy stools daily. She recently returned from a 2-week backpacking trip in Nicaragua. Stool studies are positive for Giardia. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?

bullets.text: Giardia lamblia infection presents with greasy diarrhea, abdominal pain, and nausea after exposure in areas with poor sanitation; fever and vomiting are uncommon.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Giardia is a parasitic cause of diarrheal illness found globally but especially prevalent where sanitary conditions and water treatment are limited. Transmission occurs via waterborne, foodborne, or fecal-oral routes. The incubation period is typically 1–2 weeks, and the classic presentation includes greasy/fatty stools, diffuse abdominal pain, and nausea. Fever and vomiting are notably uncommon, helping distinguish it from bacterial causes of traveler's diarrhea.

bullets.text: Symptomatic Giardia infection should be treated with metronidazole, tinidazole, or nitazoxanide to relieve symptoms and prevent further transmission.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While some Giardia infections are self-limited, treatment is recommended for all symptomatic individuals. First-line agents include metronidazole (Flagyl), tinidazole, and nitazoxanide. Azithromycin and ciprofloxacin are commonly used for bacterial causes of traveler's diarrhea (e.g., Campylobacter, E. coli), and ivermectin is used for parasitic infections such as Strongyloides or scabies—none of these are effective against Giardia.

explanation_raw: Giardia is a parasite that causes diarrheal illness. While found globally, it is especially common in areas where sanitary conditions are poor and water treatment facilities are limited. Transmission may be waterborne, foodborne, or fecal-oral. The incubation period is usually 1–2 weeks, and symptoms include greasy diarrhea, abdominal pain, and nausea. Fever and vomiting are uncommon. While some infections are self-limited, treatment is recommended for symptomatic individuals to improve their symptoms and prevent transmission to others. Metronidazole, nitazoxanide, or tinidazole are recommended for treatment of Giardia infection. Azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, and ivermectin are antimicrobials that are commonly used to treat other causes of traveler's diarrhea.

stem: A 49-year-old female with a past medical history of epilepsy presents to your office because of sadness, sleep disruption, generalized anhedonia, and a recent increase in appetite. Her Patient Health Questionnaire–9 (PHQ-9) score is elevated at 14. Which one of the following medications should be AVOIDED in this patient?

bullets.text: Bupropion should be avoided in patients with epilepsy due to its dose-dependent risk of lowering the seizure threshold.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Antidepressants including bupropion, trazodone, and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are associated with an increased risk of seizures and should be avoided in patients with a history of epilepsy. In general, SSRIs and SNRIs are considered safer first-line choices for depression in this population. Mirtazapine and vortioxetine are also preferred alternatives, as they have a more favorable seizure safety profile.

explanation_raw: Antidepressants including bupropion, trazodone, and tricyclic antidepressants are associated with an increased risk of seizure and should be avoided in patients with epilepsy. In general, SSRIs or SNRIs are safer choices. Mirtazapine and vortioxetine would also be preferred choices.

stem: A 20-year-old female presents for a health maintenance examination. She has no significant past medical history and no concerns. Based on U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines, screening for which one of the following would be most appropriate at this time?

bullets.text: The USPSTF gives a B recommendation for hepatitis C screening in all adults aged 18–79, making it appropriate for this 20-year-old at her health maintenance visit.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF gives a B recommendation for hepatitis C screening in all adults aged 18–79, making it appropriate for this 20-year-old at her health maintenance visit. Cervical cancer screening is not recommended until age 21 (A recommendation), so it would not apply here. Evidence for hyperlipidemia screening in young adults without risk factors is insufficient, and visual skin cancer screening has an I recommendation (insufficient evidence), though counseling about UV exposure is recommended (B) for fair-skinned persons aged 6 months to 24 years.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force gives a B recommendation for screening for hepatitis C in individuals 18–79 years of age. Cervical cancer screening is not recommended until at least age 21 (A recommendation). Evidence for screening for hyperlipidemia and skin cancer is uncertain. Current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of the benefits and harms of visual skin examination to screen for skin cancer (I recommendation), but counseling for ultraviolet exposure is recommended for persons 6 months to 24 years of age with fair skin types (B recommendation).

stem: A 75-year-old male with acute confusion presents to the emergency department and is found to have a blood pressure of 280/140 mm Hg. Which one of the following potential etiologies would provide the strongest indication for lowering his systolic blood pressure to a target of 120 mm Hg within 20 minutes?

bullets.text: Acute aortic dissection requires the most aggressive blood pressure reduction — systolic to 100–120 mm Hg within 20 minutes — along with heart rate reduction to <60 bpm to minimize shear stress and prevent dissection propagation or rupture.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute aortic dissection is the one hypertensive emergency that mandates rapid, aggressive blood pressure lowering (systolic to 100–120 mm Hg within 20 minutes) combined with heart rate control (<60 bpm). This dual approach reduces aortic wall shear stress, limits propagation of the dissection, and decreases the risk of rupture and aneurysmal degeneration. In contrast, other hypertensive emergencies such as acute ischemic stroke, acute renal failure, hypertensive encephalopathy, and intracerebral hemorrhage require much more cautious and gradual blood pressure reduction, as overly rapid lowering in these conditions can worsen end-organ ischemia and lead to serious complications.

explanation_raw: Treatment of acute aortic dissection includes aggressive lowering of the systolic blood pressure to 100–120 mm Hg within 20 minutes and concomitant lowering of the pulse rate to <60 beats/min to reduce shear stress on the aortic wall, minimize the risk of propagating the dissection, and reduce the risk of other complications, including rupture and aneurysmal degeneration. The optimal treatment of acute ischemic stroke, acute renal failure, hypertensive encephalopathy, and intracerebral hemorrhage requires blood pressure to be lowered more cautiously to avoid the risk of complications that may be seen with overly rapid and aggressive blood pressure–lowering.

stem: A 56-year-old male sees you because he has been falling asleep at work in the afternoon. Upon questioning he notes that he is very tired all the time. Although he is in bed 8 hours per night and wakes with an alarm, he gets up 3 times nightly to urinate. He says that he has been told he snores. He does not have any constipation, dry skin, mood changes, stomach pain, changes in urine stream, shortness of breath, or chest pain. The patient is 173 cm (68 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (209 lb). His vital signs include a blood pressure of 140/88 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 79 beats/min, and a respiratory rate of 16/min. Which one of the following is most likely to yield the correct diagnosis?

bullets.text: Polysomnography is the definitive diagnostic study for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which is strongly suggested by the classic triad of obesity, loud snoring, and daytime fatigue.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with the classic triad of obstructive sleep apnea: obesity, loud snoring, and excessive daytime fatigue despite adequate time in bed. Polysomnography (overnight sleep study) is the gold-standard test to confirm OSA by measuring apneic and hypopneic episodes, oxygen desaturation, and sleep architecture disruption.

bullets.text: TSH, B12/folate/iron studies, and a comprehensive metabolic panel are less likely to identify the cause of fatigue here because the patient lacks supporting symptoms such as mood changes, dry skin, constipation, nutritional deficiencies, shortness of breath, or abdominal pain.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A TSH would be appropriate if hypothyroidism were suspected (e.g., mood changes, dry skin, constipation), but those features are absent. Low B12, folate, or iron are possible causes of fatigue but are not supported by this presentation. A comprehensive metabolic panel to evaluate kidney or liver dysfunction would be warranted if the patient had shortness of breath, stomach pain, or chest pain, which he does not. The clinical picture overwhelmingly points to OSA as the etiology of his fatigue.

explanation_raw: The combination of obesity, loud snoring, and fatigue is suspicious for obstructive sleep apnea, and polysomnography is the definitive diagnostic study. A TSH level would be useful if hypothyroidism were suspected as the cause of this patient's fatigue, but it is less likely because he does not have any mood changes, dry skin, or constipation. Low vitamin B12, folate, and iron levels are also less likely based on this patient's presentation. A comprehensive metabolic panel would be useful if kidney or liver function were suspected as the cause of the patient's fatigue, but these are less likely because he does not have shortness of breath, stomach pain, or chest pain.

stem: A 16-year-old female presents for a routine well child examination. She has never been sexually active and does not use illicit substances. Based on guidelines from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, screening patients such as this for which one of the following has the strongest evidence of benefit?

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends screening for anxiety in children and adolescents aged 8–18 years (Grade B recommendation), making it the strongest evidence-based screening option for this non-sexually active adolescent.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF gives a Grade B recommendation for anxiety screening in children and adolescents aged 8–18 years, meaning there is high certainty of moderate net benefit. For this 16-year-old who is not sexually active, chlamydia/gonorrhea screening (also Grade B) does not apply. Screening for eating disorders, elevated blood pressure, and scoliosis in adolescents all carry an 'I' (insufficient evidence) recommendation from the USPSTF, meaning the current evidence is lacking to assess benefits and harms.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for anxiety in children and adolescents 8–18 years of age (B recommendation). The USPSTF does recommend screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea for sexually active females in this patient's age group (B recommendation); however, this patient is not sexually active. Screening adolescents for eating disorders, elevated blood pressure, and scoliosis all have insufficient evidence to assess the benefits and harms (I recommendation).

stem: A 50-year-old female presents for evaluation of unilateral shoulder pain without a history of acute injury. She has tried ibuprofen with minimal symptomatic relief. Plain radiographs of the affected shoulder taken at an urgent care clinic last week demonstrated no abnormal findings. Which one of the following physical examination findings would best support a diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis as the primary etiology of this patient's shoulder pain?

choices.A: Apprehension in a 90° position with abduction and external rotation
choices.B: Crepitus on passive abduction with preserved passive range of abduction
choices.C: Restricted active range of abduction with preserved passive range of abduction
choices.D: Restricted passive range of abduction and external rotation
choices.E: Weakness on resisted abduction and external rotation

correct_label: Restricted passive range of abduction and external rotation

bullets.text: The hallmark of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is pain with restricted passive range of motion, especially in external rotation, flexion, and abduction, with normal plain radiographs.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The hallmark finding of adhesive capsulitis, also known as frozen shoulder, is pain associated with restricted passive range of motion, particularly in external rotation, flexion, and abduction. Radiographs are typically normal in adhesive capsulitis, although characteristic findings can be seen on MRI. This distinguishes it from glenohumeral osteoarthritis, which also causes limited passive range of motion but shows radiographic changes such as joint space narrowing, sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and subchondral cystic change.

bullets.text: Apprehension with abduction/external rotation suggests instability; crepitus is nonspecific; limited active but preserved passive range of motion points to extra-articular causes; and weakness on manual testing suggests a high-grade rotator cuff tear.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Apprehension in a position of abduction and external rotation would suggest shoulder instability rather than adhesive capsulitis. Crepitus on passive range of motion suggests a mechanical abnormality (intra- or extra-articular) and is nonspecific. Limited active range of motion in abduction with preserved passive range of motion is characteristic of extra-articular sources of shoulder pain such as rotator cuff tendinitis, impingement, subacromial bursitis, biceps tendinitis, or partial/complete rotator cuff tears. Weakness on manual muscle testing in abduction and external rotation raises concern for a high-grade or full-thickness rotator cuff tear.

explanation_raw: The hallmark finding of adhesive capsulitis, also known as frozen shoulder, is pain associated with restricted passive range of motion, particularly in external rotation, flexion, and abduction. Osteoarthritis of the glenohumeral joint also commonly causes pain and stiffness with limited passive range of motion; however, radiographs would show evidence of osteoarthritis, with joint space narrowing, sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and subchondral cystic change. With adhesive capsulitis, radiographs are typically normal, although characteristic findings are seen on MRI. Limited passive range of motion occurs with adhesive capsulitis and osteoarthritis because both conditions involve structural changes within the intra-articular space of the glenohumeral joint, thus resulting in mechanical restriction of the range of motion. Apprehension in a position of abduction and external rotation would suggest a diagnosis of shoulder instability. Crepitus on passive range of motion would suggest a mechanical abnormality within the shoulder girdle (either intra- or extra-articular) and is nonspecific to any one condition. Limited active range of motion in abduction with preserved passive range of motion is common to extra-articular sources of shoulder pain, such as rotator cuff tendinitis and impingement, subacromial bursitis, biceps tendinitis, and partial or complete rotator cuff tears. Weakness on manual muscle testing in abduction and external rotation would raise concern for a high-grade or full-thickness rotator cuff tear.

stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes presents to your office because he is concerned about an ulcer on the bottom of his right foot. He is uncertain how long the ulcer has been present. He is afebrile and otherwise asymptomatic. His most recent hemoglobin A1c is 9.7% and was obtained 9 months ago. His medications include metformin, 2000 mg daily, and insulin glargine (Lantus), 34 units nightly. He does not regularly check his blood glucose levels. On examination, the patient has an ulcer on the plantar surface of the right foot overlying the head of the fifth metatarsal, measuring 1.0 cm in diameter. The ulcer appears deep with erythema that extends approximately 2.5 cm from the margin of the ulcer. A probe-to-bone test is positive. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next test to evaluate for osteomyelitis?

bullets.text: Plain radiography is the recommended initial imaging modality for suspected osteomyelitis in diabetic foot ulcers due to its low cost, safety, and wide availability.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In a patient with diabetes mellitus and suspected osteomyelitis of the foot, initial evaluation should include a probe-to-bone test, a serum inflammatory marker such as ESR, and plain radiography. Plain radiography is the recommended first-line imaging modality because it is inexpensive, safe, and readily available. If plain radiographs suggest osteomyelitis, advanced imaging (such as MRI) may not be necessary. A highly elevated ESR is suggestive of osteomyelitis, whereas WBC count can be normal in up to half of patients with severe diabetic foot infections and is therefore not helpful in diagnosing osteomyelitis.

bullets.text: WBC count, superficial wound cultures, and peripheral vascular studies each have significant limitations and do not contribute meaningfully to the diagnosis of osteomyelitis in diabetic foot infections.
bullets.sub_paragraph: WBC count is used to grade severity of diabetic foot infections but is normal in roughly half of severe cases, making it unreliable for diagnosing osteomyelitis. Superficial wound cultures are poorly sensitive and specific for identifying causative organisms compared to deep tissue cultures and are not recommended for assessing diabetic foot infections or osteomyelitis. While evaluation of peripheral vasculature and oxygenation may be relevant to overall management of diabetic foot disease, it does not contribute to the diagnosis of osteomyelitis itself.

explanation_raw: In a patient with diabetes mellitus and suspected osteomyelitis of the foot, initial evaluation should include a probe-to-bone test, a serum inflammatory marker such as an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and plain radiography. Plain radiography is the recommended initial imaging modality in the diagnosis of osteomyelitis due to its low cost, safety, and availability. If a plain radiograph suggests osteomyelitis, advanced imaging may not be necessary. While an elevated WBC count can be used to grade the severity of a diabetes-related foot infection, it can be normal in about half of patients with a severe diabetes-related foot infection and is not helpful in the diagnosis of osteomyelitis. A highly elevated ESR, however, is suggestive of an osteomyelitis infection. Superficial wound cultures are poorly sensitive and specific for identifying diabetes-related wound organisms compared to deep tissue cultures and are not used in the assessment of diabetes-related foot infections or osteomyelitis. While evaluation of peripheral vasculature and oxygenation may be warranted in the management of diabetes-related foot infections and osteomyelitis, it does not contribute to the diagnosis of osteomyelitis.

stem: A 63-year-old female with hypertension sees you for routine follow-up. She has been bothered by swelling in her legs for the last several months. Her blood pressure is well controlled and she does not have any shortness of breath, cough, difficulty breathing while lying down, or pain in her legs when walking. She thinks the swelling is better earlier in the day. Her current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril (Zestril), estrogen, levothyroxine (Synthroid), and as-needed acetaminophen. A physical examination demonstrates mild pitting edema of both legs from the ankle to the distal third of each calf. There are 2+ pedal pulses and no skin changes. Examinations of the heart and lungs are normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Holding estrogen, and monitoring for improvement in peripheral edema
choices.B: Holding lisinopril, and monitoring for improvement in peripheral edema
choices.E: Bilateral venous duplex ultrasonography with reflux

correct_label: Holding estrogen, and monitoring for improvement in peripheral edema

bullets.text: Adverse medication effects, including estrogen-induced peripheral edema, should always be considered before pursuing further diagnostic workup for new symptoms.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient's bilateral leg swelling in the setting of estrogen use is most likely a medication side effect. Since she is 63 years old and likely remote from menopause, there may no longer be a strong indication for continued estrogen therapy. Discontinuing the estrogen and monitoring for improvement is the most appropriate first step before ordering additional tests or escalating management.

bullets.text: ACE inhibitors do not cause peripheral edema, ankle-brachial indices are for suspected arterial disease, and venous compression ultrasonography is reserved for suspected DVT—none of which fit this clinical picture.
bullets.sub_paragraph: ACE inhibitors do not cause peripheral edema; in fact, they may reduce edema caused by calcium channel blockers. Ankle-brachial indices are indicated for arterial disease, which typically presents with exertional leg pain and diminished pulses—not bilateral swelling. Venous compression ultrasonography is used to evaluate for DVT, which is unlikely in the setting of chronic bilateral edema; DVT more commonly presents as acute unilateral edema, and the Wells score plus D-dimer should guide that workup. Venous duplex ultrasonography with reflux can evaluate chronic venous insufficiency, but medication-induced edema should be ruled out first given the absence of alarm features such as heart failure signs or lower extremity ulcerations.

explanation_raw: Adverse medication effects should always be considered when evaluating new symptoms, such as the association between estrogen use and peripheral edema. This patient's age suggests that she is likely remote from menopause, which provides a reason to consider discontinuing estrogen therapy. Peripheral edema is not associated with ACE inhibitor use. In fact, combining an ACE inhibitor with a calcium channel blocker (CCB) may decrease the edema attributable to CCB use. Ankle-brachial indices are indicated for the evaluation of suspected arterial disease. Arterial disease typically presents as lower extremity pain during activity that improves with rest. Arterial disease may lead to decreased arterial pulses. Arterial disease should be ruled out in those at risk before starting compression therapy for venous disease. Venous compression ultrasonography is indicated when deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is suspected. DVT is unlikely in the presentation of chronic bilateral lower extremity edema. DVT should be considered in acute unilateral edema, and the Wells score should be used to determine if there is an intermediate or high risk. The combination of a low-risk Wells score and a negative D-dimer level safely rules out DVT. Venous duplex ultrasonography with reflux is helpful in evaluating for chronic venous insufficiency. While this patient may have chronic venous insufficiency, her current medication use could be causing her edema. This should be evaluated before pursuing additional diagnostic testing given her lack of alarm symptoms, such as signs of heart failure or lower extremity ulcerations.

stem: Which one of the following antibiotics would be recommended for the treatment of syphilis in a pregnant patient who has a history of penicillin allergy?

bullets.text: Parenteral penicillin G benzathine is the only therapy with documented effectiveness for syphilis in pregnancy; penicillin-allergic pregnant patients must undergo desensitization followed by penicillin treatment.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Parenteral penicillin G benzathine is the only therapy with documented effectiveness for treating syphilis in a pregnant person. In pregnant patients with any stage of syphilis and a reported penicillin allergy, the CDC recommends desensitization followed by treatment with penicillin G benzathine. There is no acceptable antibiotic substitute in pregnancy: azithromycin and erythromycin are insufficient to cure maternal infection or treat fetal infection; ceftriaxone lacks sufficient data to recommend its use for maternal infection or prevention of congenital syphilis; and doxycycline/tetracycline are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters due to fetal harm.

explanation_raw: Parenteral penicillin G benzathine is the only therapy with documented effectiveness for treating syphilis in a pregnant person. In pregnant patients with any stage of syphilis and a reported penicillin allergy, the CDC recommends desensitization followed by treatment with penicillin G benzathine. Azithromycin and erythromycin are insufficient to cure maternal infection or treat fetal infection. There is insufficient data to recommend cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone for the treatment of maternal infections and the prevention of congenital infections. Doxycycline and tetracycline are not recommended for use in the second and third trimesters.

stem: A 7-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents with his parents for a well child visit. His BMI has consistently been above the 80th percentile. His parents have both struggled with maintaining healthy weights. To help them promote a healthy lifestyle for their child, you should tell the parents which one of the following?

choices.A: An hour per day of moderate or vigorous physical activity is recommended starting at age 6
choices.B: Calorie restriction alone is sufficient in maintaining a healthy weight
choices.C: Children should avoid video screen–based physical activity
choices.D: Organic fruit juices can be provided to achieve the recommended daily servings of fruits and vegetables

correct_label: An hour per day of moderate or vigorous physical activity is recommended starting at age 6

bullets.text: Children aged 6–17 years should engage in 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous physical activity, and this is a core component of anticipatory guidance for healthy weight management.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Anticipatory guidance for lifestyle management in children should incorporate multiple approaches addressing nutrition, physical activity, and behaviors that contribute to energy imbalance. The recommended goal is 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous physical activity for children aged 6–17 years. Calorie restriction can be beneficial in reducing weight in adolescents when combined with additional strategies such as physical activity and behavioral changes.

bullets.text: Children should consume 5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day, and the AAP recommends against fruit juice as a substitute for whole fruit due to its high calorie content; screen-based physical activity (e.g., active video games) can help reduce weight in children with overweight.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While excessive video screen time has been associated with increased pediatric obesity, screen-based physical activity such as video games requiring whole-body movement can actually help reduce weight in children with overweight and obesity. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends against the use of fruit juices as a substitute for whole fruit due to their high calorie content, and children should aim for 5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day as part of a balanced diet.

explanation_raw: Anticipatory guidance for lifestyle management in children should incorporate multiple approaches that address nutrition, physical activity, and behaviors that contribute to possible energy imbalance. These recommendations include 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous physical activity for children 6–17 years of age. Calorie restriction is beneficial in reducing weight in adolescents when combined with additional strategies, such as physical activity and behavioral changes. While excessive video screen time has been associated with increased pediatric obesity, screen-based physical activity (eg, video games that require whole-body movement) can help reduce weight in children with overweight and obesity. Children should consume 5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends against the use of fruit juices as a substitute for whole fruit due to its high calorie content.

stem: A 56-year-old female presents with numbness of her bilateral feet. She first became aware of this during a recent pedicure when she had difficulty feeling the nail technician work on her toes and the plantar surface of her feet. Since that time, she has noted a feeling of "walking on cotton gauze" and has started wearing slippers around her home. She had intense pruritus of her feet approximately 6 months ago that persisted for several weeks, but it was not accompanied by paresthesia. She is otherwise in good health and participates in an aerobics class 3 days per week. She takes lisinopril (Zestril), 10 mg daily, for essential hypertension. She does not have any other symptoms. On examination, her cranial nerves, muscle strength, and reflexes are normal. Sensation is diminished over the plantar surface and toes of both feet. She has 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally. Routine laboratory studies, including a CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, hemoglobin A1c, serum protein electrophoresis, and TSH, vitamin B12, and folate levels, are all in normal range. She is concerned that she may be developing multiple sclerosis. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

bullets.text: In a patient with symmetric distal paresthesias and normal routine labs, nerve conduction testing and EMG is the recommended next step to characterize the type and pattern of peripheral neuropathy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with a symmetric, length-dependent pattern of paresthesias (bilateral feet, 'walking on cotton gauze') without any red flag features such as ataxia, diplopia, speech disturbance, or asymmetry. This presentation makes a central nervous system lesion or radiculopathy less likely. When routine laboratory workup is unrevealing, electrodiagnostic testing (nerve conduction studies and EMG) is the appropriate next step, as it can distinguish axonal from demyelinating neuropathy and guide further targeted workup—for example, Lyme antibody testing or B-vitamin levels if an axonal pattern is identified.

bullets.text: Gabapentin addresses symptoms but not etiology; MRI brain/spine is not indicated without central neurologic signs or asymmetry; Lyme and vitamin testing are secondary steps guided by EMG results rather than first-line workup.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Gabapentin can reduce neuropathic pain symptoms but does not identify the underlying cause and should not precede diagnostic evaluation. MRI of the brain or spine is reserved for patients with central neurologic signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, cranial nerve deficits) or asymmetric findings, which are absent here. Lyme serology and vitamin level testing may be appropriate follow-up after electrodiagnostic testing reveals an axonal pattern, but ordering them without first characterizing the neuropathy type is premature and less efficient.

explanation_raw: This patient demonstrates a symmetric pattern of paresthesia without red flag symptoms such as ataxia, double vision, or speech issues, which makes a lesion of the central nervous system or a nerve root less likely. Because the results of her routine laboratory studies are normal, electrodiagnostic testing would be the recommended next step. While gabapentin can be helpful in treating painful peripheral neuropathy, further workup is needed to determine the cause of this patient's symptoms. Lyme antibody testing and vitamin level testing plus supplementation may be helpful if electrodiagnostic testing exhibits an axonal pattern. Imaging of the brain or spine, such as with MRI, is not recommended in patients without central neurologic signs or asymmetry.

stem: A 56-year-old female presents for evaluation of right heel pain. She recently returned from a hiking trip during which she developed progressive heel discomfort. The patient's only medication is losartan (Cozaar), which she takes for hypertension. After a thorough examination, you diagnose Achilles tendinopathy. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in diagnosis and management?

choices.C: Corticosteroid injection of the Achilles tendon

bullets.text: Physical therapy with activity modification and targeted eccentric exercises is the recommended first-line treatment for Achilles tendinopathy; complete rest and corticosteroid injections are not recommended.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Achilles tendinopathy is a common overuse injury in active individuals diagnosed clinically, making additional imaging unnecessary unless an alternate diagnosis is suspected. Current guidelines favor referral to physical therapy for activity modification and targeted eccentric strengthening exercises. Complete rest is not recommended as it does not promote tendon remodeling. Corticosteroid injections are also discouraged due to risk of tendon weakening and rupture. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection remains investigational, with mixed evidence regarding superiority over placebo for pain relief and return to activity, and is therefore not considered first-line management.

explanation_raw: Achilles tendinopathy is a common injury in active individuals. The diagnosis is made clinically; therefore, additional imaging is not indicated unless there is concern for an alternate diagnosis. Current recommendations for management include physical therapy for activity modification and targeted exercises. Neither complete rest nor corticosteroid injection are currently recommended for management of Achilles tendinopathy. While platelet-rich plasma injection continues to be studied in tendon injuries, it is not currently recommended as first-line management. Furthermore, studies remain mixed as to whether platelet-rich plasma injections are superior to placebo for pain control and return to normal activity.

stem: A 45-year-old male with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is anxious about managing his condition and uncertain about his ability to meet the demands of treatment and self-care. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate strategy to help him understand his diagnosis and follow through on lifestyle and/or medication changes?

choices.A: Emphasizing the seriousness of the condition by showing pictures of patients with complications
choices.B: Explaining the diagnosis and treatment plan with medical language to ensure professional communication
choices.C: Supplying only detailed written instructions about his condition immediately after the appointment
choices.D: Using motivational interviewing to identify what is most important to the patient and create impetus for change

correct_label: Using motivational interviewing to identify what is most important to the patient and create impetus for change

bullets.text: Motivational interviewing is the communication strategy with the best evidence for facilitating behavior change in patients with chronic conditions like type 2 diabetes.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Motivational interviewing works by identifying what is most important to the patient and creating internal impetus for change, rather than relying on external pressure or fear. Scare tactics have not been shown to be effective, and physicians should avoid medical jargon. Providing excessive detail not tailored to the individual's goals can overwhelm the patient and reduce engagement with self-care.

explanation_raw: Motivational interviewing is the communication strategy with the best evidence of leading to a change in behavior. Scare tactics have not been shown to be effective. Physicians should speak in language that the patient can understand rather than use jargon. Supplying too much detail may overwhelm the patient, especially if it is not tailored to the individual's goals.

stem: A generally healthy 15-year-old female presents to your office with a history of frequent, generalized abdominal pain and loose stools daily for the last few months. She has not noted any relationship to food or a specific frequency. She has not had any previous surgeries and is up to date on routine vaccinations. At her 14-year-old well child visit, her height was at the 50th percentile and her weight was at the 60th percentile. Today, her height is at the 35th percentile and her weight at the 20th percentile. She has had a weight loss of 1 kg (2 lb). Her vital signs are normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Reassurance and dietary monitoring to evaluate for a relationship to symptoms

bullets.text: IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG) is the preferred initial screening test for celiac disease due to its high sensitivity (95%) and specificity (95%), and total IgA levels should also be checked given the 2–3% rate of IgA deficiency in this population.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Patients with classic symptoms of diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, bloating, malabsorption, and failure to thrive should undergo evaluation for celiac disease. Serologic testing for IgA tTG is the preferred initial screening in all age groups. When celiac disease is strongly suspected, total IgA levels should also be obtained because 2–3% of these patients will have IgA deficiency. If IgA tTG serology is positive, most patients will require esophagogastroduodenoscopy with small-bowel biopsy for confirmation, though some organizations state that a no-biopsy technique is safe for children with very high IgA tTG levels.

bullets.text: Reassurance is inappropriate given classic malabsorption symptoms; fecal fat testing is a secondary consideration; and carbohydrate breath testing is used for SIBO, which typically occurs in patients with abnormal anatomy or risk factors like diabetes or scleroderma.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Reassurance would be inappropriate given this patient's unexplained weight loss and malabsorption signs. Fecal fat testing may be useful in the workup of malabsorption, but the initial test is usually a qualitative single-specimen assessment rather than the more costly 72-hour collection; the latter is reserved for cases with high suspicion after negative initial testing. Carbohydrate breath testing evaluates for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), which generally occurs in individuals with abnormal gut anatomy or conditions affecting intestinal motility (e.g., diabetes mellitus, scleroderma), and typically presents with bloating and flatulence rather than this clinical picture.

explanation_raw: Patients with classic symptoms of diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, bloating, malabsorption, and failure to thrive should undergo evaluation for celiac disease. Serologic testing for IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG) is the preferred initial screening in all age groups due to its high sensitivity (95%) and specificity (95%). When celiac disease is strongly suspected, total IgA levels should also be obtained because 2%–3% of these patients will have IgA deficiency. If IgA tTG serology is positive, most patients will require esophagogastroduodenoscopy with small-bowel biopsy for confirmation, but it is not used as an initial test and some organizations state that a no-biopsy technique is safe for children with very high IgA tTG levels. This patient has classic signs of malabsorption and unexplained weight loss, indicating need for further evaluation. Reassurance would be inappropriate at this time. Fecal fat testing may be useful in the workup of suspected malabsorption symptoms, but the initial test is usually a qualitative assessment of fat in a single specimen because it is less expensive and easier to perform than 72-hour testing. If high suspicion remains after negative initial testing, a 72-hour fecal fat test should be performed. Carbohydrate breath testing can be used to evaluate for suspected small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). SIBO generally occurs in individuals with abnormal anatomy or other risk factors for abnormal intestinal mobility, including diabetes mellitus or scleroderma. The majority of patients with SIBO present with bloating and flatulence.

stem: A 60-year-old male asks you about testosterone supplementation during a routine office visit. He reports that he has had decreased energy, decreased libido, and loss of upper and lower body strength over the last year. He would like to have his testosterone level checked today. Which one of the following symptoms, if present in this patient, would be most concerning for testosterone deficiency?

choices.C: Loss of axillary and pubic hair
choices.D: Thinning of hair at the temples

correct_label: Loss of axillary and pubic hair

bullets.text: Loss of axillary and pubic hair is one of the more specific signs of male hypogonadism, making it more diagnostically useful than nonspecific symptoms like fatigue or memory issues.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Loss of axillary and pubic hair is one of the more specific symptoms of male hypogonadism. In contrast, many other symptoms have broad differential diagnoses: memory issues can stem from attention disorders, mood disorders, or sleep apnea; fatigue and diminished stamina may reflect endocrine, musculoskeletal, or rheumatologic disorders; temporal hair thinning is common with aging and androgenic alopecia; and eyebrow thinning is more characteristic of thyroid disorders. Therefore, when evaluating a patient for possible hypogonadism, loss of axillary and pubic hair carries greater diagnostic specificity.

explanation_raw: Loss of axillary and pubic hair is one of the more specific symptoms of male hypogonadism. Memory issues have myriad etiologies; they may be secondary to attention disorders, mood disorders, sleep apnea, or other neurologic disorders. Fatigue or diminished stamina may be a symptom of male hypogonadism but also can be indicative of other endocrine, musculoskeletal, or rheumatologic disorders. Thinning hair at the temples may occur with aging and with androgenic alopecia. Thinning of the eyebrows may be related to thyroid disorders.

stem: A 3-year-old female is brought to your office by her parents for a preschool examination. She had a normal birth and is up to date on her vaccinations. On examination she appears to be healthy, and her development is appropriate for her age. She is in the 50th percentile for height and weight. You note a grade 1–2/6 continuous murmur best heard in the infraclavicular region when she is upright. The murmur changes slightly in intensity with head movement and is absent when she is supine. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Reassuring the parents that this is a benign venous hum that needs no follow-up
choices.B: Scheduling a follow-up appointment in 1 month to recheck the murmur
choices.C: Recommending that the patient undergo echocardiography when she reaches adulthood
choices.D: Sending the patient for evaluation for repair of a patent ductus arteriosus

correct_label: Reassuring the parents that this is a benign venous hum that needs no follow-up

bullets.text: A venous hum is an innocent murmur caused by vein vibration, commonly heard in children aged 3–6 years, and requires only parental reassurance with no further follow-up.
bullets.sub_paragraph: A venous hum is an innocent heart murmur caused by vibration in the veins. It is commonly heard in children and typically appears between 3 and 6 years of age. A key distinguishing feature is that it is audible only when the child is upright and changes with head movement. Because it is entirely benign, reassurance of the parents is the appropriate management, and no additional follow-up or workup is necessary.

explanation_raw: A venous hum is an innocent heart murmur that is caused by vein vibration. It is commonly heard in children and may appear between 3 and 6 years of age. It is typically audible only when the child is upright, and changes with head movement. In a child with a venous hum, reassurance of the parents is appropriate, and no follow-up is necessary.

stem: A 40-year-old female presents to your office after an episode of anaphylaxis. She has a known tree nut allergy and developed oral swelling, dyspnea, and chest pain after eating a muffin from a coffee shop. Her symptoms initially improved after she used her epinephrine auto-injector but began to worsen 10 minutes later. She used a second dose of her auto-injector 10 minutes prior to presentation and is feeling much better. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Starting famotidine (Pepcid), 20 mg daily, and follow-up in 1 week
choices.B: Starting prednisone, 40 mg for 5 days, and follow-up in 5 days
choices.C: Starting fexofenadine (Allegra), 180 mg daily, and immediate follow-up with an allergist
choices.D: with observation for 1–2 hours prior to discharge
choices.E: Transfer to the ED with observation for 6–12 hours prior to discharge

correct_label: Transfer to the ED with observation for 6–12 hours prior to discharge

bullets.text: Patients with refractory anaphylaxis requiring multiple doses of epinephrine should be transferred to the ED for observation for 6–12 hours due to the risk of a biphasic reaction.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient experienced refractory anaphylaxis requiring 2 doses of epinephrine, which indicates a severe reaction that warrants a higher level of care. Even after initial symptom improvement, patients with severe or refractory anaphylaxis are at significant risk for a biphasic reaction — a recurrence of anaphylactic symptoms hours after the initial episode — and therefore require observation for 6–12 hours in an emergency department setting before discharge can be considered.

bullets.text: H1/H2-blockers and corticosteroids are adjunctive agents in anaphylaxis management but are not sufficient as the primary intervention for severe or refractory anaphylaxis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: While antihistamines (H1- and H2-blockers) and corticosteroids can play a supportive role in post-anaphylaxis care — helping to reduce urticaria, itching, and potentially mitigating prolonged reactions — they are not the mainstay of therapy for severe or refractory anaphylaxis. Epinephrine remains the drug of choice, and transfer to a higher level of care is necessary when anaphylaxis is refractory, as home discharge or office observation alone would be inappropriate given the biphasic reaction risk.

explanation_raw: This patient experienced anaphylaxis due to her tree nut allergy. Her anaphylaxis was refractory and required 2 doses of epinephrine for treatment. Although she is feeling better, patients with refractory anaphylaxis should be transferred to a higher level of care, such as an emergency department, for further evaluation and management. Patients who have had severe or refractory anaphylaxis are at risk for a biphasic reaction and should be observed for 6–12 hours before discharge. Although medications such as H1- and H2-blockers and corticosteroids can be helpful in the postanaphylaxis care of patients, they are not the mainstay of therapy for patients who have had severe anaphylaxis.

stem: A 42-year-old male has been admitted to the hospital for hypotension and electrolyte disturbances due to chronic diarrhea. He was stabilized in the ICU and transferred to the inpatient floor. His gastroenterologist is asking for a colonoscopy with biopsies. His medical history is significant for congenital heart disease with a mechanical aortic valve replacement, an embolic stroke resulting in right hemiparesis, a deep vein thrombosis, and a solitary kidney. He is currently anticoagulated with warfarin and has an INR of 2.6. He has a creatinine level of 2.8 mg/dL (N 0.7–1.3) and a glomerular filtration rate of 28 mL/min/1.73 m2. In addition to holding warfarin for the planned colonoscopy, how should you manage this patient’s anticoagulation while he is hospitalized?

choices.A: Resuming warfarin post procedure with a goal INR of 2.0–3.0
choices.B: Vitamin K for reversal, and resuming warfarin post procedure with a goal INR of 2.5–3.5
choices.E: A heparin drip titrated to achieve therapeutic aPTT or anti-factor Xa levels

correct_label: A heparin drip titrated to achieve therapeutic aPTT or anti-factor Xa levels

bullets.text: Patients with mechanical heart valves requiring procedures with high bleeding risk (e.g., colonoscopy with biopsy) need bridging anticoagulation with a heparin drip titrated to therapeutic aPTT or anti-factor Xa levels until the procedure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient has a mechanical heart valve (INR goal 2.5–3.5) and requires a colonoscopy with biopsies, which carries a high bleeding risk. Warfarin should be held perioperatively, and bridging with a therapeutic heparin drip is appropriate given his high thromboembolic risk. Vitamin K reversal is unnecessary as he is hemodynamically stable and not actively bleeding. The heparin drip can be stopped shortly before the procedure and restarted afterward once hemostasis is confirmed.

bullets.text: Enoxaparin is contraindicated due to his reduced renal function (low GFR), and subcutaneous heparin 5000 units is a prophylactic dose — not sufficient for therapeutic bridging in a high thromboembolic risk patient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Enoxaparin (low molecular weight heparin) is renally cleared and should be avoided in patients with significantly reduced GFR due to risk of drug accumulation and bleeding. Subcutaneous heparin at 5000 units three times daily is a VTE prophylaxis dose and does not provide adequate anticoagulation for a patient with a mechanical heart valve at high risk for thromboembolism. Vitamin K administration is reserved for patients with supratherapeutic INR who are actively bleeding or require emergent reversal, which does not apply here.

explanation_raw: This patient requires a procedure with a high likelihood of bleeding and should not be anticoagulated at the time of the procedure. He also has a high likelihood of thromboembolic disease and should receive bridging with a heparin drip until his INR has normalized for the planned procedure. With his mechanical heart valve, the correct INR goal is 2.5–3.5. Reversal with vitamin K is not necessary because he is stable and not actively bleeding. He is not a candidate for enoxaparin due to his glomerular filtration rate. Heparin, 5000 units subcutaneously, is a prophylactic dose, not a treatment dose.

stem: A 4-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his parents after tripping and falling on his hand in an outstretched position. An x-ray reveals a buckle (torus) fracture of the distal radial metaphysis. Which one of the following management strategies would be most appropriate?

choices.A: A short arm splint for 3 weeks with follow-up radiography
choices.B: A short arm splint for 3 weeks with follow-up radiography only if pain or tenderness persists
choices.C: A short arm cast for 6 weeks with follow-up radiography
choices.D: A short arm cast for 6 weeks with follow-up radiography only if pain or tenderness persists

correct_label: A short arm splint for 3 weeks with follow-up radiography only if pain or tenderness persists

bullets.text: Distal radius buckle (torus) fractures in children should be treated with short arm immobilization (splint, soft cast, or wrap) for 3 weeks; full casting is unnecessary, and follow-up radiography is only needed if pain or tenderness persists.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Buckle (torus) fractures are incomplete compression fractures that cause cortical bulging without cortical disruption. They are common in children due to the elasticity of their bones. A short arm splint, soft cast, or wrap for 3 weeks provides adequate immobilization. Complete casting is not required given the stable, non-displaced nature of the injury. Per the Choosing Wisely campaign, routine follow-up radiography is unnecessary unless the patient continues to experience pain or tenderness, avoiding unnecessary radiation exposure.

explanation_raw: Buckle (torus) fractures are incomplete compression fractures that cause cortical bulging of the bone without cortical disruption. They are common in children because of the elasticity of their bones. Distal radius buckle fractures should be treated with short arm immobilization using a short arm splint, soft cast, or wrap for 3 weeks. Complete immobilization with a cast is unnecessary. According to the Choosing Wisely campaign, follow-up radiography is unnecessary unless the patient continues to experience pain or tenderness.

stem: A 19-year-old female presents for a wellness visit while home on college break. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which one of the following screenings is indicated?

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends screening for unhealthy drug use in all adults ≥18 years of age (Grade B recommendation).
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF recommends screening for unhealthy drug use in all adults ≥18 years of age (Grade B recommendation). Unhealthy drug use is defined as using psychoactive medications for purposes other than as prescribed or illegally obtaining drugs for personal use.

bullets.text: For this age group, the USPSTF has assigned an 'I' (insufficient evidence) recommendation for screening of cavities/periodontal disease, dyslipidemia, skin cancer, and suicide risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For this age group, the USPSTF has determined the evidence to be insufficient (I recommendation) to recommend for or against screening for cavities or periodontal disease, dyslipidemia, skin cancer, or suicide risk. An 'I' statement means the current evidence is lacking, of poor quality, or conflicting, and the balance of benefits and harms cannot be determined.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for unhealthy drug use in adults ≥18 years of age (B recommendation). Unhealthy drug use is defined as using psychoactive medications for purposes other than as prescribed or illegally obtaining drugs for personal use. For this patient's age group, the USPSTF has determined the evidence to be insufficient to recommend for or against screening for cavities or periodontal disease, dyslipidemia, skin cancer, or suicide risk (I recommendation).

stem: A 33-year-old oyster fisherman presents because of a 3-day history of diarrhea. He describes frequent, large-volume, watery stool that is milky white. His vital signs are normal and he appears nontoxic. Infection with which one of the following pathogens is most likely?

bullets.text: Large-volume, rice-water or milky-white stools are the classic presentation of Vibrio species infection, and testing should occur regardless of known shellfish or brackish water exposure.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In patients presenting with large-volume rice-water or milky-white stools, the most likely pathogen is Vibrio species. This fisherman's occupational exposure to oysters and marine environments raises further suspicion, but guidelines indicate testing should be pursued based on stool characteristics alone, without requiring a confirmed exposure history.

explanation.heading: When to Test for Other Pathogens

bullets.text: IDSA guidelines recommend testing for C. difficile, enteropathogenic E. coli, enterotoxigenic E. coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica when diarrhea is accompanied by fever, bloody or mucoid stools, signs of sepsis, or severe abdominal cramping.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The other pathogens listed—Clostridioides difficile, enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, enterotoxigenic E. coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica—are more strongly associated with presentations that include fever, bloody or mucoid stools, systemic signs of sepsis, or severe abdominal pain and tenderness. This patient's watery, milky-white stool without these features makes Vibrio species the most likely etiology.

explanation_raw: In patients presenting with large-volume rice-water or milky-white stools, the most likely pathogen is Vibrio species. Patients with this presentation should be tested for infection regardless of exposure to undercooked shellfish or brackish waters. Guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend testing for infection with Clostridioides difficile, enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, enterotoxigenic E coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica in patients with diarrhea and fever, bloody or mucoid stools, signs of sepsis, or severe abdominal cramping or tenderness.

stem: A 35-year-old female with Down syndrome presents for a health maintenance examination. She does not have any new symptoms or concerns today. Her only medication is an etonogestrel implant (Nexplanon) that was placed 2 years ago. She is monogamous with a male sex partner. On examination you note normal vital signs with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. At her most recent laboratory evaluation 2 years ago, she had an LDL-cholesterol level of 104 mg/dL, a fasting glucose level of 89 mg/dL, and a TSH level of 2.67 μU/mL (N 0.4–4.2). Which one of the following screening evaluations should you order today?

choices.A: The National Task Group–Early Detection Screen for Dementia tool

explanation.heading: Screening Recommendations for Adults with Down Syndrome

bullets.text: TSH testing every 1–2 years starting at age 21 is recommended for adults with Down syndrome, given an estimated hypothyroidism prevalence of ~50% in those over 30.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Per the 2020 Global Down Syndrome Foundation evidence-based guidelines, hypothyroidism is highly prevalent in adults with Down syndrome (~50% in those >30 years). TSH screening is therefore recommended every 1–2 years beginning at age 21. This patient's TSH was last checked 2 years ago, making it due today. Dementia screening is not recommended until age 40 (using a validated tool such as the NTG-EDSD), as dementia is rare before that age in this population. Cardiovascular lipid screening follows standard USPSTF guidelines, and this patient's LDL was checked recently and is not yet due. DXA screening is not recommended before age 65 in Down syndrome, as evidence for earlier screening is lacking. Cervical spine radiography for atlantoaxial instability is also not recommended; instead, clinicians should monitor for signs of cervical myelopathy (incontinence, altered gait, brisk reflexes, clonus).

explanation_raw: In 2017, the U.S. nonprofit group Global Down Syndrome Foundation convened a workgroup to create an evidence-based guideline for clinicians and adults with Down syndrome and their supporters. This guideline was published in 2020 and includes responses to 10 questions that were created using the Population/Intervention/Comparator/Outcome (PICO) format. They address screening for conditions known to be of higher prevalence in individuals with Down syndrome. In the United States, hypothyroidism is common in individuals with Down syndrome, with an estimated prevalence of approximately 50% in adults >30 years of age. Screening is therefore recommended with TSH testing every 1–2 years starting at age 21. This patient's TSH level was last checked 2 years ago and is due today. Dementia occurs on average at younger ages in those with Down syndrome than those without Down syndrome; however, it is rare before the age of 40. If any concerning symptoms arise in this age group, a thorough investigation for alternative causes is recommended. Routine screening for dementia is recommended beginning at age 40 for individuals with Down syndrome. A validated tool such as the National Task Group–Early Detection Screen for Dementia should be used. Cardiovascular disease prevention is recommended for individuals with Down syndrome per U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines. This patient's LDL-cholesterol level was last checked 2 years ago and is not due for recheck today. The prevalence of osteoporosis in individuals with Down syndrome has been estimated with a wide degree of variation (1.4%–45.1%). There is no evidence that DXA screening at ages younger than recommended for adults without Down syndrome (age 65) is of benefit. Although atlantoaxial instability (AAI) is known to have a higher prevalence in those with Down syndrome than those without Down syndrome, no studies have assessed the use of cervical spine radiography for diagnosing AAI. Screening radiography is therefore not recommended; instead, it is recommended that clinicians remain alert for signs and symptoms of cervical myelopathy, such as incontinence, altered gait, brisk reflexes, and clonus.

stem: You are participating in a continuing medical education (CM

choices.E: Oxygen supplementation, and descending to a lower elevation

correct_label: Oxygen supplementation, and descending to a lower elevation

bullets.text: This patient presents with high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), a medical emergency distinct from mild acute mountain sickness.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute mountain sickness risk increases when sleeping above ~8200 ft (2499 m) and typically causes difficulty sleeping, headache, and decreased appetite. HAPE represents a more severe, life-threatening form of altitude illness requiring immediate intervention.

bullets.text: Immediate supplemental oxygen and descent to a lower elevation are the definitive treatments for HAPE.
bullets.sub_paragraph: At a modern ski resort, descent is feasible and should be prioritized. Nifedipine can be used as an emergency treatment for HAPE when descent or a hyperbaric chamber is unavailable, but it is not the first-line choice when descent is possible. Dexamethasone is used for high-altitude cerebral edema, not HAPE.

bullets.text: Acetazolamide is for prevention of acute mountain sickness, not treatment of HAPE; COVID-19 infection is unlikely given the clinical context.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acetazolamide helps prevent acute mountain sickness but has no established role in treating HAPE. Nifedipine is a backup option only when evacuation is not available. Dexamethasone targets high-altitude cerebral edema. COVID-19 is an unlikely diagnosis in this altitude-exposure scenario.

explanation_raw: The risk for acute mountain sickness increases when sleeping above altitudes of about 8200 ft (2499 m). Symptoms can include difficulty sleeping, headaches, and decreased appetite. This patient has more severe symptoms of high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), which is a medical emergency, and should begin supplemental oxygen and descend to a lower altitude if possible. Acetazolamide can be used to prevent acute mountain sickness, but it is not a treatment. Dexamethasone is a supplemental treatment for high-altitude cerebral edema. Nifedipine can be used in the prevention of HAPE and as a treatment in emergency situations in which descent or a hyperbaric chamber is not available. In this case, the patient is at a modern ski resort and descent should be feasible. COVID-19 infection is unlikely in this scenario.

stem: Which one of the following antibiotics is most commonly associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

bullets.text: Sulfonamide antibiotics, particularly sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, are the most common antibiotic cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Antibiotics as a class are responsible for more than one-quarter of SJS and toxic epidermal necrolysis cases worldwide. Among antibiotics, sulfonamides such as sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim account for the majority of antibiotic-associated SJS cases. This underscores the importance of antibiotic stewardship and careful consideration of both common and potentially life-threatening adverse effects before prescribing.

explanation_raw: Antibiotics are the most common cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis, accounting for more than one-quarter of cases worldwide. Sulfonamide antibiotics, such as sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, are associated with the majority of antibiotic-associated SJS cases worldwide. Antibiotic stewardship is always important, and consideration for both relatively benign and life-threatening side effects should be considered with every prescription written.

stem: During an annual visit, a 62-year-old female reports an episode of vaginal spotting that lasted for a few days in May. It is now July and she has not had another recurrence. A transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial stripe of 4 mm, no fibroids, and no polyps. Which one of the following would be most appropriate regarding follow-up evaluation?

bullets.text: An endometrial stripe ≤4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound has a >99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer, so no further evaluation is needed unless bleeding recurs.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Transvaginal ultrasonography or endometrial biopsy are both appropriate initial diagnostic tests for postmenopausal bleeding. An ultrasound showing an endometrial stripe ≤4 mm is associated with a >99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer, and no further evaluation is needed unless the bleeding is recurrent. If bleeding is persistent or recurrent, a tissue sample (endometrial biopsy) would be appropriate. If biopsy is non-diagnostic and bleeding continues to persist or recur, further evaluation with hysteroscopy and curettage would be indicated.

explanation_raw: Transvaginal ultrasonography or endometrial biopsy are both appropriate initial diagnostic tests for postmenopausal bleeding. An ultrasound showing an endometrial stripe ≤4 mm is associated with a >99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer and no further evaluation is needed unless the bleeding is recurrent. If bleeding is persistent or recurrent, then a tissue sample would be appropriate. If an endometrial biopsy is not helpful and bleeding continues to persist or recur, then further evaluation with hysteroscopy and curettage would be indicated.

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with shoulder pain after having fallen on his arm in an outstretched position. He reports a sensation of catching and popping in the shoulder. With the patient seated and hands placed on his hips, you apply force to the elbow and direct the humerus anteriorly and superiorly, while asking the patient to resist your motion, which produces pain in the affected shoulder. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: A positive anterior slide test combined with a history of catching or popping sensation after a fall on an outstretched arm is highly suggestive of a glenoid labral tear, with a positive likelihood ratio of 6.0.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The anterior slide test is performed with the patient seated, hands on hips, as the examiner applies anterior and superior directed force to the elbow. This test, when positive alongside a catching or popping sensation, has a positive likelihood ratio of 6.0 for diagnosing a glenoid labral tear, making it a clinically significant finding in the workup of shoulder instability following trauma.

bullets.text: Acromioclavicular arthritis, adhesive capsulitis, glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and rotator cuff tears each have distinct clinical presentations and are not associated with catching or popping sensations, nor are they identified by the anterior slide test.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acromioclavicular joint arthritis presents with superior shoulder pain and a positive cross-body adduction test. Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by diffuse pain and restricted passive range of motion. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis typically presents with gradual onset pain and loss of motion in older patients. Rotator cuff tears present with pain and weakness on overhead activities, identified by the empty can and external rotation tests. None of these conditions are associated with a catching or popping sensation, and the anterior slide and crank tests are not specific for these diagnoses.

explanation_raw: This patient's history of a catching or popping sensation combined with a positive anterior slide test, as described in the physical examination, is highly suggestive of a glenoid labral tear. This combination of history and the positive anterior slide test has a positive likelihood ratio of 6.0 in diagnosing a glenoid labral tear. Acromioclavicular joint arthritis presents with superior shoulder pain and tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint, often with a positive cross-body adduction test. Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by diffuse shoulder pain and restricted passive range of motion. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis usually presents with a gradual onset of pain and loss of motion, particularly in older patients. A rotator cuff tear typically presents with pain and weakness, especially with overhead activities, and positive findings on the empty can and external rotation tests. Acromioclavicular joint arthritis, adhesive capsulitis, glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and rotator cuff tears are not associated with catching or popping sensations, and the crank and anterior slide tests are not specific for these conditions.

stem: According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which one of the following is the recommended next step for adults who screen positive for unhealthy alcohol use?

choices.E: Referral for alcohol use disorder treatment

bullets.text: The USPSTF recommends screening all adults for unhealthy alcohol use and providing brief counseling interventions for those who screen positive (B recommendation), using the SBIRT approach.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF recommends screening all adults for unhealthy alcohol use and implementing brief counseling interventions for those who screen positive (B recommendation). The screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT) approach has been shown to decrease the number of patients with risky drinking after the intervention. Motivational interviewing is commonly used as the brief counseling technique in primary care settings.

bullets.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, and interpersonal psychotherapy are longer-term approaches not appropriate as brief interventions; patients meeting DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder (AUD) should be referred for formal treatment rather than managed with brief counseling alone.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, and interpersonal psychotherapy are different psychotherapy modalities used as longer-term counseling methods and would not be appropriate for use as brief counseling interventions for adults with unhealthy alcohol use. Patients identified as having alcohol use disorder (AUD) by DSM-5 criteria should be referred for specialized treatment rather than managed solely with brief primary care interventions.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening all adults for unhealthy alcohol use and implementing brief counseling interventions for those who screen positive (B recommendation). The screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT) approach has been shown to decrease the number of patients with risky drinking after the intervention. Motivational interviewing is often used for brief counseling in primary care settings. Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, and interpersonal psychotherapy are different psychotherapy approaches that are used as longer-term counseling methods and would not be appropriate for use as brief counseling interventions for adults with unhealthy alcohol use. Patients identified as having alcohol use disorder (AUD) by DSM-5 criteria should be referred for treatment.
