stem: A 30-year-old female presents with constipation and severe anal pain following bowel movements. On examination, you observe an anal fissure. In addition to increasing fluids, fiber, and warm sitz baths, which one of the following would be effective and least likely to result in side effects?

bullets.text: Topical calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem) are the preferred first-line sphincter relaxant for anal fissures due to their efficacy and favorable side effect profile compared to topical nitroglycerin.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For anal fissures, topical sphincter relaxants applied externally around the anus 2–4 times per day help reduce sphincter tone and promote healing. Topical calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem are best tolerated. Topical nitroglycerin is also effective but is associated with more side effects such as headaches and lightheadedness, causing approximately 1 in 5 patients to discontinue therapy. Botulinum toxin injections are another effective option. Topical capsaicin should be avoided as it is an irritant, and oral calcium channel blockers are not effective for anal fissures.

explanation_raw: For anal fissures, topical sphincter relaxants applied externally around the anus 2–4 times per day help reduce sphincter tone and promote healing. Topical calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem are best tolerated. Topical nitroglycerin is also effective but is associated with more side effects such as headaches and lightheadedness, which results in 1 in 5 patients stopping therapy. Botulinum toxin is also effective. Topical capsaicin is an irritant. Oral calcium channel blockers are not effective for treatment of anal fissures.

stem: Which one of the following interventions lowers the risk of diverticulitis?

choices.A: Avoiding consumption of popcorn, nuts, and seeds

bullets.text: A vegetarian diet lowers the risk of diverticulitis, while red meat consumption, long-term NSAID use, tobacco use, obesity, and lack of exercise are known risk factors.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Diverticulitis is an inflammation of diverticula caused by protrusion through the intestinal wall. Risk factors include constipation, a low-fiber diet, increasing age, red meat consumption, smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, aspirin and NSAID use, and genetic susceptibility. Consuming a vegetarian diet may help prevent diverticulitis. Notably, consumption of nuts, seeds, and popcorn is NOT a risk factor for diverticulitis (SOR B), contrary to older teaching.

bullets.text: Left lower quadrant tenderness is the most specific physical finding; workup includes CBC, basic metabolic panel, CRP, urinalysis, and CT with contrast if the diagnosis is uncertain.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The incidence of diverticulitis is increasing, yet routine screening is not recommended. Tenderness in the left lower quadrant is the most specific finding on exam. Evaluation includes a CBC, basic metabolic panel, C-reactive protein level, and urinalysis. CT with contrast is the imaging modality of choice when the diagnosis is uncertain.

bullets.text: Treatment is based on severity and ranges from oral antibiotics and a clear liquid diet for mild cases to IV antibiotics, bowel rest, or surgery for abscess, peritonitis, or recurrent disease.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment of diverticulitis is guided by severity. Mild cases may be managed with oral antibiotics and a clear liquid diet. More severe cases require hospitalization with IV antibiotics and bowel rest. Surgical management is indicated for complications such as abscess formation or peritonitis, as well as for prevention of recurrences.

explanation_raw: Diverticulitis is an inflammation of diverticula caused by a protrusion through the intestinal wall. Risk factors include constipation, a low-fiber diet, increasing age, red meat consumption, smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, aspirin and NSAID use, and genetic susceptibility. Consuming a vegetarian diet may help to prevent diverticulitis. Red meat intake, long-term NSAID use, and tobacco use are risk factors for diverticulitis. After years of research, it was concluded that consumption of nuts, seeds, and popcorn is not a risk factor for diverticulitis (SOR B). The incidence of diverticulitis is increasing, yet screening is not recommended. Tenderness located in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen is the most specific finding of diverticulitis. Evaluation includes a CBC, a basic metabolic panel, a C-reactive protein level, and urine analysis. CT with contrast is the imaging modality of choice if the diagnosis is uncertain. Treatment is based on severity and includes oral and intravenous antibiotics, bowel rest and a clear liquid diet, and surgical management for abscess formation or peritonitis as well as for prevention of recurrences.

stem: An 82-year-old male presents to your office because he has been experiencing severe, stabbing pain that feels like an electric shock on the left side of his face in his cheek, lips, and chin. The episodes are usually triggered by light touch or eating and last for a few seconds. Which one of the following cranial nerves is associated with this disorder?

bullets.text: Trigeminal neuralgia involves severe paroxysmal pain in the distribution of cranial nerve V (trigeminal), classically triggered by light touch or eating and lasting seconds.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by severe paroxysms of electric shock-like pain in the distribution of one or more branches of cranial nerve V. In this patient, the pain involves the cheek, lips, and chin on the left side — consistent with the V2 (maxillary) and V3 (mandibular) branches of CN V. The episodes are brief (seconds) and triggered by light touch or eating, which are hallmark features of this condition.

bullets.text: Other cranial nerves produce distinct deficits: CN VII causes facial muscle paralysis (Bell's palsy), CN X causes dysphagia/dysphonia, CN XI causes neck weakness, and CN XII causes tongue paralysis — none of which match this presentation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Impairment of cranial nerve VII (facial nerve) results in paralysis of facial muscles, as seen in Bell's palsy — not pain. Cranial nerve X (vagus) involvement may cause dysphagia and dysphonia. Cranial nerve XI (accessory) damage results in neck and shoulder weakness, and cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal) damage leads to tongue paralysis. None of these cranial nerves are responsible for the sensory pain distribution described in this case.

explanation_raw: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by severe paroxysms of pain in the distribution of 1 or more branches of cranial nerve V. Impairment of cranial nerve VII results in paralysis of facial muscles, such as Bell palsy. Impairment of cranial nerve X may cause dysphagia and dysphonia, cranial nerve XI involvement results in neck weakness, and cranial nerve XII damage leads to tongue paralysis.

stem: Which one of the following social determinants of health has a protective effective against Alzheimer disease and related types of dementia?

bullets.text: Higher levels of social engagement have a protective effect against Alzheimer disease and related dementias (ADRDs), while many other social determinants of health increase risk.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions in which people are born, work, live, and age, as well as the wider set of forces and systems shaping daily life. Among these, higher levels of social engagement are protective against ADRDs. In contrast, SDOH such as decreasing BMI with older age, early-life adversity, low education level, food insecurity, midlife obesity, manual labor, and low socioeconomic status are all associated with a greater risk of developing ADRDs.

explanation_raw: Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions in which people are born, work, live, and age as well as the wider set of forces and systems that shape the conditions of daily life. Several SDOH affect cognition and risk of Alzheimer disease and related dementias (ADRDs). For example, higher levels of social engagement have a protective effect against ADRDs. Conversely, SDOH such as decreasing BMI with older age, early-life adversity, low education level, food insecurity, midlife obesity, manual labor, and low socioeconomic status are associated with a greater risk of ADRDs.

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to your office for evaluation of muscle aches and fatigue. His current medications include rosuvastatin (Crestor), dapagliflozin (Farxiga), and semaglutide (Ozempic). Over the past month he has noticed increasing pain in his hips, thighs, and shoulders without any apparent trigger. He feels so stiff in the morning that it is becoming difficult to get out of bed. On examination his strength is diminished (4/5) in the proximal muscle groups. You do not note any swelling or redness of any joints, muscles, or extremities. He has normal reflexes and no clonus. Laboratory Findings Hemoglobin A1c 6.4% Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL (N 13.2–16.6) Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (N 0.7–1.3) Potassium 4.2 mEq/L (N 3.5–5.1) Creatine kinase 84 U/L (N 55–170) Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 88 mm/hr (N 0–20) C-reactive protein 9.2 mg/L (N 0–0.3) Antinuclear antibody <1:40 (N <1:40) Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's myalgias?

bullets.text: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) presents in adults ≥50 with proximal muscle pain/fatigue, elevated ESR and CRP, mild anemia, and a characteristically normal creatine kinase level.
bullets.sub_paragraph: PMR is an inflammatory condition diagnosed clinically in older adults. Key features include proximal muscle pain (hips, thighs, shoulders), fatigue, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP), and mild anemia. A normal creatine kinase level is an important distinguishing feature. It is treated with oral glucocorticoids, and rapid improvement is expected; lack of response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. PMR is also associated with giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis), which can cause temporal headaches, visual changes, and risks permanent vision loss if untreated.

bullets.text: Fibromyalgia does not cause elevated inflammatory markers; polymyositis and statin-induced myopathy typically elevate creatine kinase; and SLE is associated with a positive ANA — none of which are present in this patient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not produce elevated ESR, CRP, or anemia. Polymyositis and statin-induced myopathy (rosuvastatin being a potential culprit) both typically cause elevations in creatine kinase, which this patient lacks. Systemic lupus erythematosus almost universally presents with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer, which is absent here. The combination of proximal myalgias, elevated inflammatory markers, normal CK, and age >50 strongly favors PMR over these alternatives.

explanation_raw: These findings are concerning for polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), an inflammatory condition that typically affects adults ≥50 years of age. This patient's proximal muscle pain, fatigue, and decreased proximal muscle strength are consistent with this diagnosis, as are the elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level) and mild anemia. A normal creatine kinase level is expected in patients with PMR. PMR is diagnosed clinically and treated with oral glucocorticoids. Rapid improvement with therapy is expected; if improvement does not occur, an alternate diagnosis should be explored. Giant cell arteritis, also known as temporal arteritis, is associated with PMR. It causes temporal headaches, visual changes, and constitutional symptoms. Early identification and treatment are essential to prevent permanent vision change. Fibromyalgia does not cause elevated inflammatory markers. Polymyositis and statininduced myopathy may cause myalgias but are typically associated with elevations in creatine kinase, which this patient does not have. Almost all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus have an elevated antinuclear antibody titer, which this patient also does not have.

stem: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends which one of the following regarding screening asymptomatic adolescents and adults for herpes simplex virus?

bullets.text: The USPSTF gives a Grade D recommendation against routine serologic screening for HSV in asymptomatic adolescents and adults, including pregnant patients, concluding with moderate certainty that harms outweigh benefits.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The USPSTF concluded with moderate certainty that the harms outweigh the benefits for routine, population-based serologic screening for herpes simplex virus (HSV) in asymptomatic adolescents and adults, including pregnant patients (Grade D recommendation). High false-positive rates are common when serologic testing is performed in asymptomatic individuals, and treatment is not recommended even for those who test positive without symptoms. Therefore, no testing is the recommended approach for this population.

explanation_raw: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force concluded with moderate certainty that the harms outweighed the benefits for routine, population-based serologic screening for infection with herpes simplex virus (HSV) in asymptomatic adolescents and adults, including pregnant patients (D recommendation). High false-positive rates are common in asymptomatic patients who undergo serologic testing for infection with HSV. In addition, treatment is not recommended in asymptomatic patients with a positive test.

stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the urgent care clinic by their parents with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. The child has been irritable over the past 2 days with intermittent abdominal pain and several episodes of associated emesis, and just had a bloody stool that the parents describe as resembling jelly. The child appears uncomfortable but is alert and afebrile, with normal blood pressure. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

bullets.text: Intussusception presents with a classic triad of intermittent abdominal pain, emesis, and 'red currant jelly' (blood-tinged mucous) stools, most commonly at the ileocolic junction in infants and toddlers.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Intussusception occurs when a segment of intestine telescopes into an adjacent section. It classically presents with the triad of intermittent colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and blood-tinged mucous stools ('red currant jelly' stools). It most commonly occurs at the ileocolic junction and typically affects infants and toddlers aged 6 months to 3 years. Initial evaluation begins with ultrasonography, and an air or contrast enema can both confirm and reduce the intussusception. Surgical correction is required if the enema fails.

bullets.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis, pyloric stenosis, and volvulus can each cause abdominal pain and vomiting, but none characteristically produce the 'red currant jelly' bloody stools seen in intussusception.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Necrotizing enterocolitis typically presents with severe abdominal pain, lethargy, and hemodynamic instability, usually in premature neonates. Pyloric stenosis is characterized by projectile (non-bloody) vomiting in young infants without bloody stools. Volvulus presents with sudden-onset vomiting and abdominal pain and possible distension, but bloody stools are not a hallmark feature. The combination of intermittent pain, vomiting, and 'red currant jelly' stools in a toddler specifically points to intussusception.

explanation_raw: Intussusception is a condition in which a part of the intestine slides or "telescopes" into an adjacent section. It presents with a classic triad of intermittent abdominal pain, emesis, and blood-tinged mucous stools that are sometimes called "red currant jelly" stools. It most commonly occurs at the ileocolic junction and typically affects infants and toddlers. The initial evaluation begins with ultrasonography. An enema with air or contrast can both confirm the diagnosis and reverse the intussusception. If this procedure does not relieve the condition, surgical correction is necessary. Necrotizing enterocolitis is a severe intestinal infection that typically presents with severe abdominal pain, lethargy, and unstable vital signs. Pyloric stenosis is notable for projectile vomiting, but not bloody stools. Volvulus typically involves a sudden onset of vomiting and abdominal pain and even distension, but without bloody stools.

stem: A generally healthy 54-year-old male with a 20-pack-year smoking history presents to discuss smoking cessation. His first grandchild was just born and he is eager for help in quitting cigarette smoking. He quit smoking 2 years ago using nicotine gum (Nicorette Gum), but resumed smoking 5 months later. He has also explored telephone helplines and support groups, but did not find them beneficial. He currently smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day. Which one of the following would be most likely to help this patient quit smoking?

bullets.text: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation (NNT=7), and combining varenicline with NRT is more effective than either alone or bupropion plus NRT.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Seven FDA-approved pharmacotherapies exist for smoking cessation: varenicline, bupropion, and five forms of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT). Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy compared to NRT and bupropion, with a number needed to treat of 7. Recent meta-analyses demonstrate that combination pharmacotherapy is superior to monotherapy, and specifically that varenicline plus NRT yields higher rates of sustained smoking cessation compared to bupropion plus NRT. For this patient who previously failed NRT monotherapy (nicotine gum), the combination of varenicline plus nicotine gum represents the most evidence-based and effective approach.

explanation_raw: Seven pharmacotherapies are approved by the FDA for smoking cessation, including bupropion, varenicline, and 5 forms of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT). All of these have been shown to be beneficial in smoking cessation compared to placebo. Compared to NRT and bupropion, varenicline appears to be the most effective monotherapy with a number needed to treat of 7. Recent meta-analyses suggest that a combination of pharmacotherapies is more effective than monotherapy. Varenicline plus NRT is more likely to result in sustained smoking cessation compared to bupropion plus NRT.

stem: A 60-year-old female returns to discuss management of her recurrent nephrolithiasis. She has a history of calcium stones and just recently passed her fourth stone this year despite appropriate lifestyle changes, including a fluid intake of 3 L per day and a diet high in fiber and low in animal protein. She would like a medication to help prevent the development of more kidney stones. She has a past medical history of asthma for which she takes a budesonide/formoterol inhaler (Symbicort) as needed. Today, her vital signs and a physical examination are normal. A recent basic metabolic panel was normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate prevention strategy?

bullets.text: When lifestyle modifications fail to prevent recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated with high-dose thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg daily), allopurinol, or potassium citrate.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Lifestyle changes such as appropriate fluid intake (2.5–3.0 L per day), a high-fiber/low-animal-protein diet, lower sodium intake (<4–5 g per day), and moderate calcium intake (1200 mg per day) can reduce calcium stone recurrence. However, when patients continue to form recurrent stones despite these measures, pharmacologic therapy is warranted. First-line options include high-dose thiazide diuretics, allopurinol, and potassium citrate, all of which have evidence supporting reduction in stone recurrence.

bullets.text: Furosemide increases urinary calcium excretion and is associated with kidney stone formation; magnesium oxide has not been shown to reduce stone development; and tamsulosin aids stone expulsion but does not prevent new stone formation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Furosemide (a loop diuretic) promotes hypercalciuria and is actually associated with nephrolithiasis, making it contraindicated in this setting. Magnesium oxide lacks sufficient evidence for stone prevention. Tamsulosin (an alpha-blocker) relaxes ureteral smooth muscle to facilitate passage of existing stones but has no role in preventing future stone formation.

explanation_raw: Lifestyle changes such as appropriate fluid intake (2.5–3.0 L of liquid per day), a diet high in fiber and low in animal protein, lower sodium intake (<4–5 g per day), and moderate calcium intake (1200 mg per day) can help reduce recurrence of calcium stones. However, if patients continue to develop recurrent calcium stones, it is reasonable to initiate pharmacologic therapy. Appropriate medications include high-dose thiazide diuretics, allopurinol, and potassium citrate. Furosemide would not be appropriate as it has been associated with kidney stone formation. Magnesium oxide has not been shown to decrease the risk of stone development. Tamsulosin can be used to help with stone expulsion, but it does not help to prevent stones.

stem: A 72-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after her neighbor found her on the floor in her home. She is drowsy and confused, and unable to provide any history. An initial laboratory evaluation reveals the following: Glucose 95 mg/dL BUN 9 mg/dL (N 6–20) Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (N 0.5–1.1) Estimated glomerular filtration rate 63 mL/min/1.73 m2 Sodium 118 mEq/L (N 135–145) Potassium 3.0 mEq/L (N 3.3 –5.0) Chloride 88 mEq/L (N 101–115) Bicarbonate 22 mEq/L (N 16–30) Anion gap 8 mEq/L (N 5–14) Calcium 8.8 mg/dL (N 8.4–10.5) Which one of the following would be the most appropriate intervention at this time?

bullets.text: Symptomatic severe hyponatremia (Na <125 mEq/L) should be treated with a 100-mL bolus of 3% hypertonic saline, which may be repeated up to 2 times at 10-minute intervals to raise sodium by 4–6 mEq/L.
bullets.sub_paragraph: This patient presents with symptomatic severe hyponatremia (sodium level <125 mEq/L). The most appropriate intervention is a 100-mL bolus of 3% hypertonic saline (SOR B), which may be repeated up to 2 times at 10-minute intervals with the goal of increasing the sodium level by 4–6 mEq/L. Serum sodium levels should be monitored after every bolus and every 6 hours during the first 24 hours of treatment (SOR C).

bullets.text: Rapid correction of severe hyponatremia must be avoided to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome; correction should be limited to 8–12 mEq/L over 24 hours or 18 mEq/L over 48 hours.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Avoiding rapid correction of severe hyponatremia is critical to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Depending on risk factors, sodium correction should be limited to 8–12 mEq/L over 24 hours or 18 mEq/L over 48 hours (SOR C).

bullets.text: Normal saline is appropriate only for nonsevere hypovolemic hyponatremia (Na ≥125 mEq/L); IV desmopressin (DDAVP) is indicated for diabetes insipidus or overcorrection of hyponatremia, not initial treatment of severe hyponatremia.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Normal saline is appropriate treatment for nonsevere hypovolemic hyponatremia (a sodium level ≥125 mEq/L but <135 mEq/L), not for symptomatic severe hyponatremia. Intravenous desmopressin (DDAVP) is indicated for treatment of diabetes insipidus, which usually presents with high-normal sodium levels or hypernatremia. Desmopressin may also be given with 5% dextrose in water if overcorrection of severe hyponatremia has occurred, but it is not the initial treatment of choice here.

explanation_raw: This patient presents with symptomatic severe hyponatremia (sodium level <125 mEq/L). The most appropriate intervention at this time is a 100-mL bolus of 3% hypertonic saline (SOR B), which may be repeated up to 2 times at 10-minute intervals with the goal of increasing the sodium level by 4–6 mEq/L. Serum sodium levels should be monitored after every bolus and every 6 hours during the first 24 hours of treatment (SOR C). Avoiding rapid correction of severe hyponatremia is important to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Depending on risk factors, sodium correction should be limited to 8–12 mEq/L over 24 hours or 18 mEq/L over 48 hours (SOR C). The use of normal saline is appropriate treatment for nonsevere hypovolemic hyponatremia (a sodium level ≥125 mEq/L but <135 mEq/L). Intravenous desmopressin (DDAVP) is indicated for treatment of diabetes insipidus, which usually presents with highnormal sodium levels or hypernatremia. Desmopressin may also be given with 5% dextrose in water if overcorrection of severe hyponatremia has occurred.

stem: A 35-year-old construction worker presents to your office with an acute onset of lower back pain that began 3 days ago. The patient describes the pain as a burning sensation that radiates down his left leg. He has no bowel or bladder dysfunction and has been in good health. A straight leg–raising test is positive at 45° on the left without motor deficit. Which one of the following does evidence support as the first step in treatment of this patient's condition?

bullets.text: For acute lumbar radiculopathy without red flags, conservative management with mobilization and manipulation is first-line, supported by level B evidence.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In the absence of red flags (fracture, malignancy, epidural abscess, or cauda equina syndrome), the approach to acute lumbar radiculopathy should be conservative. Most patients improve over the first 2 weeks, and there is level B evidence that mobilization and manipulation is of benefit. Bed rest was previously recommended, but current data supports allowing the patient to be as active as the pain allows. While corticosteroids, NSAIDs, and muscle relaxants are often used, evidence to support their use is lacking. In the subacute stage, neurodynamic mobilization and strength training can be added. If there is no improvement over 6 weeks, MRI should be ordered.

explanation_raw: In the absence of red flags (fracture, malignancy, epidural abscess, or cauda equina syndrome), the approach to acute lumbar radiculopathy should be conservative. Most patients improve over the first 2 weeks, and there is level B evidence that mobilization and manipulation is of benefit. Bed rest was previously recommended, but current data supports allowing the patient to be as active as the pain allows. While corticosteroids, NSAIDs, and muscle relaxants are often used, evidence to do so is lacking. In the subacute stage, neurodynamic mobilization and strength training could be added. If there is no improvement over 6 weeks, then MRI should be ordered.

stem: A 46-year-old male with chronic hypertension presents to your clinic for routine follow-up. Due to issues with insurance coverage, he has not been taking his antihypertensive medications for the last 2 months. Today, he is asymptomatic and an examination is normal, except for a blood pressure of 162/100 mm Hg, which is confirmed on repeat testing. In addition to addressing insurance and social determinants of health, which one of the following would be most appropriate for this patient?

choices.A: Monotherapy with a calcium channel blocker (CC
choices.C: Combination therapy with a CCB and an ACE inhibitor
choices.D: Combination therapy with a diuretic and a β-blocker
choices.E: Combination therapy with a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist

correct_label: Combination therapy with a CCB and an ACE inhibitor

bullets.text: This patient has stage 2 hypertension, defined as systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥100 mmHg (or >20/10 mmHg above goal).
bullets.sub_paragraph: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg or a diastolic blood pressure ≥100 mm Hg (or a systolic blood pressure >20 mm Hg above goal or a diastolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg above goal). This classification is important because it drives the recommendation for combination therapy rather than monotherapy.

bullets.text: The vast majority of patients with essential hypertension require 2 or more agents for adequate control; combination therapy with a CCB and an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the preferred first-line approach for stage 2 hypertension.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Monotherapy is unlikely to achieve adequate blood pressure control in stage 2 hypertension. Combination therapy with a calcium channel blocker (CCB) and an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) is most appropriate. Race-based prescribing that advises preferential use of thiazides or CCBs for Black patients has demonstrated insufficient blood pressure control and is falling out of favor. β-Blockers are not first-line for hypertension unless specific comorbidities (e.g., coronary artery disease, heart failure) are present. Aldosterone antagonists are reserved for cases where multiple drug classes fail to achieve adequate control.

explanation_raw: The vast majority of patients treated for essential hypertension will require 2 or more agents to achieve adequate blood pressure control. Combination therapy with a calcium channel blocker and an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) would be most appropriate for this patient with stage 2 hypertension. Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg or a diastolic blood pressure ≥100 mm Hg (or a systolic blood pressure >20 mm Hg above goal or a diastolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg above goal). Race-based prescribing, which advises preferential use of thiazide or calcium channel blockers for Black patients, has demonstrated insufficient blood pressure control and is thus falling out of favor. β-Blockers are not used as first-line treatment for hypertension, but they may be indicated in patients with specific comorbidities, such as coronary artery disease or heart failure. Aldosterone antagonists are also not typically used as first-line treatment for hypertension, but they may be used if multiple other drug classes cannot achieve adequate blood pressure control. Monotherapy is unlikely to produce adequate blood pressure control in this patient.

stem: A 14-year-old female presents to your office with her mother who is concerned about her daughter's recent 15-lb weight loss and severe fatigue. After ruling out other etiologies, you diagnose anorexia nervosa. Which one of the following findings, if present in this patient, would indicate the need for inpatient care?

bullets.text: A potassium level of 2.6 mEq/L represents severe hypokalemia and indicates the need for inpatient care in anorexia nervosa, as it can lead to life-threatening cardiac complications.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Eating disorders can often be managed in the outpatient setting with a multidisciplinary team including physicians, therapists, and dietitians. However, severe electrolyte abnormalities — such as a potassium of 2.6 mEq/L (normal 3.5–4.9 mEq/L) — require a higher level of care due to the risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Other findings commonly seen in eating disorders, such as hair loss, muscle atrophy, parotid gland enlargement, and mildly elevated sodium, do not independently mandate inpatient admission.

explanation_raw: A potassium level of 2.6 mEq/L would indicate the need for inpatient care of this patient's anorexia nervosa. Eating disorders can often be treated in the outpatient setting with a multidisciplinary care team including physicians, therapists, and dietitians. However, certain findings, including severe hypokalemia, require higher levels of care. While hair loss, muscle atrophy, parotid gland enlargement, and elevated sodium can all be found in patients with eating disorders, severe electrolyte abnormalities can lead to life-threatening cardiac complications and require immediate treatment.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents to your office for an annual wellness visit. She reports a family history of Lynch syndrome and recently tested positive herself. Which one of the following should you recommend regarding colon cancer screening in this patient?

bullets.text: Patients with Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) should begin colonoscopy screening between ages 20–25 and repeat every 1–2 years, regardless of current age.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), formerly called Lynch syndrome, significantly elevates colorectal cancer risk. Guidelines recommend initiating colonoscopy screening between ages 20 and 25 (or earlier based on family history) and repeating every 1–2 years. This contrasts with average-risk individuals, who begin screening at age 45. Since this 30-year-old patient has already confirmed Lynch syndrome, colonoscopy should be recommended starting this year.

bullets.text: Fecal occult blood testing, stool DNA testing, and sigmoidoscopy are insufficient screening modalities for this high-risk population; colonoscopy is the required standard.
bullets.sub_paragraph: In high-risk patients such as those with Lynch syndrome, less sensitive or less complete tests (fecal occult blood testing, stool DNA testing, flexible sigmoidoscopy) are not considered adequate substitutes for full colonoscopy. Colonoscopy allows visualization and biopsy of the entire colon, which is essential given the elevated and distributed cancer risk in Lynch syndrome patients.

bullets.text: Lynch syndrome also confers increased risk for endometrial, ovarian, stomach, small-bowel, and pancreatic cancers, requiring broader surveillance beyond colonoscopy.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Lynch syndrome is not limited to colorectal cancer risk. Affected individuals have elevated risks for endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small-bowel, and pancreatic cancers, among others. Clinicians should counsel patients on comprehensive cancer surveillance strategies and consider referral to genetic counseling services for ongoing management and family screening guidance.

explanation_raw: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), formerly called Lynch syndrome, is a hereditary cancer syndrome that increases the risk for several types of cancer, especially colon cancer. Guidelines recommend that patients with HNPCC should start colon cancer screening with colonoscopy between 20 and 25 years of age and repeat every 1–2 years. Patients at average risk for colon cancer should begin colon cancer screening at age 45. Fecal occult blood testing, stool DNA testing, and sigmoidoscopy are not adequate screening tests in this high-risk population. Lynch syndrome is associated with increased risk for several other cancers including endometrial, ovarian, stomach, small-bowel, and pancreatic.

stem: A 53-year-old male without a significant past medical history presents to the emergency department for evaluation of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Pertinent findings on presentation include notable tenderness in the epigastrium and a lipase level >3 times the upper limit of normal. He is admitted for acute pancreatitis. Intravenous lactated Ringer solution, antiemetics, and pain control are initiated. At the time of your evaluation he has normal vital signs and reports improved symptoms, although you still note abdominal tenderness. When entering admission orders for this patient, which one of the following diets would be most appropriate?

bullets.text: Patients with acute pancreatitis should be started on a low-fat solid diet early (within 24 hours of admission), as this is associated with shorter hospital stays compared to liquid or soft diets.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Acute pancreatitis increases caloric needs due to intense inflammation and reduces intestinal mucosal perfusion, leading to increased gut permeability. Early enteral feeding within 24 hours improves splanchnic blood flow, bowel wall integrity, and gut motility. A Cochrane review demonstrated that enteral nutrition is associated with lower mortality, less multiple organ failure, and less systemic infection compared with parenteral nutrition — benefits that are even more pronounced in severe acute pancreatitis (RR of death 0.18, 95% CI 0.06–0.58). Liquid and soft diets have no evidence of benefit over a low-fat solid diet, and some studies show a shorter length of stay with solid diets. If oral intake is not tolerated within 72 hours, nasogastric or nasojejunal tube feeding should be initiated; parenteral nutrition is reserved for those who cannot tolerate enteral feeding.

bullets.text: Low-carbohydrate diets are not recommended in acute pancreatitis because they tend to be high in fat, which can worsen pancreatic inflammation.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Low-carbohydrate diets are contraindicated in acute pancreatitis as their higher fat content may exacerbate pancreatic inflammation. Liquid and soft diets, while historically used, lack evidence of superiority over a low-fat solid diet and may prolong hospitalization. Parenteral nutrition is not the preferred initial approach; it is reserved only for patients who cannot tolerate enteral or oral feeding, as it carries higher risks of infection and organ failure compared to enteral nutrition.

explanation_raw: Pancreatitis is associated with an intense inflammatory response that increases caloric needs, and nutrition management is a key component of care. Acute pancreatitis is also associated with reduced perfusion of the intestinal mucosa, leading to tissue damage and increased intestinal permeability. Enteral feeding provides calories and increases splanchnic blood flow, leading to improved integrity of the bowel wall and improved gut motility. Patients with acute pancreatitis benefit from early enteral feeding within 24 hours of admission. A Cochrane review found that enteral nutrition has been associated with lower mortality, less multiple organ failure, and less systemic infection compared with parenteral nutrition. In severe acute pancreatitis, the benefits of enteral nutrition appear to be even more notable with a relative risk of death of 0.18 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.58). Liquid and soft diets have no evidence of benefit over a low-fat solid diet, and some studies found a shorter length of stay in patients started on solid diets rather than liquid diets. If patients cannot tolerate an oral diet within 72 hours, enteral nutrition should be provided via nasogastric or nasojejunal tube. Parenteral nutrition should be administered in patients who cannot tolerate tube feeding. Low-carbohydrate diets are not recommended because they are often high in fat and may worsen pancreatic inflammation.

stem: A healthy 57-year-old female presents for an annual health maintenance visit. Her last menstrual period was 2 years ago. She exercises 5 times per week, does not smoke, and rarely drinks alcohol. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her 80-year-old mother has no history of fractures, but takes alendronate (Fosamax), 70 mg weekly. According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which one of the following would be the preferred strategy to screen for osteoporosis in this patient?

choices.A: Using the FRAX tool now to determine the need for DXA screening
choices.B: Using the FRAX tool at age 65 to determine the need for DXA screening

bullets.text: Per USPSTF, routine osteoporosis screening with DXA begins at age 65 for all women, regardless of risk factors; postmenopausal women under 65 are only screened early if they have significant risk factors such as smoking, heavy alcohol use, or parental history of hip fracture.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Per USPSTF, routine osteoporosis screening with DXA begins at age 65 for all women, regardless of risk factors. Postmenopausal women under 65 qualify for earlier screening only if they have additional risk factors such as smoking, excessive alcohol use, or a parental history of hip fracture. This patient is a healthy 57-year-old with a normal BMI, no smoking or alcohol use, and regular exercise—her mother takes alendronate but has no documented hip fracture, so this does not meet the USPSTF threshold for early screening. She should therefore wait until age 65 for DXA screening.

bullets.text: FRAX is a useful tool for counseling patients about future fracture risk but is not intended to determine who should undergo DXA screening.
bullets.sub_paragraph: FRAX calculates a 10-year probability of major osteoporotic or hip fracture and can guide treatment decisions or patient counseling. However, it is not a tool to identify which patients should receive DXA screening—that decision is governed by USPSTF age- and risk factor–based criteria. Conflating FRAX use with screening eligibility is a common error.

explanation_raw: According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), women ≥65 years of age should be screened for osteoporosis using DXA bone mineral density testing, regardless of fracture risk assessment. Postmenopausal women <65 years of age with 1 or more additional risk factors such as smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, or parental history of hip fracture should also be screened with DXA. This patient does not have any significant risk factors. Tools such as FRAX can be used to help counsel patients regarding the future risk of fracture, but they are not intended to be used to determine who should receive further screening with DXA.

stem: You are evaluating a patient with acute-on-chronic kidney disease and a serum potassium level of 6.5 mEq/L (N 3.3–5.0). In addition to peaked T waves, which one of the following additional electrocardiogram changes is most likely to be present?

bullets.text: Hyperkalemia produces a progressive sequence of ECG changes: peaked T waves → prolonged PR interval → loss of P waves → prolonged (widened) QRS interval, which signals severe, life-threatening toxicity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: As serum potassium rises above 5.0 mEq/L, the resting membrane potential is depolarized, slowing conduction throughout the cardiac system. Early changes include peaked (tall, narrow) T waves. With worsening hyperkalemia, the PR interval lengthens, P waves flatten and disappear, and the QRS complex widens. A prolonged QRS interval in the setting of hyperkalemia indicates severe toxicity and is associated with progression to bradycardia, junctional rhythm, ventricular fibrillation, and death within hours if untreated.

bullets.text: ECG findings such as flattened T waves, prolonged QT, ST depression, U waves, and delta waves are not associated with hyperkalemia—they reflect hypokalemia or other conditions like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Flattened T waves, prolonged QT interval, ST segment depression, U waves, and T-wave inversion are characteristic of hypokalemia (potassium <3.5 mEq/L), not hyperkalemia. Delta waves (a slurred upstroke on the QRS) are the hallmark of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome due to an accessory conduction pathway and are entirely unrelated to potassium disorders. Recognizing these distinctions prevents misidentification of the underlying electrolyte disturbance on ECG.

explanation_raw: Hyperkalemia (potassium level >5.0 mEq/L) can occur with impaired renal excretion, transcellular shifts, and increased potassium intake. Management of severe hyperkalemia includes using diagnostic EKG to identify cardiac conditions requiring emergent treatment. EKG changes associated with hyperkalemia include peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, loss of P waves, and prolonged QRS interval. Hyperkalemia resulting in prolonged QRS interval, bradycardia, and junctional rhythm is associated with adverse events, including ventricular fibrillation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and death within 6 hours of measurement. Findings associated with hypokalemia (potassium level <3.5 mEq/L) include flattened T waves, prolonged QT interval, ST segment depression, U waves, and Twave inversion. Delta waves are not associated with potassium disorders but are present in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

stem: A 15-year-old male comes to your clinic 30 minutes after being hit in the face by a baseball during practice. He is alert and answers questions appropriately. After clearing the blood, you find that his upper front tooth (No. 8) is quite loose and the root is visible. The tooth is lying lower than his other teeth. The tooth appears intact and without fracture. There is no crepitus or pain when palpating the alveolar and mandibular bones. You immediately call his dentist to arrange an emergency appointment. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step prior to sending the patient to the dentist's office?

choices.B: Repositioning the tooth in the socket and having the patient bite down on gauze
choices.C: Gently removing the tooth and placing it in saline or milk

correct_label: Repositioning the tooth in the socket and having the patient bite down on gauze

bullets.text: For a luxated or avulsed permanent tooth, immediate repositioning in the socket and having the patient bite down on gauze is the recommended first-line intervention; time is critical, as reimplantation after 1 hour has little chance of success.
bullets.sub_paragraph: For dislodged or fully avulsed permanent teeth, immediate reimplantation or repositioning is recommended (SOR C). If possible, replace the tooth in its anatomic position and have the patient bite down on a washcloth or gauze to keep it in place. It is not advised to remove a loose tooth, as the socket is the safest medium for the tooth. If the tooth is fully avulsed, hold it by the crown, rinse with saline, and reimplant. A tooth that cannot be reimplanted should be placed in saline solution or milk until definitive care is available.

bullets.text: Antibiotic treatment is not imperative at the time of acute injury, and immediate imaging is not necessary without evidence of dental or bony fracture, as it would only delay reimplantation and referral to a dentist.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Antibiotic treatment is not imperative at this time. Without evidence of a dental or bony fracture, immediate imaging is not necessary as it would delay reimplantation and referral to a dentist. Removing a loose tooth is also incorrect, as leaving it in the socket — or promptly repositioning it — provides the best chance of tooth survival.

explanation_raw: For dislodged or fully avulsed permanent teeth, immediate reimplantation or repositioning is recommended (SOR C). Time is imperative in saving teeth. If reimplantation does not occur within 1 hour, there is little likelihood that it will be successful. If possible, replace the tooth in its anatomic position and have the patient bite down on a washcloth or gauze to keep it in place. It is not advised to remove a loose tooth, as the safest medium for the tooth is the socket. If the tooth is fully avulsed, hold it by the crown, rinse with saline, and reimplant. A tooth that cannot be reimplanted should be placed in a saline solution or milk. Antibiotic treatment is not imperative at this time. Without evidence of a dental or bony fracture, immediate imaging is not necessary as it would delay reimplantation and referral to a dentist.

stem: A 50-year-old female presents for follow-up of laboratory studies. At her last visit, she presented with palpitations, anxiety, and unintentional weight loss. An examination was notable for exophthalmos. Her laboratory results show a very low TSH level with elevated free T4 and normal total T3 levels. A radioactive iodine uptake scan demonstrates a high, homogeneous uptake of iodine. Which one of the following medications is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?

bullets.text: This patient has Graves disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, characterized by exophthalmos, low TSH, elevated free T4, and diffusely high radioactive iodine uptake.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Graves disease can be differentiated from other causes of hyperthyroidism by radioactive iodine uptake pattern: diffusely elevated uptake in Graves disease, focal uptake in toxic adenoma, multiple foci in toxic multinodular goiter, and low uptake in thyroiditis. Classic symptoms include palpitations, anxiety, weight loss, and exophthalmos.

bullets.text: Methimazole is the preferred antithyroid medication for Graves disease due to its superior safety profile compared to propylthiouracil (PTU), which carries a higher risk of severe hepatotoxicity.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Treatment options for Graves disease include antithyroid medications (methimazole preferred, PTU second-line), radioactive iodine ablation, and surgical thyroidectomy. The notable exception is the first trimester of pregnancy, where PTU is preferred over methimazole due to methimazole's higher teratogenic risk. Treatment choice is otherwise guided by risks, benefits, and patient preference.

bullets.text: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, prednisone is reserved for thyroid storm, and verapamil (a calcium channel blocker) is only indicated for symptom control when beta-blockers are contraindicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Levothyroxine would worsen hyperthyroidism and is indicated for hypothyroidism. Prednisone may be used in severe hyperthyroidism such as thyroid storm but is not first-line for Graves disease. Calcium channel blockers like verapamil can manage adrenergic symptoms (e.g., palpitations) when beta-blockers cannot be used, but are not definitive therapy for Graves disease.

explanation_raw: This patient has hyperthyroidism, specifically Graves disease. Diffusely high radioactive iodine uptake differentiates Graves disease from other thyroid conditions, including toxic adenoma (high uptake concentrated in one spot), toxic multinodular goiter (high uptake in multiple spots), and thyroiditis (low uptake). Treatment options for Graves disease include antithyroid medications, radioactive iodine ablation, and surgical thyroidectomy. The most appropriate treatment is usually determined based on the risks and benefits of each option and patient preference. Methimazole is the preferred antithyroid medication for treatment of Graves disease due to its improved safety profile compared to propylthiouracil, which has a greater risk of severe liver injury. Pregnant patients in the first trimester should be treated with propylthiouracil because it has a lower teratogenic risk than methimazole. Levothyroxine is used to treat hypothyroidism. Prednisone is used to treat severe hyperthyroidism, such as thyroid storm. A calcium channel blocker such as verapamil would be indicated if a β-blocker is contraindicated or not tolerated.

stem: An 85-year-old male on the third day of hospitalization for the treatment of pneumonia develops symptoms of altered mental status. Evaluation of his medications does not identify a reason for his altered mental status. The nursing staff has been unable to successfully redirect him to keep him calm. Which one of the following medications would be appropriate for the management of the patient's delirium?

bullets.text: When non-pharmacologic redirection fails and no reversible cause is identified, second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine are the preferred agents for managing delirium in hospitalized patients.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness, and cognition. Initial management focuses on identifying and correcting underlying causes along with non-pharmacologic redirection. When these measures fail, pharmacologic intervention is warranted to ensure patient safety. Although no medications are FDA-approved specifically for delirium, second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine) are preferred over first-generation agents due to a more favorable side effect profile in older adults.

bullets.text: Haloperidol carries a higher risk of QT prolongation in elderly patients; benzodiazepines (lorazepam) worsen delirium in older adults; lithium is for chronic bipolar management; and oxycodone, while sedating, is not appropriate for delirium.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Haloperidol (a first-generation antipsychotic) is a less preferred option because of its risk of QT prolongation and other adverse effects in elderly patients. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are generally avoided in older adults with delirium because they can paradoxically worsen confusion and increase fall risk. Lithium is indicated for the chronic management of bipolar disorder and has no role in acute delirium. Oxycodone is an opioid analgesic that may cause sedation but is not an appropriate or targeted treatment for delirium and could further cloud cognition.

explanation_raw: Delirium is a syndrome characterized by an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness, and cognition. Initial efforts should focus on identifying and addressing any underlying causes while providing redirection. However, if no reversible cause is found, managing delirium using medications becomes the most appropriate next step to ensure the patient's safety. While there are no FDA-approved medications for the management of delirium, second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine are preferred for this indication. Haloperidol is a less preferred option, compared to a second-generation antipsychotic. It is known to cause QT prolongation and other concerning side effects in older patients. Lithium is indicated for chronic management of bipolar disorder and does not have a role in the acute management of this patient's delirium. The side effects of benzodiazepines such as lorazepam make them undesirable for managing delirium, particularly in an older adult. Oxycodone is an opioid analgesic that would likely provide some degree of sedation but would not be appropriate for managing this patient's delirium.

stem: An 84-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease, mild cognitive impairment, and type 2 diabetes is admitted to your hospital for a hip fracture after a recent fall. On examination the patient has normal speech but is confused. He is clearly unable to articulate his understanding of the risks and benefits of surgery. You should do which one of the following to determine this patient's decision-making capacity regarding surgery?

choices.A: Administer the Aid to Capacity Evaluation assessment tool
choices.B: Administer the Montreal Cognitive Assessment evaluation tool
choices.C: Document a lack of capacity and consult his designated durable power of attorney

correct_label: Document a lack of capacity and consult his designated durable power of attorney

bullets.text: When a patient clearly lacks decision-making capacity, the treating clinician documents this and defers to the designated durable power of attorney for health care as the surrogate decision-maker.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Decision-making capacity is determined by the treating clinician — not by a psychiatrist, not by the court. In straightforward cases where the patient is clearly unable to understand, appreciate, reason about, or communicate a treatment decision (as in this confused 84-year-old), formal structured assessments (e.g., Mini-Cog, MacCAT-T) are not necessary. Psychiatry consultation is rarely appropriate for capacity determination. Once lack of capacity is documented, the legally designated durable power of attorney for health care assumes the role of surrogate decision-maker and should be consulted immediately.

explanation_raw: This patient clearly lacks the capacity to make decisions, and a surrogate decision-maker should be consulted. If designated, a durable power of attorney for health care should make decisions for this patient. Structured assessments for determining decision-making capacity or cognitive function may help in uncertain cases but are not necessary in this situation. Psychiatry consultation is rarely necessary to determine decision-making capacity and would not be appropriate in this situation. Decision-making capacity is determined by the treating clinician, not the court.

stem: A 36-year-old backcountry skier becomes separated from her group during a blizzard. The ski patrol locates her several hours later, sitting on the ground and not moving or shivering. She is conscious but confused. Which one of the following would be the most important initial step?

choices.B: Providing a warm drink and high-calorie snack, and reconnecting her with her group
choices.C: Having her remove her wet clothes and wrapping her in an insulated vapor barrier
choices.D: Placing large heat pads around her upper body and wrapping her in an insulated vapor barrier
choices.E: Performing emergency rapid sequence field intubation and preparing for evacuation

correct_label: Placing large heat pads around her upper body and wrapping her in an insulated vapor barrier

bullets.text: Field assessment of hypothermia relies on level of consciousness, presence of shivering, alertness, and spontaneous movement — this patient's findings (conscious but confused, not moving or shivering) indicate moderate hypothermia requiring immediate intervention.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Core temperature measurement is impractical in the field and unnecessary for management decisions. A simplified field assessment categorizes hypothermia by level of consciousness, presence or absence of shivering, alertness, and spontaneous movements. This patient is conscious but confused and not shivering or moving, placing her in the moderate hypothermia category, which demands prompt action.

bullets.text: Moderate hypothermia is managed in the field by keeping the patient horizontal, placing large heat packs in the axillae and around the upper chest, and wrapping her in an insulated vapor barrier ('burrito method') prior to transport to a facility with an ICU.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The correct initial step is applying large warming packs to the upper body and wrapping the patient in an insulated vapor barrier. The patient should remain horizontal to prevent cardiovascular collapse. Wet clothing should NOT be removed in the field unless shelter is available and rescue is more than 30 minutes away, as this risks further heat loss. Warm fluids and high-calorie foods are appropriate only for cold-stressed or mildly hypothermic patients who can protect their airway and swallow safely. Intubation is unnecessary here because the patient is conscious and protecting her airway, and it would provide no rewarming benefit.

explanation_raw: Hypothermia is a potentially life-threatening condition that physicians and first responders should be able to promptly recognize and treat. While core temperature is useful for academic purposes or in a hospital, it is impractical to obtain and unimportant in the field. A simplified hypothermia assessment for field use evaluates the patient's level of consciousness, presence or absence of shivering, level of alertness, and spontaneous movements to categorize the severity of hypothermia. This patient is not moving or shivering, and although she is conscious she is not alert. This patient is experiencing moderate hypothermia and requires immediate intervention. A patient with moderate hypothermia should be kept horizontal, have large warming packs placed in the axillae and around the upper chest, be wrapped in an insulated vapor barrier (the burrito method), and be prepared for transport to the nearest medical facility, ideally one with an ICU. Warm fluids and high-calorie foods can be used for a patient who is cold stressed or has mild hypothermia. Wet clothes should not be removed in the field unless shelter is available and rescue is more than 30 minutes away because this risks further lowering the patient's core temperature. Intubation is not necessary because the patient is protecting her airway and is conscious. Furthermore, it would not warm her.

stem: A 63-year-old male presents for his annual health maintenance examination. He maintains a healthy lifestyle, eats well, and exercises regularly. A physical examination is normal. His most recent prostate cancer screening revealed a PSA level of 4.6 ng/mL (N 0.3–4.0), and his previous result 2 years ago was normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

bullets.text: For a newly elevated PSA, the AUA recommends repeating the PSA level in 4–8 weeks before pursuing additional biomarkers, imaging, or biopsy, as PSA may normalize in up to 40% of individuals.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Prostate cancer screening recommendations vary across organizations. The American Academy of Family Physicians does not recommend routine PSA-based screening, while the AUA recommends screening every 2–4 years for men aged 50–69. Importantly, when a PSA is newly elevated, the AUA advises confirming with a repeat PSA before escalating workup, since PSA can normalize in as many as 40% of cases. Additionally, age-adjusted PSA thresholds apply—4.5 ng/mL is considered the upper limit of normal for men in this patient's age group (60–69 years), making the result only marginally elevated.

bullets.text: Empiric antibiotics are not recommended for elevated PSA in asymptomatic individuals, a digital rectal exam is not recommended as a standalone or adjunct screening tool, and proceeding directly to biopsy without repeat PSA confirmation is premature.
bullets.sub_paragraph: The Choosing Wisely AUA initiative explicitly recommends against using empiric antibiotics to treat an elevated PSA in asymptomatic patients, as there is no evidence supporting this practice. A digital rectal examination is not recommended as a screening method, either alone or in combination with PSA. Proceeding directly to biopsy or additional imaging without first confirming the elevated PSA with a repeat test is not consistent with AUA guidance, as the initial elevation may be transient and not reflective of underlying malignancy.

explanation_raw: Prostate cancer screening recommendations vary, and there is little evidence that routine screening for prostate cancer improves patient-oriented outcomes. While the American Academy of Family Physicians does not recommend routine prostate-specific antigen (PSA)–based screening for prostate cancer, the American Urology Association (AUA) recommends prostate cancer screening with PSA testing for those 45–50 years of age. For those 50–69 years of age, the AUA recommends screening every 2–4 years between ages 50-69. The AUA also recommends obtaining a follow-up PSA level for individuals with newly elevated PSA before considering additional biomarkers, imaging, or biopsy. While this is based on expert opinion, the authors note that PSA may normalize in as many as 40% of individuals. The authors also suggest a higher threshold for biopsy based on age, with 4.5 ng/mL being the upper limit of normal for this patient's age group. The Choosing Wisely AUA initiative recommends against using empiric antibiotics to treat elevated PSA levels in asymptomatic individuals. A digital rectal examination is not recommended as a screening method alone or in addition to a screening PSA.

stem: An otherwise healthy 37-year-old female presents because of a 4-day history of multiple episodes of watery, nonbloody diarrhea. She has no fever, chills, abdominal pain, or vomiting. She does not have a history of recent antibiotic use, hospitalization, or travel, but does say that her teenage son recently returned from a spring break trip and has similar symptoms. Physical examination findings include dry mucous membranes and tachycardia. The abdomen is soft with mild generalized tenderness on deep palpation. Which one of the following next steps would be most appropriate at this time?

bullets.text: In an otherwise healthy, nontoxic patient with acute, self-limited watery diarrhea, no stool testing is indicated.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Testing for fecal calprotectin, lactoferrin, leukocytes, occult blood, and Clostridioides difficile is of limited value in nontoxic patients with acute diarrhea. Fecal calprotectin lacks consistency in distinguishing infectious from inflammatory causes, fecal lactoferrin lacks specificity, and fecal leukocytes disintegrate easily, reducing test sensitivity.

bullets.text: Stool testing is warranted only when specific high-risk features are present, none of which apply to this patient.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Indications for stool testing in acute infectious diarrhea include: severe abdominal pain or tenderness, bloody or mucoid stools, clinical signs of sepsis, fever ≥38.3°C (101.0°F), immunocompromised state, recent hospitalization, recent antibiotic use, or diarrhea lasting more than 7 days. This patient has none of these features, making no testing the appropriate choice.

explanation_raw: Testing for fecal calprotectin, lactoferrin, and leukocytes is of limited value in evaluating a nontoxic patient with acute diarrhea, including infectious diarrhea. Testing for fecal occult blood and infection with Clostridioides difficile is also not recommended in these patients. Detecting fecal calprotectin in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease and bacterial diarrhea lacks consistency and is not recommended. Although the presence of fecal lactoferrin can be associated with a bacterial etiology, its lack of specificity makes it less useful. Fecal leukocytes disintegrate easily in stool samples, reducing test sensitivity. Indications for obtaining stool testing for acute infection include the presence of severe abdominal pain or tenderness, bloody or mucoid stools, clinical findings of sepsis, fever ≥38.3 °C (101.0 °F), immunocompromised state, recent hospitalization, recent antibiotic therapy, and diarrhea that lasts >7 days.

stem: Which one of the following dog bite wounds should be considered for primary closure instead of being left to heal by secondary intention?

choices.A: A crush injury to the arm
choices.B: A gaping wound to the hand
choices.C: A linear wound to the face
choices.D: A puncture wound to the leg

correct_label: A linear wound to the face

bullets.text: Dog bite wounds to the face may be primarily closed for cosmetic reasons, while higher-risk wounds (crush injuries, hand wounds, puncture wounds) should heal by secondary intention.
bullets.sub_paragraph: Dog bite wounds may be primarily closed if desired for cosmetic reasons, such as linear wounds to the face. However, wounds that carry a higher risk of infection—including crush injuries, wounds to the hand, and puncture wounds—should be left to heal by secondary intention. Additional risk factors for infection include delayed presentation (greater than 6–12 hours for bites to the arm or leg, or greater than 12–24 hours for bites to the face) and immunosuppression, including diabetes mellitus.

explanation_raw: Dog bite wounds may be primarily closed if desired for cosmetic reasons such as wounds to the face. However, dog bite wounds that carry a higher risk of infection such crush injuries, wounds to the hand, and puncture wounds, should be left to heal by secondary intention. Other factors that increase the risk of infection include delayed presentation (>6–12 hours for bites to the arm or leg and >12–24 hours for bites to the face) and bites in people who are immunosuppressed, including those with diabetes mellitus.
